t: Persist in implementing the political responsibility for governing the Party
zh: 坚持落实管党治党政治责任
paras: Writing in the People's Daily (22 September 2026), Nie Pingping, a professor at Nanjing University, examines the last of the "fourteen adherences" in Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building: persisting in implementing political responsibility for governing the Party. Nie argues that this item is the logical conclusion and anchor of the whole system, because it turns theory and deployment into action. For a ruling party of more than 100 million members, the author holds, vigilance in governing the Party cannot be relaxed for a moment.

The commentary has four parts. It first explains why responsibility links theory to practice, then describes the mechanisms through which political responsibility is carried out. It goes on to set out a four-step chain of responsibility and ends with proposals for tightening responsibility further, based on Xi Jinping's speech at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Nie draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, and on volumes of Xi Jinping's selected writings on Party building.

Nie argues that the first thirteen adherences set the leadership, strategy, values and the seven areas of Party building, and that responsibility is the "rigid force" that converts them into an operable, checkable and accountable system. Three mechanisms are said to do this work: pressure transmission, running from the central leadership to grassroots organisations; rigid constraint through accountability rules; and systemic integration, in which Party committees bear primary responsibility, secretaries are the first persons responsible and discipline commissions supervise. Responsibility is then divided into knowing, bearing, discharging and being held to account for it, a closed loop that Nie says rests on institutions. The author contrasts this with Western public-governance theory, where responsibility is described as dispersed and legal or contractual, whereas the Party's political responsibility is described as centralised and answerable to the people's fundamental interests.

Nie calls for responsibility to be tightened in line with the "three more" requirements: more resolute implementation of central decisions, more effective confinement of power within institutional "cages", and a clearer and firmer anti-corruption struggle. Nie reads the Party's history as showing that Party building is strong when responsibility is firmly applied and falters when it slackens, and concludes that this is how the Party will remain the core of leadership guiding Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how the Party presents responsibility, accountability and discipline as the working core of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.
quoteEn: Persisting in implementing the political responsibility for governing the Party is the fulcrum that turns theory into practice.
quoteZh: 坚持落实管党治党政治责任，是将理论转化为实践的支点。

t: Using strict discipline to govern the whole Party
zh: 坚持用严明的纪律管全党治全党
paras: This commentary, first published in the People's Daily, argues that using strict discipline to manage and govern the whole Party is a key part of Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building and the fundamental measure of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Drawing throughout on the first volume of the Selected Writings of Xi Jinping on Party Building, Wang Yong holds that the Party, as a Marxist party built on revolutionary ideals and iron discipline, depends on discipline to answer the question of what it relies on to govern itself.

The article has four parts. It first reviews discipline building since the 18th Party Congress (2012), then links strict discipline to the Party's advanced and pure character and to its governing capacity. It next discusses extending discipline to every member, cadre and organisation, and closes with the joint use of Party discipline and state law as 'two yardsticks'.

Wang's central claim is that theory and practice in discipline building have reinforced each other. On the theoretical side, the author stresses that political discipline is the most important and fundamental discipline, and notes that the 19th Party Congress (2017) put discipline building into the overall plan for Party building. On the practical side, Wang lists regulations such as the Disciplinary Action Regulations, political inspections and the eight-point rules, and says these ended a previous 'lax and soft' approach. Wang also presents strict discipline as a response to the 'four tests' and 'four dangers' and as the basis for cadres to act boldly. Discipline must apply to everyone, with no exceptions and no blind spots. Wang says the Disciplinary Action Regulations, revised in 2015, 2018 and 2023, express the principle that discipline is stricter than law and comes before it. The merged work of discipline inspection commissions and supervisory commissions is said to link Party discipline with law enforcement.

Wang concludes that when discipline is strong the Party is strong, and that strict discipline is a historical lesson of the Party's growth. The author presents it as protecting Chinese modernization and keeping the Party advanced and pure, citing 101.286 million members and 5.431 million primary-level organisations at the end of 2025. Read the original if you want an official Party-school account of how current discipline building is framed, including its institutional and legal-regulatory components.
quoteEn: Using strict discipline to manage and govern the whole Party targets all Party members, all Party cadres and all Party organisations.
quoteZh: 坚持用严明的纪律管全党治全党，针对的是所有党员、所有党的干部、所有党的组织。

t: Persisting in making Party conduct building regular and long-term
zh: 坚持推进作风建设常态化长效化
paras: This commentary, published in the People's Daily, takes up one of the "fourteen persistences" that the author identifies in Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building: making the building of Party conduct (zuofeng) regular and long-term. He argues that Party conduct is the Party's image and bears on its survival. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), he says, the Central Committee has pursued conduct building continuously, and the task now is to fight a protracted campaign so that it supports the building of a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

The article has three parts. The first sets out why the principle matters. The second explains its theoretical content, drawing on several texts in the Selected Works of Xi Jinping on Party Building. The third proposes practical paths for carrying it out.

On significance, He gives three reasons. Conduct building keeps the Party's flesh-and-blood ties with the people, and the public fears campaigns that leave only a superficial effect. Conduct problems are stubborn and recurrent, so one-off drives cannot remove them. And because conduct problems are at root problems of Party spirit, conduct building drives Party building as a whole. On content, He treats "regular" (changtaihua) and "long-term" (changxiaohua) as one unit. Regularity means continuous attention to thinking, supervision and discipline, and routine self-examination in Party life. Long-term effect means moving from treating symptoms to tackling root causes through Party regulations, so that cadres move from "not daring" to "not being able" and finally to "not wanting" to violate norms.

For practice, He calls for three things. Cadres should temper their Party spirit and put political cultivation first. Regulations should be improved and enforced rigidly, so that the "four undesirable work styles" cannot mutate in hidden forms. Chains of responsibility should be tightened, and unhealthy conduct and corruption should be investigated and handled together. He concludes that this approach will let good Party conduct set the tone for social conduct and customs and create a good environment for high-quality development. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party-building discourse frames conduct building, discipline and institutional constraint in the Xi era.
quoteEn: Unhealthy conduct and corruption are two sides of the same problem, and the former is a hotbed in which the latter grows.
quoteZh: 不正之风和腐败问题互为表里，是腐败滋长的温床。

glossary.explanation: The Party's long-standing effort to correct the working style and behaviour of its members and cadres. It has been a central strand of Party-building campaigns since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

t: Persisting in building a high-calibre cadre corps capable of shouldering the great task of national rejuvenation
zh: 坚持建设堪当民族复兴重任的高素质干部队伍
paras: This commentary, first published in the People's Daily, asks how the Party should build a cadre corps able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Liu Jingbei argues that selecting and appointing officials is a historic Party tradition, and that Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building supplies the guiding principles for doing so. Liu presents strict governance of officials as the key to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

The article is organised as seven study themes drawn from Xi's writings, including the Selected Works on Party Building. They cover the principles of selecting and appointing officials, the criteria for a good cadre, the primacy of political standards, the "five systems" of cadre work, strict management combined with care, talent strategy, and the training of young cadres as successors.

Liu's core move is to set out a chain running from selection to management. Political loyalty comes first, including support for the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and failure on this standard means a one-vote veto. Around it Liu arranges five systems: cultivating quality, assessing and knowing cadres, selection and appointment, strict management, and positive incentives. Each is paired with a named risk, such as promoting officials with problems, mismatching people and posts, or going through the motions. Liu also holds that strict supervision and encouragement to take responsibility are inherently unified, and that protecting officials who act, and clearing those falsely accused, belongs to management.

For talent work, Liu lists eight elements of Xi's thinking and calls for more active, open and effective talent policies to support Chinese modernization. For young cadres, Liu proposes long-term planning, strict selection, graduated training in hard posts, bold and timely promotion, and constant supervision, which Liu likens to tending a field. The aim is reliable successors for socialism with Chinese characteristics, so that the "red country" never changes colour. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned statement of current Party doctrine on cadre selection, management and succession.
quoteEn: Good Party cadres are not only selected but, above all, shaped through management.
quoteZh: 党的好干部既是选出来的，更是管出来的。

t: Upholding the building of an organisational system that is connected from top to bottom and effective in execution
zh: 坚持健全上下贯通、执行有力的组织体系
paras: This commentary, first published in the People's Daily in September 2026, explains one of the "fourteen upholds" of Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building: keeping up the effort to build an organisational system that is connected from top to bottom and strong in execution. Zhang Peng argues that a tight organisational system is the strength of a Marxist party. In the author's account, it is a precondition for upholding the leadership of the Party Central Committee and for pursuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

The piece has two main sections. The first sets out why such a system matters: Zhang cites Xi's statements on organisation, the size of the Party, and the risks it faces on the new journey. The second addresses how to build the system and what it is meant to achieve. It treats the Central Committee, the intermediate Party committees and grassroots organisations in turn, and then links the system to Party leadership, Party discipline and national rejuvenation.

Zhang's central claim is that organisation turns scale into strength. The article cites 101.286 million members and 5.431 million primary organisations at the end of 2025. It says that this size brings problems of managing members, covering new sectors and tackling lax discipline, and that a tight system can convert size into quality and political advantage. The Central Committee is described as the brain and hub, with the Party's leading position resting on the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Zhang assigns each level a role in carrying out central decisions: central bodies are the "first kilometre", local committees the "middle section" and grassroots branches the "last kilometre". Each level must avoid specific failures: obstacles, blockages and broken links. The author also stresses a priority on the grassroots, including rectifying weak and lax branches.

Zhang concludes that the Party's overall leadership and all its work depend on a strong organisational system. The article cites poverty alleviation, the response to the pandemic, disaster relief and technological breakthroughs as examples of organisational strength becoming national governance capacity. It calls for a complete system of organisational rules and for stricter enforcement of democratic centralism. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how Party organisation is justified as the basis of leadership and governance in the Xi era.
quoteEn: Only by working to build an organisational system that is connected from top to bottom and effective in execution, and by making every level of Party organisation sound and strong, can Party leadership work "as the body commands the arm, and the arm the fingers".
quoteZh: 只有着力健全上下贯通、执行有力的组织体系，让党的各级组织都健全、都过硬，党的领导才能“如身使臂，如臂使指”。

t: Persist in forging strong Party spirit
zh: 坚持锤炼坚强党性
paras: This commentary, published in the People's Daily, asks why and how Communist Party members and cadres should keep forging "strong Party spirit" (dangxing). Chen Jiaxi argues that doing so is a foundational task of the Party's new great project of self-building in the new era and an important part of Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building. In Chen's account, strong Party spirit guarantees the Party's advanced nature and purity and its capacity to lead and govern.

The article has three parts. It first sets out why forging Party spirit is necessary, then analyses the internal logic of Xi Jinping's statements on it since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and finally proposes practical requirements for the new journey. It draws on quotations from Xi Jinping, including texts in the Selected Works on Party Building.

On necessity, Chen names three requirements: strengthening political building and unity around the Party Central Committee, building an ideological barrier for long-term rule and advancing the Party's self-reform, and shaping cadres who are loyal, clean and ready to take responsibility. On logic, Chen reads Xi's remarks as answering questions of essence (Party spirit is ultimately a question of standpoint, tested by public versus private interest), of mechanism (a lifelong task, combining self-discipline with institutional constraint) and of cultural roots (Party-spirit education as the Communists' "study of the mind", linked to Chinese self-cultivation traditions). Chen holds that this moves Party-spirit work from individual self-improvement to the strategic level of a long-ruling party.

Chen proposes four practical paths: arming members with theory through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, tempering them through rigorous inner-Party political life, testing them in practical work for the people, and reinforcing them through discipline and supervision. The author concludes that members should treat Party-spirit cultivation as a lifelong task and convert it into strength for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-building discourse presents Party spirit, loyalty and self-reform as linked themes.
quoteEn: When Party spirit is strong, convictions are firm and action is forceful; when Party spirit is pure, work style is sound and the cause prospers.
quoteZh: 党性坚强，则信念坚定、行动有力；党性纯洁，则作风过硬、事业兴旺。

glossary.explanation: The qualities of political standpoint, loyalty, discipline and commitment expected of Communist Party members. In Chinese Party discourse it covers both the Party's essential character and each member's personal cultivation.
A slogan stressing that the Party must continually examine and correct itself, used prominently under Xi Jinping.
The official name for China's development path, stressed since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

t: Persistently using the Party's innovative theory to unite hearts and forge souls
zh: 坚持用党的创新理论凝心铸魂
paras: Feng Yanli, writing in the People's Daily (10 September 2026), takes up the task of using the Party's innovative theory to "unite hearts and forge souls", which the article calls the fundamental task of the Party's ideological work. Feng argues that this task gives Party building in the new era an ideological foundation and spiritual support. The commentary opens with Xi Jinping's remark that a strong theory gives the world's largest Marxist governing party clear direction, unity and confidence.

The piece has four parts. The first explains what the formula means. The second presents it as an answer to major questions facing a long-governing Marxist party. The third reviews practical results since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The fourth sets out how theoretical armament should be pursued further. Feng draws throughout on Xi Jinping's writings on Party building.

Feng reads the formula in three ways: as a scientific orientation grounded in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, as a strategic measure for strengthening the Party's foundations, and as a requirement of unified thinking and firm belief. "Uniting hearts" is defined as unifying thought, will and action. "Forging souls" is defined as firming ideals and convictions. The two are said to support each other. Feng says the formula answers three questions: how to forge the soul (belief rests on theoretical clarity), how to consolidate the foundation (theoretical identification builds political identification, inside and outside the Party), and how to stay evergreen (clear theory and firm belief drive the Party's self-reform). As evidence, Feng cites firmer ideals among Party members, stronger unity, and better links between study and practice through campaigns such as the study of Party history and the theme-based education campaign.

Feng calls for deeper, more practical and more heartfelt theoretical study. Party members should read original works and study genuinely, understand, believe and apply the theory. Study should be tailored to different groups, with leading cadres as the "key minority", and should reach enterprises, villages, schools, communities and online platforms in accessible forms. Study should also connect with investigation and research and with concrete work, so that it supports Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official press frames ideological education and theoretical study in the new era.
quoteEn: Uniting hearts and forging souls complement and support each other.
quoteZh: 凝心与铸魂相辅相成、互为支撑。

t: A detailed investigation of Ren Bishi's return to support the Central Red Army's Long March
zh: 任弼时等率部回援中央红军长征一事详考
source: Journal of the Long March Studies, 2026 no. 3
paras: The article takes up a little-documented episode of Red Army history. In 1941–42 the historian Ye Huosheng heard comrades of the former Second Front Army recall that Ren Bishi, leading the Sixth Army Corps on its westward expedition, turned back to support the Central Red Army's Long March. The authors, from the Ren Bishi Memorial Hall, argue that the episode really happened and set out to establish it from Nationalist and Communist documents, telegrams, battle reports and memoirs.

The study follows the Sixth Army Corps from its departure in August 1934 to its meeting with He Long's Second Army Corps on 24 October 1934. It has three parts: the existence and content of the recall orders of 3–4 October; the decision taken by Ren, Xiao Ke and Wang Zhen at Houchang on 4–5 October; and the military significance of the marches and battles from 5 to 24 October. The sources include the Central Revolutionary Military Commission's telegrams, Otto Braun's (Li De's) recollections, Xiao Ke's and Zhang Ziyi's memoirs, and Nationalist battle reports and recollections.

The authors first compare the Commission's orders with the corps' route. Up to 2 October the route matched the instructions. Only the three urgent telegrams of 3–4 October forbade a move west across the Wu River and ordered the corps to Jiangkou, and the authors treat these as the recall orders. They link the orders to the Central Committee's decision to break out, and cite Xiao Ke and others to argue that the corps was meant to provide a foothold in western Hunan and to scout the route. The authors infer that the Army Corps' military and political committee gave up a feasible Wu River crossing at Houchang and turned northeast. No source records the discussion directly, so they reason from circumstances: the corps' leaders had foreseen a westward shift of the Central Red Army, and they were told to reach the new area by mid-October. They then show that the breakout at MaSangchangping and the Jiagou gorge, at heavy cost at Ganxi, drew off large Nationalist forces. They cite Li Jue's and Yang Shangkun's memoirs to argue that this eased the Central Red Army's passage through the first blockade lines.

The authors conclude that the episode is genuine military history. In their account the Sixth Army Corps took heavy losses but completed its task: it joined the Second Army Corps, served as a scout and diverted enemy troops. They present the episode as showing the political loyalty, firm conviction and spirit of sacrifice of Ren, Xiao Ke, Wang Zhen and their troops. Read the original if you work on Long March history or Ren Bishi and want a source-based reconstruction of the Sixth Army Corps' movements in October 1934.
quoteEn: The Sixth Army Corps' marches and battles of 5–24 October were in essence also a way of supporting the Central Red Army's Long March by "scouting the road".
quoteZh: 红六军团10月5—24日的行军和作战实质上也是通过“探路”来回援中央红军长征。

glossary.explanation: The supreme military body of the Chinese Soviet Republic and the Red Army in the early 1930s. It sent the telegraphed orders to the Sixth Army Corps.
A Red Army force from the Hunan–Jiangxi base area. It set out westward in August 1934 under Ren Bishi, Xiao Ke and Wang Zhen to link up with the Second Army Corps.
The strategic retreat of the Chinese Red Army from 1934 to 1936. The Central Red Army began it from Jiangxi in October 1934.

t: The distinctive contribution of the Long March Spirit to inheriting and carrying forward the great founding spirit of the Party
zh: 长征精神对传承弘扬伟大建党精神的独特贡献
source: Journal of the Party School of the CPC Central Committee (National Academy of Governance), 2026 no. 4
paras: Marking the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March, Wang asks how one specific form in the Spirit Genealogy of Chinese Communists inherits and extends the great founding spirit of the Party. The author treats the founding spirit as the source and the genealogy as the stream that flows from it. Wang argues that earlier studies tend to read single spirits statically or list them chronologically, and that the Long March Spirit's bridging role has been under-examined. The thesis is that the Long March Spirit inherits the founding spirit in every dimension and also enriches it through its own distinctive features.

The article has four parts. It first sets the four components of the founding spirit (upholding truth and ideals, practising the original aspiration and mission, fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely, being loyal to the Party and true to the people) against Long March episodes. It then examines what is unique about the Long March Spirit, then its influence on Chinese society from the revolution to the present, and finally its international dissemination. The evidence ranges from Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping to accounts by foreign journalists, scholars and politicians.

In the author's reading, the Long March Spirit is distinctive for three reasons. It carries a historical turning-point character, because the Zunyi Meeting ended dogmatic leadership and began genuinely independent exploration. It also fuses Party spirit with the national spirit, which Wang calls the highest embodiment of that spirit. And it has unusual reach, since, unlike regional or sector-specific spirits, it worked at the level of the whole revolution and spread through texts, poetry, songs and slogans. Wang then traces how the 'new Long March' idiom was used from Deng Xiaoping's 1978 speech through later leaders to Xi Jinping's image of each generation's own Long March. The author also cites the naming of rockets, submarines, parks and hospitals after the Long March. Wang adds that Snow, Salisbury and Brzezinski, the Comintern's reassessment, and Time magazine's 1999 listing helped spread the founding spirit abroad.

Wang concludes that the Long March Spirit turns the abstract founding spirit into concrete, widely felt strength, and that it has become a shared spiritual asset of humanity. The author suggests it can feed a community with a shared future for mankind and broaden the founding spirit's reach abroad. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of how the Long March is used in official discourse and how its foreign reception is presented, with many cited sources.
quoteEn: If the great founding spirit is the core gene of the Communist Party of China, then the Long March Spirit is the "explicit expression" of that gene under the test of life and death.
quoteZh: 如果说伟大建党精神是中国共产党的内核基因，长征精神就是这种基因在生死考验中的“显性表达”。

glossary.en: great founding spirit of the Party
glossary.explanation: A formulation, set out by Xi Jinping in 2021, of the Party's founding values: upholding truth and ideals, practising the original aspiration and mission, fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely, and being loyal to the Party and true to the people.

glossary.zh: 中国共产党人精神谱系
glossary.explanation: An official list of named revolutionary, construction-era and reform-era 'spirits' (such as the Jinggangshan, Long March and Yan'an spirits), presented as flowing from the founding spirit.
The official name for the values attributed to the Red Army's Long March of 1934–36: firm ideals, selflessness, independence, discipline and reliance on the masses.
A January 1935 Politburo meeting during the Long March that criticised the earlier military leadership and is officially seen as establishing Mao Zedong's leading position.
A metaphor used by Party leaders, notably since 1978, to describe the current task of national development as a continuation of the Long March.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign-policy and global-governance concept, calling for shared interests and values among nations.

t: Characteristics of the Central Committee's meetings during the Long March
zh: 长征时期中共中央会议特点论析
source: Journal of Long March Studies (Changzheng xuekan), 2026 no. 3
paras: Li Zequan asks what distinguished the dozens of important meetings the CPC Central Committee held during the two-year Long March, and why they proved decisive. Earlier scholarship, the author notes, has mostly catalogued their number, type, date, place, topics and participants. Li instead identifies three defining features: fixing on the most important agenda item and pursuing it to the end, handling the tactics of inner-Party struggle correctly, and upholding democratic centralism.

The article is organised around these three features. It draws on more than twenty meetings, from Tongdao, Liping and Zunyi through Lianghekou, Eijie (Russian-border) and Maoergai to Wayaobao after the Central Committee reached northern Shaanxi. It concentrates on Mao Zedong's role and on the conflicts with the 'Left' dogmatist leadership of Bo Gu and Otto Braun (Li De), and with Zhang Guotao. It closes with the contemporary lessons the author draws.

On the first feature, Li argues that the 'first agenda item' was line and leadership. Before arrival in Shaanxi the issue was the military line, and afterwards the political and organisational lines. The author also points to the tight, sustained pace of meetings, such as six in eleven days at Zhaxi. On the second, Li contends that at Zunyi Mao won over Zhang Wentian, Wang Jiaxiang and Zhou Enlai, and confined the meeting to the military line without attacking the earlier political line. In dealing with Zhang Guotao, Li says, Mao combined principle with flexibility and refused expulsion so as to preserve Party and army unity. On the third, Li reads Zunyi as a victory of the majority over a small minority. Li cites the enlarged-meeting format used in 14 sessions and the Gougba meeting, where Mao accepted a vote against him and then persuaded colleagues. Zhang Guotao's defeat is likewise attributed to his violating democratic centralism.

Li concludes that these meetings were the most critical factor in turning the Long March from crisis to success and in establishing Mao's correct line and leadership. The article presents them as a guide for improving decision-making today. It calls for the traditions of the Long March to be carried forward under the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, and for formalism and bureaucratism in meetings to be opposed. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of how Long March meetings are interpreted in current official scholarship, including the Zunyi, Gougba and Zhang Guotao episodes.
quoteEn: Viewed institutionally, what ultimately enabled our Party to defeat Zhang Guotao's erroneous line was still inner-Party democratic centralism.
quoteZh: 从制度上看，我们党最终战胜张国焘错误路线的还是党内民主集中制。

glossary.explanation: The Party's fundamental organisational principle, combining inner-Party discussion with binding unity of action. It is commonly summarised as individual subordinate to organisation, minority to majority, lower level to higher level, and the whole Party to the Central Committee.

The Party's official label for the line of Wang Ming and the Bo Gu leadership. It is said to have mechanically applied Soviet experience and Comintern instructions without regard to Chinese conditions.
In Party usage, the overall strategic, political and organisational orientation of the Party. Disputes over the 'correct line' are treated as the central questions of Party history.

t: Origins and discursive evolution of the Chinese Communist Party's concept of the "political check-up"
zh: 中国共产党政治体检概念的源流考释与话语变迁
paras: The "political check-up" (zhengzhi tijian) entered Party discourse in 2018, when Xi Jinping called on members and cadres to undergo regular check-ups to "sweep away political dust". It was written into Party regulations in 2019 and restated in 2024. Wu asks where this concept comes from and how its meaning developed. Wu argues that, although the term appeared only in the new era, related ideas and practices run through the Party's whole history, and that the concept matured through inheritance and innovation rather than appearing without precedent.

The article is a conceptual history in five parts. It first traces the concept's sources in classical Chinese culture and in Marxist writings on Party building. It then follows its development through the New Democratic Revolution, the period of socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and finally the new era.

On the sources, Wu reads the term as a medical metaphor applied to politics and finds precursors in the traditional ideas of self-examination (canxing), official assessment (kaoke) and public critique (qingyi). Wu also draws on Marxist writings about Party spirit, criticism and self-criticism, and ideological struggle and political education. For the revolutionary period, Wu argues that struggle was itself the test of members' loyalty, and that the Party built a system of political screening covering admission, assessment and purges. In the socialist period the equivalent expressions were \"passing the socialist test\" and \"clearing up politics\", which the author says combined institutionalised screening with campaign-style purification. Wu acknowledges that the latter caused harmful consequences. In the reform era, \"democratic appraisal\", \"checking against standards\" and \"Party-spirit analysis\" made the practice more regular, with clearer standards.

For the new era, Wu identifies three innovations: a statement of the concept's function (for individuals, for intra-Party political life and for selecting cadres), explicit standards (Central Committee requirements and Party rules, the people's expectations, and the example of revolutionary forebears), and methods (political inspection tours, organisational life and mass supervision). Wu concludes that the century-long history should be viewed objectively and as a whole, despite detours and misunderstandings, so that its revolutionary and political significance is properly understood. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language genealogy of this Party-building term and its precursors, from imperial-era ideas to current Party regulations.
quoteEn: As a figurative expression, the political check-up extends the medical concept of the "physical examination" into the political field, and refers mainly to examining and assessing a person's political qualities.
quoteZh: 政治体检作为一种形象化表达，将医学中的“体检”概念引申到了政治领域，主要指的是对人的政治品质进行检查与评估。

glossary.explanation: A Party-building practice, named by Xi Jinping in 2018, in which members and organisations regularly examine their political stance and conduct. It was written into Party regulations in 2019.
A Party practice, drawn from Leninist tradition, of members openly criticising each other and themselves. It is used in meetings such as democratic life meetings.
Inspection teams sent by higher Party bodies to examine lower-level Party organisations for political and disciplinary problems.

t: Basic paths for the orderly connection of Party discipline and state law in the new era
zh: 新时代党的纪律与国家法律有序衔接的基本路径
paras: How should Party discipline and state law be linked so that the two work together without displacing each other? Wang and Bi take up this question of "discipline–law connection" (jifa xianjie). They argue that the connection has moved from a principle to be advocated to a mechanism to be implemented. Even so, they hold that institutional design, drafting procedures and enforcement still need strengthening if intra-Party supervision and state supervision are to be integrated.

The article has three parts. It first sets out the value of the connection, then identifies four priority problem areas, and finally proposes remedies for each. It traces the policy line from the Fourth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2014) to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Along the way it covers the revised Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of January 2024 and the Supervision Law.

The authors ground the connection in three needs. Drawing on Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, they present discipline as essential to a Marxist party's vanguard character. They also treat the connection as a component of the socialist rule-of-law system with Chinese characteristics and as a requirement of the joint effort against corruption. They then name four weaknesses: blurred boundaries (Party discipline spilling over into society, or "discipline replacing law" and the reverse); poor enforcement links in case transfer, evidence conversion and cooperation; unclear allocation of responsibility among Party discipline, administrative sanctions and criminal liability; and weak awareness and skills among officials. Their remedies include applying "law reservation" and proportionality limits, and keeping discipline stricter than, and ahead of, the law. They also propose joint meetings, joint case teams and a shared clue platform, different conversion rules for physical and verbal evidence, and early involvement of procuratorates. Finally, they propose training, publicity and stronger accountability.

Wang and Bi conclude that clear boundaries, working mechanisms, defined responsibilities and stronger awareness together make the connection operate stably. They present this as serving full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the legal governance of power. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-school account of how discipline inspection, supervision and judicial organs are meant to coordinate in practice, including proposed procedures on case transfer, evidence and sanctions.
quoteEn: The discipline–law connection is the key link between intra-Party regulations and state law, and it plays a critical role in keeping the two coordinated and raising the overall effectiveness of the rule of law.
quoteZh: “纪法衔接”是连接党内法规与国家法律的关键环节，对于保障二者协调一致、提升法治的整体效能有着极为关键的作用。

glossary.explanation: The articulation of Party discipline with state law, through institutional design and procedures. It covers case transfer, evidence, responsibility and the boundaries between the two systems.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: Official term for the Party-building and anti-corruption drive promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

Disciplinary penalties imposed on public officials for duty-related violations of law, such as warnings and demerits. They are governed by the Law on Sanctions for Public Officials and are distinct from Party discipline and from criminal punishment.

t: On the cultural subjectivity of the Communist Party of China
zh: 论中国共产党的文化主体性
paras: The article takes up "cultural subjectivity", which Liu calls a signature concept of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. It asks what the Communist Party of China's (CPC) cultural subjectivity consists of. Liu defines it as the Party's inherent cultural consciousness and capacity as the political agent driving the development of Chinese culture. The article argues that this subjectivity has been formed, consolidated and developed through more than a century of cultural practice led by the Party.

Liu distinguishes three nested levels of cultural subject: the Chinese nation, the Chinese people and the Party. The Party's cultural subjectivity is then analysed through four attributes: cultural consciousness, cultural autonomy, cultural creativity and cultural transcendence. Each is broken into sub-dimensions and illustrated with episodes from the revolutionary, socialist-construction and reform periods up to the new era. The sources are speeches by Xi Jinping, works by Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, Party congress reports, the Constitution and passages from Marx and Engels.

Consciousness is shown in the Party's acceptance of cultural missions, its changing view of culture's place (from a supporting instrument to a goal, a livelihood matter and a productive force), and its grasp of the laws of cultural development. Autonomy means keeping cultural identity and shedding the dependence of late-developing countries. Liu contrasts the CPC's self-chosen path with the Kuomintang's alleged dependence on imperialism and feudal forces, and traces the Party's cultural strategies from the 1950s to the goal of a cultural powerhouse by 2035. Creativity covers people-centred cultural values, new content (revolutionary and socialist culture, and the creative transformation of traditional culture) and methods such as the Two Integrations. Transcendence rests on the relative independence of culture from the economic base, citing Marx on Greek art and Engels on philosophy. Liu argues that the Party has made culture advance beyond its material conditions, and that this is also embedded in constitutional and legal cultural institutions.

Liu concludes that the Party's cultural subjectivity is closely tied to the fate of Chinese culture, and that the Party's leadership of culture, rooted in a people-oriented value stance, underpins the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text presents Party leadership over ideology and culture, together with the defence of cultural security against Western infiltration, as essential to this subjectivity. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how current Chinese Party scholarship frames the CPC as a cultural agent, along with its periodisation of Party cultural policy.
quoteEn: The CPC's cultural subjectivity refers to the cultural-subject attributes the Party holds as the political agent driving the development of Chinese culture; it is the cultural-subject consciousness and capacity inherent in the Party itself.
quoteZh: 中国共产党的文化主体性，意指中国共产党作为推动中华文化发展的政党主体所具有的文化主体属性，是中国共产党自身内在具有的文化主体意识与能力。

glossary.explanation: The formula of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Xi Jinping stressed it in 2021–2023 as the key method of adapting Marxism to China.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: Official goal of restoring China to national strength and prosperity, a central theme of Party discourse since Xi Jinping took office in 2012.

A national strategy, first set out at the 18th Party Congress (2012), to build a country with strong cultural production, influence and soft power. The Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020) set the goal of achieving it by 2035.

t: The Communist Party of China's historical process, basic experience and practical paths in building an international united front
zh: 中国共产党推动构建国际统一战线的历史进程、基本经验和实践路径
paras: Wang Xinying and Zhang Xianyan ask how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has built an international united front over its history, and how it should build a new one today. They argue that the united front, long treated by the Party as a key instrument of revolution, construction and reform, has always had an international dimension. Placing the question against the interwoven "two overall situations" (the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and profound global change), they hold that the Party's historical record offers lessons and a practical route for the present.

The article has three parts. The first periodises the history: the New Democratic Revolution (including the anti-Japanese war and the world anti-fascist front), socialist revolution and construction (anti-hegemony fronts, the "intermediate zone" and "three worlds" theories), reform and opening up (peace and development, partnerships, a harmonious world), and the new era (shared human values, a community with a shared future for mankind, the Belt and Road Initiative and the four global initiatives). The second part distils three lessons. The third proposes four practical paths for the present.

On experience, the authors identify three points. First, the CPC has handled self-reliance and the international front dialectically: independence and leadership are preserved inside the front, while international aid is treated as necessary though not a substitute for self-reliance. Second, domestic and international fronts must be coordinated, as in the mutual reinforcement of the anti-Japanese national front and the world anti-fascist front. Third, strategic principle (peace, anti-hegemony, solidarity with colonial and developing countries) must be joined with tactical flexibility, shown in Mao Zedong's wide 1964 definition of anti-imperialist forces and the 1970s cooperation with Western states against Soviet hegemony.

For the new era the authors propose four paths: take a community with a shared future for mankind as the guiding goal and supply international public goods; make Global South countries the main targets of the front; build issue-based coalitions on development, climate and, in the authors' account, selected areas of China–US cooperation; and shape China's national image through a shift from "unilateral telling" to "shared narrative". The authors conclude that China should use the united front's distinctive strengths to secure a favourable international environment for national rejuvenation and for world peace and development. Read the original if you want a Party-centred, periodised account of Chinese united front thinking in foreign affairs, from Mao to the present, and its policy recommendations.
quoteEn: The key to the united front lies in uniting the majority, and building an international united front must likewise win over the majority of international actors.
quoteZh: 统一战线的关键在于团结大多数，国际统一战线的构建也必须抓住国际行为体中的大多数。

glossary.explanation: A strategy of alliance with non-Party forces against a main enemy, which the CPC has treated since the revolutionary period as one of its key instruments. It is applied domestically and, as this article discusses, internationally.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept associated with Xi Jinping since 2012–13. It calls for cooperation among states on security, development and governance.
A term for developing countries, used in Chinese official discourse to denote the main partners of China's foreign policy.
An infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched by Xi Jinping in 2013, linking China with countries across Asia, Africa and Europe.
Mao Zedong's 1970s division of the international order into the superpowers, other developed states and the developing countries. It placed China among the third world.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: A historical examination of the Communist Party of China's upholding of cultural leadership since reform and opening up
zh: 改革开放以来中国共产党坚持文化领导权的历史考察
paras: Yang and Zhang ask how the Communist Party of China has understood and upheld its cultural leadership (wenhua lingdaoquan, often rendered cultural hegemony) since reform and opening up. They note that the Party named "the CPC's cultural leadership" as an explicit proposition only in Xi Jinping's June 2023 speech at a symposium on cultural inheritance and development. Taking an intellectual-history approach, they argue that the Party's exploration moved through challenge, innovation and gradual maturity, and that it now forms a systematic theory.

The article divides the period into three stages. The first covers the early reform years of ideological emancipation and the return to order after the Cultural Revolution. The second runs from the 1990s to the early 2000s, under the socialist market economy and all-round opening up. The third is the new era under Xi Jinping, set against what the authors call great changes unseen in a century and the Party's push to strengthen its overall leadership. Each stage is tied to leaders' statements and Party documents.

In the authors' account, early reform leaders such as Deng Xiaoping upheld cultural leadership through the Four Cardinal Principles, opposing both "Left" and Right deviations. They also held that literature and art should neither be subordinate to politics nor detached from it, and that journalism is the Party's mouthpiece. Their fourth measure was building socialist spiritual civilization. From the 1990s the emphasis shifted to "building rather than criticising" and to establishing a leading role amid pluralism, summed up as one dominant strand with many coexisting ones, an image of a wild-goose formation replacing a single rigid line. The authors also list advanced socialist culture, the core socialist value system, and the claim that "only by occupying the market better can more ground be occupied". In the new era they describe a strengthened socialist ideology, core socialist values, control of public opinion on the internet, and comprehensive Party leadership over propaganda, ideology and culture, including its personnel. They present this last stage as a historic shift in the ideological situation.

The authors conclude that early problems were largely legacies of history, while later ones, such as cultural pluralism and cultural markets, were new and called for fresh thinking. They say the Party under Xi has now set out fundamental principles, key tasks and institutional safeguards, which marks a new stage. They add that new situations will keep arising and that the Party must uphold fundamental principles while innovating. Read the original if you want a Party-historical account, built from official texts, of how the concept of cultural leadership developed from Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping.
quoteEn: Occupying the market and occupying the ideological front are dialectically united: \"only by occupying the market better can more ground be occupied.\"
quoteZh: 占领市场和占领意识形态阵地是辩证统一的，“只有更好地占领市场，才能更多地占领阵地”。

glossary.explanation: The Party's authority to guide a society's ideas, values and cultural life. It corresponds to the Gramscian idea of cultural hegemony, though Chinese texts frame it through Party leadership.

Deng Xiaoping's 1979 formulation: keeping to the socialist road, the people's democratic dictatorship, the leadership of the Communist Party, and Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought. They serve as a political bottom line.
A Party goal, developed from 1979 onward, of cultivating ideals, morality, discipline and culture alongside material development.
A set of twelve values at national, social and individual levels, formally put forward at the 18th Party Congress in 2012.

t: "The warmth and cold of revolution": clothing and bedding supply for the people's army in the revolutionary war years
zh: “革命的冷暖”：革命战争时期人民军队被服供给问题研究
paras: Qi Xiaoguang takes up a basic but little-studied question in the logistics history of the people's army led by the Chinese Communist Party: how it obtained clothing and bedding (quilts, blankets, uniforms) during the revolutionary wars. Qi argues that the problem affected soldiers' survival and the army's capacity to keep fighting. In Qi's account, solving it required mass mobilisation of production and the gradual building of supply institutions, and the process shows the army's revolutionary optimism and the close bond between army and people.

The article follows the army from the Jinggangshan base area to the final stage of the civil war and has four main sections. The first describes the hardships of supply in the Soviet period and the Long March, the War of Resistance against Japan and the War of Liberation. The second traces the move towards self-sufficient production behind enemy lines, with mass participation. The third examines how supply standards and management were systematised. A short conclusion reflects on the symbolic meaning of clothing. Qi draws on recollections of commanders such as Xu Xiangqian and Nie Rongzhen, Party directives, military orders and folk songs.

Qi's core claim is that shortage drove self-reliance. Early supply depended mainly on capture from the enemy, then on the Nationalist blockade and the later cutting-off of funds, especially after the Southern Anhui Incident of 1941, pushed the army towards full self-supply. Qi describes army workshops, production competitions and above all the labour of peasant women, tailors and villagers, summed up in the phrase that the "largest clothing factory is the masses". Qi then shows how, after the 1940 logistics meetings, supply became standardised: unified management, issue by unit level, fixed quotas and service lives for items, accounting and discipline rules, economies in cloth use, and, in 1949, nationwide unified standards. Uniform styles and colours moved from disorder to regularity.

Qi concludes that clothing was both a soldier's means of survival and a carrier of political identity, revolutionary feeling and class belonging. Patched uniforms and the labour of people at the rear are presented as a "living fossil" of revolutionary spirit and of the "fish and water" relationship between army and people. Qi sees the history as reflecting the Party's political skill in mobilisation, institution-building and revolutionary narrative, with continuing spiritual value today. Read the original if you are interested in the social and institutional history of Communist military logistics, or in how current Party-history scholarship frames material culture and army–people relations.
quoteEn: From bodily warmth to emotional warmth, the figures of soldiers fighting undaunted by the cold and of the people labouring hard in production make up a precious memory of the revolutionary war years.
quoteZh: 从身体的暖到情感的暖，部队战士不畏严寒的战斗身影和人民群众奋力劳作的生产身影，构成了革命战争年代的珍贵记忆。

glossary.explanation: A Party image, associated with Mao Zedong's wartime writings, saying that the army relates to the people as fish to water, depending on popular support. It is used in Party history to describe army–civilian solidarity.

The January 1941 clash in which Nationalist forces attacked the headquarters units of the New Fourth Army in southern Anhui. Afterwards the Nationalist government stopped funding Communist forces, according to the article.
The Party's officially shaped account of the revolution and its history, used to convey values and legitimacy.

t: Mao Zedong's planning and direction of the strategic offensive during the War of Liberation
zh: 解放战争时期毛泽东关于战略进攻的谋划与指导
paras: Peng Houwen asks how Mao Zedong planned and directed the People's Liberation Army's shift to the strategic offensive in the War of Liberation (1946–1949). The article argues that the PLA went on the offensive before its strength had overtaken that of the Nationalist (Kuomintang) forces. Its main forces moved to exterior-line operations and carried the war into Nationalist-held areas, which Peng presents as a vivid application of Mao's military strategic thought. In Peng's account this reversed the course of the war and hastened the fall of the Nationalist regime.

The study is organised around three turning points, drawn mainly from Mao's telegrams and Central Committee directives. The first is the southern-front operational plan of 22 June 1946, drafted on the eve of the full-scale civil war. The second is the Central Committee meeting of 21 November 1946, which adopted the line of "overthrowing Chiang Kai-shek". The third is the Xiaohe Conference of 21–23 July 1947 in northern Shaanxi, which fixed the offensive's overall deployment.

Peng's central claim is that Mao's thinking moved in stages. The 1946 southern plan was defensive in strategy but offensive in form, and it pointed south into Nationalist territory. As military victories mounted and the peace talks collapsed in November 1946, the aim changed from securing peace and democracy to overthrowing Nationalist rule. Mao then set out a blueprint: destroy 70 to 80 Nationalist brigades, bring the two sides' strength into balance, and push beyond the Yangtze within three to five years. Peng then identifies a further shift after Liu Bocheng and Deng Xiaoping's forces crossed the Yellow River on 30 June 1947. Mao no longer waited to crush the Nationalist offensives in Shandong and northern Shaanxi, or for overall superiority. Peng attributes this to two causes: the liberated areas' resources were close to exhaustion, and inner-line operations in Shandong were going less well than expected.

Peng concludes that the Xiaohe Conference settled the offensive's goals, policy and concrete plans. Its principles were set out in Mao's directive of 1 September 1947, "The Strategic Policy for the Second Year of the War of Liberation". Three armies then advanced into the Central Plains, and by October 1947 the PLA's slogan was to overthrow Chiang Kai-shek and liberate all China. In Peng's reading, the Nationalist regime's collapse was by then clearly in prospect. Read the original if you study Mao's military thought, the Party's documentary record of the War of Liberation, or the decision-making behind the 1947 advance into the Dabie Mountains and the Central Plains.
quoteEn: This shows that, while the Nationalist forces' overall strength still exceeded that of our army, trying to destroy their main attacking forces in a short time through inner-line operations remained difficult.
quoteZh: 这说明，在当时国民党军队的整体力量仍然超过我军的情况下，企图在短时期内通过内线作战歼灭国民党进攻的主力部队，仍然是有困难的。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese Communist Party's term for the civil war with the Nationalist government from 1946 to 1949, which ended with the founding of the People's Republic.
In Mao's military writings, the stage at which the PLA moved from defence to a general offensive, which Chinese historiography dates to mid-1947.
Fighting outside one's own base areas, in enemy-held territory, as opposed to inner-line operations within the base areas.
An enlarged Central Committee meeting chaired by Mao in Xiaohe village, Jingbian county, northern Shaanxi, on 21–23 July 1947, which decided to shift the main forces to exterior-line operations.

t: High-quality Party building leading high-quality development: theoretical logic and strategic paths
zh: 高质量党建引领高质量发展：理论逻辑与战略路径
source: Studies on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics, 2026 no. 1
paras: Tang and Han take up Xi Jinping's 2025 formula of "leading high-quality development through high-quality Party building". They ask why the quality of Party building should shape the quality of economic and social development, and how the link can be strengthened. Their answer is that the Party's leadership is the fundamental tie between the two, so that improving Party building turns the Party's political and organisational strengths into development momentum and governance capacity.

The article has three parts. It first sets out the theoretical logic, tracing it through Marx, Engels and Lenin on the active role of the superstructure, then through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. It then assesses the current situation, giving achievements and problems. It closes with strategic paths along four dimensions: political and ideological guidance, institutional arrangements, working mechanisms, and cadre capacity. The authors cite examples such as industrial-chain Party alliances in Jiangsu.

The core argument is that the formula follows the Marxist principle that the superstructure acts back on the economic base, and that a ruling party is the concrete agent of this. The authors describe the formula as continuing the tradition while innovating on it in five areas: Party leadership, Party organisations' functions, the driving mechanism of the Party's self-reform, the orientation towards new quality productive forces, and systemic method. They present the two sides as mutually dependent. Party building supplies direction, organisation and institutions, while development results serve as the yardstick of Party-building quality. Against the achievements they set four problems: superficial understanding of "Party leadership", organisational coverage that is formal rather than effective, weak resource integration and merely formal fusion with business, and thin personnel capacity. The authors cite figures showing that misconduct such as inaction or false action made up 84.1 per cent of the formalism and bureaucratism cases handled in November 2025.

The authors propose that Party organisations change how they understand the link between Party building and development, and that institutions be built into corporate governance, science and technology, and emerging sectors. They also call for more flexible, networked working mechanisms and for cadres who combine political and business competence, selected and assessed under a correct view of performance. They conclude that Party building should be embedded in every stage of development through organised, institutionalised channels. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party-building scholarship justifies and operationalises Party leadership of the economy, including its diagnosis of grassroots problems in new economic and social organisations.
quoteEn: In essence, high-quality Party building leading high-quality development is an organic interaction between political logic and economic logic, and between the logic of Party building and the logic of development.
quoteZh: 高质量党建引领高质量发展本质上是政治逻辑与经济逻辑、党建逻辑与发展逻辑的有机互动。

glossary.explanation: The official goal of China's economy since the late 2010s, replacing the earlier emphasis on high-speed growth. It stresses quality, innovation and meeting people's needs for a better life.
A concept associated with Xi Jinping since 2023, referring to advanced productive forces driven by technological innovation. Official discourse links it to high-quality development.

An official term for the Party's efforts to correct its own faults and maintain discipline. Xi Jinping presents it as the Party's second answer to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and decline.

t: The core meaning, historical necessity and scientific method of upholding the Party's cultural leadership
zh: 坚持党的文化领导权的核心要义、历史必然性和科学方法
source: Marxist Studies (马克思主义研究), 2026 no. 5
paras: Chen Wanqiu asks what it means to uphold the Party's cultural leadership, why this is historically necessary, and how it should be done. The article treats the Party's cultural leadership (cultural hegemony in the sense of leading influence) as an extension of political leadership and as a proposition Xi Jinping put forward in the new era. Chen argues that existing scholarship has examined its origins, texts and countermeasures but rarely interpreted it through historical materialism, and sets out to do so.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the core meaning from three Marxist angles: the contradictory movement between social being and social consciousness, the internal logic of strengthening the Party's overall leadership, and the principle that the people are the creators of history. The second presents four grounds for historical necessity, and the third proposes methods built on Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Chen draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and on the Party's record from the revolutionary period to the present.

Chen's central claim is that, because consciousness reacts back on social being, contesting cultural leadership means contesting the power to shape people's thinking. Giving it up, in this reading, would expose society to capital's logic, Western values and historical nihilism, and would shake the socialist system. Chen also holds that cultural leadership cannot be separated from the Party's overall leadership, and that it expresses the cultural agency of the people rather than simple administrative interference. For practice, Chen distinguishes three linked powers: leadership (the goal), management (the institutional support, including control of the internet and online literature and art) and discourse (the means of narrative and interpretation). Chen adds two further requirements: a path of socialist cultural development with Chinese characteristics, aimed at building a culturally strong country by 2035, and the organic union of the "soul line" (Marxism) and the "root line" (traditional Chinese culture) in the Second Integration.

Chen concludes that upholding cultural leadership is not an expedient but a fundamental matter for the fate of the Party and country, supported by the claim that the Party's undertakings have advanced when it used cultural power well and met setbacks when it did not. The article presents this as essential to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and as guided by Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how Chinese Party theorists ground cultural leadership in historical materialism and translate it into policy on media, the internet and discourse.
quoteEn: Upholding the Party's cultural leadership is, in essence, converting the political advantage of upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership into the spiritual advantage of cultural self-confidence and self-reliance.
quoteZh: 坚持党的文化领导权，本质上是将坚持和加强党的全面领导的政治优势转化为文化自信自强的精神优势。

glossary.explanation: The Party's leading and guiding authority in the cultural and ideological field. It is related to Gramscian "cultural hegemony", and Xi Jinping has framed it as the Party's cultural leadership.
A body of ideas on cultural work formally presented in 2023, treated as part of Xi Jinping Thought. It puts the Party's leadership of culture first.
The Party's formula for combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture. It is the second of the Two Integrations.
A Party goal of building a country with strong cultural influence, competitiveness and security, with 2035 as the target date.
The idea that Chinese culture and the Chinese people should be the independent creators and bearers of their own culture, a theme Xi Jinping stressed in 2023.

t: Grasping the great significance and key requirements of Party building leading grassroots governance
zh: 深刻把握党建引领基层治理的重大意义与重要要求
paras: This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 3 August 2026, asks why Party building should lead grassroots governance and what that leadership requires. Tan Xiaoyan argues that, amid a changing social structure, more diverse popular demands and growing pressure to control risks, grassroots governance has an increasingly foundational and strategic place in national governance. The author concludes that Party building must lead it, as a safeguard for Chinese modernization.

The piece has two parts. The first sets out the significance of Party-led grassroots governance, which the author calls political, theoretical and practical. The second turns to four requirements: improving the system of overall Party leadership, pursuing reform and innovation, serving and benefiting the people, and putting risk prevention first. Tan frames the whole discussion with Xi Jinping's statements on grassroots work and on the Party's roots among the people.

In the first part Tan gives four reasons. Grassroots Party organizations, which the author says numbered 5.431 million at the end of 2025, are the foundation of the Party's long-term rule. Grassroots governance underpins the modernization of national governance. Rising popular expectations require responsive services. Grassroots units are also the first line of defence in coordinating development and security. In the second part, Tan proposes that major grassroots matters be decided by Party organizations after discussion. The author also calls for trimming township and sub-district administrative structures, giving them fuller powers and cutting formalistic burdens. Tan further urges combining self-governance, rule of law and moral governance, and strengthening emergency management, using the updated 'Fengqiao experience' and big-data tools.

Tan concludes that the Party's organizational strengths must be converted into governance capacity at the grassroots, so that effective governance supports high-quality development and a high level of security. The author holds that the people should be the judges of results, and that governance should be tested by whether people gain real benefits and whether their rights are protected. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of the current Party-building approach to grassroots governance, including its institutional proposals on township powers, burden reduction, cadre training and risk control.
quoteEn: The effectiveness of all grassroots governance work should be tested by whether the people have truly received tangible benefits and whether their rights and interests have truly been protected.
quoteZh: 检验基层治理一切工作的成效，要看人民是否真正得到了实惠，人民权益是否真正得到了保障。

glossary.explanation: The official formulation of China's development path, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models of modernization.

glossary.en: combining self-governance, rule of law and moral governance
glossary.explanation: An official model of grassroots governance, often called the 'three-governance integration'. It combines resident self-government, legal norms and moral or cultural guidance, all under Party leadership.
A model of resolving disputes locally, which originated in Zhuji, Zhejiang in the 1960s. It has been promoted as a template for grassroots conflict mediation.

t: International communication strategies of Yan'an woodcuts during the War of Resistance
zh: 抗战时期延安木刻的国际传播策略
paras: This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2026, asks how Yan'an woodcuts reached foreign audiences during the War of Resistance against Japan. Xue argues that, facing a Kuomintang news blockade of the Border Region, the Communist Party used woodcuts as a visual medium that crossed language barriers. In the author's account, they presented an image of united resistance and democratic construction and were notably effective in international communication.

The article has two main parts. The first maps the transmission network: Party leaders, progressive art organisations, and foreign journalists and friends who visited Yan'an. The second looks at the channels (printed anthologies and overseas periodicals, international exhibitions, and published reportage) and then at why the content suited foreign audiences.

Xue gives concrete cases. Zhou Enlai took Yan'an works to the 1942 national woodcut exhibition in Chongqing and gave Yan Han's picture-story on the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain to an American journalist. Works were sent to the Soviet Union and to the United States, and illustrated Gunther Stein's 1945 book The Challenge of Red China. The author holds that the woodcuts focused on resistance and democracy, as in Gu Yuan's Marriage Registration and Village Election. They combined Western printmaking technique with Chinese folk traditions, and drew on real events, so that they served as credible visual evidence against stigma and blockade.

Xue concludes that this was a successful strategy by which the Party actively built a visual political discourse and contested discursive power under information blockade. The author presents it as a historical reference for exploring how China's stories are communicated internationally today. Read the original if you want a brief overview of Yan'an woodcuts as wartime Party external propaganda and the specific channels and examples the author cites.
quoteEn: Yan'an woodcuts were not propaganda products invented subjectively and detached from reality; their creation was deeply rooted in the fighting, production and daily life of the soldiers and people of the Border Region.
quoteZh: 延安木刻并非脱离现实主观臆造的宣传品，其创作深深植根于边区军民的战斗、生产与生活实践之中。

glossary.explanation: Woodblock prints made by artists in the Communist-led Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region during the 1930s–40s, often depicting resistance, production and village life. Many were produced by teachers and students of the Lu Xun Academy of Arts.
The Communist-led Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, with Yan'an as its centre, which the Kuomintang government restricted and blockaded during the war.

t: Understanding in depth the thesis that "upholding Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics"
zh: 深入理解“坚持党的领导是中国特色社会主义最本质的特征”
paras: This commentary, published in Guangming Daily, explains a thesis placed first among the "fourteen upholds" of Xi Jinping's Party-building thought, which a national Party-building conference in June 2026 formally set out. The thesis is that upholding Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Gong Yun argues that this claim rests on the basic principles of scientific socialism, develops the Marxist theory of Party-building, and expresses the inherent unity of CPC leadership and the socialist cause.

The article has three parts. The first distinguishes "features" from the "most essential feature" in socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second explains why Party leadership determines the nature, direction and fate of that socialism. The third sets out practical measures for ensuring that the Party remains the strong leadership core.

In the first part, Gong uses the Marxist pairing of essence and appearance. Essence is an inherent determination and features are its outward expression. Public ownership as the mainstay, rule of law, common prosperity, a people-centred approach and harmony between humanity and nature all derive from socialism's essence. Gong holds that Party leadership governs all of them, so that without it they lose their foundation and drift from the socialist course. In the second part, Gong argues that Marxism requires the proletariat to form its own party, and that the CPC embodies this principle in China. According to Gong, its founding mission, its representation of the broadest interests of the people without special interests of its own, and its capacity to coordinate the whole situation make it irreplaceable.

Gong calls for four tasks: safeguarding the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Party Central Committee, including through the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; improving institutions of comprehensive Party leadership so that leadership is neither absent nor overreaching; advancing the Party's self-reform, with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and anti-corruption work; and uniting the people through the mass line. Gong concludes that the thesis reflects the will of the Party and the state and the fundamental interests of the people. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how current Party-theory writing justifies Party leadership as the defining feature of Chinese socialism.
quoteEn: Among these features, Party leadership is the most essential one. It governs all the others, which are all determined by Party leadership and take shape, develop, play their role and show their advantages under it.
quoteZh: 在这些特征中，党的领导是最本质的特征，统领其他所有特征，其他特征都是由党的领导所决定的，都是在党的领导下形成发展、发挥作用、彰显优势的。

glossary.explanation: A body of ideas on Party-building attributed to Xi Jinping. The article says it was formally set out at the national Party-building conference of June 2026 and comprises "fourteen upholds".

A formulation from the 6th Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). It affirms Xi Jinping's position as core of the Party Central Committee and of the whole Party, and the guiding role of his thought.
A Party requirement to uphold Xi Jinping's core position in the Central Committee and the whole Party, and to uphold the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's disciplinary and anti-corruption drive since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
An official term for the Party's continual self-purification, self-improvement and self-renewal, used in current Party-building discourse.
The official name for China's political and economic system and its guiding ideology since the reform era.

t: Carrying forward the great Long March spirit to build a firm ideological foundation of ideals and convictions among young people
zh: 弘扬伟大长征精神 筑牢青年理想信念根基
paras: Song Xiaodong, a researcher at Beihang University's School of Marxism, takes up how universities can use the Long March spirit to strengthen the ideals and convictions of young people. Writing in a newspaper commentary, Song argues that today's youth are at a formative stage and face a mix of competing ideas and cultures, so they need this spirit to "supplement the calcium" of their ideological backbone. Universities, as the main site of moral and civic education, should work the spirit into the whole process of ideological and political education.

The article follows Xi Jinping's five-part definition of the Long March spirit and organises its proposals under four headings. These are upholding Party leadership to set the direction of youth education, promoting patriotism to nurture feelings for family and country, tempering the will to struggle to build a sense of responsibility, and committing young people to national development through practical action. Each section links episodes from the Long March to concrete measures for higher education.

In the first section, Song reads the Long March's success as proof that Party leadership is decisive. From this the author draws the conclusion that Party committees must lead universities, with the president responsible under the committee's leadership. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era should enter textbooks, classrooms and minds, and stories such as the Zunyi Meeting and the crossing of snow mountains and grasslands should become teaching material. The later sections turn the Long March into educational methods. Stories such as "half a quilt" illustrate patriotism and the people's standpoint. Military training, labour education and sport build endurance, and the "seeking truth from facts" attitude is applied to academic rigour. Song also calls for young people to take on "chokepoint" technological problems as their own long march.

Song concludes that every generation must walk its own Long March, citing Xi Jinping, and that the challenges of building a modern socialist country require this spirit. The practical proposals include red study tours to Long March sites, links with the "Three Going to the Countryside" activities and the Western Development volunteer programme, and encouraging graduates to work at the grassroots and in fields such as artificial intelligence and quantum technology. The author also proposes publicising role models such as poverty-alleviation village cadres and border-defence soldiers. Read the original if you want to see how Party-affiliated scholars translate Long March commemoration into concrete university ideological education measures.
quoteEn: Universities, as the main front for fostering virtue and nurturing talent, should dig deeply into the educational value of the great Long March spirit and integrate it into the whole process of ideological and political education.
quoteZh: 高校作为立德树人的主阵地，要深入挖掘伟大长征精神的育人价值，将其融入思想政治教育全过程

glossary.explanation: A set of values the Party associates with the Red Army's Long March of 1934–36. Xi Jinping defined it in 2016 as putting the people's interests first, firm revolutionary ideals, self-reliance, discipline and unity, and reliance on the masses.
The system of courses and activities in Chinese schools and universities that teaches Marxism, Party theory and patriotic values.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.

t: Grasping the rich meaning of the Communist Party of China's outstanding qualities
zh: 深刻把握中国共产党的优秀特质的丰富意蕴
paras: This commentary in Guangming Daily takes up the six "outstanding qualities" of the Communist Party of China that Xi Jinping set out in his speech marking the Party's 105th anniversary.
