The six are: pursuing truth and keeping the right direction; being rooted in the people; shouldering historical missions and holding the strategic initiative; keeping pace with development trends; daring and being able to struggle; and strengthening itself. Chen Jinlong argues that these qualities are a systematic summary and a "key code" to why the Party has been able to succeed.

The article has three parts. The first examines how the qualities came about. The second discusses the internal unity the author finds in Xi's formulation. The third assesses what the formulation contributes. Chen defines a party's qualities as distinctive attributes formed from its nature, guiding ideology, values and practice, and describes them as its "genes" and an inner support for its growth.

On origins, Chen names four factors: the scientific guidance of Marxism, including its materialist conception of history and its view of the people as the creators of history; the tempering of revolution, construction, reform and the new era; the nourishment of fine traditional Chinese culture, with the Two Integrations as the concrete route; and a conscious response to the demands of the times. On internal unity, the author sees four pairings: cause and effect; theoretical character, practical exploration and Party-building experience; past, present and future; and historical confidence and historical initiative. Chen illustrates each with the wording of Xi's six formulations.

Chen concludes that the formulation offers new ways to describe the Party's character and to answer why the Party has succeeded. In the author's reading it also supports the shaping of the Party's image and gives international audiences a way to understand the Party and its long period in power. Chen says that, grounded in a "grand view of history", it supplies a new reference point for interpreting Party history and will shape how that history is narrated. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated scholar presents and systematises the official account of the Party's qualities after the 105th anniversary speech.
quoteEn: The Communist Party of China's outstanding qualities are a convergence and fusion of historical confidence and historical initiative.
quoteZh: 中国共产党的优秀特质是历史自信与历史主动的交汇融合。

glossary.explanation: A formula promoted under Xi Jinping: integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Chen presents it as the concrete route by which the Party's qualities formed.
In Chen's definition, the confidence and conviction of the agents of history in the history of their nation, state or party.
In Chen's definition, the spirit and ability to grasp the broad trend of history on the basis of its laws and to drive historical change consciously.

t: The Party's self-reform focuses on governing power
zh: 党的自我革命重在治权
paras: This newspaper commentary takes up Xi Jinping's formulation that the Party's self-reform 'focuses on governing power', because the "Four Forms of Decadence" mostly stem from privilege-seeking thinking and corruption is chiefly the use of power for private gain. Wu and Liu argue that self-reform is in essence a project of purifying power turned inward. In their view, treating the governance of power as the key lever is the only way to uproot the soil of misconduct and corruption and keep the Party advanced and pure.

The article is organised around four practical paths: regulating how power operates, strengthening whole-process supervision, cultivating an ethics of power, and fixing responsibility for governing power. Each section is built from quotations from Xi Jinping, followed by the authors' suggestions on implementation. The authors refer to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as the time when the Party revised many internal regulations and laws and built a power-list system.

On regulating power, Wu and Liu say that loss of control arises from poor allocation: vague boundaries lead to overreach, excessive concentration to monopolised power, and weak oversight to abuse. They call for clearer limits in areas such as major policy, project approval, large funds and cadre appointments. They also call for democratic centralism and collective decision-making, and for a 'technology plus institutions' approach that leaves traces of how power is used. On supervision, they stress the 'key few', especially top leaders, and the coordination of Party, supervisory, inspection, mass and media oversight. They also stress investigating work-style problems and corruption together. They treat institutional constraint and supervision as 'external discipline' that must be paired with the 'self-discipline' of an ethics of power, grounded in power serving the people, disciplinary awareness and caution in small matters.

The authors conclude that responsibility must be passed down in a chain. Party organisations bear primary responsibility, discipline inspection and supervisory bodies bear supervisory responsibility, and accountability must be strict, covering both direct and leadership responsibility. They hold that this closed loop of responsibility underpins the effort to govern power. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-theory commentary in 2026 presents power governance as the core of the Party's self-reform, and how it links institutional design, supervision, ethics and accountability.
quoteEn: The Party's self-reform is in essence a project of purifying power, turned inward like a blade against oneself.
quoteZh: 党的自我革命本质上是刀刃向内的权力净化工程

glossary.explanation: A concept stressed under Xi Jinping describing the Party's claimed capacity to correct its own faults and fight corruption from within, without external pressure.
Formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, which the Party targeted in its work-style campaign launched after the 18th Party Congress in 2012.
Senior leading officials, especially top leaders of units, whom the Party treats as the main targets of supervision because of the power they hold.
The Party's fundamental organisational principle, combining discussion and collective decision-making with strict obedience to the decision once made.
A graded approach to discipline, from early reminders and criticism to serious disciplinary and legal sanctions, aimed at catching problems early.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: The historical course and contemporary mission of the great project of Party building
zh: 党的建设伟大工程的历史进程和时代使命
paras: Published in the People's Daily on 3 July 2026, this commentary takes its cue from Xi Jinping's speech marking the 105th anniversary of the Communist Party of China. It asks how the Party has built itself over 105 years and what that task requires now. Song Yuehong argues that the "great project of Party building" has been a continuous process that has equipped the Party to lead each stage of national development, and that it remains the fundamental guarantee for building a strong country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

The article follows four historical stages. These are the pre-1949 revolution, the early years of the People's Republic and socialist construction, reform and opening up from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). A final section turns to the present and sets out five tasks for the future.

Song's core claim is that at each stage the Party advanced its own construction alongside theoretical innovation through the Two Integrations. In the revolutionary period this meant building the Party ideologically, democratic centralism and the "three magic weapons". After 1978 it meant raising the Party's governing and anti-corruption capacities. Since 2012, in Song's account, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the Central Committee's eight-point regulations and Xi Jinping's Party-building thought have strengthened unity and the Party's political ecology. Song presents this thought as an original contribution to the Marxist theory of the party.

Song concludes that, given the unprecedented complexity of the current environment, Party building must be strengthened further. The article calls for upholding the Party's overall leadership and the authority of the Central Committee, and for making full and rigorous self-governance of the Party genuinely effective. It also calls for putting political building first, combining ideological education with institutional governance, and keeping up work on conduct, discipline and anti-corruption. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party-building history and priorities are presented in the Party press at the 105th anniversary.
quoteEn: To govern the country, one must first govern the Party; only when the Party flourishes can the country be strong.
quoteZh: 治国必先治党，党兴才能国强。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A Party-building policy line promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It covers political, ideological, organisational, conduct and discipline building, together with anti-corruption work.
A formula in Party theory: combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's specific realities and with China's fine traditional culture.
The part of Xi Jinping Thought concerned with how a long-ruling Marxist party should be built. The Party presents it as a development of Marxist party theory.
Rules adopted by the Central Committee in December 2012 to curb formalism, bureaucratism, extravagance and hedonism among officials.
The Leninist organisational principle of the Party, combining discussion and decision-making with binding discipline and centralised leadership.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: The key to why the Communist Party of China can succeed
st: On the Party's six outstanding qualities
zh: 中国共产党为什么能的关键密码
paras: Writing in the People's Daily after the 105th anniversary of the Party's founding, Xie Chuntao, a vice president of the Central Party School, sets out to explain why the Communist Party of China has been able to succeed. The commentary presents itself as an exposition of Xi Jinping's anniversary speech, which summarised six "outstanding qualities" of the Party. Xie argues that these qualities are a major theoretical innovation and the "key code" to the Party's achievements, and that history and the people chose the Party because other parties lack them.

The article takes the six qualities in turn, giving each a section: pursuing truth and keeping the right direction; being rooted in the people; shouldering the historical mission and holding strategic initiative; keeping pace with the times; daring and being able to struggle; and strengthening itself so as to stay vital. Each section moves from historical examples, from the Party's early years through reform and opening up to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), to a statement of what the Party should do next. Each ends with a line that "history profoundly shows" the lesson in question.

Xie's central claim is that the qualities are mutually supporting and explain results in concrete areas. Scientific theory, culminating in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, is said to have guided the achievement of a moderately prosperous society and Chinese modernization. Closeness to the people is credited with the poverty-alleviation campaign and the mass line. Strategic planning, from the "four modernizations" to the 2035 and mid-century goals and five-year plans, is said to let the Party "keep drawing one blueprint to the end". On self-governance, Xie holds that the Party's rigorous self-discipline and its anti-corruption campaign are "unique in the history of world political parties".

Xie concludes that Party members must absorb these qualities "into their blood and bones" so that the Party never changes in character, and that it remains the firm leadership core of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The practical tasks named include study of Xi's thought, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, implementing the 15th Five-Year Plan, and continued full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want an authoritative, officially aligned account of how the Party now explains its own success, and of the vocabulary used for it.
quoteEn: A party guided by scientific theory is invincible and unbeatable.
quoteZh: 一个拥有科学理论指导的政党是无坚不摧、无往不胜的。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions after the 19th Party Congress (2017). It is presented as the latest stage in adapting Marxism to China.
A formula adopted in 2022 that affirms Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Party Central Committee and of the whole Party, and the guiding role of his thought.
A Party requirement to uphold Xi Jinping's core position and the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Party Central Committee.
The official term for China's own path of modernization, described as distinct from Western models. It is the central goal of the Party's current strategy.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: The policy of tightening Party discipline and conduct and fighting corruption, which has been prominent since 2012.
A Party method, associated with Mao Zedong, of drawing on the views of ordinary people and then returning policy to them. It is presented as the basis of the Party's links with the people.

t: From Yan'an to Xibaipo: an important exploration by Chinese Communists in establishing a correct view of performance
zh: 从延安到西柏坡：中国共产党人树立正确政绩观的重要探索
paras: This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 3 June 2026, asks how the Communist Party of China forged and held to a "correct view of performance" (zhengjiguan) between the Yan'an period and the Xibaipo period. Wu Yin argues that, under extreme hardship, the Party kept to a people-centred stance, its founding aspiration of serving the people, incorruptibility and plain living. In Wu's account, this laid the foundation for victory in the New Democratic Revolution and for building the new China.

The piece is a short historical essay in two parts. The first covers Yan'an, when the Party governed the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia border region in wartime. The second covers Xibaipo, where the Central Committee was based from May 1948 and which Wu calls the "last rural command post" of the revolution. Wu draws on Mao Zedong's writings, anecdotes of leaders' daily lives, accounts by visitors such as Edgar Snow, Tan Kah Kee and Huang Yanpei, and figures on land reform.

For Yan'an, Wu cites leaders farming their own vegetable plots, minimal cadre allowances, and the execution of the corrupt official Xiao Yubi as evidence of a "trust–supervision–punishment" system. Wu adds the "Serve the People" speech, the 1945 writing of wholehearted service to the people into the Party constitution, and measures such as the "three-thirds" system and rent reduction. For Xibaipo, Wu points to land reform, which the author says gave land to some 160 million people and drew over 8.8 million labourers into supporting the three great campaigns. Wu also stresses Mao's warning at the Second Plenum of the Seventh Central Committee (1949) to keep up modesty and hard struggle, and his "examination" remark about avoiding the fate of Li Zicheng.

Wu concludes that the view of performance was not static. It moved from creating visible material welfare for base-area peasants under war conditions to restoring production in cities once the Party took national power. Throughout, Wu says, it stayed tied to the fundamental interests of the majority, which Wu describes as the inner logic and historical dialectic of the Party's outlook. The author presents this trajectory as historical experience for establishing and practising a correct view of performance in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how current Party discourse draws on the revolutionary period for lessons on cadre conduct and assessment.
quoteEn: The more victories follow one another, the more one must keep a clear head; the greatest achievement is always to stay close to the masses and to preserve the true colours of hard struggle.
quoteZh: 越是接连取得胜利时，越要保持清醒，最大的政绩就是始终不脱离群众、始终保持艰苦奋斗的本色。

glossary.explanation: The criteria by which officials understand and judge their own achievements in office. Party discourse stresses establishing a "correct" view, in which results serve the people rather than personal advancement.
The title of Mao Zedong's 1944 speech at Zhang Sude's memorial meeting. It became the Party's stated fundamental purpose and was written into the Party constitution in 1945.
A system of power-sharing in the anti-Japanese base areas. Communists, non-Party left-progressives and middle-of-the-road figures were each to hold roughly one third of government seats.
Mao Zedong's term for the Chinese revolution from 1919 to 1949, led by the proletariat and aimed at overthrowing imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism as a step toward socialism.

glossary.en: Second Plenum of the Seventh Central Committee
glossary.explanation: A meeting held at Xibaipo in March 1949. Mao warned there of the dangers of complacency and set out the tasks of shifting the Party's work to cities.

t: A great expedition that opened a new situation: the Red Army's Long March, its strategic shift and historical significance
zh: 开创新局的伟大远征：红军长征实现战略大转移及其历史意义
paras: This newspaper article by two Party historians argues that the Red Army's Long March was more than a feat of preserving the revolution's seed of fire. In the authors' account it was a strategic shift that changed the fate of the Chinese revolution, turned danger into safety and laid an important foundation for later victory. The authors present the march as 'a great expedition that opened a new situation'.

The article has three parts. The first traces how the northward course evolved, from the departure from the Central Soviet Area to the arrival at Wuqi in northern Shaanxi on 19 October 1935. The second explains why settling in northern Shaanxi mattered, drawing on the geography of the revolution and the changed national situation. The third discusses how the Party's anti-Japanese policy and its image among the people were affected.

The authors' central claim is that the destination was not chosen deliberately at the start. They describe a shift from 'unconscious' to 'conscious' choice and from 'seeking survival' to 'planning the overall situation'. Plans moved from joining forces in western Hunan, to a base around Zunyi, to crossing the Yangtze, and then to a Sichuan–Shaanxi–Gansu base after the Mao-led crossings of rivers and the meeting of the First and Fourth Front Armies. They say that Japanese aggression, the Huabei Incident of 1935 and the rise of the Sino-Japanese national contradiction to the principal contradiction made north China the front line. In their reading the revolution's earlier southern centre of gravity could no longer win broad support. They list the advantages of the Shaanxi–Gansu–Ningxia area: strategic depth, weak Nationalist control, commanders open to resisting Japan, and an existing base and army.

The authors conclude that after the Long March the aim was no longer only the army's survival but leading the nation's resistance. They credit the Wayaobu meeting with launching the anti-Japanese national united front and the shift from civil war to war of resistance. They say this raised the Party's standing among the people and countered Nationalist stigmatisation. The Long March, they write, moved the revolution 'from south to north' geographically, 'from narrow to broad' politically and 'from passive to active' strategically. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party historians present the Long March's strategic logic and significance.
quoteEn: Thus the Long March was not only a geographical move 'from south to north', but also achieved a political shift 'from narrow to broad' and a strategic shift 'from passive to active'.
quoteZh: 因此，长征不仅是地理上的“由南向北”，更实现了政治上的“由窄向宽”、战略上的“由被动向主动”。

glossary.explanation: The Party's policy from the mid-1930s of uniting all classes and political forces willing to resist Japan, including the Nationalists. The article links its formulation to the Wayaobu meeting of December 1935.
The 1934–36 retreat of the Chinese Red Army from its southern bases to the north-west, ending for the Central Red Army in northern Shaanxi. Party history treats it as a founding episode.
Japan's 1935 pressure to extend its control over north China, which the article treats as making north China the anti-Japanese front line.
A Party concept for the main social contradiction at a given time, which shapes strategy. The article says the Sino-Japanese national contradiction replaced the class contradiction in this role.

t: From Yan'an to the world: the international dissemination of Chinese literary theory
zh: 从延安到世界：中国文论的国际传播
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 8 April 2026
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary, Deng Haili asks what the 80-year translation and circulation of Mao Zedong's Talks at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art can teach about taking Chinese literary theory abroad. Deng argues that the Talks' international career offers a historical model for telling China's story well and building Chinese discourse and narrative systems.

The piece surveys English translations in two groups: those led by the Chinese government and those produced by foreign research institutions and scholars. It runs from versions around 1950 to the Harvard multi-volume edition of Mao's writings completed in 2023.

Deng describes the official translations of the 1950s and 1960s, including the Foreign Languages Press Selected Works of Mao Zedong, as state-level cultural dissemination. In Deng's account they served Cold War solidarity with Western leftists, sinologists and Third World revolutionaries. Foreign-led translations, by contrast, moved from political-historical readings, as in the 1952 Harvard documentary history, to aesthetic ones. Bonnie McDougall's 1980 translation criticised ideologically biased scholarship and stressed the text's aesthetic content. Deng presents the Harvard edition under Stuart Schram as combining political, historical and aesthetic perspectives.

Deng concludes that international dissemination is a complex process of discourse generation, re-signification and cultural dialogue, not simple language conversion. In this reading the Talks moved from a revolutionary document to a theme in world literary theory, showing the vitality of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Deng sees lessons for helping Chinese culture "go out" and "go in" and for mutual learning among civilisations. Read the original if you want a brief overview of the Talks' English translation history and how a Chinese scholar frames its lessons for international communication.
quoteEn: The international dissemination of Chinese literary theory has never been a simple matter of language conversion, but a complex systemic undertaking involving discourse generation, reconstruction of meaning and cultural dialogue.
quoteZh: 中国文论的国际传播，从来不是简单的语言转换，而是涉及话语生成、意义重构与文化对话的复杂系统工程。

glossary.zh: 在延安文艺座谈会上的讲话
glossary.pinyin: Zài Yán'ān wényì zuòtánhuì shàng de jiǎnghuà
glossary.en: Talks at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art
glossary.literal: Speech at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art
glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's 1942 speeches setting out the Communist Party's line that literature and art should serve workers, peasants and soldiers and the revolution. It remains a foundational text of Party cultural policy.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formulation for the Party's project of fitting Marxism to China's conditions and to contemporary circumstances.

t: Making the responsibility for governing the Party effectively a reality
zh: 推动管党治党责任落实到位
paras: Writing in the People's Daily (29 May 2026), Wang Xipeng takes up the relationship between the responsibility for managing and governing the Party and the effort to form and act on a correct view of performance. The article argues that the two are mutually reinforcing: the tighter and more concrete Party governance is, the steadier a correct performance outlook becomes, and the more it yields achievements that benefit the people and are recognised by them.

The piece is a commentary in three parts. The first sets out five ways in which Party governance supports a correct performance outlook: political guarantee, ideological foundation, work-style safeguard, a yardstick for testing results, and institutional safeguard. The second turns to how responsibility is to be enforced, and the third to democratic centralism as the basis of scientific decision-making and practical implementation.

Wang's central claim is that a performance outlook is a "soft constraint" that Party governance turns into a "hard" one, through quantified assessment, accountability and personnel decisions. The author describes distortions such as vanity projects, falsified data and formalism as ultimately problems of Party spirit, and treats failure to pursue full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as itself evidence of a wrong performance outlook. Responsibility must run vertically through every level and horizontally across clearly defined bodies: Party committees bear primary responsibility, secretaries are first responsible persons, other leaders carry "one post, two responsibilities", and discipline commissions supervise. Wang also argues that democratic centralism, combining collective leadership with individual division of responsibility, prevents both one-man rule and diffusion of responsibility.

Wang concludes that democratic centralism should run through the whole process of creating achievements: collective wisdom to judge at the decision stage, divided responsibility at the implementation stage, and institutional constraint at the oversight stage. This, the author holds, removes the ground for a distorted performance outlook and encourages foundation-laying, long-term work that answers to history and the people. Wang also stresses that strict management should be combined with care for officials, so that rigour does not stifle initiative. Read the original if you want to see how official Party-building discourse in 2026 links cadre evaluation, accountability systems and democratic centralism to the idea of a correct performance outlook.
quoteEn: The process of putting responsibility for governing the Party into effect is also the process by which a correct performance outlook turns from a "soft constraint" into a "hard rule".
quoteZh: 管党治党责任落实的过程，也是正确政绩观从“软约束”变为“硬杠杠”的过程。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the Xi Jinping era, prominent since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering ideological, organisational, work-style and disciplinary discipline and anti-corruption work within the Communist Party.
An official concept concerning how officials understand and pursue achievements in office. Party documents contrast it with vanity projects and short-term growth chasing.
The Communist Party's fundamental organisational principle, combining discussion and democratic input with centralised decision-making and obligatory compliance with decisions.
The rule that every Party leader is responsible both for their own professional or administrative work and for Party conduct and discipline in their area.

t: Polishing the "golden calling card" of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation
zh: 擦亮中央八项规定这张“金色名片”
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 26 March 2026
paras: This newspaper commentary asks how the Central Committee's eight-point regulation on Party conduct, issued after the 18th Party Congress (2012), can keep advancing the Party's self-reform. Lü Yongxiang calls the regulation a "golden calling card" and a fulcrum for changing how the Party is governed. The author argues that thorough implementation of its spirit gives the Party's self-reform a concrete lever and supplies a conduct guarantee for building a strong country and national rejuvenation.

The piece is set against the learning and education campaign on implementing the regulation, which the whole Party began in March 2025. After a short opening on the regulation's record since 2012, it sets out three orientations for implementation, each tied to a different foundation of self-reform: values, integrity and institutions.

First, Lü holds that putting the people first must be the value stance. Officials should check whether their view of power, of performance and of career has been distorted, and should deal with formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance. Second, the author urges a mechanism for investigating work-style problems and corruption together, so that the chain from bad conduct to corruption is cut. This means tracing the funds, participants and interest exchanges behind banquets and gifts. Third, Lü stresses making conduct-building regular and long-term. The author points to Party regulations on accountability, thrift and official reception, and to case analysis that finds the institutional roots of recurring problems.

Lü concludes that work-style building is a protracted struggle and that the regulation is a long-term "iron rule", not a short-term measure. The author calls for combining reform spirit with strict standards, and for linking conduct, discipline and anti-corruption work. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official line on how the eight-point regulation is tied to the Party's self-reform and to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.
quoteEn: Work-style building is a protracted struggle. The eight-point regulation is not a short-term rule but a long-effective iron rule and hard line.
quoteZh: 作风建设是持久战。中央八项规定不是短期的规定，是长期有效的铁规矩、硬杠杠。

glossary.explanation: A set of rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012 to curb extravagance, bureaucracy and formalism among officials, covering matters such as meetings, travel and official reception. Its implementing rules were issued later.
An official concept, stressed under Xi Jinping, that the Party must correct its own problems and keep itself pure through internal discipline and anti-corruption work.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official slogan for the Party's internal discipline and anti-corruption drive since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
The official goal of restoring China's strength and international standing, usually dated to 2049.

t: Advancing the Party's self-reform requires systematic guidance
zh: 推进党的自我革命要实现系统化指引
paras: This short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (26 March 2026) asks how the Party should govern itself in the new era. Liang Fei argues that Xi Jinping's call for "five more steps into place" in advancing the Party's self-reform gives systematic guidance on this question. The author presents the five as the key practical levers for applying Xi's thinking on the Party's self-reform.

The article draws on Xi's remarks at the 21st group study session of the Political Bureau of the 20th Central Committee. There, Xi called self-reform the Party's "second answer" to escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. The five areas are understanding, Party spirit, regulated exercise of power, strict supervision and discipline, and fulfilment of responsibility for Party governance. Liang groups them under three headings: motivation, rigid constraints, and coordination of the governance system.

Liang's central claim is that governance effectiveness depends on moving from piecemeal to systemic governance. Awareness and Party spirit are treated as the ideological drive, which turns external pressure into internal motivation. Regulating power and joint investigation of misconduct and corruption, with Party supervision linked to other forms of supervision, supply the rigid constraints. A closed loop of assigning, performing, supervising and holding to account responsibility ties the system together. Liang assigns each element a role: understanding answers "why", Party spirit "who", power regulation "what", supervision "how well", and responsibility "relying on whom".

Liang concludes that the five steps form an organic whole and must be pursued with a systems outlook, so that the elements resonate together. The aim, in the article's account, is a governance pattern that covers all content, all objects, the full chain of responsibility and every institution. This would strengthen the Party's creativity, cohesion and combat capacity and support the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholars frame the "five steps" as a systematic governance framework.
quoteEn: The \"five more steps into place\" are not five isolated dimensions, but an organic whole that is logically rigorous and internally unified.
quoteZh: “五个进一步到位”不是五个孤立的维度，而是逻辑严密、内在统一的有机整体。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building. It holds that the Party must keep correcting itself through rigorous discipline and anti-corruption work, and it is presented as the answer to the problem of Party decay.

glossary.en: the historical cycle of rise and fall
glossary.explanation: The idea, associated with a 1945 exchange between Huang Yanpei and Mao Zedong, that regimes tend to flourish and then decline. The Party presents supervision by the people as a first answer and self-reform as a second.

t: Digital technology empowering primary-level Party building: advantages and pathways
zh: 数字技术赋能基层党建的优势及进路
paras: Gao Qi and Nie Hongna ask how big data, artificial intelligence and related technologies can be used to raise the quality of primary-level Party building, and what risks must be managed along the way. Their thesis is that digital technology offers three distinct advantages (integration, precision and interactivity), but that these are accompanied by five risks that call for deliberate countermeasures. The article, published in Theoretical Horizons in 2025, presents itself as offering theoretical grounds and practical reference for the digital transformation of grassroots Party organisations.

The article opens by citing Xi Jinping's call for full online and offline coverage of Party organisations and several Party documents on primary-level Party building. It then moves in three steps: the technological advantages, the risks, and a set of corresponding remedies. The authors draw illustrations from cloud storage, integrated digital Party-building platforms, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection's 2015 anti-'four undesirable work styles' app, and VR and metaverse training.

On advantages, the authors argue that integration breaks down hierarchical barriers to information sharing and converts resources into practical effectiveness. Precision shifts work from experience to data and from after-the-fact exposure of misconduct to early-warning systems. Interactivity turns one-way governance into interactive governance and enables immersive training. On risks, they identify a 'technology-first' tendency in which instrumental rationality displaces value rationality, digital formalism (such as compulsory app check-ins and 'digital traces'), data-security weaknesses linked to outsourced platforms, algorithmic bias and 'information cocoons', and digital divides, especially between urban and rural Party members.

The remedies follow the risks. The authors call for embedding a people-centred value orientation in technology design, reforming assessment systems and the view of performance, and establishing tolerance-for-error and correction mechanisms. They also call for stronger data and system security, algorithmic ethics rules with monitoring and accountability, and tiered digital-skills training with long-term incentives for Party members and cadres. Digital tools, they stress, remain auxiliary to serving the masses and winning hearts. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how digitalisation of grassroots Party organisation is being justified and where its problems are officially acknowledged.
quoteEn: Technology should be a people-centred tool of service, and should not run counter to the Party's original aspiration and mission.
quoteZh: 技术本应成为以人为本的服务工具，而不应适得其反与党的初心使命相背离。

glossary.explanation: The work of building and running Party organisations at the lowest levels, such as villages, neighbourhoods, enterprises and schools. It is treated as the foundation of the Party's organisational system.

A term for formalism carried out through digital means, such as compulsory app check-ins, repeated data reporting and showy websites. It is criticised in Party discourse as adding to the burdens on grassroots cadres.
Formalism, bureaucracy, hedonism and extravagance, targeted in the Party's campaign on conduct launched after the 18th Party Congress (2012).

The practice of requiring grassroots workers to document their activity online, through records, photos or logins, so that it can be inspected. Critics within the Party see it as a source of formalism.
A mechanism that allows leniency toward cadres' mistakes made in good-faith innovation or reform, while requiring that errors be identified and corrected.

t: The ideological value of Party conduct building
zh: 党的作风建设的意识形态价值论析
paras: Cao Jinlong and Liu Jianjun ask what ideological significance the Communist Party's work on its "style of conduct" (zuofeng jianshe) carries beyond its place in Party discipline. They argue that conduct building is part of ideological work as well as of Party building. In their view it has three kinds of ideological value: it shapes the Party's image, it expresses the Party's nature and purpose, and it helps guard against ideological risks.

The article starts from the Party's long record of emphasising good conduct, including the practices of linking theory with practice, staying close to the masses, criticism and self-criticism, and plain living. It also covers the work since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, notably the Central Committee's eight-point regulations. The argument is organised in three parts: the direct value of image-building, the core value of reaffirming Party spirit and purpose, and the potential value of preventing risk. Historical examples include the contrast between "Yan'an style" and "Xi'an style", and a series of education campaigns since 2013.

The authors' first move is to treat the Party's conduct as its image. They trace the shift in official wording from conduct "affecting" the Party's image to conduct "being" the image, and say that people judge the Party by the behaviour of its members. Where conduct matches ideological propaganda, they argue, ideology gains recognition and cohesion, and where it does not, trust is lost. Second, they follow Xi Jinping in holding that conduct problems are at root problems of Party spirit. They link such problems to a weakened commitment to the people's standpoint and say they damage the Party-masses relationship, which underpins the Party's legitimacy. Third, they list internal and external ideological risks, including "Westernisation", "colour revolution", social trends and digital platforms. They describe formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance as an especially dangerous internal risk. They argue that a disciplined Party is the precondition for resisting external ones as well.

The authors conclude that conduct building is both a way of solving present problems and a pre-emptive move against future risks. They contend that the greater the risks and tasks on the path of building a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the more conduct building must be strengthened. They say this would raise the cohesion and guiding force of socialist ideology. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party-building scholars link discipline and conduct campaigns to the Party's legitimacy and ideological security.
quoteEn: Party conduct is the practical embodiment of ideological ideas, and conduct building carries extremely important ideological value.
quoteZh: 党的作风是意识形态理念的实践体现，作风建设具有极其重要的意识形态价值

glossary.explanation: A long-standing Party campaign concept covering the attitudes and behaviour of Party members and cadres in thought, work and daily life. It has been stressed especially since 2012, with measures against formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: Official term for the strategy of tightening Party discipline, supervision and anti-corruption work, closely associated with Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
Rules issued by the Politburo in December 2012 to curb extravagance, formalism and bureaucratism among officials, for instance on meetings, travel and hospitality.

The ideological and organisational qualities expected of a Communist Party member, including loyalty to the Party's beliefs, principles and purpose. Official discourse treats it as the root of conduct.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official national goal of restoring China's strength and international standing, central to Party discourse since Xi Jinping took office in 2012.

t: Systematically constructing a long-term mechanism for Party conduct building
zh: 论党的作风建设长效机制的体系化建构
paras: Writing after the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (October 2025), Wang Jianqin asks how the Party's work on conduct (zuofeng jianshe) can be made routine and lasting, and argues that a mature long-term mechanism has now taken shape. In Wang's account, the Eight-point Regulations adopted after the 18th Party Congress (2012) served as the anchor that moved conduct building from 'frequent campaigns' to 'long-term governance'. The article presents this mechanism as an institutional guarantee for upholding the Party's overall leadership and for implementing the 15th Five-Year Plan.

The article is organised around four components of the mechanism. These are the creation of Party regulations, the internalisation of values, the execution of rules, and supervision. Wang first traces how the Eight-point Regulations changed the way intra-Party regulations are drafted, then examines education and demonstration effects, then responsibility systems and monitoring, and finally the supervision system and its link to state supervision.

Wang's central claim is that the Eight-point Regulations combined rigidity with effectiveness. They carried no 'trial' label, were framed around concrete problems, and were revised through a standing practice at the start of each Politburo term. Wang describes a 'small incision' drafting method, a 'core norm plus supporting rules' structure, and phased development from 2013 to 2027. On implementation, Wang stresses a 'dual-responsibility' arrangement. It pairs the 2019 trial regulations on responsibility for enforcing Party regulations with the regulations on Party committees' principal responsibility for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. It is backed by five linked steps, including joint supervision and the 'one case, two investigations' accountability rule. Wang adds big-data monitoring that targets hidden variants of the 'four forms of decadence', and list-based governance. In supervision, the author argues that the Eight-point Regulations widened the scope of intra-Party oversight. They also helped align it with the national supervision reform through joint investigation of misconduct and corruption.

Wang concludes that the mechanism has matured into an integrated whole, moving from treating symptoms to addressing root causes. In the author's view it shows the Party's historical consciousness in carrying out the Party's self-reform. Wang expects it to supply institutional support for the Party's leadership system, major national strategies, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and Chinese modernization during the 15th Five-Year Plan period. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party discipline and conduct rules are designed, enforced and supervised, and how this work is justified institutionally.
quoteEn: The institutionalisation of the spirit of the Eight-point Regulations is not only a landmark innovation in the methodology of drafting intra-Party regulations, but also an active exploration of systematically building a long-term mechanism for conduct building.
quoteZh: 中央八项规定精神的制度化历程，不仅是党内法规制定方法论的标志性创新，更是围绕作风建设长效机制进行体系化建构的主动探索。

glossary.explanation: A set of rules on official conduct adopted by the Politburo in December 2012. They restrict extravagance, formalism and bureaucratism in meetings, travel, hospitality and documents.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's discipline and anti-corruption drive. It has been a leading theme since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
An official term for the Party's efforts to correct its own problems through internal discipline and supervision. It is prominent in Xi Jinping-era discourse.
Formal rules issued by Party bodies to govern Party organisations and members. Their official system has been codified and expanded since 2012.

glossary.en: joint investigation of misconduct and corruption
glossary.explanation: A principle that treats breaches of conduct rules and corruption as linked and investigates them together.
The official name for the Party's model of modernisation. It is presented as distinct from Western paths.

t: Spirit-building and image construction of the Communist Party of China in the Yan'an period
zh: 延安时期中国共产党的精神塑造与形象建构
source: Teaching and Research (教学与研究), 2025 no. 11
paras: This research article asks how the Communist Party of China's spirit and its public image shaped each other in the Yan'an period (1935–48), and what that interaction means today. He and Cao argue that Party members under Mao Zedong's leadership developed the Yan'an spirit, and that this spirit was the inner core around which the Party built three images: a leadership image, a revolutionary image and an advanced image. They note that existing scholarship describes these images but rarely links them to the Yan'an spirit.

The article has three main parts. The first treats the Yan'an spirit as the core and value guide of image-building, tracing its origins in model figures and in Mao's essays. The second examines the three images in turn. The third draws lessons for the Party's spiritual inheritance and image-building in the new era, including international communication. The authors draw on Mao, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and on Yan'an-period sources such as the Liberation Daily and the labour-model campaigns.

The central claim is that a party's image is the practical form of its spirit. The authors say the Yan'an spirit grew from exemplars such as Norman Bethune, Zhang Side and the labour model Zhao Zhankui, then was condensed into four elements: a correct political direction, an ideological line of emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts, the fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, and a self-reliant, hard-working pioneering spirit. The leadership image rested on the line of all-out resistance, Mao's theoretical works and his personal example in the production campaign. The revolutionary image rested on the Rectification Movement and self-criticism, which the authors present as the Party leading social revolution through self-reform. The advanced image rested on communist ideals joined to concrete goals, expressed in the proposition of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions.

The authors conclude that the new era should carry forward these practices in four ways. The Party should rely on its leading core, draw on exemplars, combine internal improvement with external perception, and build the image systematically. They add that the image depends on governing capacity, on serving the people's fundamental interests, and on interaction between the Party and the people. They also call for stronger research on the Party's spiritual lineage, use of digital media and a modern international communication system. Read the original if you study Yan'an-period Party history, or want to see how Chinese scholars link Party spirit to political image-building.
quoteEn: A party's image is the practical form of its spirit; it takes spiritual strength as its core and shows itself concretely as the real effect of unified thinking within and unified action outside.
quoteZh: 政党形象就是政党精神的实践形态，它以精神力量为内核，具体表现为对内统一思想、对外统一行动的现实效果。

glossary.explanation: The set of values attributed to Party members in the Yan'an base area, summarised by Xi Jinping as political direction, seeking truth from facts, serving the people and self-reliance. The term was formulated after the period itself.

glossary.zh: 中国共产党人精神谱系
glossary.explanation: The official series of named 'great spirits' formed in the Party's history, from the founding spirit to the Yan'an spirit and later ones. Xi Jinping has promoted it as a resource for Party building.
The Party-wide education and discipline campaign of 1942–45 in Yan'an. It targeted dogmatism, sectarianism and bureaucratic work styles.
The campaign from 1939–40 onwards in which Party, army and officials grew food and made goods in the border region to ease economic blockade.

t: How to combine strict management with care and balance incentives with constraints
zh: 怎样做到严管厚爱结合、激励约束并重
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts, Wang Ruijun takes up a line from the Recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025): combine strict management with loving care, and give equal weight to incentives and constraints, so as to stimulate the endogenous drive and overall vitality of the cadre corps. Wang argues that strictness and care are not opposites but a single unity, and that the 15th Five-Year Plan period requires cadres who dare to take responsibility and know how to deliver.

The article has three parts. It first describes the challenges facing cadres in the new era and the problems Wang sees in the cadre corps. It then explains why strict supervision and encouragement of initiative are organically unified. It closes with four practical areas of work for Party committees and organisation departments: Party-spirit training, incentives and care, enforcement of rules, and motivating cadres to act.

Wang names several problems: formalism and bureaucratism, a lack of capability, passive attitudes of "doing less so as to err less", and a minority who treat strict constraint as an excuse for inaction. The causes lie in distorted views of political achievement, weak skills, and inadequate systems that do not coordinate material, spiritual and promotion incentives. Strict management, in Wang's account, sets rules and bottom lines; care and incentives supply motivation. Strictness is both a "tightening spell" and a "protective talisman" because it catches problems early, while care without supervision turns into indulgence. Good cadres are therefore both strictly supervised and sincerely cared for.

Wang proposes strengthening ideals, loyalty and warning education, and pursuing the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Wang also calls for a performance-and-merit approach to appointments, support for grassroots cadres, lighter formalistic burdens, and checks on "top leaders" through power, responsibility and negative lists. Cadres should also be assessed on livelihoods, ecology and public satisfaction, and be led to build new quality productive forces and pursue high-quality development. Read the original if you want a representative example of current Party-building discourse on cadre management, including its institutional measures and official vocabulary.
quoteEn: Strict management and loving care are both indispensable and internally connected: strict management is the greatest care, and supervision is the best protection.
quoteZh: 严管和厚爱缺一不可、内在贯通，严管就是最大的厚爱、监督就是最好的保护。

glossary.explanation: A formulation from the 6th Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) affirming Xi Jinping's position as the Party's core and the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought. Party documents present it as decisive for the Party and country.
The requirement that Party members firmly uphold Xi Jinping's core position in the Central Committee and the Party's centralised, unified leadership.
A concept advanced by Xi Jinping in 2023–24 for productivity driven by technological innovation and emerging industries.
An official goal of shifting from fast growth to growth emphasising quality, efficiency and innovation, prominent since the 19th Party Congress (2017).

t: How the CPC Central Committee's organs established themselves in Shanghai after the failure of the Great Revolution
zh: 大革命失败后中共中央机关在上海何以立足？
source: Documents of the Party (Dang de wenxian), 2025 no. 6
paras: After the failure of the Great Revolution in 1927, the CPC Central Committee moved from Wuhan back to Shanghai and went underground. Ma Xiaohan asks how the Party sited and shielded its organs under the White Terror. The article argues that the Party moved from improvised methods, such as using members' homes and borrowed or feigned shops, to a mature model of 'independently run businesses', and that this model explains how the centre survived in Shanghai until 1933.

The study covers the Central Committee's Shanghai organs from 1927 to 1933. It begins with the early Party's two cover strategies in the foreign concessions, 'using the family to cover the Party' and 'using commerce to cover the Party'. It then follows the post-1927 stage of 'family-style organs', the reorganisation after the defection of Gu Shunzhang in 1931, and the later results of the business model. Evidence includes memoirs, Party circulars, the 1928 'Common Knowledge of Secret Work' and accounts by defectors and Guomindang agents.

Ma's central claim is that each model's weaknesses led to the next. 'Family-style organs' (large pretend families, or real or pretend couples) helped with tenancy checks but depended on neighbours and comrades, left the Party short of funds and exposed it to informers. Ma cites the betrayal of Luo Yinong in 1928 as an example. From 1928 the Party therefore pursued 'socialization of organs' and 'professionalization of members', opening real shops, clinics, bookshops, antique dealers and 'husband-and-wife' stores, while borrowed or feigned cover remained a supplement and a risk. Ma credits independent businesses with three benefits: safer cover (the Central Committee survived nearly three years after Gu's defection), closer links with the masses, and financial self-reliance, including 'red-white trade' with the Soviet areas.

Ma concludes that independent business combined security, economic autonomy and mass work, and that the Party's adaptability and resilience in extreme conditions rested on it. The author adds that the experience laid a foundation for hidden-front work in the War of Resistance and the civil war. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of the Central Committee's underground arrangements in Shanghai, including named safe houses, shops and Special Branch practices, as seen through Party-history writing in the journal Documents of the Party.
quoteEn: The 'independent business' model took account of both underground work and economic work, and showed the Communists' firm convictions and their revolutionary spirit and political ability to fight to the end.
quoteZh: “独立办商”模式，兼顾了地下工作和经济工作，展现出中国共产党人坚定信念、斗争到底的革命精神和政治能力。

glossary.explanation: The Central Committee's intelligence and security organ, set up in Shanghai in 1927 under Zhou Enlai. It protected leaders, chose and guarded safe houses and gathered intelligence.
A cover practice from 1927 in which Party members lived together as a 'family', large or small, to pass tenancy checks in the concessions.
The practice of the Party opening and running real shops and firms as cover, as opposed to merely borrowing or pretending to be a business.
The 1924–1927 revolutionary movement of the First United Front between the Communists and the Guomindang. It ended with the Guomindang's 1927 purge of Communists.
Trade between the Communist-held 'red' Soviet areas and the Guomindang-held 'white' areas, used to obtain scarce goods and funds.

t: From domestic confrontation to international debut: the CPC and the question of representation at the San Francisco Conference
zh: 从国内交锋到国际亮相：中共与旧金山会议代表权问题
paras: Zhou Tianyu asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) handled the composition of the Chinese delegation to the 1945 San Francisco Conference, which founded the United Nations, and how its propaganda changed along the way. Existing scholarship has examined the delegation's makeup, the Party's fight to attend and Dong Biwu's activities in the United States. Zhou argues that it has paid less attention to the link between the Kuomintang–CPC talks on a "coalition government" and the delegation question, and to the propaganda around Dong's trip. The article contends that the episode shows the CPC growing from a party with little international experience into one with both international and domestic horizons.

Drawing on archival documents, the article follows events from the Dumbarton Oaks talks of 1944 to the conference of mid-1945. It covers the CPC's growing foreign-affairs work after the Kuomintang's military collapse in the Henan–Hunan–Guangxi campaign and the arrival of the US Army observer group in Yan'an. It then traces the failed talks mediated by the US envoy Patrick Hurley and the Yalta announcement. The last sections cover the naming of Dong Biwu as delegate and his publicity work on the way to and in San Francisco.

Zhou's central claim is that the Party's approach had two phases. From mid-February to late March 1945, the CPC treated the delegation list as a political instrument. It demanded that the Kuomintang receive at most one third of the seats and that the CPC, the Democratic League and non-party figures hold the rest. It tied this demand to "coalition government" in the Yan'an press and English-language broadcasts, in order to expose one-party rule and mobilise domestic opinion. Zhou argues that this pressure, together with the Democratic League's lobbying and Roosevelt's suggestion, helped lead Chiang Kai-shek to accept one Communist delegate, though far fewer than the CPC wanted.

In the second phase, once Dong was named, the Party shifted its main audience abroad. Despite Kuomintang obstruction, Dong spoke to the American press and overseas Chinese and distributed 5,000 copies of an English booklet on the liberated areas. Zhou concludes that the Party moved from "exposing the Kuomintang" to "constructing the image of the liberated areas". In this reading, the episode taught the Party a lesson in linking international and domestic issues that proved useful in the Civil War period. Read the original if you study CPC diplomacy, the Kuomintang–CPC negotiations of 1944–45 or early Communist propaganda, and want an archive-based account of the San Francisco delegation dispute.
quoteEn: The CPC linked the domestic Kuomintang–CPC negotiations with the international San Francisco Conference, achieving a propaganda effect that coordinated the domestic and international situations.
quoteZh: 中共将国内的国共谈判与国际的旧金山会议相联系，实现了国内外局势的联动宣传效果。

glossary.explanation: The CPC's 1944–45 demand to end Kuomintang one-party rule and form a government of all anti-Japanese parties. Mao Zedong set it out in his 1945 report "On Coalition Government".

A coalition of smaller non-Communist political groups and intellectuals, founded in 1941 and 1944 in its later form. It sought a third path between the Kuomintang and the CPC and was close to the CPC on the coalition-government demand.
The term the CPC used for the base areas it governed behind Japanese lines and elsewhere during the war.

t: Techniques of rapid night marching in mountain terrain by the Red Army
zh: 红军山地夜路快速行军技术探赜
paras: Niu Zelin takes up a question that, the author says, has not yet received detailed scholarly study: how did the Red Army march quickly along mountain roads at night during the Agrarian Revolutionary War (the Soviet period of the late 1920s and 1930s), and how was that capacity built? Facing a much stronger Nationalist army, the Red Army had to rely on mountain and night marches to turn passivity into initiative. Niu argues that these marches rested on concrete technical training, field expedients and organisational discipline, not simply on evasion.

Drawing on historical sources, diaries and memoirs, the article starts from the strategic shift of going "up the mountains" after 1927, associated with Mao Zedong. It then moves through training (hill-climbing, physical competitions, military geography courses), guides and local recruitment, bridging and river crossing, and signalling by flags, bugles and relayed orders. It goes on to route choice, night-march methods, examples of speed, and the political work and discipline behind the pace.

The core argument has three parts. First, Niu holds that route selection decided outcomes: circling and detour tactics worked in the first four encirclement campaigns, but straight-line marching under Li De and Bo Gu in the fifth campaign lost the Red Army its flexibility, while the post-Zunyi Conference manoeuvres, notably the four crossings of the Chishui River, regained it. Second, night marching was drilled for secrecy: silent movement, soldiers dyeing clothing and horses, limited torches, and white towels as guides, with the 1931 passage between enemy forces and the Gansu night escape as cases; Niu also notes risks such as getting lost, bad weather and slow bottlenecks. Third, the article cites daily marching rates of roughly 80 to over 100 li and the 240-li dash to the Luding Bridge, and attributes this speed to political work, singing, strict discipline and detailed crossing regulations.

Niu concludes that the Red Army's way of marching was meant to find favourable moments to fight, and that it grew from the reality of enemy strength and Red Army weakness, as well as from the adjustment of strategy by Mao Zedong and Zhu De. The author adds that this style shaped later Chinese military practice, citing a US veteran's memoir about Chinese night flanking marches in Korea. Read the original if you are interested in the tactical and logistical detail of Red Army marching, with its sources, rather than in strategy alone.
quoteEn: This distinctive way of marching was, objectively speaking, required by the reality of a strong enemy and a weak Red Army.
quoteZh: 这种独特的行军方式，从客观上讲是敌强我弱的现实所需。

t: "Making the Party truly mass-based": the development paths of the Chinese Communist Party's early grassroots organizations
zh: “使党真正群众化”：中国共产党早期基层组织的发展路向
paras: How did the Chinese Communist Party build grassroots organizations during its founding years and the Great Revolution (1924–27)? Yi Fenglin argues that existing scholarship has examined local cases, operating mechanisms and individual explorations, but has not synthesised the multiple paths and underlying logic at both macro and micro levels. The article contends that the Party's early grassroots development combined several paths, and that together they produced what the Party then called its "massification" (qunzhonghua).

The article draws on Party documents, regional committee circulars and reports, Comintern resolutions and membership statistics. It covers five dimensions: the shift in recruitment method from traditional social ties to a more revolutionary and standardised approach; expansion into new regions and sectors; the balance between quantity and quality of members; the working of democratic centralism between higher and lower organizations; and the role of the Comintern.

Yi's first main point is that early recruitment relied on networks of schoolmates, fellow-townspeople and workmates, as in Jiangxi, which helped secrecy. After the May Thirtieth Movement this was judged inadequate: in 1926 the Shanghai regional committee and Chen Duxiu called for recruiting through the branch's collective work. Second, the Party extended from core cities to surrounding regions and from factories to schools, villages and offices, supported by study societies, trade unions and peasant associations. The article cites membership rising from 994 before the Fourth Congress to 57,967 before the Fifth, with workers at 53.8 per cent. Third, active recruitment targets and shortened probation periods were followed by branch reorganisation, member education, vetting and anti-corruption measures. Regular reports, special commissioners and inspections sustained democratic centralism, though Yi notes that the Comintern's excessive focus on workers and its failure to guide organizational policy after the 1927 coup had negative effects.

Yi concludes that these varied paths rooted the Party in grassroots society and reflected Marxist guidance together with an ability to adjust organizational policy to revolutionary conditions. The article presents a balanced growth in numbers and quality as the Party's overall approach. Read the original if you study early Chinese Communist Party history, organizational development, or the documentary sources on regional Party committees in the 1920s.
quoteEn: "Balanced development of quantity and quality" was the overall approach to organizational development in the early Chinese Communist Party.
quoteZh: “数量与质量均衡发展”是早期中国共产党组织发展的总体思路。

glossary.explanation: The Leninist organizational principle adopted by the Party, combining discussion within the organization with strict obedience of lower bodies to higher ones. The article treats it as the basis of reporting and guidance between Party levels.
A term used in 1920s Party documents for turning the Party from a small body of intellectuals into one with a broad base among workers and peasants.
The basic unit of Party organization. The Fourth Congress (1925) renamed the earlier "group" as "branch", and the Fifth Congress (1927) defined it as the Party's basic organization.

The 1925 anti-imperialist movement of strikes and protests that began in Shanghai after British-led police shot demonstrators on 30 May. The article presents it as a turning point for Party expansion.
The Chinese name for the 1924–27 revolutionary period of Guomindang–Communist cooperation and the Northern Expedition, which ended with the 1927 coup against the Communists.

t: The genesis and logic of upholding the Party's cultural leadership
zh: 坚持党的文化领导权的发生逻辑
paras: Tian Xuming examines why the Communist Party of China (CPC) now stresses upholding its cultural leadership (wenhua lingdaoquan, often rendered cultural hegemony), a concept the article calls an original idea of Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The author argues that the concept is both a product of applying Marxist party theory to Chinese cultural work and a response to the Party's own history and to present-day demands. Tian contends that a party holding cultural leadership can guide social values, command discursive authority, unite the people, integrate resources and resist cultural colonisation.

The article moves in three steps. It first reconstructs the theoretical sources in Marx, Engels and Lenin. It then surveys the CPC's practice from the May Fourth period through the Party's founding, the Gutian Conference, the Yan'an rectification, the post-1949 years and reform and opening up, citing Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. Finally it explains, under three headings, why the concept is stressed in the new era.

On the classics, Tian reads Marx and Engels' claim in The German Ideology that the ruling material force is also the ruling intellectual force, and Marx's remark that theory becomes a material force when it grips the masses, as implying that the proletarian party must contest cultural leadership. Lenin is presented as making this explicit: he opposed the Proletkult's claim to cultural autonomy and demanded that publishing and libraries be Party institutions. In Tian's account, the CPC's history shows the same pattern, with cultural struggle opening the way for each stage of its work. For the new era, Tian gives three reasons: safeguarding the Party's governing security, citing Xi's remark that regimes often collapse first in the ideological sphere and the author's view of the Soviet collapse; meeting the inner requirements of Chinese modernization; and answering the great changes unseen in a century, in which the author sees Western cultural infiltration as a continuing means of containing China.

Tian concludes that a party's strength lies not only in organisation but in its ideological and cultural leadership, and that the CPC must keep strengthening this leadership to secure its long-term rule and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Tian says the concept supplies a political guarantee for building a socialist cultural power. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of how Chinese scholars trace the lineage of the cultural leadership concept from Marx and Lenin through to Xi Jinping's era.
quoteEn: Upholding cultural leadership is an important experience by which the Communist Party of China has built and strengthened the Party and continually led its cause forward.
quoteZh: 坚持文化领导权是中国共产党立党强党，不断引领事业发展的一条重要经验。

glossary.explanation: The Party's authority to direct culture, ideology and public values; the term echoes Gramsci's 'hegemony' but is used in the official discourse of the Party's leadership over cultural work.
The official name for China's path of modernisation under CPC leadership, presented as distinct from Western models and emphasising both material and cultural-ethical progress.
The policy of economic reform and engagement with the world economy launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.
The Party-wide ideological campaign of the early 1940s, centred in Yan'an, aimed at unifying thinking and combating subjectivism, sectarianism and formulaic writing.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official goal of restoring China to national strength and prosperity, set out as the central aim of the Party's mission in the Xi Jinping era.

t: Advancing the Party's self-reform by improving the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
zh: 以健全全面从严治党体系推进党的自我革命
source: Journal of Harbin Institute of Technology (Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 6
paras: Xi Jinping has described improving the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as the "effective path" to advancing the Party's self-reform. Sun and Zhao note that existing scholarship mostly studies how to build this system in practice, while the basic question of why it is an effective path has not been settled. They answer by asking what makes it effective, in what sense it is a path, and how it can drive the Party's self-reform. Their thesis is that the system's own properties match the inner demands of self-reform.

The article, published in the Journal of Harbin Institute of Technology (Social Sciences Edition), is organised in three steps. It first sets out the criteria of effectiveness: results, speed, cost-benefit and overall function. It then treats the system as a path formed by history, theory and practice, and surveys the Party's rigorous self-governance from the Mao Zedong period through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Finally it describes the system's structure and proposes ways to improve it.

The authors argue that effectiveness has three parts: strengthening the Party's overall leadership, pooling the forces of Party governance and securing long-term rule. They say it also needs speed, quality, controlled cost and returns that the people can see. They describe a vertical hierarchy of institutions, from the Party Constitution and democratic centralism down to Party regulations. It spans six areas of Party building and runs through a "establish–implement–revise" cycle. Three features, in their account, link the system to self-reform. Its integrated, interlocking nature ties self-reform to the Party's mission of social revolution. Its linkage reflects the dialectical "self-negation" by which the Party must overcome corruption, which they define as the alienation of power. Its emergence and adaptability allow gains to accumulate like compound interest and let the Party respond to new risks.

The authors call for refining the vertical institutional system, planning the six areas systematically, and strengthening the supply, operation and updating of rules. They also call for using AI and big data in Party governance. They conclude that the system's central task is to bring Party power within the rule of law, so that power belonging to the people stays under popular control and reflects the people-oriented nature of Party rule. Read the original if you want to see how Party-building scholarship justifies the system through systems theory, dialectics and cost-effectiveness reasoning, or want to track the official vocabulary around the Party's self-reform.
quoteEn: The essence of corruption is the alienation of power, and the basic requirement of the Party's self-reform is that the Party itself recognise the danger of this alienation of power.
quoteZh: 腐败的本质是权力异化，党的自我革命的基本要求就是要自己意识到这种权力异化的危险

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It covers Party discipline, anti-corruption work and institutional building across all areas of the Party.
Official term for the Party's efforts to correct its own problems, said to be a second answer to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall.

t: Three-dimensional interpretation of shaping the image of a Marxist party from the perspective of self-reform in the new era
zh: 新时代自我革命视域下马克思主义政党形象塑造的三维阐释
source: Journal of Harbin Institute of Technology (Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 6
paras: Xu Fengzhen and Zheng Pei'e take up the relationship between the Communist Party of China's self-reform and the shaping of its image as a Marxist party. Starting from the 2021 Party resolution's conclusion that an advanced Marxist party is forged through constant self-reform, they argue that the two are bound by an internal logic: the process of self-reform is itself the process of building the Party's image. They treat this as necessary for keeping the Party advanced and pure, and for advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization.

The article is organised around three questions: why, what and how. The first part sets out the value of image-building, the second describes how it has appeared in practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and the third proposes ways to deepen it. It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements and on Party documents, regulations and statistics, such as figures on Party membership, intra-Party regulations and anti-corruption cases.

On the first question, the authors hold that Xi Jinping Thought on self-reform supplies theoretical guidance, while the spirit of self-reform supplies moral support. They say this spirit shapes the Party as responsible, mission-driven and clean. On the second, they link each strand of Party building to a specific image: political building to a Party that takes charge of the whole situation, ideological building to firm belief, organisational building to tight organisation, conduct to a clean political climate, discipline to strict order, institutions to rule-based governance, and anti-corruption work to integrity. On the third, they propose that the Party solve the "unique problems of a large party" through the "six always" questions, tell the story of its self-reform, and use home-hosted diplomacy, new media and scholarly exchange to spread it. They also suggest recasting that story in terms that international audiences can accept, with anti-corruption cooperation as an example.

The authors conclude that self-reform and image-building are an organic whole, with theory, practice and values reinforcing one another. They call for the Party to keep pursuing self-reform without pause, so that it becomes a Marxist governing party that is vigorous, trusted by the people and able to withstand all tests. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party-building scholarship links discipline, anti-corruption and institutional reform to the Party's public image and external communication.
quoteEn: The Party's self-reform in the new era and the shaping of the image of a Marxist party form an organic whole, in which theory is isomorphic, practice is interembedded and values coexist.
quoteZh: 新时代党的自我革命与马克思主义政党形象塑造之间，是理论同构、实践互嵌、价值共生的有机整体。

glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's term for the Party's continuous effort to purify, improve and renew itself. Official texts present it as the Party's second answer to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall.
The official term for China's path of modernization under Party leadership, presented as distinct from Western models.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central official goal of the Party since the 18th Party Congress, referring to restoring China's national strength and international standing.

glossary.en: unique problems of a large party
glossary.literal: problems unique to a large party
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's phrase for the challenges of governing and managing the world's largest political party. It is summed up in the "six always" questions, which concern mission, unity, governing capacity, work spirit, problem-solving and political climate.

t: The development and practice of the theory of Party-spirit cultivation in the new era
zh: 新时代党性修养理论的发展与实践探析
source: Journal of China Jinggangshan Cadre Institute, 2025 no. 6
paras: Zhu Yan, Zhou Zhudong and Huang Li ask how the theory and practice of Party-spirit cultivation (dangxing xiuyang) have developed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They argue that Xi Jinping's statements on the subject, which call it the \"study of the heart\" of Communists and a lifelong required course, form an original body of ideas.
