In the authors' account, these ideas are part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and guide the Party's self-reform.

The article first sets out why cultivation is needed and what it means, then lists three routes: theoretical study, tempering through work practice, and criticism and self-criticism. It then reviews how the Central Committee has strengthened Party spirit through eight rounds of concentrated education campaigns between 2013 and 2025, the anti-corruption drive, and Party regulations. The final sections assess results in six areas: theoretical, political, moral, disciplinary and work-style cultivation.

The authors' central claim is that Party spirit does not rise automatically with seniority or rank and must be built through lifelong effort. They treat campaigns, such as the mass-line campaign of 2013 and the study of Party discipline in 2024, as the main vehicle for concentrated education. Daily branch study and Party school training provide the regular kind. Anti-corruption work targets the \"key minority\" of leaders, grassroots \"flies and ants\" and fugitives abroad. The article cites official figures: 4.648 million cases filed since 2012 and 97.4 per cent satisfaction in a 2022 survey. Rules are to be made systematically and enforced strictly, so that discipline becomes a \"high-voltage line\".

The authors conclude that cultivation is a systematic, long-term project. They call for better institutional supply, for including it in the modernization of state governance capacity, and for turning Party spirit from an \"organisational requirement\" into a \"value pursuit\". They also urge the \"key minority\" to set an example, and they want problems of \"disconnect between knowing and doing\" and formalism to be resolved. Read the original if you want a Party-school account of how the post-2012 education campaigns and anti-corruption statistics are presented as evidence of improved Party discipline and conduct.
quoteEn: Party-spirit cultivation is a systematic project and also a long-term project.
quoteZh: 党性修养是一项系统工程，也是一项长期工程。

glossary.explanation: The process by which Party members train their ideological conviction, discipline, morality and work style. Party leaders describe it as a lifelong task for every member.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology since it was written into the Party Constitution in 2017.
Official term for senior leading cadres, who are held to have a decisive influence on Party conduct and are therefore the focus of supervision and discipline.
Official phrase for the Party's claimed capacity to purify, improve and renew itself through internal supervision and discipline.

t: Basic experience of the Communist Party of China in Party-spirit education
zh: 中国共产党党性教育的基本经验
source: Journal of China Executive Leadership Academy Jinggangshan, 2025 no. 6
paras: How has the Communist Party of China (CPC) cultivated "Party spirit" (dangxing) in its members over more than a century, and what lessons follow? Han Qiang and Ma Jingming define Party-spirit education as the Party's internal education of members, with leading cadres as the main focus, aimed at preserving its character as the vanguard of the working class, the Chinese people and the Chinese nation. They argue that political cultivation comes first, and they draw out six basic experiences from this history.

The article opens with the 2023 revised regulations on cadre education and Xi Jinping's December 2024 remarks on lifelong self-cultivation. It cites 2024 discipline-inspection figures (877,000 cases filed) to show that the anti-corruption situation remains severe and that this education is never finished. It then moves through the Party's history, from the Anyuan and Beijing Party schools of the Great Revolution period through Yan'an to the present, and cites the key regulations and five-year plans of the Xi Jinping era.

The core claim is that Party spirit is not innate and does not rise automatically with seniority or rank, so it must be built through education and practice. The authors list the experiences: keep ideals and convictions at the centre; uphold Party leadership and the authority of the Central Committee; test Party spirit in practice; safeguard unity as the Party's life; use persuasion and the formula "unity–criticism–unity", learned after past excesses such as the expanded anti-rightist campaign; and rely on institutional safeguards. They add that confronting major questions of each era produces ideological unity. In their account the Yan'an rectification campaign is the model of concentrated education. Party schools, cadre academies and the national Party-education plans carry out the work.

The authors conclude that Party-spirit education is a key means of keeping the Party advanced and pure. They call for continuing its traditions while widening content and methods. They also call for tackling superficiality, formalism and activity-for-its-own-sake, so that cadres are moved for a lifetime rather than for a moment. They want a multi-actor, multi-channel pattern consolidated, with lasting mechanisms. Read the original if you want a Party-school perspective on how Chinese scholars summarise the history, institutions and regulations of Party-spirit education.
quoteEn: Practice is the touchstone of Party spirit.
quoteZh: 实践是党性的试金石。

glossary.explanation: The sum of the stance, worldview, work style and image expected of a Communist Party member. In the article it is the concentrated expression of class character.

The various forms of education the CPC gives its members, especially leading cadres, on ideals, discipline, work style and loyalty. It is delivered through Party schools, cadre academies and campaigns.
A formula associated with Mao Zedong for handling disagreement within the Party. It starts from a wish for unity, passes through criticism or struggle, and reaches a new unity on a new basis.
The 1940s Party-wide campaign of study and criticism at Yan'an. The CPC treats it as a model of concentrated education for unifying thought.

t: A theoretical account of how the Eight-Point Regulation has changed China
zh: 八项规定改变中国的学理化阐释
source: Journal of China Executive Leadership Academy Jinggangshan, 2025 no. 6
paras: The article asks how and why the Central Committee's Eight-Point Regulation on improving Party conduct and staying close to the masses, adopted after the 18th Party Congress (2012), has changed China. The authors say existing scholarship covers its content, origins and implementation, but has not explained the underlying mechanism. They argue that a modest rule on conduct became a lever for the Party's self-reform and for wider social change, and that this rests on uniting the "power of truth" with the "power of personality".

After a literature review, the article is built in three parts. The first sets out what the regulation changed in three dimensions: the governing actors (Party cadres), the organisation of power and public spending, and social customs. The second explains why it could have such effects. The third proposes ways to turn the new conduct into lasting custom, which the authors call "transforming conduct into custom".

The core argument is that the regulation joins the truth of correct theory with the personal example of the Party's fine traditions, and turns the principle of putting the people first into concrete daily rules. The authors say it worked through a governing logic of three steps: starting from "key small matters" such as banquets, official cars and meeting styles, building a systematic network of rules, and enforcing them rigidly through accountability, routine supervision and special campaigns. They add that it spread through pressure and example from the "key minority" of leading cadres to the Party majority. In the authors' account this moved discipline from external constraint towards habit, and its example influenced government conduct and then popular customs.

For lasting effect, the authors call for three things. The first is more precise rules, with refined implementation measures, list-based management and feedback on rectification. The second is education: theoretical study and Party-spirit training so that cadres move from outside constraint to inner conviction. The third is cultural work, including a culture of integrity, drawing on traditional and revolutionary resources, and public opinion that supports the rules. Read the original if you want a Party-school scholarly account of how the Party explains the Eight-Point Regulation's wider effects and its plans to make it permanent.
quoteEn: The Eight-Point Regulation unites the power of truth with the power of personality: truth gives personality its direction and confidence, personality gives truth its vehicle and drive, and together they turn the Party's lofty ideals and fine conduct into rules of behaviour for cadres, so that these take root.
quoteZh: 八项规定将真理力量与人格力量相统一，真理力量为人格力量提供方向和底气，人格力量为真理力量提供载体和动力，二者相辅相成，将党的崇高理想和优良作风转化为党员干部的行为准则，使其真正落地生根。

glossary.explanation: A set of rules adopted by the Politburo of the 18th Central Committee in December 2012 on improving work style and staying close to the masses. It limits official banquets, travel, meetings, publicity and similar matters, and has become a byword for the Party's conduct campaign.
A Party term for leading cadres, whose example is said to shape the conduct of the wider Party and society.
The Party's official term for its efforts to correct its own problems without outside pressure.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: A systematic account of how the Communist Party of China can achieve long-term governance
zh: 中国共产党何以能够实现长期执政的系统性认识
source: Journal of China Jinggangshan Cadre Academy, 2025 no. 6
paras: Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that achieving long-term governance is a fundamental question the Party must answer, the authors ask why the Communist Party of China (CPC) is able to govern over the long term. They argue that existing scholarship explains mainly why long-term governance is necessary and how to achieve it, but not why it is possible. Their answer is that the Party, as a mission-driven party, has unified political, historical and practical logic into a distinctive system of governing advantages.

The article reviews recent studies and then builds a composite analytical framework: Party authority, Party adaptation, value consensus, institutional resilience and civilizational genes. Each element corresponds to one of five sections: Party leadership, self-reform, the supremacy of the people, the socialist system, and the Two Integrations. The sections draw on the Party's history from the new-democratic revolution through the post-1949 period and reform and opening up to the post-18th Congress (2012) era.

On leadership, the authors hold that centralised and unified leadership, with the Party Central Committee at its core, gives strategic continuity, mass mobilisation and the capacity to concentrate resources, and they contrast China's stability with what they call Western turmoil. On self-reform, they present it as the Party's defining political strength and its "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall, advanced through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. On the people, they describe a shift from "representing" to "becoming" the people, realised through whole-process people's democracy, and set it against Western party systems they portray as serving narrow interests. The socialist system and the Two Integrations, especially integration with fine traditional Chinese culture, are said to supply institutional durability and cultural legitimacy.

The authors conclude that long-term governance rests on unifying five things with it: Party leadership, the supremacy of the people, institution-building, cultural integration and self-reform. They warn that global uncertainty, heavy reform tasks and problems peculiar to a large party threaten this governance. They call for continued strengthening of governing capacity, the Party's overall leadership, risk awareness and a firm people's stance in pursuit of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how current Party-building scholarship justifies the CPC's long-term governance through a five-part framework.
quoteEn: The value advantages of the CPC's long-term governance, internalised through institutions, build a dynamic mechanism for converting them into effective state governance.
quoteZh: 中国共产党长期执政的价值优势通过制度内化而构建起国家治理效能转化的动力机制

glossary.explanation: A theme in Party discourse about how the CPC can remain the ruling party over the long run. Xi Jinping has called it a fundamental question the Party must answer.
The Party's term for rectifying itself and combating corruption and misconduct from within. It has been central to Party discourse since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official slogan for strict Party discipline, anti-corruption work and institutional regulation of Party conduct.
Official concept, introduced by Xi Jinping, describing Chinese democracy as covering every stage of political and policy processes rather than only elections.
Formula for combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities (first) and with fine traditional Chinese culture (second).

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's overarching national goal of restoring China's strength and international standing.

t: A scientific path for implementing democratic centralism in the new era
zh: 新时代贯彻民主集中制的科学路径
source: Journal of Jinggangshan Cadre Academy of China, 2025 no. 6
paras: Wu Hui and Ding Yongqiang ask how democratic centralism, which they call the Communist Party's fundamental organisational principle and leadership system, can be carried out more effectively in the new era. Following Xi Jinping's remark that it must be advanced through both cadres and mechanisms, they argue that persistent implementation problems can be solved only through a systematic path: educating and training leading cadres, having leaders set an example, and building up institutions.

The article opens by setting out four reasons the principle matters: it upholds the authority of the Party Central Committee, underpins the modernisation of state governance, joins scientific decision-making to efficient execution, and sustains a clean political ecology within the Party. It then examines four shortcomings that Xi Jinping has identified since 2013, and their causes. The remainder is divided into two parts, one on leading cadres as the "key minority" and one on institutional mechanisms.

The authors describe the four shortcomings as too little promotion of democracy, too little correct centralisation, too little criticism and too little strict discipline. They attribute these to weak Party spirit, unclear theoretical understanding, imprecise institutional design (for example vague definitions of "major matters") and lax enforcement of accountability. For cadres, they propose training in theory, Party rules and working methods, drawn from Mao Zedong's "Methods of Work of Party Committees" and the "sixteen-character principle". They also call for example-setting by Politburo members, by first secretaries ("squad leaders" rather than "patriarchs") and by team members. For institutions, they propose collective-leadership rules, wider participation by Party members and Party congress delegates, and the Two Upholds. They add a request-and-report system with "must request", "should report" and "no need to request" lists, together with supervision, graded accountability and an early-warning system with indicators such as collective-decision rates and the share of dissenting views adopted.

The authors conclude that democratic centralism is the Party's greatest institutional advantage. They call for institutional confidence and continued refinement of the system, so that democracy and centralism are united and the Party becomes "a piece of hard steel", providing institutional support for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-school account of how the current leadership proposes to operationalise democratic centralism, including its proposed lists, indicators and accountability measures.
quoteEn: Democratic centralism is a scientific, rational and efficient system, and it is our Party's greatest institutional advantage.
quoteZh: 民主集中制是科学合理且有效率的制度，是我们党最大的制度优势。

glossary.explanation: The Communist Party's organisational principle, combining internal democratic discussion with centralised, binding decisions and discipline. It originates in Leninist party theory and is written into the Party Constitution.
A political requirement, formalised after 2016–2018, to uphold the core position of General Secretary Xi Jinping and the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Party Central Committee.
A phrase used by Xi Jinping for leading cadres, whose conduct is held to determine whether Party policies and rules are carried out.
The top official of a Party committee or organisation, usually the secretary. The article treats this figure as the main bearer of responsibility for implementing democratic centralism.

t: The historical significance and lessons of leading the troops to Jinggangshan and the Tongdao change of course
zh: 引兵井冈与通道转兵的历史意义及启示
source: Journal of the Jinggangshan Executive Leadership Academy of China, 2025 no. 6
paras: Writing in a Party-school journal in 2025, Zhang Youliang takes up two turning points in the history of the Communist Party of China: Mao Zedong's decision in 1927 to lead the Autumn Harvest Uprising troops to Jinggangshan, and the change of the Central Red Army's route at Tongdao in December 1934. Zhang argues that the two events are comparable, since each combined historical necessity with contingency, and that both opened the way to revolutionary victory. The article draws lessons from them for present-day officials.

The article compares the two events under three headings borrowed from the traditional triad of favourable timing, terrain and human harmony: deep historical causes, geographical and popular advantages, and Mao's personal role. It then moves to lessons. It is organised as a parallel narrative, from the failed attacks on cities and the Wenjiashi and Sanwan decisions to the Xiang River defeat and the emergency meeting at Tongdao, followed by a set of contemporary implications.

On causes, Zhang holds that the Party's dependence on Comintern instructions and the successive 'Left' errors of Qu Qiubai, Li Lisan and Wang Ming produced the failures that forced both changes of course. On terrain and people, Zhang cites Jinggangshan's remoteness and economic base, local armed forces under Yuan Wencai, Tongdao's strategic position and the weak Guizhou forces, and the loss of confidence in Bo Gu and Otto Braun among Red Army commanders. On Mao, the article stresses his insistence on turning from cities to the countryside, his reorganisation of the army at Sanwan, and his persuasion of colleagues on the long march. Zhang presents the Tongdao decision as the start of Mao's emergence as the core of the leadership.

Zhang draws five lessons: seeking truth from facts; adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times; the Two Establishes and the importance of a leadership core; the Party's self-reform; and the ability to recognise, adapt to and initiate change amid a rapidly shifting international environment. The author links these to Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Party-history account that ties the Jinggangshan and Tongdao decisions to current Party doctrine on leadership and self-reform.
quoteEn: The main reason for this major change lies in the Party's insistence on proceeding from reality and adopting strategies and tactics that practice had proved effective.
quoteZh: 这一重大变化的主要原因，就在于我们党坚持从实际出发，采取被实践证明行之有效的战略策略。

glossary.explanation: A formula from the 20th Party Congress period that affirms Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Central Committee and the whole Party, and the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought. Official texts present it as a conclusion drawn from the Party's history and recent practice.
The official term for China's path of modernization, promoted since the 20th Party Congress (2022) as distinct from Western models and rooted in Chinese conditions.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for applying Marxism to Chinese realities and to the demands of the contemporary era, a process the Party treats as its central theoretical task.

An official term for the Party's efforts to correct its own errors and enforce discipline, presented by Xi Jinping as the second answer to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's long-term national goal, associated with the Chinese Dream and used to frame its policy aims for the middle of the twenty-first century.
The Party's official label for ultra-radical lines in the late 1920s and early 1930s, such as putschism and adventurism, which later Party history judges to have caused serious losses.

t: Why Soviet-area cadres developed a good work style, and what it means for today
zh: 苏区干部好作风成因及时代启示
source: Journal of the Jinggangshan Cadre Academy of China, 2025 no. 6
paras: Xiao Xiaohua asks why cadres in the Central Soviet Area (1931–34) acquired the work style summed up in a Xingguo folk song, and what that experience offers Party building today. The article holds that the style, which it defines as wholehearted service to the people, truth-seeking and pragmatism, hard struggle, honesty in office and striving for first-class work, followed from the Party's nature and purpose and was then shaped by its environment, leadership example, institutions and cultural inheritance.

The article, published in the Journal of the Jinggangshan Cadre Academy of China in 2025, works through five sets of causes. These are the Party's class character, ideals and mission; the political atmosphere inside the Party; the example set by leaders such as Mao Zedong, Zhu De and Zhou Enlai; systems of education, supervision and discipline; and inherited resources. These include the Jinggangshan period, traditional Chinese culture, and Hakka and Luling local culture. A final section draws lessons for the present.

Xiao's central argument is that style expresses a party's nature and purpose. The Soviet constitutional documents defined the regime as a democratic dictatorship of workers and peasants, and revolutionary conviction gave cadres their resolve. Xiao then shows how organisational life, criticism and self-criticism, and model-praising newspaper columns kept the Party's political atmosphere healthy. Leaders led by example in studying theory, conducting investigations, doing voluntary labour and saving grain and oil. Education programmes, inspection bodies, audit and anti-corruption regulations and inspection tours added institutional constraints. Xiao also argues that traditional values such as seeking truth from facts and putting the people first were transformed into the new style.

Xiao draws four lessons for the new era, linking them to the Eight-point Regulation and Xi Jinping's statements. They are to arm cadres theoretically with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; to keep close ties with the people and oppose formalism and bureaucracy; to have leading cadres set an example as a "lead goose"; and to build a mechanism of education, restraint, supervision and punishment, with zero tolerance for violations. Xiao adds that culture, including the Soviet Area spirit, should be drawn on to purify the Party's political ecology. Read the original if you study the history of Party work style and discipline in the Central Soviet Area, or how Party scholars link revolutionary-era experience to current campaigns.
quoteEn: The formation of a work style is a systematic project, related both to each Party member's and cadre's thinking and habits and to the external environment and institutional constraints.
quoteZh: 作风的形成是个系统工程，既与每个党员干部的思想、习惯有关，也与外部的环境和制度约束有关。

glossary.explanation: The main Communist-held base area in southern Jiangxi and western Fujian in the early 1930s. It was the seat of the Chinese Soviet Republic, proclaimed in 1931.
Rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012 to curb extravagance, formalism and bureaucracy among officials. They form the base of the Party's work-style campaigns since then.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official guiding ideology of the Chinese Communist Party, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–18.
Official labels for work habits that stress show and procedure over real results, and for officials who are detached from the public. They are targets of Party work-style campaigns.
A Party practice of openly pointing out one's own and others' faults to correct them. Party documents treat it as a basic internal discipline.

t: Leading economic and social development through the Party's self-reform
zh: 以党的自我革命引领经济社会发展
paras: Zhu Lingjun takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) that the Party's self-reform and economic and social development are closely linked and mutually reinforcing. The commentary argues that self-reform is the essential means by which the Party leads what it calls the great social revolution, and that it must be strengthened as the 15th Five-Year Plan period begins.

The article has three parts. The first explains why self-reform matters for development, drawing on Marxist views of the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, on the record since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and on the harsher conditions Zhu expects in the 15th Five-Year Plan period. The second identifies four problem areas among Party members and officials and their causes. The third sets out measures, anchored in the Plenum's decision to write full and rigorous self-governance of the Party into the guiding thinking for that period.

Zhu's central claim is that more effective Party governance gives development firmer guarantees. The article credits the eight-point regulation, the campaign against the "four malpractices" and anti-corruption work with creating a healthier political climate and fairer market conditions. The four problems it names are: distorted views of political achievement (favouring showy results, local interests, the short term and announcing over implementing); gaps in officials' competence; a weak work style, including formalism and passivity; and inadequate integrity. On the last, Zhu cites 789,000 cases filed by discipline inspection and supervision bodies in the first three quarters of 2025. Zhu attributes these problems to a changing environment, weak Party spirit in some officials, and gaps in how power is regulated and cadres are motivated.

Zhu calls for five things: upholding the Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; using Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to unify thinking; strengthening Party organisation, especially at the grassroots and in new economic sectors, together with a correct view of political achievement; making the eight-point regulation a lasting practice; and pressing on with anti-corruption work as an "offensive, protracted and all-out" struggle. Read the original if you want an official Party School account, published in Qiushi, of how self-reform is linked to the 15th Five-Year Plan period and which cadre problems it prioritises.
quoteEn: The more effective the governance of the Party, the stronger the guarantee for economic and social development.
quoteZh: 管党治党越有效，经济社会发展的保障就越有力。

glossary.explanation: A formula in Xi Jinping-era Party discourse for the Party's continual efforts to correct its own faults, discipline its members and combat corruption. It is presented as the means by which the Party keeps its capacity to lead.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party-building and discipline agenda promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering ideology, organisation, work style, discipline and anti-corruption.
A formulation from the 6th Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) affirming Xi Jinping's core position in the Party and the guiding role of his thought.
A Party requirement to uphold Xi Jinping's core position in the Central Committee and the Party as a whole, and to uphold the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership.

Rules on officials' work style adopted by the Politburo in December 2012. They restrict extravagance, formalism and bureaucratism, and have been a basis of later campaigns against the "four malpractices" (formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism, extravagance).
China's national development plan for 2026–2030. Its guiding principles were discussed at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025).

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: An analysis of cultural construction in the anti-Japanese base areas behind enemy lines during the War of Resistance
zh: 抗日战争时期敌后根据地文化建设论析
paras: Wu Ying asks what made cultural work possible in the anti-Japanese base areas behind Japanese lines (1937–1945), what that work consisted of, and what it contributed. The article defines this cultural construction as purposeful, organised activity of creation, dissemination and popularisation in the Party-led base areas. It was centred on serving the war, mobilising the masses and shaping revolutionary culture. Wu argues that it was a special cultural practice that became a weapon of the revolution and offers lessons for cultural development today.

The article is built in four steps. It first sets out five foundations of cultural construction in the base areas. It then examines the content and the characteristics of that culture. Next it assesses its place in the revolution and the war. It closes with lessons for building a culturally strong country in the new era. Examples include Tian Jian's street poems, the Yellow River Cantata, the opera The White-Haired Girl, the new yangge movement, woodcuts, winter schools and the Lu Xun Academy of Arts.

Wu identifies five foundations: Party leadership and correct policy, a mass base created by rent reduction and mass organisations, organisational backing from propaganda departments and arts troupes, flexible forms close to reality, and a spirit shaped by national crisis. Citing Mao Zedong's On New Democracy, Wu says the cultural content was national, scientific and mass-oriented, and served the war and the people. It also reshaped culture and treated the "cultural war" as a second front beside the military one. Wu lists six features: political and combative character, mass orientation, practicality, flexible organisation, combining inheritance with innovation, and the union of intellectuals with workers, peasants and soldiers.

Wu concludes that this work consolidated political mobilisation, ideological education and popular support, helped break down enemy morale, and trained cultural cadres. It also laid foundations for socialist culture after 1949. For the present, Wu draws five lessons: uphold Party leadership under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, keep a people-centred orientation, align culture with the times and Chinese modernization, balance tradition and innovation, and build an integrated system for talent. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of wartime cultural policy and its use as a model for current cultural strategy.
quoteEn: The foundations of cultural construction in the anti-Japanese base areas behind enemy lines form an organic whole.
quoteZh: 敌后抗日根据地文化建设的基础是一个有机整体

glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's January 1940 essay setting out the political, economic and cultural programme for the stage between the old order and socialism. It defines the "national, scientific and mass" culture that Wu treats as the guiding line.
The official term for China's path of modernisation, used in Party documents since the early 2020s. Wu invokes it when linking wartime cultural work to present tasks.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology since 2017, written into the Party and state constitutions. Wu names it as the guide for cultural construction today.
An official goal of raising China's cultural strength and influence, stressed in recent Party documents. Wu presents the wartime experience as a source for this aim.

keywords: intellectuals and workers, peasants and soldiers

t: Mao Zedong and people's petitions (xinfang) in New China
zh: 毛泽东与新中国人民信访
paras: This article from Mao Thought Studies (2025, no. 5) asks how Mao Zedong received and handled letters and visits from ordinary people (renmin xinfang) after 1949, and what that practice means today. He Quansheng argues that petitioning was an important channel linking the Party to the masses and a concrete expression of the mass line. In He's account, it gave Mao practical material for decisions and became a regular part of how he governed.

The article draws on three published sources: Selected Letters of Mao Zedong, volumes six to eight of the Collected Works of Mao Zedong, and the Chronology of Mao Zedong (1949–1976). From these He sorts the letters and visits into six types. They report on economic and social conditions; discuss culture, education and theory; ask Mao to arrange jobs, schooling, Party entry or promotion; ask for relief or assistance; recall old acquaintance; and seek rehabilitation of revolutionary martyrs and people wrongly accused. A second part sets out Mao's statements on petitioning, and a third draws lessons for the present.

He's central claim is that Mao treated letters as a way to learn conditions and correct bureaucratism. The author cites Mao's instruction that people's letters must be taken seriously and handled properly. They cite his 1952 call to start checking bureaucratism and commandism "from handling people's letters", and his 1959 "Inner-Party Correspondence" on consulting grassroots cadres. He also highlights Mao's refusal to use his position for relatives and friends. Mao declined to recommend his wife's brother, schoolmates and maternal relatives for posts, schools or Party membership, and he turned down special relief, offering help from his own royalties instead. Other cases show letters changing policy or outcomes, including a 1951 revision on the leading class and several rehabilitations in the 1970s. He also notes Mao's objection to Party organisations mobilising masses to write letters of tribute.

He concludes that Mao's theory and practice of petitioning is part of his thinking on socialist construction. It offers guidance for upholding the mass line, practising a people-centred development philosophy, and strengthening investigation and research, as well as mass work and learning within the Party. The article ties these points to Xi Jinping's remarks and the 20th Party Congress report (2022). Read the original if you want a source-based catalogue of Mao's correspondence with citizens and relatives, or an example of how Chinese Party-history scholarship links Mao-era practice to current petition (xinfang) work.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong held that upholding the mass line and warmly receiving people's letters and visits is the fundamental path and scientific working method by which our Party stays close to the masses and overcomes bureaucratism.
quoteZh: 毛泽东认为，坚持群众路线，热情接待人民群众来信来访，是我们党密切联系人民群众、克服官僚主义的根本路径和科学工作方法。

glossary.explanation: A Party working method associated with Mao Zedong: gathering the views of the masses, turning them into policy, and testing the policy among them. The Party describes it as its lifeline.
In Party usage, an official style marked by detachment from the people, indifference to their problems and reliance on orders. The Party has repeatedly campaigned against it.

glossary.zh: 以人民为中心的发展思想
glossary.pinyin: yǐ rénmín wéi zhōngxīn de fāzhǎn sīxiǎng
glossary.literal: development thinking with the people at its centre
glossary.explanation: A formula from the Xi Jinping era stating that development should be for the people, rely on them and have its results shared by them.
The official reversal of a wrongful verdict or political judgement against a person, often after death, restoring their reputation.

t: Clarifying three misconceptions about the Yan'an Rectification Movement
zh: 澄清对延安整风的三个误识
paras: Marking the 80th anniversary of the end of the Yan'an Rectification Movement (1942–45), Zhu Jun takes up what the article calls misreadings and deliberate distortions of this episode in Chinese Communist Party history, circulating in Chinese and foreign scholarship. The author argues that these accounts amount to historical nihilism, whose real aim is to deny Mao Zedong's contribution to the revolution and, through that, the historical legitimacy of Communist Party rule. Drawing on historical sources, Zhu seeks to refute three claims.

The article is organised around three charges: that the movement was a power struggle against Wang Ming, that it was a campaign of persecution through criticism and self-criticism, and that it was a vehicle for a Mao personality cult and Mao's personal dictatorship. Zhu treats the rectification's origins, its method of starting with senior cadres, the 1945 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party, and the Seventh Party Congress. Sources include Mao's speeches, accounts of Ren Bishi, Zhou Enlai, Zhang Wentian and Bo Gu, and Stuart Schram's biography of Mao.

On the first charge, Zhu argues that the Comintern and the Party already backed Mao as leader by 1938, so there was nothing to fight over. In this reading, the target was subjectivism, whether leftist or rightist, and the policy was to attack the errors while keeping the people. On the second, the author presents criticism and self-criticism as a principled, comradely method, citing the self-examinations of senior leaders. On the third, Zhu distinguishes rational respect for a leader from blind worship. Mao's prestige is explained by wartime conditions, the Comintern's dissolution in 1943 and the rivalry with the Nationalists. Citing Mao's refusal of a birthday celebration, the author says the movement guarded against a personality cult. Mao Zedong Thought, Zhu adds, came out of collective drafting under democratic centralism, which restrains personal arbitrariness.

Zhu concludes that Mao's leadership position rested on political, ideological, mass and practical foundations and was chosen by history and the people. The author holds that a proletarian party needs a firm leadership core whose authority is upheld. Closing in the present, Zhu calls for a deeper grasp of the Two Establishes and a stronger consciousness of the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party historiography currently rebuts Western and Chinese critical accounts of the Yan'an period and ties them to present-day political principles.
quoteEn: Cherishing the leader is in essence safeguarding the interests of the Party, the class and the people, not deifying an individual.
quoteZh: 爱护领袖本质上是维护党、阶级和人民的利益，而非神化个人。

glossary.explanation: A Party-wide ideological education and discipline campaign (1942–45) conducted in the Yan'an base area. It targeted dogmatism, sectarianism and stereotyped Party writing.
In official Chinese usage, a label for interpretations seen as denying or belittling the Party's revolutionary history and leaders.
The Leninist organisational principle combining internal discussion and election with strict obedience to decisions once taken.
A formula from the 20th Party Congress period that affirms Xi Jinping's position as the Party's core and the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought.
The Party requirement to uphold Xi Jinping's core position in the Central Committee and the whole Party, and to uphold the Central Committee's authority and centralised leadership.

t: The theoretical implications and institutional advantages of the Communist Party of China's consolidation of cultural subjectivity in the new era
zh: 新时代中国共产党巩固文化主体性的理论蕴涵与制度优势
paras: Wang Zhen asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) consolidates what Xi Jinping calls the 'cultural subjectivity' (wenhua zhutixing) of Chinese civilisation, and why it is able to do so. The article argues that this consolidation rests on a historical-materialist foundation, on the Party's integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, and on its accumulated theory of cultural construction. It adds that the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics give the project a distinctive advantage. The author writes under the guidance of Xi Jinping's cultural thought.

The article has three main parts. The first sets out the theoretical foundations, drawing on Marx and Engels's views of practice, objectification, the masses and social intercourse, and on the 'second integration' with traditional thought (Laozi, Xunzi, the idea of great unification, the continuity of civilisation). The second traces the Party's thinking on culture through the New Democratic revolution, the socialist period and reform and opening up, up to the new era, and summarises three theoretical features of current practice. The third turns to institutions and sorts them into fundamental, basic and important systems.

In Wang's account, culture is the objectified product of labour and practice, so a nation's cultural subjectivity is created by the people and has to be defended by them. Wang adds that it is not closed: cultural intersubjectivity and mutual learning among civilisations are needed. Drawing on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, the author claims the Party has consistently sought a leading role for Marxism within cultural diversity. The new-era theory is characterised as seeking truth from facts, keeping pace with the times and putting the people first. On institutions, Wang argues that the socialist system and Party leadership secure cultural security and direction, that the people's congress system and consultative bodies bring in popular input, and that public ownership keeps the products of labour in the people's hands. Wang also lists the system for cultivating core socialist values, heritage-protection inspection and integrated education, science and talent development.

Wang concludes that the Party's consolidation of cultural subjectivity has a theoretical basis and institutional guarantees that other approaches lack. Wang presents these as turning into momentum for cultural innovation and for building a strong cultural nation. The article treats this as showing the world significance of a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-theory scholar links historical materialism, traditional Chinese philosophy and the institutional order to the Party's current cultural policy.
quoteEn: The socialist system and the leadership of the Communist Party of China are the fundamental institutional advantage for consolidating and developing cultural subjectivity.
quoteZh: 社会主义制度和中国共产党领导是巩固和发展文化主体性的根本制度优势。

glossary.explanation: A concept stressed by Xi Jinping in 2023. It refers to a civilisation's capacity to develop itself, respond to challenges and open new paths while keeping its own cultural identity.
The part of Xi Jinping Thought dealing with culture, formally set out in October 2023. It covers cultural confidence, the Party's cultural leadership and the 'second integration'.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilisation
glossary.explanation: An official phrase, used since 2021, for the civilisation said to result from Chinese modernization, in contrast to Western modernisation.

t: On the cultural subjectivity of the Communist Party of China
zh: 论中国共产党的文化主体性
paras: Cultural subjectivity is described in the article as a signature concept of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Liu Hongchang asks what it means for the Communist Party of China (CPC) to hold cultural subjectivity, and how that subjectivity has taken shape over a century of Party practice. The answer is that the Party is the political agent driving the development of Chinese culture, and that its cultural subjectivity consists of four linked attributes: cultural consciousness, cultural autonomy, cultural creativity and cultural transcendence.

Liu first distinguishes three nested levels of cultural subject: the Chinese nation, the Chinese people and the Party. The Party's cultural subjectivity is defined as the cultural awareness and capacity inherent in the Party itself. The article then works through the four attributes in turn, drawing on Party documents, the writings of Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and episodes from the revolutionary period, the early People's Republic and the reform era up to the present.

On consciousness, Liu argues that the Party has taken up a cultural mission, deepened its understanding of culture's place (from a supporting tool to a livelihood and economic force), and grasped cultural laws in time and space. On autonomy, the Party is said to have chosen its cultural path, planned its cultural strategy (from Deng's call for socialist spiritual civilization to the 'cultural power' goal for 2035) and defended cultural security, in contrast to a Kuomintang portrayed as dependent on imperialism. On creativity, Liu points to the people-centred orientation of culture, the creation of revolutionary and socialist culture, and methods such as the Two Integrations and 'drawing the essence, discarding the dross'. On transcendence, Liu draws on Marx's remarks on Greek art and the relative independence of culture. The Party is said to have pushed culture ahead of its economic base through the 'Double Hundred' policy and literacy campaigns, and through constitutional and legal provisions on cultural leadership.

Liu concludes that the Party's cultural subjectivity rests on its leadership of cultural work and on a people-centred stance, and that it underpins the Party's ability to create new culture in the new era. The article treats this subjectivity as tied to the fate of Chinese culture and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theory account of how Chinese scholars frame the Party's cultural role, with its historical periodisation and the official policy documents it cites.
quoteEn: The Communist Party's cultural subjectivity refers to the cultural-subject attributes the Party holds as the political agent driving the development of Chinese culture; it is the cultural awareness and capacity inherent in the Party itself.
quoteZh: 中国共产党的文化主体性，意指中国共产党作为推动中华文化发展的政党主体所具有的文化主体属性，是中国共产党自身内在具有的文化主体意识与能力。

glossary.explanation: A concept associated with Xi Jinping's thought on culture. It refers to a collective subject's awareness of, and capacity for, cultural creation and development.
The formula of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with China's fine traditional culture. It has been prominent in Party theory since 2021–2023.
A national strategy first set out at the 18th Party Congress (2012). It aims to build a country with strong cultural influence, with 2035 as the target date.

glossary.pinyin: bǎi huā qífàng, bǎi jiā zhēngmíng
glossary.literal: Let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend
glossary.explanation: A cultural and scientific policy line announced by Mao Zedong in the 1950s. It is presented in Party writing as encouraging diversity under the leadership of the mainstream.

t: Fully understanding and grasping the Party's leading position and role in whole-process people's democracy
zh: 充分认识和把握党在全过程人民民主中的领导地位和作用
paras: This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 5 March 2026, asks why and how the Communist Party's leadership must be upheld within whole-process people's democracy. Zhu Xiqun argues that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of this form of democracy. In Zhu's account it runs through every link, field and stage of democratic practice and must be kept up and strengthened throughout. The piece opens with Xi Jinping and with the recommendations of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), which call for the organic unity of Party leadership, the people as masters of the country, and law-based governance.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical, historical and practical logic behind Party leadership. The second describes how that leadership is embodied in institutions. The third proposes ways of strengthening it further. Examples include the drafting of the 15th Five-Year Plan, the way the Party group of the National People's Congress Standing Committee handles legislation, and the State Council's reports to the Standing Committee on state-owned assets.

On theory, Zhu argues that Marxist classics hold that popular rule cannot arise spontaneously and needs organisation by a vanguard proletarian party. Zhu holds that the Party has no special interests of its own, so it can integrate the demands of different social strata. In this reading whole-process people's democracy avoids what the author calls the capital-driven games and political theatre of Western democracy. On history, Zhu traces the Party's pursuit of people's democracy from the 'three-thirds' system in the anti-Japanese base areas to the people's congress system, and concludes that without Party leadership there is no people's democracy. On institutions, Zhu says Party leadership works through the people's congresses, multi-party cooperation and political consultation, and the Party-group system, which Zhu calls a 'converter' and 'connector'. It also runs through the five links of democratic election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight.

Zhu calls for deeper understanding of the unity of Party leadership, the people as masters and law-based governance. Zhu also asks for better institutions through which the Party coordinates all organs, clearer rules for Party groups, and oversight led by intra-Party supervision. Zhu further proposes using intra-Party democracy to drive people's democracy and developing the 'Fengqiao experience'. Zhu presents this as a political guarantee for the 15th Five-Year Plan and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise, authoritative statement of how Party writers justify Party leadership within the Chinese democratic model and describe its institutional mechanisms.
quoteEn: Party leadership and people's democracy are inherently unified, and only the Communist Party of China can lead and safeguard the people's position as masters of the country.
quoteZh: 党的领导与人民民主内在统一，只有中国共产党才能领导和保障人民当家作主。

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2019 to describe China's democratic model. Official texts present it as covering the full chain from election to oversight, under Party leadership.

glossary.en: the people as masters of the country
glossary.literal: the people being masters of the house
glossary.explanation: An official formulation for the essence of socialist democracy, meaning that the people hold state power. It is usually paired with Party leadership and law-based governance.
A Party body set up inside state organs, people's organisations and other non-Party institutions to ensure that Party policy is carried out there.

A model of grassroots conflict resolution that began in Fengqiao town, Zhejiang, in the 1960s. It relies on mobilising local residents to settle disputes locally, and has been promoted in recent years as a model of social governance.

glossary.pinyin: Dǎng de èrshí jiè sì zhōngquánhuì
glossary.en: the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee
glossary.explanation: The plenary meeting of the Central Committee in October 2025. It adopted recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030).

t: Red documentary imagery in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region: communication and lessons
zh: 陕甘宁边区红色纪实影像传播及启示
paras: How could the Party turn its land policy into voluntary action among a largely illiterate peasantry in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region? Lin and Liang argue that documentary imagery, chiefly photography and newsreel film, closed the gap that written propaganda could not. In their account it delivered land policy precisely and also served political mobilisation.

The short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2026, examines four dimensions of this practice in the Anti-Japanese War period: the organised and professional character of the communicators, the segmentation of audiences, the narrative and symbolic content of the images, and the layered, scene-based channels of distribution.

On the first, the authors point to the Yan'an Film Group, under the Eighth Route Army's General Political Department, whose filming was tied to cadre research and a layered review process. On audiences, they say poor peasants were shown side-by-side 'accounting' comparisons, middle peasants were reassured that their property was protected, soldiers were told to defend land-reform gains, and landlords received model and critical examples. Images followed a 'suffering–struggle–new life' sequence, as in Gu Yuan's woodcut of burning old land deeds. Travelling exhibitions embedded in mass meetings, and photo pages in Liberation Daily with first-hand testimony, extended reach.

Lin and Liang conclude that the experience offers a historical reference for spreading mainstream values today, citing audience-centredness, content innovation, systematic operation and channel building. Effective political communication, they contend, must follow media rules while adhering to the mass line. Read the original if you want a brief overview of visual propaganda in the Yan'an-era land policy.
quoteEn: Effective political communication must follow the laws of the media and, above all, take root in reality; only by going deep among the masses, avoiding empty talk and adhering to the mass line can it produce lasting and far-reaching communicative power and appeal.
quoteZh: 有效的政治传播既要遵循媒介规律，更要扎根现实土壤，“深入群众，不尚空谈”，坚持走群众路线，方能产生持久深远的传播力和号召力。

glossary.explanation: The Communist-led base area in northwest China, with Yan'an as its capital, that existed from the 1930s to 1950 and served as the Party's wartime centre.
A Party working method, associated with Mao Zedong, of drawing ideas from the masses and bringing policy back to them, stressing close ties with ordinary people.
A film unit founded in 1938 under the Eighth Route Army's General Political Department, which produced newsreels and documentaries in the Border Region.

t: Full and rigorous Party self-governance as a safeguard for economic and social development
zh: 全面从严治党保障经济社会发展
paras: Writing in the Economic Daily in February 2026, Chen Jinlong asks how Party discipline relates to economic and social development during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030). The article takes as its starting point Xi Jinping's speech at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Chen argues that upholding the Party's overall leadership is the first principle of development in this period, and that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is what allows that leadership to run through every aspect and stage of development.

The commentary has three parts. The first sets out why the Party's overall leadership must be upheld, drawing on the 'six upholds' principles of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee. The second explains why full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is required by that leadership. The third proposes four areas where standards should be raised and measures made more practical.

Chen contends that leadership steers direction and policy, coordinates relations such as central and local or efficiency and fairness, concentrates resources on major undertakings, and mobilises the people's initiative. In Chen's account, strict Party governance serves three purposes: it improves the Party's capacity to lead development amid old problems, such as uneven development, and new ones, such as strong supply and weak demand. It also keeps the Party the core of leadership for socialism with Chinese characteristics and consolidates its long-term governing position. Chen presents the Party's self-reform as the means by which the Party leads a wider social revolution.

For the Plan period, Chen calls for four things. The first is to uphold the authority of the Party Central Committee and its centralised, unified leadership. The second is to confine power in an institutional cage by refining rules, enforcing them without exception and having 'top leaders' set an example. The third is to pursue the anti-corruption struggle with clarity, including through joint handling of unhealthy work styles and corruption and attention to new and hidden forms of graft. The fourth is to strengthen officials' political responsibility and sense of historic mission, with a performance outlook centred on benefiting the people. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links Party discipline to the goals of the 15th Five-Year Plan.
quoteEn: Only through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party can the Party always maintain its advanced nature and purity, and lead the great social revolution through its own self-reform.
quoteZh: 全面从严治党，才能始终保持党的先进性和纯洁性，以党的自我革命引领伟大社会革命。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan introduced after the 18th Party Congress (2012) for strengthening Party discipline, organisation and conduct, including the anti-corruption campaign.
A term in Xi Jinping-era Party theory for the Party's continual effort to correct its own faults and keep its discipline, presented as its second 'answer' to the problem of historical cycles.

glossary.zh: 把权力关进制度的笼子
glossary.pinyin: bǎ quánlì guān jìn zhìdù de lóngzi
glossary.en: confine power in an institutional cage
glossary.literal: lock power in the cage of institutions
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Xi Jinping for restraining the exercise of public power through rules and supervision.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: Resolutely getting things implemented is the ideal and conviction of Communists in action
zh: 狠抓落实是共产党人行动着的理想信念
paras: Writing in the People's Daily on 25 February 2026, Wang Yubo, Yunnan's governor, argues that implementing the Party Central Committee's major decisions is a basic requirement of upholding the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership. The article's thesis, echoed in its title, is that resolute implementation is the ideal and conviction of Communists put into action. It is framed by the start of the 15th Five-Year Plan period and by Xi Jinping's January 2026 call for cadres to build practical working ability.

The piece has three parts. The first presents Xi Jinping's remarks on implementation as the "philosophy of action" of Communists in the new era, tracing them from his work in Zhengding, Fujian, Zhejiang and Shanghai to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second reports how Yunnan has put Xi's instructions into practice. The third sets out how the 15th Five-Year Plan period should be approached.

In the first part, Wang says Xi's remarks answer why, for whom and how to implement. They cover the significance, political requirements, scientific methods, responsible actors and value orientation of implementation, with the "top leader" as key and the people's livelihood as the destination. For Yunnan, Wang cites four lines of work: the Dianchi and Erhai lake clean-up, with Dianchi water quality held at Grade IV; green electricity and "West-to-East power transmission", with over 2 trillion kWh sent; rural living-environment gains; and a cross-jurisdictional trusteeship model for Mohan town on the China–Laos Railway. For the coming period, Wang proposes five unities: Party spirit and the people's character; ideas and practice; the local and the whole; the whole course and its stages; and inheritance and innovation. A sixth pairs struggle with scientific method.

Wang concludes that cadres should show "real, bold, skilful and sustained" effort in implementation, avoid formalism and bureaucratism, and treat the people's welfare as their greatest achievement. The article ends by urging high-quality development that withstands the test of history, practice and the people. Read the original if you want to see how a provincial leader presents Xi Jinping's theory of implementation, and how it is tied to concrete Yunnan examples, in an official Party-building text.
quoteEn: Resolutely getting things implemented is the ideal and conviction of Communists in action.
quoteZh: 狠抓落实是共产党人行动着的理想信念。

glossary.explanation: An official goal, stressed since 2017, of shifting from rapid growth to development that emphasises quality, innovation and efficiency.

t: Revolutionary music and women's work in the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Border Region
zh: 革命音乐与晋察冀边区妇女工作
paras: This short piece, published in Guangming Daily in February 2026, asks how the Communist Party used revolutionary music in its work among women in the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Border Region during the War of Resistance against Japan. Wang argues that the Party used music skilfully and that it played an important role in mobilising women for the war and in changing their thinking. The article opens by calling the region the first anti-Japanese democratic base area behind enemy lines and notes that the Party had stressed song as a propaganda tool since 1923.

The article is built in three sections, each supported by Party directives, local newspapers, memoirs and reportage from the period. The first covers how songs, plays and ballads raised women's wartime awareness, including winter-school songs. The second covers the formation of women's self-defence corps. The third covers how music spread progressive ideas and encouraged women's emancipation, with the example of the local activist Liu Yaomei.

Wang's central claim is that vivid melodies, plain lyrics and concrete storytelling resonated with women. Familiar songs such as "On the Songhua River", reportage plays about model figures like Rong Guanqiu, and "seeing off" songs urging husbands to enlist are said to have stirred their patriotic feeling. Citing the article's sources, Wang says some 270,000 women in the region were organised into armed groups by June 1940, and that songs such as "Sisters Go to the Battlefield" helped to recruit them. The third section argues that songs like the "Song of Women's Liberation" encouraged women to cut their hair and unbind their feet. Wang also describes women moving from onlookers to participants and then to creators, as village drama troupes and women's troupes staged stories drawn from their own lives.

Wang concludes that the Party's policy of women's liberation, carried through music, strengthened women's sense of themselves as agents. This in turn led them to take part in making revolutionary music, which raised their political awareness and helped them contribute to the war effort. The article presents the Border Region as a case of effective cultural mobilisation under Party leadership. Read the original if you want a brief, source-rich overview of how songs and village theatre were used in wartime mobilisation of women, as presented in current Party-history writing.
quoteEn: Through musical works, women in the Border Region came to understand deeply the Chinese Communist Party's stance on resisting Japan, which better awakened their wartime consciousness.
quoteZh: 边区妇女在音乐作品中深刻认识到中国共产党的抗战主张，更好地激发了其抗战意识的觉醒。

glossary.explanation: A Communist-led anti-Japanese base area established behind Japanese lines in North China from 1937, covering parts of Shanxi, Chahar and Hebei. Mao Zedong called it a model base area.

t: Village governance and the remaking of the village cadre corps in the Shandong anti-Japanese base areas
zh: 山东抗日根据地的村政建设与干部群体重塑
paras: How did the Communist Party turn village governance in Shandong, where early in the War of Resistance grassroots power was largely held by local bullies and gentry, into a working base for wartime mobilisation? Ma Mingchong argues that institution-building came first in remaking the village cadre corps. In the author's account, a series of measures produced a body of village cadres drawn mainly from poor and middle peasants, who took on mobilising the masses, supporting the war and governing the countryside.

The article, a historical study based largely on Shandong and Hebei-Shandong-Henan border-region archives and document collections, covers the period from the early war years to 1944. It is organised around four lines of work: adjusting the administrative-village system and reforming village power; integrating mass organisations and building Party branches in natural villages; constructing a top-down management system for village cadres; and perfecting cadre education and training.

Ma first describes the shift from a centre-village system to administrative villages (set by a 1941 decision at 100 households or 400 people) and a wave of democratic village elections. By the end of 1942, the article cites 8,170 of 10,128 villages in the base areas as already reformed, with old cadres replaced and village affairs committees formed. Peasant associations and other mass organisations supplied many village heads and Party recruits, and Party branches were set up in villages. Ma argues that this extended Party leadership to village level, broke the gentry's monopoly of local control and increased the Party's capacity to draw resources from the countryside. A defined hierarchy followed, with elected cadres confirmed by district offices, fixed terms, democratic centralism, and a monthly grain allowance for village heads so that poor peasants could serve. Ma notes limits, including corruption and slow reform in the Hebei-Shandong-Henan area in 1942, and the district-level leadership problems that later measures tried to fix. Training came through rotating courses for village heads, collective sessions, daily study hours, rectification and advanced people's schools.

Ma concludes that the Party's remaking of the village cadre corps was unprecedented. In the article's view, it produced politically conscious grassroots cadres, tied revolutionary power to the people through democratic means and strengthened the revolutionary forces. Read the original if you want a documented account of the institutional mechanics of Communist rural governance in wartime Shandong, as told in current Party-history scholarship.
quoteEn: The Party's remaking of the village cadre corps in the Shandong anti-Japanese base areas was unprecedented.
quoteZh: 我们党对山东抗日根据地村干部群体的重塑是史无前例的。

glossary.explanation: A system that grouped natural villages into larger administrative units, set in Shandong in 1941 at 100 or more households or 400 or more people. It replaced the earlier centre-village arrangement.
Democratic elections of village heads and committees, promoted from 1940–41 in the base areas to replace old village officials.

t: The explanatory power, tensions and limits of emotion research in the study of Party history
zh: 情感研究在党史研究中的解释力、张力与边界
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2026, Wang Xiaosi asks what the international "emotional turn" in historiography can and cannot contribute to the study of the history of the Communist Party of China. Wang argues that the history of emotions offers a fresh analytical angle on why the Party won popular support and gathered forces for change, but that its rising prominence also exposes methodological tensions and limits. The key task, in Wang's view, is to balance borrowed theory with empirical work, and emotional interpretation with structural analysis.

The piece is organised in three parts. The first sets out how emotion research extends the explanatory reach of Party history. The second identifies four internal tensions. The third discusses the limits of interpretation and proposes three directions for methodological integration. Examples include the 1937 uniform change of the Red Army, which Wang has studied, "speaking bitterness" in land reform, mobilisation during the Korean War, and the Yan'an "cave dialogue".

Wang contends that emotion history enriches a tradition focused on lines, policies and organisation by recovering the anxieties and meaning-making of Party members and ordinary people. Mid-level concepts such as "emotional governance" and "emotional mobilisation" link macro structure to micro experience, and Wang presents the Party's mass-line practices as a distinctive tradition on which an autonomous Party history narrative can be built. The four tensions are: narrated versus lived emotion in diaries and memoirs; the poor fit of Western concepts such as Hochschild's "emotional labour"; the assumption of universal emotions against specific historical contexts, as in "turning grief into strength"; and the need to balance emotion against other explanatory factors. Wang insists that emotion catalyses and reinforces but is never the fundamental driving force, and warns against "emotional determinism".

Wang concludes that researchers should cross-check varied sources, combine discourse, content and narrative analysis, and use materialist dialectics to bound emotion's role. The three proposed directions are reading texts and historical context against each other, linking micro case studies with broader comparison, and joining humanistic interpretation with social-science methods. Wang says emotion history can become indispensable once researchers know what it can and cannot do, and that it should serve the building of a Chinese philosophy and social science system. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese historian justifies and limits the use of emotion history within official Party history scholarship.
quoteEn: Although emotion can strengthen identification, catalyse action and influence decisions, it can ultimately hardly become, on its own, the fundamental driving force of historical development.
quoteZh: 情感虽然能够强化认同、催化行动、影响决策，但终究难以单独成为历史发展的根本动力。

glossary.explanation: A mid-level analytical concept used by some Chinese historians for how the Party shapes, manages and channels emotions in governing and mobilising society.
The use of emotional appeals to rally people behind a political campaign, as in land reform or the Korean War.
A land-reform-era practice in which peasants publicly recounted past suffering to build class consciousness and legitimise class struggle.
A 1945 Yan'an conversation between Mao Zedong and Huang Yanpei about escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall, often cited in Party discourse on popular support.

t: The operating mechanism of red financial regulations in the Central Soviet Area
zh: 中央苏区红色金融法规的运行机制
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 3 February 2026
paras: This newspaper commentary examines how the financial regulations of the Central Soviet Area worked in practice. Tang argues that the government of the Chinese Soviet Republic built an integrated financial mechanism covering audit, supervision, cash management, credit and discipline. In Tang's account, it supported economic growth, countered Kuomintang sabotage of the base areas' finances, and left lessons for later financial systems.

The article is organised around four components: a banking and audit structure, currency and cash controls, credit policy for workers and peasants, and supervision with punishment. It draws on regulations issued mostly between 1931 and 1934, including the State Bank's provisional statutes, the cash-export registration rules and the 1934 audit regulations.

Tang stresses three points. First, a three-tier State Bank and an audit commission independent of the banking system, later made parallel to the People's Commissars, created external oversight. Second, the State Bank held a monopoly on note issue, foreign currencies were exchanged and unified, and the registration of cash exports checked silver outflow. Third, the credit rules abolished usury, voided old usurious contracts and promoted credit cooperatives. Tang adds that prosecutors and the graded penalties of the 1933 directive on corruption, plus reform through labour, backed this system.

Tang concludes that these regulations combined unified finance, sound banking, independent audit and clean conduct, and were a legal experiment under wartime conditions. The article presents them as a useful reference for developing finance with Chinese characteristics, and holds that the rule of law is the foundation of financial work and Party leadership its soul. Read the original if you want a concise Party-history overview of early Communist financial institutions and how current commentary draws lessons from them.
quoteEn: It shows us that the rule of law is the foundation of financial work, and Party leadership is its soul.
quoteZh: 它昭示我们，法治是金融事业的根基，党的领导是金融工作的灵魂。

glossary.explanation: The main Communist-held revolutionary base in southern Jiangxi and western Fujian in the early 1930s. It was the seat of the Chinese Soviet Republic's central government.
The Communist-led government proclaimed in 1931 in the Jiangxi base area. It existed until the Red Army's Long March began in 1934.
Mass-membership lending bodies in the Soviet areas that offered low-interest loans to members as an alternative to usurers.

t: Opening new fields in the development of the theory sub-discipline of CPC history and Party building studies
zh: 拓展中共党史党建学理论学科发展的新领域
paras: Chu Zhuwu takes up a practical problem in Chinese academic organisation. The theory sub-discipline of CPC history and Party building studies is one of four second-level sub-disciplines of that field, and it has only just been created. The author argues that it is now a "soft spot" and a "weak link" because it has low recognition and slow progress in building the discipline. Chu calls on scholars to open up new fields for it, as part of building an autonomous system of knowledge for the field.

The commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in January 2026, has three parts. The first clarifies what the sub-discipline is. The second assesses its present state, covering research output, how universities have set it up and the main problems. The third sets out four routes for building it. Chu draws on the Academic Degrees Committee of the State Council's definition of the discipline, on the views of Song Xueqin, Wei Weicen and Wang Binglin, and on the published doctoral admissions catalogues of several institutions.

Chu's central point is that the theory sub-discipline has two tasks. It must study the theory and methods of the first-level discipline as a whole. These include Marxism's general principles and the specific theory that arises when they are combined with CPC history and Party building. It must also develop its own second-level discipline system, with its own ontology, epistemology and methodology. Otherwise there would be no reason to set it up separately. Chu names three problems. Its importance is underrated, and some units doubt that it should exist. It has not developed enough internally, because some universities lack staff and cannot teach its required courses. It also has low standing, because students prefer sub-disciplines with better job prospects. Chu reports few studies of the subject and no systematic ones. Institutions have organised it in very different ways.

Chu proposes four measures. Higher-level bodies should improve top-level design and planning. Research should be strengthened on topics such as Marxist party theory, the history of the discipline, documentation studies, overseas studies of CPC history and the relationship between the CPC and the world. A textbook introducing the field should be written and placed in the Marxist theory research and construction project's textbook programme. Talent training should be supported through publicity and favourable doctoral and master's admission quotas. Read the original if you follow how Chinese universities are organising CPC history and Party building studies as a discipline and want one professor's account of its weak points.
quoteEn: The theory sub-discipline of CPC history and Party building studies has, after all, only just been established, and it currently faces problems such as low disciplinary recognition and slow progress in building the discipline in practice.
quoteZh: 中共党史党建学理论学科毕竟刚刚设立，目前正面临着学科认可度低、学科建设实践进展缓慢等问题

glossary.en: CPC history and Party building studies
glossary.literal: Studies of CPC history and Party building
glossary.explanation: A first-level academic discipline in China that brings together the history of the Communist Party of China and the study of Party building. It has four second-level sub-disciplines, including the theory sub-discipline discussed in the article.

A term in Chinese official discourse for a body of concepts, theories and disciplines developed in China rather than drawn from Western academia. It is often paired with the discipline system, academic system and discourse system.

glossary.en: Marxist theory research and construction project
glossary.explanation: A national project, launched in the early 2000s, to compile standard textbooks and research on Marxist theory for use in Chinese universities. Its textbooks are regarded as authoritative.

glossary.en: Academic Degrees Committee of the State Council
glossary.explanation: The Chinese state body that sets the catalogue of disciplines and the rules for awarding degrees. Its decisions fix which disciplines and sub-disciplines universities may establish.

keywords: CPC history and Party building studies

t: Advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party with higher standards and more practical measures
zh: 以更高标准更实举措推进全面从严治党
paras: This commentary, published in Economic Daily, interprets Xi Jinping's speech at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection.
