Li Xianzong and Tang Di argue that political mobilisation was the decisive mechanism: through ideological education, organisational networks and the alignment of material interests, the Party converted scattered national energies into a unified popular force. They organise their account around three dimensions: motives, practice and lessons for today.

The article, published in Red Culture Journal in 2025, has three parts. The first sets out the historical motives: the national crisis created by Japanese aggression and the appeasement or inaction of Western powers and the League of Nations, popular anti-Japanese enthusiasm, and the mobilising experience the Party had accumulated in the Great Revolution and the land revolution. The second part surveys wartime practice under three headings: propaganda and education, organisation-building, and interest-linking policies. The third part draws lessons for the present.

On practice, the authors describe mass cultural propaganda (slogans, drama, the Yellow River Cantata, newspapers such as Liberation Daily), literacy campaigns, and international publicity through Xinhua, overseas newspapers and visiting foreign journalists. They cite the growth of Party membership from about 40,000 to over 1.2 million, mass associations for peasants, women and youth, and an army that grew from some 50,000 to 1.2 million, with 2.6 million militia. They also treat rent and interest reduction, the production campaign (with 2 million additional mu of arable land in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region in 1942–44, per the article) and the 'three-thirds' system of government as ways of tying popular interests to the war effort.

The authors draw three lessons. First, adhering to the Two Integrations, meaning the integration of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its traditional culture, is the 'golden key'; they link it to Xi Jinping Thought and to the concept of new quality productive forces. Second, the mass line is described as the Party's institutional strength in organising the people. Third, strategies must be adapted to circumstances, as in the shift from 'opposing Chiang and resisting Japan' to 'pressing Chiang to resist Japan' and in 'life as mobilisation' methods such as kang-side meetings. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of wartime mobilisation, with local examples and figures, framed to draw lessons for contemporary Party work.
quoteEn: This practical wisdom of 'life as mobilisation' allowed political work to permeate the capillaries of the masses' daily lives.
quoteZh: 这种“生活即动员”的实践智慧,使政治工作渗透到群众生活的毛细血管。

glossary.explanation: A formula associated with Xi Jinping: integrating the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.

The Party's method of leadership, summarised as 'from the masses, to the masses': gathering popular views, systematising them into policy and returning them to the people. Mao Zedong developed it in the 1930s–40s.
A wartime power-sharing formula in the base areas under which Communists, left-progressives and middle-of-the-road figures each held about one third of government seats.
A concept promoted since 2023 that stresses innovation-led, technology-intensive productive forces as the basis of high-quality development.
The wartime land policy that capped landlords' rents and loan interest rather than confiscating land, in order to sustain the united front against Japan.
The campaign launched from 1939, notably in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, in which troops, officials and peasants grew food and made goods to achieve self-sufficiency under blockade.

t: The CPC's perception of and policy towards Britain during the Second KMT–CPC Cooperation, 1937–1940, and its effects
zh: 第二次国共合作背景下中共对英国的认识、政策及其影响（1937—1940）
source: Studies on CPC History (Zhonggong dangshi yanjiu), 2025 no. 3
paras: Wen Cheng asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) viewed British policy between the outbreak of full-scale war in 1937 and the Tripartite Pact of September 1940, and how that view fed back into its handling of relations with the Kuomintang (KMT). The article opens with Mao Zedong's 1940 remark tracing a 'vertical line' from Neville Chamberlain to the KMT's anti-communist 'friction expert' He Shaonan. Wen argues that the CPC's attitude to Britain rested on domestic and international conditions, above all the state of KMT–CPC relations, and in turn shaped its handling of those relations.

The author notes that existing scholarship concentrates on British aid after the Pacific War began in 1941, leaving the earlier period unstudied. The article follows three phases. It begins with the united-front line adopted after the Comintern's Seventh Congress (1935) and the search for a pro-British, anti-Japanese alignment. It then covers the deterioration of Anglo-Soviet relations from the Munich Conference to the Soviet–German pact of August 1939, and ends with the CPC's push for the KMT to reject Britain and ally with the Soviet Union, up to 1940. Sources are mainly CPC leaders' speeches and internal documents.

Wen's central claim is that the CPC read international alignments through the lens of KMT–CPC cooperation. Early on it treated Britain as a vital but wavering ally. After Munich and the 1939 Soviet–German pact, it feared a 'Far Eastern Munich' in which Britain, Japan and Chiang Kai-shek would form an anti-Soviet, anti-communist bloc. The CPC therefore revived anti-British criticism, partly in line with Comintern instructions, to keep the KMT from joining the Anglo-French camp. Wen holds that the main aim was to preserve the anti-Japanese united front. He adds that the fear of a full Anglo-Japanese settlement proved exaggerated, though it was understandable for the weaker party, and that the criticism also harmed relations with Britain and with the KMT.

In 1940 the Anglo-Japanese rift widened, Soviet standing rose and France fell. The CPC then replaced anti-British rhetoric with a drive to ally with the Soviet Union and to reconcile with the KMT. Wen reports that Mao and Zhang Wentian later acknowledged that opposing KMT entry into the Anglo-American bloc had been too sharp as policy. The author concludes that 1937–1940 CPC policy must be understood within a five-sided relationship involving Britain, the Soviet Union, Japan, the KMT and the CPC, and that this period of adjustment was made independently of Moscow. Read the original if you study CPC wartime diplomacy, the united front or Sino-British relations and want a source-based account of how foreign policy judgements shaped Party strategy.
quoteEn: The reason the CPC worked to influence the KMT government's diplomatic choices, urging it to keep its distance from Britain and strengthen ties with the Soviet Union, was to sustain KMT–CPC cooperation.
quoteZh: 中共之所以努力影响国民党政府的外交抉择，促使其与英国保持距离、强化对苏联系，是为了维系国共合作。

glossary.explanation: The wartime alliance between the CPC and the KMT, and wider social forces, against Japanese aggression. It took shape after 1936–37 and underpins what is called the Second KMT–CPC Cooperation.
A term used by the CPC and the Comintern for a feared deal in which Britain would appease Japan at China's expense, as Czechoslovakia had been sacrificed at Munich in 1938.
The Moscow-led international organisation of communist parties (1919–1943). Its Seventh Congress (1935) endorsed broad anti-fascist popular fronts, which shaped CPC strategy.
The CPC's term for armed and political clashes between KMT and communist forces during the war. Anti-communist surges are called 'anti-communist high tides'.

t: The Central Eight-point Regulation: the "institutional blade" of the Party's self-reform
zh: 中央八项规定：党的自我革命的“制度利刃”
paras: This newspaper commentary asks how the Central Eight-point Regulation, adopted in December 2012, has served the Party's self-reform. Li argues that the regulation used a "small incision" to bring about large change: it reshaped the Party's political ecology through institutional innovation and became a model for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

The article starts from the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's claim that self-reform is the second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall. It then takes in turn the regulation's response to the "four tests" and "four dangers", its problem-oriented method, the pairing of rules with technology, the link between Party and state governance, its theoretical significance, and its international meaning.

Li's central claim is that rules and technology work together. The author cites a closed-loop mechanism of public complaints, discipline inspection and departmental correction, and the writing of the regulation into Party discipline rules. Li also cites digital platforms: monitoring of over a million official vehicles and budget disclosure covering 98% of county governments. The author adds that Party regulations were aligned with state law and that a "Party supervision + state supervision + mass supervision" network was built. Li argues that this moved style-building from campaign-style governance to routine practice, and joined institutional governance with ideological Party-building.

Li concludes that the regulation shows strong vitality and has enriched Marxist Party-building theory. The author reports that its "institution + technology" anti-corruption model has been recognised by the United Nations and promoted in 56 countries. Li calls for continued rule-based Party governance and self-reform. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the eight-point regulation within self-reform theory.
quoteEn: The Central Eight-point Regulation used a "small incision" to bring about a "big change", reshaping the Party's internal political ecology through institutional innovation and providing a methodological model for full and rigorous Party self-governance.
quoteZh: 中央八项规定以“小切口”推动“大变局”，通过制度创新重塑了党内政治生态，为全面从严治党提供了方法论典范

glossary.explanation: A set of rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012 on officials' working style, covering research visits, meetings, official receptions and writing style. It is a signature measure of the Party's campaign against formalism and extravagance.
Official term for the Party's efforts to purify, improve and renew itself, presented since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as its answer to the risk of degeneration.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: Official slogan for the post-2012 drive to tighten Party discipline and conduct, including anti-corruption work.

t: Grasping the contemporary meaning of Party spirit and forging a firm political character
zh: 把握党性时代内涵 锻造坚定政治品格
paras: This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks what Party spirit (dangxing) means for Chinese Communists and how it is to be cultivated. Lu Han argues that Xi Jinping's statements on the subject answer what Party spirit is, why it must be strengthened and how, and that they enrich Marxist Party-building theory and give Party members a basic guide to self-cultivation.

The article is organised as a sequence of seven requirements, each presented as a way of tempering Party spirit. It draws on Xi's remarks since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and quotes him on ideals, struggle and Party-spirit education.

Lu's core claim is that Party spirit starts from political standpoint: the Party has no interests of its own and represents only the proletariat and the people, so members must put the public interest first. From this follow firm belief in communist ideals and in the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, a clear stance on politics and discipline, and the unity of Party spirit and the people's character. Lu holds that the two are inseparable, since there is no Party spirit apart from the people's character. Work style is treated as a question of Party spirit, with Party spirit as the root, style as its expression and discipline as its safeguard.

Lu also calls for the courage and skill to struggle, handling contradictions dialectically in the course of Chinese modernization. Finally, Lu proposes cultivating the Communist's "learning of the heart" through Party-spirit education, organisational life, daily self-discipline and the Party's self-reform. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-spirit cultivation is framed in official discourse under Xi.
quoteEn: Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline are one whole: Party spirit is the root, Party style is its expression, and Party discipline is its safeguard.
quoteZh: 党性、党风、党纪是一体的，党性是根本、党风是表现、党纪是保障。

glossary.explanation: The qualities, principles and standpoint expected of a Communist Party organisation and its members, reflecting the Party's nature. It is a long-standing term in Party-building discourse.
The official term for China's path of modernization, promoted in Party documents especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
An official formula for the Party's efforts to correct its own problems and maintain discipline, emphasised under Xi Jinping.
A term borrowed from Chinese philosophy, which Xi applies to Party-spirit education as inner self-cultivation.

t: The construction logic and pathways of an autonomous knowledge system for the discipline of CPC history and Party building
zh: 中共党史党建学自主知识体系的建构逻辑及路径探析
paras: Li Jia asks how the newly established first-level discipline of CPC history and Party building (zhonggong dangshi dangjianxue) can build its own autonomous knowledge system. The article starts from Xi Jinping's statement that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics ultimately means building China's autonomous knowledge system, and from the 2024 regulations on Party history study and education. Li argues that the discipline must achieve academic independence and standardisation while upholding Party leadership and ideological security, and that an autonomous knowledge system is the way to overcome the discipline's subordinate status and marginal discourse.

The article is organised in three parts: theoretical foundations, internal structure, and practical pathways. Li names three foundations: Marxist party theory, historical materialism, and the Party-building theory of Sinicised Marxism, from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The structure is then divided into a disciplinary system, an academic system and a discourse system, and the final part gives measures for each.

Li's central claim is that the three systems form one organic whole: the disciplinary system is the 'skeleton', the academic system the 'flesh and blood', and the discourse system the 'medium of expression'. The disciplinary system has four modules: Party history, Party leadership and Party building, the discipline's own metatheory, and the practical work of Party affairs. The academic system rests on theory-building, summing up experience, problem orientation and methodological innovation, including data science and social network analysis. The discourse system needs a chain of concepts, propositions, theories and categories, and must manage the tension between political and academic language. Li also sets out three relationships to handle: political and academic, theoretical and practical, national and global.

For practice, Li proposes four second-level disciplines, interdisciplinary tracks such as 'Party history plus digital humanities', a course and textbook matrix, a staged training model from undergraduate to doctoral level, dual supervisors drawn from Party and government, and reform of academic evaluation. For discourse, Li calls for three communicating teams, integrated traditional and new media, accurate translation of core terms such as full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and international communication through the Belt and Road Initiative and comparative study of party systems. Li concludes that the discipline, as the foundation, the core and the bridge respectively, should develop in a systematic way to support Party building. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese scholars plan the curriculum, methods and international communication of this new discipline.
quoteEn: The disciplinary system is the foundation, providing institutional support for academic research and discourse building; the academic system is the core, determining the discipline's theoretical depth and the scientific character of its discourse; the discourse system is the link, both the form in which academic ideas are expressed and an important vehicle of the discipline's influence.
quoteZh: 学科体系是基础，为学术研究和话语构建提供制度性支撑；学术体系是核心，决定学科的理论深度和话语体系的科学性；话语体系是纽带，既是学术思想的表达形式，也是学科影响力的重要载体。

glossary.explanation: A concept stressed by Xi Jinping in 2022–2023 for China's own system of concepts, theories and methods in philosophy and the social sciences, as distinct from reliance on Western frameworks. It is usually described as comprising disciplinary, academic and discourse systems.

glossary.literal: Study of CPC history and Party building
glossary.explanation: A first-level academic discipline that the article says was created in 2022. It brings together the study of Party history, Party leadership and Party building, which were previously spread across other disciplines.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the Xi Jinping era for strengthening Party discipline, supervision and internal governance. The article treats it as a core concept for the discipline's discourse.
China's international infrastructure and cooperation initiative launched in 2013. The article cites it as a platform for exchanges between parties.

t: The tactical evolution and strategic use of the CPC's tunnel warfare in Central Hebei during the War of Resistance against Japan
zh: 抗战时期中共冀中地道战的战术演进与策略运用
paras: Wang Guangyao asks how tunnel warfare (didao zhan) arose on the Central Hebei plain during the War of Resistance against Japan, and under what conditions it became an effective tactic. The article argues that it was an innovation in plain guerrilla warfare guided by Mao Zedong's theories of guerrilla and protracted war, and that its development depended on shifts in the balance of forces as well as on Party leadership.

The article follows the tunnels in four stages. It begins with the Japanese 'cage policy' of blockhouses and strongpoints, then turns to the early, limited use of tunnels, using the 1942 Beitan massacre in Dingxian as its main case. It next examines how tunnel warfare was perfected after 1942, and closes with a short assessment. Wang draws on Japanese commanders' memoirs and reports, Chinese Communist directives, local statistics and combat accounts.

Wang contends that the cage policy, with the 'May 1st sweep' of 1942 as its peak, destroyed the older mobile guerrilla methods and forced the use of tunnels. Early tunnels were scattered, unconnected and used only for hiding, and some cadres dismissed them as 'flightism'. Digging was also costly, and at Beitan the lack of armed protection, anti-gas measures and neighbouring tunnels led to the deaths of over 800 civilians. The article then credits several factors for the change: Japanese overextension and strategic contraction from 1943; Liu Shaoqi's October 1942 instruction to turn tunnels from purely defensive works into a form that could also attack; and mass mobilisation, with government-organised digging from 1944. The result, in Wang's account, was the village-tunnel tactic, which combined fortified villages, rooftop and ground passages, concealed entrances and mines. Wang presents the December 1944 defence of Shijing village as a model case.

Wang concludes that tunnel warfare moved ordinary ground guerrilla fighting underground and created a three-dimensional battlefield behind enemy lines. The article attributes its success to unified leadership, organisation, mass mobilisation, independence and innovation. In this reading it spread to southern and eastern Hebei and remained in use during the Liberation War. Read the original if you study the CPC's military history, Party documents on guerrilla strategy, or Japanese counter-insurgency in North China, and want detailed local evidence.
quoteEn: The formation and development of tunnel warfare depended on unified leadership, effective organisation, broad mobilisation and vigorous promotion, and was the result of the CPC's persistence in the struggle against Japan, the mass line, independence and self-reliance, and innovation.
quoteZh: 地道战的形成和发展依赖于统一的领导、有效的组织、广泛的动员、有力的推广，是中共坚持对日斗争、坚持群众路线、坚持独立自主、坚持创新创造的结果。

glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's 1938 theory that China would defeat Japan through a long war in three stages: defence, stalemate and counter-offensive. The article treats tunnel warfare as a product of the stalemate stage.
The Chinese label for the Japanese strategy of blockhouses, strongpoints, roads and trenches built to divide and blockade Communist-held areas in North China.
The large Japanese offensive against the Central Hebei base area from 1 May to 20 June 1942, which the article describes as severely damaging the base.

t: Cognitive shaping and the construction of revolutionary discourse in Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region exhibition narratives: a textual analysis based on the CPC's main newspapers
zh: 陕甘宁边区展览叙事中的认知塑造与革命话语建构——基于中共主要报刊的文本分析
paras: How did the Communist Party use exhibitions in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region during the Yan'an period to shape popular perceptions and build a revolutionary discourse? Wang and Chen argue that exhibitions, which were given the political purpose of 'serving the War of Resistance and production', worked as open 'narrative texts'. In their account, these texts shaped the Party's image and ordinary people's understanding of economic and cultural construction, scientific knowledge and wartime mobilisation. They also strengthened the revolutionary narrative of national unity in resisting Japan.

The study draws mainly on reports in Liberation Daily and the New China Daily, which the authors say carried 168 reports, editorials and speeches on exhibitions between 1936 and 1946. The first part describes six forms of presentation: ceremonial layout and spatial arrangement, slogans and inscriptions, physical exhibits, graphic displays, newspaper coverage, and interpersonal communication such as guides, symposia and comments from foreign visitors. The second part sets out six themes: the 'most advanced party', support for resistance and construction, 'labour creates everything', improved production technology, the border region's hygiene campaign, and women's liberation. The third part assesses the significance of these exhibitions.

The authors' central move is to treat the exhibition as a text that visitors 'read' from the moment they enter. Portraits of leaders and labour heroes, calligraphy by Mao Zedong and Zhu De, prizes and statistical charts conveyed Party policy in ways the authors consider hard for other propaganda forms to match. Repeated pairings of words such as production, technology, resistance and national defence are said to have linked everyday labour to the war effort. The authors also present praise from Kuomintang officers and foreign guests as an 'other-shaping' effect that strengthened the Party's image beyond the border region.

Wang and Chen conclude that the exhibitions broadened people's horizons, spread scientific and hygienic knowledge, challenged feudal ideas and won support from outside the base area. They credit the exhibitions with increasing political identification with the Party and achieving what the authors call political integration. They describe the exhibitions as an important part of the Party's revolutionary cultural work in the New Democratic period and as an example of 'telling the story of the War of Resistance well'. Read the original if you study Yan'an-era propaganda, the history of Party exhibition work, or the use of press sources to analyse revolutionary discourse.
quoteEn: The exhibition is itself an open 'narrative text': the forms of its exhibits, spatial layout and ceremonial performance are its core elements, and they can effectively shape popular perceptions and construct revolutionary discourse.
quoteZh: 展览会本身是一个开放的“叙事文本”，其展品样态、空间布局、仪式展演等丰富形式构成了“叙事文本”的核心要素，能够有效塑造民众认知、建构革命话语。

glossary.explanation: The Communist-led base area in northwest China (parts of Shaanxi, Gansu and Ningxia) with its capital at Yan'an. It was the Party's central base from the late 1930s to the 1940s.
The years from about 1935 to 1948 when the CPC leadership was based in Yan'an. Party historiography treats it as the formative period of Mao Zedong Thought and wartime mobilisation.
Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution (roughly 1919–1949) led by the proletariat and aimed at a broad anti-imperialist, anti-feudal coalition before a socialist transition.

t: The multidimensional construction of the Chinese Communist Party's "Zhonghua minzu" discourse during the War of Resistance against Japan
zh: 抗战时期中国共产党“中华民族”话语的多维构建
source: Journal of Minzu University of China, 2025 no. 3
paras: Zhao Chao asks what the term "Zhonghua minzu" (the Chinese nation) meant in the Chinese Communist Party's wartime discourse, and why the Party used it as it did. Responding to Xi Jinping's calls in 2023 and 2024 to build an autonomous discourse system for the community of the Chinese nation, the article sets aside scholarly disputes over the concept and looks at the Party's own usage. Its thesis is that, between 1931 and 1945, the term carried three distinct meanings, those of state, citizenry and nation. It also served as a tool for mobilising people and competing for discursive authority, not only as a description of an objective entity.

The article first criticises existing scholarship for treating discourse as a neutral expression of the Party's views and for reading the term mainly through domestic ethnic relations. It then sets out a semantic framework built from example sentences and their common co-occurring words. Three sections follow, one for each meaning, each tied to the Party's aims and to the historical setting. Sources include Party documents, manifestos, editorials in Jiefang Ribao and Xinhua Ribao, and statements by Mao Zedong, Zhang Wentian, Wang Ming, Zhou Enlai and others.

In the "state" sense, equivalent to China, Zhao argues that after the Japanese invasion and the North China Incident of 1935 the Party moved from internationalist class language to patriotic language. Phrases such as "national liberation" and "the Party and the Zhonghua minzu" presented the Party as a defender of state interests and as "the advanced sons and daughters" of the nation. This also served in a contest with Chiang Kai-shek's China's Destiny over who represented the nation. In the "citizenry" sense, equivalent to the Chinese people, the term countered Japanese enslaving education and defeatism, using the "450 million" formula and appeals to history and national spirit. In the "nation" sense, the Party answered Japanese separatist propaganda aimed at Hui and Mongol groups by presenting a pluralistic and unified nation. It also criticised Chiang's "clan theory" as Han chauvinism.

Zhao concludes that the concept's content is multidimensional and must be read in context. The Party's wartime construction of it was also constrained by its own understanding, by domestic and international politics, and by rival political actors. Zhao suggests that later research should separate meanings by context and purpose, and that this helps in understanding the value of building an autonomous discourse system for the community of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you study Chinese Communist Party history, wartime nationalism or Party ethnic-policy discourse and want a close, example-based analysis of how the term was used.
quoteEn: Therefore, this article advocates understanding the Chinese Communist Party's "Zhonghua minzu" discourse of the War of Resistance through three layers of meaning: state, citizenry and nation.
quoteZh: 因此，本文主张从国家、国民与民族三重语义理解抗战时期中国共产党的“中华民族”话语

glossary.explanation: A modern term for the Chinese nation as a whole, coined in the late Qing period. It can denote the state, all its people, or the multi-ethnic national community, depending on context.

A concept in current Party ethnic policy, stressing that all ethnic groups in China form one national community. Xi Jinping has called for building its own historical, discourse and theoretical systems.

t: How the Communist Party promoted the formation of a sense of community of the Chinese nation during the War of Resistance against Japan
zh: 抗战时期中国共产党推动中华民族共同体意识的形成
source: Journal of the Party School of the CPC Central Committee (National Academy of Governance), 2025 no. 4
paras: Zheng Dahua asks how the Communist Party helped bring about, during the War of Resistance against Japan (1931–45), what Xi Jinping now calls the sense of community of the Chinese nation: a community of shared weal and woe, honour and disgrace, life and death, and destiny. The article argues that the Chinese nation moved from an "in-itself" to a "self-aware" community in modern times, and that this transition was completed in the war years, especially during the period of all-nation resistance. Zheng says earlier scholarship has covered Party ethnic theory and policy but has paid little attention to this particular consciousness.

The article has three parts. The first traces the Party's theoretical understanding of the "Chinese nation", from its first use of the term in 1922 through Yang Song's 1938 lectures to Mao Zedong's 1939 text The Chinese Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party. The second looks at propaganda and education stressing that all ethnic groups faced the same threat of national extinction. The third examines the mobilisation of "comprehensive all-nation resistance" and the anti-Japanese national united front. Zheng draws on Party resolutions, telegrams, editorials and leaders' writings.

Zheng contends that the Party first had to settle who belongs to the Chinese nation. Yang Song, following Stalin's definition, treated it as a modern nation. Mao instead described a long-established nation made up of the Han and dozens of minority peoples, which Zheng calls a major contribution and the groundwork for shared consciousness. The Party then stressed a common fate under Japanese aggression and used the figure of the Yellow Emperor as common ancestor. It also held that the nation's supreme interest outranks that of any individual, class or ethnic group. A 1940 outline on the Hui people ranked the contradiction with Japan above ethnic and class contradictions. Finally, Zheng argues, building the united front, countering Han chauvinism and mobilising minorities produced genuine all-nation resistance, which made the "live together, die together" consciousness possible.

Zheng concludes that the consciousness formed under Party leadership laid the foundation for the turning point in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation that victory in the war represented. The article presents the Party as the driving force behind both the concept of the nation and the sense of common destiny. Read the original if you want a documented account, drawn from Party sources, of how wartime Party texts defined the Chinese nation and its relation to minority peoples, and of how this is now linked to the contemporary concept of the community of the Chinese nation.
quoteEn: It was on the basis of the ideas that arose in the struggle against Japanese imperialist aggression — \"if we die, we die together; if we live, we live together\" — that the peoples of all ethnic groups formed the awareness that the Chinese nation, composed of all its ethnic groups, is a community of shared life and death and shared destiny.
quoteZh: 各族人民正是在反对日本帝国主义侵略的斗争中所产生的“要死大家死，要活大家活”“生则同生，死则同死；存则同存，亡则同亡”之理念的基础上，形成了由各民族组成的中华民族是生死与共、命运与共的共同体意识。

glossary.en: sense of community of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping in recent years, stressing that all ethnic groups in China form one national community. It is expressed in the four "shared" formulas (shared weal and woe, honour and disgrace, life and death, destiny).

The Party's term for resistance to Japan by all classes, parties and ethnic groups, endorsed at the Luochuan Conference of 1937. It was contrasted with resistance conducted by the Nationalist government alone.
The broad alliance of Communists, Nationalists and other groups against Japan, built on the second Nationalist–Communist cooperation after 1937.

t: The important role of the Communist Party of China in the world anti-fascist united front
zh: 中国共产党在世界反法西斯统一战线中的重要作用
paras: Hao Ping, a professor of history, argues that the Communist Party of China was the earliest initiator and core leader of the world anti-fascist united front. The commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, holds that this history links China's War of Resistance to the global anti-fascist war. It also offers lessons for building a community with a shared future for mankind.

The article moves in three steps. It first covers the 1930s, when the Party put forward the idea of an international front. It then turns to wartime practice: the anti-Japanese base areas, foreign visitors to Yan'an, and the influence of the united-front idea on national liberation movements abroad. It ends by drawing links to present-day international cooperation.

Hao points to the August 1st Declaration of 1935 and the Wayaobao meeting as the first calls for uniting all states opposed to Japanese imperialism. The author stresses that the Party combined alliance-building with strategic autonomy. As evidence, Hao cites Mao Zedong's refusal of Comintern requests to send troops to support the Soviet Union, on the grounds that guerrilla war behind enemy lines tied down more Japanese forces. In Hao's account, the base areas pinned down large Japanese forces, and Egyptian, Indonesian and Vietnamese movements drew on the Party's united-front ideas.

Hao concludes that this history shows the unity of idea and practice, and presents the community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative as its present-day continuation. The author claims that China's cooperation gives developing countries a voice in global governance and that the Party will keep playing a core leadership role. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese academic commentary links the Party's anti-fascist war record to current foreign policy themes.
quoteEn: The Communist Party of China not only won international support for China's War of Resistance against Japan, but also reshaped the way the world's anti-fascist forces were connected.
quoteZh: 中国共产党不仅为中国抗日战争争取了国际支持，更重塑了世界反法西斯力量的联结方式。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–13. It calls for joint responses to global challenges and is presented as an alternative to bloc politics.
An infrastructure and trade initiative launched by Xi Jinping in 2013. It links China with partner countries in Eurasia, Africa and beyond.
A Party strategy of building alliances with other forces against a main enemy. In the Anti-Japanese War it meant cooperation across parties and classes, and also with foreign powers.
A 1935 appeal issued in the name of the Chinese Communist Party and Soviet government. It urged an end to civil war and a united resistance to Japanese aggression.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: On comprehensively strengthening the Party's work style
zh: 论全面加强党的作风建设
paras: Zhu Lingjun and Shan Boya ask why the Chinese Communist Party should attend to its work style (zuofeng), what the work covers and how it should be done. Their answer is that work style is the visible form of the Party's nature and purpose, bears on its survival, and has been strengthened since the 18th Party Congress (2012) through a set of tested practices. The article is a research article aimed at providing scholarly support for Party building in the new era.

The authors define work style as the way Party members, cadres and organisations show Party spirit in their conduct, covering ideology, work, leadership, daily life, study and writing, and meetings. They set out its theoretical sources in classical Chinese ideas of "wind" (feng) as custom and moral influence, in remarks by Marx, Engels and Lenin on bureaucracy and bad habits, and in statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. They then explain its significance, review historical experience, and describe innovations since 2012.

The core argument is that, in the authors' account, work style shapes the Party's image, popular support and survival, and decides whether its undertakings succeed. They cite a 2024 National Bureau of Statistics survey in which 94.9 per cent of respondents approved of implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, against 75 per cent satisfaction with Party conduct and anti-corruption work before 2012. Historical experience is grouped under seeking truth from facts, linking theory with practice, staying close to the masses, integrity, hard struggle, appointing people on merit under democratic centralism, and discipline. For the period since 2012 the authors identify six practices: choosing the right entry point (the eight-point regulations), leadership setting the example, immediate correction, reform and institutional innovation, strict standards, and concentrated education campaigns.

The authors conclude that work style needs constant attention because it rebounds if relaxed, and that economic achievement cannot substitute for it. They present the practices as experience for advancing Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and link them to the Party's self-reform and to escaping the "historical cycle" of rise and fall. They call on cadres to examine themselves first during the current study and education campaign on the eight-point regulations. Read the original if you want a systematic official-academic account of how Party School scholars justify and periodise Party work-style building from Mao to Xi.
quoteEn: Historical experience shows that the achievements of economic development cannot replace a conscious commitment to work-style building; such building is always on the road, and this is the essential requirement of strengthening the Party's work style.
quoteZh: 历史经验表明，不能以经济发展的成就代替抓作风建设的自觉，作风建设永远在路上，这是加强党的作风建设的本质要求。

glossary.explanation: Rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012 to curb bureaucratic and extravagant practices and bring leaders closer to the public. They became the starting point of Xi Jinping's campaign on Party conduct.
Official concept that the Party can correct itself through its own efforts, presented as the answer to the problem of ruling parties degenerating over time.
Official term for China's development path, promoted since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: Central official goal of national revival, tied to the Chinese Dream.

t: Party integration: a new type of social integration and a comparison
zh: 政党整合：一种新的社会整合类型及比较
source: Journal of Huazhong Normal University, 2025 no. 4
paras: Market transition has left Chinese society differentiated, atomised and weakly connected. Wang Qing asks how the state can integrate such a society at the grassroots, given that existing research offers three models: government–society coordination, administrative integration and technological integration. The article argues that each has structural limits and proposes a fourth type, "party integration", in which the ruling party works on its own organisations, administrative bodies, economic organisations and mass self-governing bodies to rebuild grassroots order.

The article begins with a literature review. It runs from Durkheim's organic and mechanical solidarity, through Parsons's AGIL scheme, to Tönnies. It then follows the stages of Chinese grassroots state-building from imperial times to the present. Wang defines social integration as the state integrating society, rather than the Western focus on individuals joining society. The three existing types are then set out, and party integration is introduced and compared with them, in the author's Table 1. The analysis uses three dimensions: form of power, organisational structure and working mechanisms.

Wang identifies a typical weakness in each existing model. Government–society coordination risks state involution when state capacity is weak, and societal dependence on the state when it is strong. Administrative integration is blocked by departmental self-interest. Technological integration is instrumentalist and cannot make autonomous decisions. Party integration is described as a "re-integration" of the three. It combines internal integration (leading small groups, party groups, centralised management by portfolio, and the party's own organisation-building) with external integration of society. Drawing on Michael Mann, the author says the party's power is both concentrated, through political authority, and diffuse, through "doing work with people" and emotional governance. Party organisations are embedded in state and non-party bodies, including new economic and social organisations and new employment groups. Flexible informal mechanisms such as work teams and the "Fengqiao experience" add to this.

Wang concludes that party integration pursues both order and vitality, moving society from compliance towards identification. The author notes that diffuse power still depends on concentrated power as its backing. The balance between the two must therefore be managed, and formalism in some localities remains a problem for later study. Read the original if you want a political-science account, in the Chinese academic mainstream, of how the Communist Party's grassroots role is theorised as a model of social integration, and how it is set against other integration models.
quoteEn: Party integration is the process by which a party promotes social integration, and it is also an important way for the party to gain authority.
quoteZh: 政党整合是政党促进社会一体化的过程，也是政党获得权威的重要方式。

glossary.explanation: The author's proposed concept: the ruling party's integration of the state apparatus, its own organisations and society, offered as a fourth type of social integration.
A model in which the government relies on social organisations and communities to share in governance and public services.
A traditional Party method of persuasion through personal conversation and attention to individuals' needs, which the author treats as a form of diffuse cultural power.
A grassroots approach, named after a locality in Zhejiang, of resolving disputes at the local level through mediation rather than litigation.
Party bodies set up inside government, legislative and state-enterprise organs to play a decision-making role in major matters.

t: "Entering the cities" and "going to the countryside": the CPC's practice of currency unification around the founding of the People's Republic
zh: “进城”与“下乡”：新中国成立前后中共的货币统一实践
paras: How did the Communist Party of China (CPC) turn a patchwork of base-area currencies into a single national currency, and make it circulate in both city and countryside? Liu Mengyan argues that the unification ran in three stages: the "birth" of the renminbi, its "entry into the cities" and its "going to the countryside". In this account, currency unification was the key link in unifying financial and economic work and in consolidating the new state.

The article is a historical study of roughly 1937 to 1952, drawing on Party directives, telegrams, conference resolutions and regional reports. It begins with the plural currencies of the War of Resistance and the Liberation War, then follows the North China financial conferences of 1947 and 1948 to the founding of the People's Bank of China on 1 December 1948. The two later sections cover urban and rural circulation, with cases including Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Wuhan, Hunan and Hebei.

Liu's central argument concerns how the renminbi was established in each setting. In the cities it faced local base-area notes, the Nationalist government's gold yuan and silver-dollar notes, foreign currencies and a dominant silver dollar, with speculation rampant. The Party handled these in sequence: fixed exchange rates and later withdrawal of local notes, conversion and expulsion of the gold yuan, step-by-step controls on foreign currency, and a two-sided campaign against silver. That campaign combined administrative suppression, such as the raid on the Shanghai securities building, with commodity-indexed savings deposits. In the countryside the obstacles were a traditional preference for goods over money and a lack of trust in the notes. Liu describes campaigns to reject silver and support the renminbi, together with propaganda, tax payment in renminbi, agricultural loans, remittance networks, and state and private trade, which the author says were chosen over mainly administrative means.

Liu concludes that by the end of 1951 a unified renminbi market, excluding Tibet, Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, had been basically established. The author cites figures for 1952: peasants held 51.6 per cent of renminbi in circulation, and the commercialised share of agricultural output rose from 30 to 37 per cent between 1950 and 1953. Liu presents currency unification as the first link in unified financial control and as a support for later industrialisation. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how the early People's Republic displaced rival currencies and built trust in its money.
quoteEn: Currency unification was precisely the first link in this chain.
quoteZh: 货币统一恰是这个链条中的首要环节。

glossary.explanation: The national currency issued by the People's Bank of China from 1 December 1948, before the People's Republic was founded.
Deposits valued in units tied to the prices of a basket of goods, which protected savers from inflation.

t: Comprehensively improving cadres' capacity for modernization
zh: 全面提高干部现代化建设能力
paras: This short commentary in the Party journal Dangjian asks how Party cadres can acquire the abilities needed to carry out Chinese modernization. Hong Xianghua and Li Mengke argue that cadre capacity must be raised across the board, and that this is a systematic and long-term task requiring several kinds of training at once.

The article has two parts. The first sets out what the requirement means, drawing on Xi Jinping's call, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), for the "eight kinds of skills" and "seven abilities" and for political, leadership and work capacity suited to Chinese modernization. The second sets out practical routes to achieving it.

On content, the authors treat political capacity as first in rank and as the basis for leadership and innovation. Leadership capacity means setting direction, planning the whole picture and balancing paired relationships such as top-level design and practical exploration, or efficiency and fairness. Work capacity is to be tailored to posts, with stress on economic work, digital governance and emergency response. The four routes are ideological tempering, political training, practical experience and professional training. These involve study of Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, loyalty and discipline, grassroots and frontline postings under the "four down to the grassroots" system, and regular, tiered, technology-assisted training.

The authors conclude that these measures will give the building of a modern socialist country a strong contingent of cadres. Read the original if you want a concise statement of current official thinking on cadre education and capacity-building under Chinese modernization.
quoteEn: Political capacity comes first and plays a leading and pivotal role.
quoteZh: 政治能力是第一位的，发挥着引领性和关键性作用。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's model of national development, promoted since the early 2020s as distinct from Western modernization.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
A working system that sends officials to grassroots units to do research, handle petitions, promote policy and solve problems. It is associated with Xi Jinping's earlier work in Fujian.
A list of competences for cadres set out by Xi Jinping, such as learning, political leadership, reform and innovation, and risk prevention.

t: Experience and lessons from building the responsibility system for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
zh: 全面从严治党责任体系建设的经验与启示
paras: Liu Xianchun and Zhang Can ask what the Communist Party of China's history can teach about building a responsibility system for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. They take as their starting point Xi Jinping's instruction at the Political Bureau study session of 27 June 2024, which for the first time put this system on the agenda and called for responsibility to be in place at three levels: responsible actors, requirements, and assessment and accountability. The authors argue that the Party's century of practice holds experience that can strengthen awareness of responsibility and make the duties of governing the Party effective.

The article has three parts. The first identifies three core elements: the Party's position as the leading core, clear and tiered responsibilities, and the building and enforcement of rules. The second examines five key mechanisms: passing responsibility down the chain, supervision and accountability, assessment and incentives, education and guidance, and democratic centralism. Each is traced from the revolutionary years through the reform era to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), with citations to Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping.

In the authors' account, Party leadership is the soul of the system because it supplies direction, motivation and safeguards. They describe the Party as moving from rough to refined definitions of duty, and from basic disciplinary bodies to a full supervision system that includes the merged Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and National Supervisory Commission, inspection tours and the "four forms" of discipline. Democratic centralism is presented as the basic mechanism that restrains power and makes decisions scientific. The third part draws seven lessons, in pairs of elements to be combined: top-level design and grassroots practice; historical wisdom and the tasks of the times; theoretical innovation and practical exploration; intra-Party supervision and external checks; accountability of organisations and of individuals; rule-making and effective enforcement; and assessment with dynamic adjustment.

The authors conclude that the responsibility system must form a complete loop from concept to practice and from rules to feedback. Their proposals include a clear list of duties for each Party organisation and cadre, accountability that is precise and neither lax nor overextended, and support for officials who take initiative under the "three distinctions". They present this as a guarantee of the Party's long-term rule and the country's lasting stability. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars historicise Party responsibility mechanisms and the Third Plenum's agenda on Party-building reform.
quoteEn: Clear responsibility is the first prerequisite for building a responsibility system: Party organisations and members must know precisely what duties and missions they bear, so that every task and every post has a responsible person.
quoteZh: 责任明确是构建责任体系的首要前提，要求党组织和党员必须清晰知晓自身所承担的具体职责和使命，确保每一项工作、每一个岗位都能找到对应的责任人。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A Party-building policy promoted under Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering political, ideological, organisational, disciplinary and stylistic discipline and the anti-corruption campaign.

A graded approach to handling rule violations, from criticism and warnings for minor problems up to expulsion and criminal referral for serious ones. It is applied by Party discipline inspection bodies.

A guideline for assessing cadres' mistakes, asking officials to distinguish errors made in exploratory reform from violations of discipline, and unintended mistakes from deliberate ones. It is meant to encourage officials to act.

The Party's fundamental organisational principle, combining intra-Party discussion with unified decisions and the obedience of lower levels to higher ones. It was written into the Party constitution in 1927.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: Chen Yun's thinking and contribution on "how to be a Communist Party member" during the War of Resistance
zh: 全民族抗战时期陈云对“怎样做一个共产党员”的思考和贡献
paras: How should a Communist Party member behave? Xiong Qiuliang takes up this question through the work of Chen Yun, who headed the Party's Organization Department during the war against Japan. Xiong argues that Chen's essay "How to Be a Communist Party Member" (30 May 1939) gave a theoretically and practically sound answer. In Xiong's account the essay grew out of the pressures of rapid Party expansion and became a key document for building the membership.

The article notes that earlier studies mainly examine the content, features and influence of Chen's six standards for members, and sets out to examine the historical background, the development of his thinking and its distinctive features. It has four parts: the background of fast membership growth after 1937; Chen's step-by-step thinking from 1938 to 1939; a reading of the essay itself; and its three main characteristics.

Xiong traces how the Central Committee's 1938 decision to recruit members on a large scale (membership reportedly passed 500,000 by the end of 1938) brought problems of quantity over quality and of petty-bourgeois social composition. Chen's response developed through speeches and drafts: "How to Be a Revolutionary", the Qu Qiubai memorial talk, his proposed oath, the memo on north-west Shanxi, and the case of Liu Ligong, expelled for refusing a Party assignment. The essay covers qualifications, social composition, procedures, probationary members and six standards: lifelong struggle for communism, revolutionary interests above all, discipline and secrecy, tenacious execution of decisions, serving as a model for the masses, and study. Xiong identifies three features: a problem-oriented approach, emphasis on members' political character, and a systematic set of entry conditions and norms.

Xiong concludes that Chen combined Marxist-Leninist requirements for members, Mao Zedong's ideas on Party building and the wartime situation. In this reading, the six standards enriched Mao's Party-building doctrine, were included among 22 required documents in the Yan'an rectification movement, and remain relevant. Xiong ends by calling for continued strict control of entry and attention to members' worldview, to support Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a detailed account of the sources, drafts and case that shaped a foundational Party-building text of the Yan'an period.
quoteEn: Observing discipline is a matter not of words but of actual conduct.
quoteZh: 遵守纪律不是在口头上，而是在实际行动上。

glossary.explanation: The Party central organ responsible for membership, cadre appointments and Party organisation. Chen Yun headed it from December 1937.
An official concept promoted by the Party since the early 2020s, describing China's own path to modernization.
A Party-wide campaign of 1942–45 to unify thought and style of work around Mao Zedong's line. Chen's essay was among its required readings.

t: The Communist Party of China's early explorations of the peasant movement in 1924
zh: 一九二四年中国共产党对农民运动的早期探索
source: Studies on CPC History (Zhonggong dangshi yanjiu), 2025 no. 2
paras: Cui Jing asks how the Communist Party of China moved, between its Third Congress in 1923 and its Fourth Congress in January 1925, from adopting a resolution on the peasant question without much follow-through to raising the worker–peasant alliance. The article argues that 1924 was the year of this "key leap" in understanding. Early exploration of the peasant movement in that year supplied both the theoretical possibility and the practical basis for the shift.

Drawing largely on the Chronicle of the Communist Party of China (New-Democratic Revolution period, 1924 volume), the article first sets out the background: earlier peasant organisations at Yanqian, Haifeng and Hengshan, and the first Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. It then examines three areas: early theoretical discussion of the peasant question; the creation of institutions to train peasant-movement cadres; and early practice in Guangdong, Hunan, Hubei and Anhui.

On theory, Cui reports that Zhou Enlai, Deng Zhongxia, Zhang Tailei, Li Dazhao, Yun Daiying and Chen Tanqiu described the peasantry as a huge, impoverished and inherently revolutionary force. They saw the movement as still at a "budding" stage, with aims such as rent reduction, abolition of surcharges and the formation of peasant associations and armed self-defence. Cui notes that the Party still placed this force within the national revolution against imperialism and warlords, and had not yet fully stated its own leading role. On cadres, the Guangzhou Peasant Movement Training Institute, run under Kuomintang–Communist cooperation with Peng Pai as director of the first class, combined revolutionary theory, agricultural knowledge and military training. Similar schools were set up in Hunan and Hainan. On practice, Guangdong's movement grew through Party-led associations and self-defence forces, backed by armed support in the Guangning conflict. Elsewhere the Party used branches, peasant study societies and rural surveys, adapting its methods to local conditions.

Cui concludes that by the end of 1924 the Party's theoretical understanding had deepened, its experience had grown and its methods had diversified, though no theoretical consensus existed and regional development was uneven. The author also credits the period with experience in cadre training. Read the original if you study early CPC history, the origins of the worker–peasant alliance, or the Kuomintang–Communist united front and peasant cadre training.
quoteEn: Carrying out the peasant movement requires not only certain objective circumstances and conditions, but, more importantly, a Party that adopts highly flexible policies and tactics according to actual conditions.
quoteZh: 开展农民运动不仅需要一定的客观环境和条件，更需要党根据实际情况采取高度灵活的政策和策略。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-Leninist notion of a political alliance between the working class and the peasantry. The article says the Fourth Congress (1925) first raised it as an issue for the Party.
A short-term school set up in Guangzhou in 1924 under Kuomintang–Communist cooperation to train peasant-movement organisers. Peng Pai directed its first class.
The first united front (1924–27) between the Kuomintang and the Communist Party. Communists joined the Kuomintang as individuals and worked within its institutions.
The 1920s movement, led by the Kuomintang with Communist participation, against imperialism and warlord rule.

t: The Communist Party of China as the mainstay of the nation-wide War of Resistance
zh: 中国共产党是全民族抗战的中流砥柱
paras: Zhang Taiyuan takes up the question of what role the Communist Party of China played in the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japan, which the article calls the first completely victorious national liberation struggle in modern Chinese history. The thesis is that the victory was a victory of the whole nation and that the Party acted as its "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu), providing direction, unity, military strength and moral example.

The article is organised in four sections, each ending with a lesson for the present. They cover the Party's overall resistance line and strategy of protracted war; its promotion and defence of the anti-Japanese national united front; guerrilla warfare, the battlefields behind enemy lines and the base areas; and the heroism of Party members and the spirit of resistance. Evidence comes from Party documents, Mao Zedong's writings, statements by Xi Jinping, campaign statistics and accounts of individual heroes.

Zhang argues first that the Party was the earliest to call for armed resistance and set the course through the Luochuan Conference (1937) and Mao's On Protracted War (1938), which relied on mobilising the masses. Second, the Party was the initiator and firm defender of the united front, maintaining it even after the Southern Anhui Incident. Third, citing figures, Zhang says that in the stage of strategic stalemate the Party-led rear battlefields faced 58 to 62 per cent of Japanese forces in China and almost all puppet troops. The article reports that Party-led forces fought over 125,000 engagements, killed or captured about 1.714 million Japanese and puppet troops and built 19 base areas. It then presents martyrs such as Yang Jingyu, the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain and Deng Yufen as embodiments of patriotism and resolve.

Zhang concludes that the Party's political programme, firm will and exemplary conduct sustained the nation's hope and forged a great spirit of resistance. The lessons drawn are to uphold the Party's overall leadership, consolidate the broadest patriotic united front, rely on the people, and use the spirit of resistance to advance Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party-centred account of the War of Resistance is presented in a Central Party School publication, including its figures and exemplary stories.
quoteEn: Without the Communist Party of China there would have been no nation-wide anti-Japanese united front, and without the anti-Japanese national united front there would have been no nation-wide War of Resistance.
quoteZh: 没有中国共产党就没有全民族的抗日统一战线，没有抗日民族统一战线就没有全民族抗战

glossary.literal: the stone pillar standing in the midstream
glossary.explanation: An idiom for a steadfast force that holds firm in a crisis. Mao Zedong used it in 1941 of the Communist-led forces, and the Party now uses it for its role in the War of Resistance.
The wartime alliance of political and military forces against Japan, centred on cooperation between the Communist Party and the Kuomintang, formally established in 1937.
Mao Zedong's 1938 strategy of a long war in three stages: strategic defence, stalemate and counter-offensive, relying on mass mobilisation to overcome a stronger enemy.
The official name for China's path of modernization under Party leadership, promoted in Party discourse since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's central national goal of restoring China's strength and international standing, closely tied to the Chinese Dream.

t: The War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression: the historical turning point on the road to the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
zh: 抗日战争：中华民族走向伟大复兴的历史转折点
paras: Writing in Modern Chinese History Studies (2025, no. 4), Zhang Hao asks why the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression (1931–45) should be seen as the turning point from national crisis to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article argues that the victory ended imperialist powers' free seizure of Chinese territory, established China's standing as a major country, and set the direction for the new China. Zhang presents this as the fundamental precondition for national rejuvenation.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Japan's long-prepared plan to conquer China, in two phases: seizing the islands and territories around the mainland from 1879 to the Russo-Japanese War, then the stepwise path from the Mukden Incident to the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of 1937. The second part examines why war was unavoidable and what kind of war it was. The third sets out four respects in which the victory marked a turning point.

Zhang's core argument draws on Japanese official statements, Mao Zedong's wartime writings and Party documents. Japan's declared national goals and its 'peace' terms of 1935 and 1937 are read as demands that China become a colony, so that negotiation could not succeed. The war is therefore characterised, following Mao, as a national revolutionary war of survival and liberation, which even the Nationalists called a necessary stage towards national revival. The four aspects of the turning point are: the first complete victory over a foreign invader after a century of defeats; a major contribution to the world anti-fascist war, with China as the Eastern main theatre; the Communist Party's role as the 'mainstay' (zhongliu dizhu), which Zhang says made it the natural leader of rejuvenation; and the emergence of a prototype of the new China.

Zhang concludes that the victory restored national self-confidence, overcame the 'fear of Japan' and prepared the ground for the People's Republic and the socialist system. The war is presented as opening a new era in the history of the Chinese revolution and in the course of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a Chinese-historiographical account of the war that links it to the Party's leadership and to the rejuvenation narrative, with many quotations from Mao and from Japanese wartime sources.
quoteEn: The victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression was the historical turning point on the Chinese nation's road to great rejuvenation, and it opened bright prospects for that rejuvenation.
quoteZh: 抗日战争的胜利，是中华民族走向伟大复兴的历史转折点，开辟了中华民族伟大复兴的光明前景。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party slogan for restoring China's national strength and international standing after the 'century of humiliation'. It is closely associated with Xi Jinping's 'Chinese Dream'.

glossary.literal: the stone pillar in the midstream
glossary.explanation: An idiom for a firm force that holds steady amid turmoil. Party historiography uses it to describe the Communist Party's role in the War of Resistance.
The clash near Beijing on 7 July 1937 that marked the start of full-scale war between Japan and China. Chinese historiography treats it as the start of the nationwide war of resistance.

t: An analysis of the distinctive advantages that allow the Communist Party of China to carry out self-reform courageously
zh: 中国共产党勇于自我革命的独特优势论析
paras: Xi Jinping has called the courage for self-reform the Party's most distinctive trait and greatest strength. Wu Bo asks not why or how the Party should carry out self-reform, but why it is able to do so. The article's answer is that the Party's practical experience, traditions and spirit have formed a set of advantages. Wu describes these as the rational development and use of the Party's own resources, and argues that they must keep being exploited if the Party is to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall.

Wu identifies six advantages: political (comprehensive Party leadership), value-based (selflessness), ideological (upholding fundamental principles while innovating), organisational (a tight structure and a capable cadre corps), disciplinary, and institutional (the system of governing a large party). Each is traced through four periods: the new-democratic revolution, the socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. Each is illustrated with statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi, and with key Party documents.

Wu makes three main moves. First, the Party is said to have no special interests of its own, and this selflessness, together with its founding mission, its commitment to correcting errors and its pursuit of advanced and pure character, supplies the courage and motive for self-reform. Second, self-reform is said to rest on centralised and unified leadership by the Central Committee, democratic centralism, the Two Upholds, and a tight organisational system. It also draws on Marxism adapted to China, on traditional Chinese culture and on the Party's revolutionary spirit. For traditional culture, the author cites concern for hardship, the idea of treating illness before it appears, and the ideal of inner sageliness and outer kingliness. Third, the author argues that discipline education, the unity of Party spirit, Party conduct and Party discipline, and a system of Party regulations, internal supervision and inspection tours turn these advantages into practice. Wu says this system answers the difficult problem of self-supervision for a long-ruling party, and contrasts it with bourgeois parties and the Soviet party.

Wu concludes that a strong Marxist party is forged through self-reform, and that pushing the Party's great self-reform through to the end requires analysing its inherent advantages as well as its necessity and methods. The author calls for continued development of these resources, so that self-reform stays "always on the road" and the Party keeps to the forefront of the times. The article is a Party-history and Party-building study that presents the Party's historical record largely in affirmative terms. Read the original if you want a systematic, period-by-period account of how Chinese Party scholarship explains the Party's capacity for self-reform and the sources it cites for each advantage.
quoteEn: The Party's self-reform cannot do without drawing together and mobilising its own reserves of advantage.
quoteZh: 党的自我革命离不开对自身优势资源的整合驱动。

glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's term for the Party's capacity to correct its own faults and purify itself from within. Official English texts render it 'self-reform' or 'self-revolution'.

The requirement to uphold Xi Jinping's core position on the Party Central Committee and in the Party as a whole, and to uphold the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee.
The Party's fundamental organisational principle: centralisation on the basis of democracy and democracy under centralised guidance. Minority submits to majority and lower levels to higher levels.

t: The "xinxue" of Communists: the "inner sage" learning of Marxists' self-reform
zh: 共产党人的“心学”：马克思主义者自我革命的“内圣”之学
paras: Xi Jinping has called Party-spirit education the "xinxue" ("learning of the mind-heart") of Communists and placed it within the Party's "self-reform". Wu Wenxin asks what this Communist xinxue is and how it differs from the Neo-Confucian tradition of Wang Yangming. The article argues that it is a Marxist-faith learning, in which cultivating an "inner sage" disposition of wholehearted devotion serves the "outer king" task of serving the people.

The article is published in Taishan Journal (2025, no. 3). It has four parts. It first names the key terms of Communist xinxue and traces its cultural source to Wang Yangming. It then treats xinxue as the study of Marxist belief and sets out its content. Next it lists five ways in which it claims to surpass traditional xinxue. Finally it applies the method to Party history study and education.

Wu reads Wang's "extending innate knowing" and "unity of knowing and acting" as Party-spirit self-awareness and unity of knowing and acting. On this reading, the Party's purpose of wholeheartedly serving the people is itself a Communist "inner sage and outer king": wholeheartedness is inner cultivation and self-reform, and serving the people is the outward work of social revolution. The author says Communist xinxue differs from the traditional kind in five ways. It is thoroughly materialist, since it rests on the materiality of consciousness. It is a xinxue of the people, extended to the roughly 99 million Party members. It stresses social practice over withdrawal. It is spiral rather than cyclical in its self-reform. And it is oriented to communist values rather than to personal sagehood or religious salvation. For practice, Wu takes Xi's formula of unifying study, thought and application, and of knowing, believing and acting. Learning and thinking must be combined, thought must lead to application, knowledge must turn into belief, and belief into action.

Wu concludes that Party history education and other regular Party-spirit cultivation are all forms of practising this xinxue. In Wu's account, study is the means, thought the key and application the aim, while knowledge is the carrier, belief the core and action the destination. The author warns that knowledge not turned into belief leads to corruption and "two-faced" officials. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school scholar draws on Wang Yangming's thought to frame Party-spirit education and self-reform.
quoteEn: The xinxue of Communists is the learning of the Communist's original aspiration and the learning of faith.
quoteZh: 共产党人的“心学”就是共产党人的初心之学、信仰之学

glossary.explanation: A Song–Ming Confucian school associated with Lu Jiuyuan and Wang Yangming, centred on cultivating the moral mind. Xi Jinping has applied the term to Party-spirit education.
A term in Xi Jinping-era Party discourse for the Party's continuous self-purification and self-improvement. The official English rendering is "the Party's self-reform".
A classical Confucian ideal in which inner moral cultivation grounds effective public governance. The article recasts it as wholehearted service to the people.
A central doctrine of Wang Yangming holding that moral knowledge and action are inseparable. The article adopts it as a key principle of Communist cultivation.

t: The westward road of educated youth to Yan'an during the War of Resistance
zh: 抗战时期知识青年奔赴延安的西行之路
paras: This short historical piece, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, describes the journey made by educated young people to Yan'an during the War of Resistance against Japan. Wang uses "westward journey" as a symbolic term for a generation's search for light and progress. The article argues that, despite great physical obstacles, the journey showed the pull of Yan'an as a revolutionary base and the young people's commitment to national salvation and their ideals.

The article first sets out the objective constraints: distance, limited transport and cost. It then traces the routes from Shanghai to Xi'an, and finally the last stretch from Xi'an to Yan'an. Evidence comes from press reports such as Shen Bao (1939) and from the recorded experiences of individual travellers, including writers, artists and students.

Wang notes that Shanghai–Xi'an travel ran along "two horizontal and one vertical" routes: the Longhai railway, the Yangtze route via Wuhan, and a southern sea route via Hong Kong, Guangzhou or Vietnam and Kunming. As Japanese advances cut each in turn, travellers shifted to the next; one artist couple took seven months. The final stretch of nearly 400 kilometres had no railway. Travellers used rough roads, mule carts and mostly walking, which Wang links to Mao Zedong's description of the Xi'an–Yan'an road as the "first lesson" at the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University.

Wang concludes that the hardships could not stop the stream of young people heading to Yan'an. In the article's view, the journey confirms the attraction of the revolutionary base and the young people's firm convictions. Read the original if you want a concise, source-based account of the practical routes and hardships of reaching Yan'an in wartime.
quoteEn: The westward road was beset with countless dangers, yet it could not stop the flood of educated youth heading for Yan'an.
quoteZh: 西行之路险阻万千，却阻挡不了知识青年奔赴延安的洪流。

t: Deepening research on the Communist Party's war of resistance behind enemy lines in North China
zh: 深化中国共产党华北敌后抗战研究
paras: Fu Jing, writing in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in October 2025, asks how research on the Communist Party's anti-Japanese resistance in North China can be extended. Fu argues that North China was strategically vital to Japan, and that the Party became the "mainstay" of the national war of resistance there. New Chinese and foreign archives, newspapers, diaries and memoirs, in Fu's view, make further work possible in three areas.

The short commentary opens with the outbreak of full-scale war in July 1937 and the region's geography, resources and transport links. It then proposes three research directions: the anti-Japanese national united front, operations behind enemy lines, and the building of grass-roots political power. Each section sketches the historical background before listing questions that deserve study.

On the united front, Fu describes a region divided among local power-holders, with a weak Nationalist government and competing British and American interests. Fu urges study of how the Party won over local forces, organised underground work in occupied cities and villages, and sought international support. On military operations, Fu cites the Pingxingguan victory, the Hundred Regiments Offensive and railway sabotage, and asks how the Party adapted tactics to terrain and linked North and Central China. On grass-roots power, Fu points to the production campaign, the "three-thirds" system and theoretical education, and calls for work on cadres, Party branches and how the centre guided local struggle.

Fu concludes that deeper study would enrich the history of the war and of the Party, and would show more fully the Party's role as the mainstay of resistance. Read the original if you want a brief guide to the research agenda that Chinese historians are setting for the Party's war of resistance in North China.
quoteEn: Strengthening research on the Communist Party's anti-Japanese resistance behind enemy lines in North China will not only deepen the study of the history of the war and of the Party, but will also help to show fully the Party's role as the mainstay of the war of resistance.
quoteZh: 加强对中国共产党华北敌后抗战研究，不仅有助于深化抗战史和党史的相关研究，更有助于充分展示中国共产党在抗战中的中流砥柱作用。

glossary.explanation: The Communist Party's policy of uniting all social classes and political forces against Japan, including the Nationalists and local power-holders. It was formalised in the later 1930s.
A principle adopted in the Communist-led base areas from 1940 for allocating seats in organs of government. Communists, progressives and middle elements were each to hold roughly one third.
A large Eighth Route Army campaign in North China in 1940, centred on the Zhengtai railway, against Japanese railway lines and strongpoints.

t: Achievements of the Party-led communications enterprise during the War of Resistance
st: Building the wartime communications system centred on Yan'an, 1937–1945
