The article cites a membership of 100.271 million in 5.25 million primary-level organisations, up from a little over fifty at the founding, and presents this as evidence of the Party's appeal and cohesion. Internal strength, Xiao argues, comes from ideological Party building and theoretical education, including eight Party-wide education campaigns since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It also comes from full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the eight-point regulation on conduct, strict control over admission, and the handling of unqualified members. For members themselves, Xiao sets out three requirements: firm ideals and service to the central tasks of the Party and state; excellent performance in one's own post; and service to the people, starting with their most pressing and practical concerns.

Xiao concludes that the Party's strength depends on both the quality of its members and the solidity of its grassroots organisations. A Party that is large, ideologically united, strictly disciplined and rooted in the people is presented as able to meet the major tests ahead. The piece is a concise statement of the official line on Party building in the new era. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Party-school scholar presents Party building in the mainstream press, or a compact summary of the stock themes and figures used in 2025 discussions of Party discipline and membership.
quoteEn: The vanguard character of a Marxist party is manifested first of all in its ideological and theoretical advancement; stressing ideological Party building and strengthening the Party through theory is a distinctive feature and glorious tradition of the Party.
quoteZh: 马克思主义政党的先进性，首先体现为思想理论上的先进性，注重思想建党、理论强党是党的鲜明特色和光荣传统。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It covers stricter discipline, anti-corruption work and tighter management of Party members and cadres.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's central goal of restoring China to national strength and international standing. It is closely tied to the 'Chinese Dream' and the two centenary goals.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping. It marks the start of the post-Mao 'new period' in official periodisation.
Rules on official conduct adopted by the Politburo in December 2012. They target formalism, bureaucratism, extravagance and similar practices among Party officials.

t: The mainstay: the great role of the Communist Party of China in the nationwide War of Resistance
zh: 中流砥柱：中国共产党在全民族抗战中的伟大作用
paras: Zhang Taiyuan and Zhao Jinghan, writing in Guangming Daily in July 2025, ask what role the Communist Party of China played in the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japan. Their answer is that the Party was the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) of the nationwide resistance and its national vanguard. In the authors' account, the Party's political line, firm will and exemplary conduct sustained the hope of national salvation and set the correct direction of the war.

The short commentary is built in three parts. The first concerns the Party's determination in defending national independence, the second its line of all-out resistance and its strategy and tactics, and the third its role as the backbone of the resistance behind enemy lines. The authors rely heavily on statements by Mao Zedong, Ye Jianying and Xi Jinping. They also cite Japanese military reports and the observations of foreign journalists and a US military observer group.

First, the authors contrast the Party's steadfastness with the Guomindang's wavering between fighting and negotiating. They support this with Mao's 1936 answer to Edgar Snow, the sacrifice of commanders and heroic units, and Japanese wartime statements that the "truly anti-Japanese force" was the Communist Party. Second, they credit Mao's On Protracted War and his writings on guerrilla warfare with foreseeing three stages of the war. They also credit the united front and the mobilisation of the masses, which they treat as the key to victory. Third, they argue that the base areas and the battlefield behind enemy lines grew until they became the main theatre of resistance. As evidence they cite the 1940 offensive by 105 regiments in North China, population and troop figures for the base areas, and 19 base areas covering nearly 1 million square kilometres with a population of nearly 100 million.

The authors conclude that the Party's mainstay role was the key to victory. They present the Guomindang-led front and the Communist-led rear battlefield as cooperating in a shared strategic posture. They add that the Party also worked to build an international anti-fascist united front, and that China's resistance was the Eastern main theatre of the world anti-fascist war. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official Party-history narrative of the War of Resistance as it appeared in the 2025 commemorations, including its use of Japanese and foreign sources.
quoteEn: Mobilising and organising the unorganised Chinese masses, so that the war already begun would develop into an all-out, nationwide war of resistance, was the central key to winning victory.
quoteZh: 把处于无组织状态的中国民众动员和组织起来，使已经发动的抗战发展为全面的全民族的抗战，是争取抗战胜利的中心关键。

glossary.literal: a rock standing in the midstream
glossary.explanation: An idiom for a steadfast force that holds firm in a crisis. Xi Jinping applied it to the Communist Party's role in the War of Resistance, and it is now standard in official accounts.
The alliance of the Communist Party and the Guomindang, together with other groups, against Japanese invasion. It took shape from 1936 to 1937.
The guerrilla theatre and base areas led by the Communist Party in Japanese-occupied territory. Official history contrasts it with the Guomindang-led "frontal battlefield".
Mao Zedong's 1938 work, which predicted three stages of the war and set out a strategy of protracted resistance and guerrilla warfare.

t: Grasping the methodology for strengthening the Party's work style
zh: 把握加强党的作风建设的方法论
paras: This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2025, asks what methods underlie Xi Jinping's remarks on strengthening the Party's work style (作风建设) since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Wang Yanlong argues that these remarks settled what to tackle and how to tackle it in work-style building under new conditions, and that they contain a coherent set of ways of thinking and working. Grasping this methodology, Wang says, would help create a clean political ecology and strengthen the Party's resolve to continue the effort.

The piece is organised around four paired principles, each opened with a quotation from Xi: unifying the elimination of the "four undesirable work styles" with the establishment of new ones; unifying breadth of vision with attention to detail; unifying prevention with consolidation of foundations; and unifying clarity of direction with firm implementation. Each pair is tied to dialectical reasoning and illustrated with examples from the Party's recent practice.

Wang's first move is to present each pair as dialectical. Breaking and establishing are said to be mutually dependent: positive models and the spirit of Chinese Communists are promoted so that bad habits can be removed, and clear rules replace unwritten ones. Second, the author treats the eight-point regulation of the Central Committee as an entry point that avoided piecemeal fixes, and treats "preventing illness before it arises" and "consolidating the foundations" as a way of treating both symptoms and root causes. This includes disciplinary education, the institutional drive for officials not to dare, not to be able and not to want to be corrupt, inspection systems and big-data supervision platforms. Third, clear direction is linked to contradiction analysis, and implementation to the law of quantitative change becoming qualitative change, the "nail-hammering" spirit. Wang cites 2024 figures from discipline inspection bodies: 118,000 cases of hedonism and extravagance, with 157,000 people criticised or punished, and 107,000 cases of formalism and bureaucracy, with 156,000 people.

Wang concludes that work-style building is a protracted struggle with no end point. It requires precise targeting, sustained effort, and routine, institutionalised and long-term mechanisms, so that good work style becomes a permanent feature of the Party and the Party never changes in character. Work style is described as a matter of Party spirit and of popular support for the Party's governing position. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary presents work-style campaigns through dialectical method and recent enforcement figures.
quoteEn: Work-style building is always on the road; it has no completion.
quoteZh: 作风建设永远在路上，没有完成时。

glossary.explanation: The Party's long-running effort to improve officials' conduct, including opposing formalism, bureaucracy, hedonism and extravagance. It is treated as part of Party discipline and of maintaining the Party's links with the people.
Formalism, bureaucracy, hedonism and extravagance, named by the Party after 2012 as the main targets of work-style rectification.

A set of rules adopted by the Political Bureau in December 2012. They aim to reduce extravagance, bureaucratic formalities and officials' perks, and became the starting point of the post-2012 work-style campaign.

glossary.pinyin: bù gǎn fǔ, bù néng fǔ, bù xiǎng fǔ
glossary.en: not to dare, not to be able and not to want to be corrupt
glossary.explanation: An official formula for anti-corruption work. It combines deterrence by punishment, institutional constraints and ideological-moral education.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: Inheriting and carrying forward the great founding spirit of the Party to advance Chinese modernization
st: A roundtable of four scholars, published for the Party's 104th anniversary
zh: 继承发扬伟大建党精神 推进中国式现代化建设
paras: This is a written roundtable, moderated by Guangming Daily reporter Wang Haokui and published on 1 July 2025, the Party's 104th anniversary. It asks how the great founding spirit of the Party can be carried forward in the new era, and how Chinese modernization can draw wisdom and strength from it. The four scholars treat the spirit as a continuing resource for the Party's central tasks, and the editors present it as guiding the Party's cause.

The participants are Dai Yanjun (Central Party School), Yan Xiaofeng (School of Marxism, Tianjin University), Liu Jingbei (former deputy president of the China Executive Leadership Academy Pudong, East China Normal University) and Chen Jinlong (South China Normal University). The discussion has four sections, each tied to one element of the spirit: upholding truth and ideals; fulfilling the original aspiration and mission; fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely; and being loyal to the Party and living up to the people's trust. The last section is linked to the current Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation.

On truth and ideals, Dai argues that the Party has held to Marxism and adapted it to Chinese conditions, correcting errors through self-reform, while Yan calls for stronger ideals and convictions and counts losing them among the Party's distinctive problems as a large party. Chen and Liu read the Party's history as one of seeking the people's happiness and national rejuvenation, and Liu ties the original aspiration and mission to the Party's central task of advancing Chinese modernization, to high-quality development and to the new development philosophy. Chen traces the spirit of fighting bravely from the war of resistance to later episodes such as the Korean War, the "two bombs, one satellite" project and reform-era flood and earthquake relief, and Dai says it remains necessary for new technological, governance and national-security challenges. Liu and Yan treat conduct as a matter of Party spirit and of the Party's ties with the people, and argue that the eight-point regulation, rectifying the "four undesirable work styles" and linking work-style rectification with anti-corruption work are the means of staying loyal to the Party and the people.

The participants conclude that the founding spirit should shape ideals, people-centred development, a readiness for struggle and Party conduct as China pursues the second centenary goal. They call for continued study and education, and for ending the pattern of campaigns that tighten and then relax. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the founding spirit in 2025 and tie it to Chinese modernization and Party conduct.
quoteEn: At bottom, the problem of work style is a problem of Party spirit, and its core is the relationship between the Party and the people.
quoteZh: 作风问题本质上是党性问题，核心是党同人民群众的关系问题。

glossary.en: the great founding spirit of the Party
glossary.explanation: A formulation set out by Xi Jinping in 2021 on the Party's centenary. It has four parts: upholding truth and ideals, fulfilling the original aspiration and mission, fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely, and being loyal to the Party and living up to the people's trust.
The official name for the Party's model of modernization, described as having Chinese characteristics, and a central term of the Party's mission since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

Rules on officials' conduct adopted by the Central Committee in December 2012, aimed at curbing formalism, extravagance and bureaucratism. A Party-wide study and education campaign on it was launched in 2025.
The Party's term for formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, which the eight-point regulation targets.
The official goal of building China into a great modern socialist country by 2049, the centenary of the People's Republic.
The guiding approach to development announced in 2015, centred on innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing.
The official priority for economic work since 2017, emphasising quality and efficiency over speed of growth.

t: The great founding spirit of the Party: the wellspring of the Communist Party's spirit
zh: 伟大建党精神：中国共产党的精神之源
paras: Writing in the People's Daily for the Party's anniversary in 2025, Qi Biao asks what it means to call the \"great founding spirit of the Party\" the \"wellspring of the Party's spirit\". The article treats the concept, introduced by Xi Jinping in his speech at the centenary in 2021, as an original conceptual label that deserves close study. Qi's thesis is that the founding spirit is the Party's spiritual source in three senses: it expresses the Party's essential nature, it is the origin of the Communist Party members' spiritual genealogy, and it explains why the Party stays vital.

The piece has three main sections. The first traces how the Party has defined its own spirit, from Mao Zedong's and Deng Xiaoping's \"revolutionary spirit\" to Xi's work from 2005 onwards on the \"Red Boat spirit\" and the call to preserve the founders' fighting spirit. The second places the founding spirit within the \"spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists\", whose first list of 46 spirits was released in September 2021. The third links the founding spirit to the Party's vitality and to the problems facing a large, long-governing party.

Qi reads the four-part formulation (upholding truth and ideals, practising the original mission, fearing no sacrifice, and being loyal to the Party and the people) as the Party's political soul, its fighting character and its purpose. The genealogy is described through four periods, from the Jinggangshan and Yan'an spirits to the poverty-alleviation and anti-epidemic spirits. In Qi's view, this genealogy records the nation's passage from \"standing up\" to \"becoming prosperous\" to \"becoming strong\", and it carries the Party's \"red genes\", which must not change. Qi argues that a party's vitality is measured by whether it keeps the striving spirit of its founding, not by how long it has existed. The article cites the Party's recoveries from setbacks, and the changes since the 18th Party Congress (2012), as products of a \"historical initiative\" spirit.

Qi acknowledges that corruption and the \"four undesirable work styles\" conflict with the founding spirit and could pollute the Party's source if they spread. The article calls for the Party's self-reform, drawing on Xi's remarks on the \"unique problems of a large party\", so that the Party does not change in character and can escape the \"historical cycle of rise and fall\". It also calls for training successors to carry on the red genes. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how Party discourse positions the founding spirit within the Party's spiritual genealogy and its self-reform agenda.
quoteEn: Whether a party's vitality is strong cannot be judged simply by how long it has existed or been in power, but by whether it can consistently preserve the striving spirit of its founding and early endeavour.
quoteZh: 一个政党的生命力强大与否，不能简单从其成立及执政时间的长短作出判断，而是要看其能不能始终如一保持创建、创业时的奋斗精神。

glossary.en: great founding spirit of the Party
glossary.explanation: A formulation Xi Jinping put forward on 1 July 2021: upholding truth and ideals, practising the original mission, fearing no sacrifice, and being loyal to the Party and the people. The Party presents it as the source of all its later "spirits".

glossary.zh: 中国共产党人精神谱系
glossary.explanation: A list of named "great spirits" (such as the Yan'an spirit and the Lei Feng spirit) arranged by historical period. Xi named it in February 2021, and a first list of 46 was published in September 2021.
Official term for the Party's internal efforts to rectify itself, including anti-corruption and discipline campaigns. It is presented as the answer to the Party's own problems.

glossary.en: unique problems of a large party
glossary.literal: difficulties unique to a big party
glossary.explanation: A phrase Xi Jinping used for challenges said to face a very large, long-ruling party, summarised as "six how-to-always" questions.
A metaphor in Party discourse for the revolutionary ideals and traditions that are meant to be passed down through generations.

glossary.en: historical cycle of rise and fall
glossary.explanation: The idea, raised in the 1945 Yan'an conversation between Huang Yanpei and Mao Zedong, that regimes tend to flourish and then decline. Party leaders say they have a way to escape it.

t: Guiding the great self-reform with the great founding spirit of the Party
zh: 以伟大建党精神引领伟大自我革命
paras: Dai Lixing and Guo Wenjing, in a commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (July 2025), ask how the great founding spirit of the Party can guide the Party's great self-reform. They argue that the two are internally unified, and that the founding spirit supplies the moral and spiritual basis on which the Party's capacity for self-reform rests.

The piece has three parts. It first sets out the mutual relationship between the founding spirit and self-reform, then explains the value the founding spirit brings to self-reform, and finally proposes practical paths tied to the "four selves".

The authors read the founding spirit as four elements, each matched to a function. Seeking truth and holding to ideals gives belief and theoretical grounding; practising the original aspiration and shouldering the mission strengthens the Party's members and its people-first stance; fearlessness and heroic struggle supplies the will to turn the blade inward; loyalty to the Party and faithfulness to the people fixes political direction. Self-reform, in turn, is described as the founding spirit carried forward and put into practice, from the Yan'an rectification campaign to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

For practice, the authors call for stronger ideological and theoretical work, cultivation of Party spirit and a sense of responsibility, sustained discipline and anti-corruption work building on the "three no-corruptions", and people's supervision, with public satisfaction as the measure of results. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party scholars link founding-spirit rhetoric to the Party's self-reform agenda.
quoteEn: The great founding spirit is the spiritual pillar of self-reform, and self-reform is the practical requirement for carrying forward the great founding spirit.
quoteZh: 伟大建党精神是自我革命的精神支柱,自我革命是弘扬伟大建党精神的实践要求。

glossary.en: great founding spirit of the Party
glossary.explanation: A formulation Xi Jinping presented in 2021 for the Party's centenary, summarised as upholding truth and ideals, practising the original aspiration and mission, fearlessness and struggle, and loyalty to the Party and the people.
An official concept for the Party's efforts to correct its own problems and maintain discipline, stressed in Party discourse since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the campaign since 2012 to tighten Party discipline, including the anti-corruption drive.
A formula calling on the Party to purify, improve, reform and raise itself (自我净化、自我完善、自我革新、自我提高).
An anti-corruption formula: officials should be unable, unwilling and not daring to be corrupt, combining deterrence, institutional constraint and ideological education.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: Building Party conduct on the foundation of firm ideals and convictions
zh: 以坚定理想信念为根基推进作风建设
paras: Writing as the Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation is under way, Zhang takes up the question of how to build Party conduct on a lasting footing. Quoting Xi Jinping's call to "return to basics and strengthen the foundation", the commentary argues that firm ideals and convictions must be treated as a lifelong task. In Zhang's view they are the root of work on conduct and of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

The piece has three parts. The first explains why firm convictions are the foundation of founding and strengthening the Party. The second surveys how the Party has pursued ideal-and-conviction education across four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third sets out five routes for strengthening convictions today.

Zhang argues that convictions are a weapon for keeping the Party advanced and pure, the base of its long-term governing strength and an essential requirement for its central tasks. In the historical survey, the author lists measures such as the Party's minimum and maximum programmes, the Three Main Rules of Discipline and Eight Points for Attention, rectification campaigns, discipline inspection bodies and the series of study-and-education campaigns since the new era began. The five routes are: raising theoretical level in Marxism; remembering the founding mission and "matters of national importance"; strengthening cultural confidence and intra-Party political culture; self-reform and a readiness to struggle; and education backed by Party regulations and institutions. Zhang presents these as a path from knowing to believing to acting.

Zhang concludes that convictions must be cultivated throughout life and tied to study of innovative Party theory, self-cultivation and practical work. The author calls for deeper grasp of the Two Establishes, strengthened awareness and confidence, and the Two Upholds, together with institutional rules that make conviction education routine. The goal, in this account, is to supply a firm political guarantee for building a strong country and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party-building discourse links ideological conviction, institutional discipline and conduct work in 2025.
quoteEn: Firm ideals and convictions are the source of strength that underpins the Party's long-term governance.
quoteZh: 坚定理想信念是稳固党长期执政的力量根基。

glossary.explanation: A set of rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012 to curb formalism, extravagance and bureaucratism among officials. It became a symbol of Xi Jinping's drive to reform Party conduct.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's campaign, strengthened since 2012, to tighten discipline, fight corruption and improve Party organisation.
A formula from the 2021 Party resolution on history, affirming Xi Jinping's position as core of the Central Committee and the Party as a whole, and the guiding role of his thought.
A Party requirement to uphold Xi Jinping's core position in the Central Committee and the Party, and to uphold the Central Committee's authority and centralised leadership.

glossary.literal: the great things of the nation
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Xi Jinping asking officials to keep in mind the issues vital to the country's overall interest when working.

t: Mastering investigation and research as a basic skill
zh: 掌握调查研究这个基本功
paras: Niu Xianfeng takes up Xi Jinping's repeated call for cadres to master diaoyan, "investigation and research", as a basic skill of governance. The article argues that this practice is the concentrated expression of Marxist world outlook and methodology, a family heirloom of the Party, and an urgent requirement for tackling the problems met in advancing Chinese modernization. It situates the call in a sequence running from the first of the Eight-point Regulations (2012), through Xi's 2021 Central Party School speech, to the 2023 work plan on promoting investigation and research across the Party.

The piece is organised in four parts. It first explains why investigation and research embodies Marxist epistemology and the mass viewpoint, tracing the practice to Mao Zedong's 1930 Xunwu investigation. It then argues that mastering the skill requires adherence to the Party's ideological line and to the mass line, and closes with the methods needed to do it well. Throughout, Niu builds the case mainly from Xi's remarks, supplemented by Mao's.

Niu's core move is to tie the practice to two Party principles. On the ideological line, seeking truth from facts is split into \"facts\" (starting from reality, rejecting perfunctory or pre-scripted visits) and \"truth\" (analysing raw material to find underlying regularities), so that conclusions come after investigation rather than before it. On the mass line, investigation is presented as going to the people, listening to them and drawing on their creative practice, which the author links to meeting the principal contradiction of the new era and to high-quality development.

On method, Niu calls for a solid work style and sincere motives, a problem-oriented approach, and a focus on practical results. The author treats staged, \"bonsai\" or token inspections as formalism and bureaucratism rooted in a distorted view of political achievement. Niu concludes that deep, rigorous research is a precondition for sound decisions in further comprehensively deepening reform and for moving towards national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how current Party-school discourse frames investigation and research within the Party's ideological line, mass line and the 2025 campaign on the Eight-point Regulations.
quoteEn: Carrying out investigation and research is itself walking the mass line.
quoteZh: 开展调查研究就是走群众路线

glossary.explanation: A Party working method of going to the grassroots to gather first-hand information and then analyse it before making decisions. It is traditionally associated with Mao Zedong's 1930s writings and has been promoted again under Xi Jinping.
The Party's principle of drawing ideas from the people and returning them as policy, summed up as "from the masses, to the masses". It is a core element of Party doctrine on leadership style.
A principle at the heart of the Party's ideological line, associated with Mao and later with Deng Xiaoping. It requires policy to start from objective reality rather than from dogma.
The official term for China's path of modernization, presented since the 20th Party Congress (2022) as distinct from Western models.
Rules on Party work style adopted in December 2012 to curb formalism, bureaucratism and extravagance and to bring officials closer to the public.
An official development goal emphasising quality, efficiency and innovation over speed of growth.

t: Improving Party conduct is always a work in progress
zh: 作风建设永远在路上
paras: This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that improving Party conduct (zuofeng jianshe) is "always on the road" and must be pursued without relaxation. Liu Xiaoxin argues that conduct is tied to the Party's image, to popular support and to its survival. The piece is written to support the study and education campaign on thoroughly implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point decision on conduct.

The article has three parts. The first explains why conduct matters, the second reviews the Party's record on conduct in four historical periods, and the third sets out how to win what Liu calls a "tough and protracted battle" on conduct. The historical survey runs from the New Democratic Revolution through the socialist revolution and construction and the reform era to the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

Liu argues that conduct is required by the Party's nature and purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, that it decides the success of the Party's cause, and that it sets the tone for social customs. On this basis Liu holds that Chinese modernization will meet serious risks, which call for stricter Party governance and the Party's self-reform. The historical review stresses Mao Zedong's "three major styles", the Yan'an rectification campaigns, the post-1949 rectification drives and the 2001 and 2009 decisions on conduct. It treats the eight-point decision adopted in December 2012 as the first major Party regulation of the 18th Party Congress era, and credits Xi Jinping's personal example with a decisive role in its implementation.

For the future, Liu calls for three measures. The first is to focus on the "key minority" of leading cadres and lead from the top down. The second is to turn conduct work into regular, standardised and lasting practice through institutions with clear red lines. The third is to investigate and address undesirable work styles and corruption together, since Liu says they share a root, by tracing corruption from conduct problems and conduct problems from corruption. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party commentary frames the history and current tasks of conduct building and the eight-point decision.
quoteEn: Unhealthy practices and corruption share the same root and source and are two sides of the same coin.
quoteZh: 不正之风与腐败问题同根同源、互为表里。

glossary.explanation: A set of rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012 on improving work style and ties with the masses. It covers streamlined meetings, documents, official travel and frugality.
The Party's term for efforts to improve the work style, discipline and behaviour of Party members and cadres. It is a recurring theme in Party-building campaigns.
A phrase for leading cadres, whose conduct is said to set the example for the whole Party and society.
An official term, prominent since the 18th Party Congress, for the Party's efforts to correct its own problems and keep itself clean.
The official name for China's path of modernization, promoted since the 20th Party Congress (2022) as distinct from Western models.
Campaigns for ideological and organisational discipline within the Party, notably the Yan'an campaign of the early 1940s against subjectivism, sectarianism and Party formalism.

t: The great founding spirit of the Party: the spiritual source of the Communist Party of China
zh: 伟大建党精神：中国共产党的精神之源
paras: Zeng Yi's commentary, published in Study Times in June 2025, asks why the "great founding spirit of the Party" is described as the "source" of the Communist Party of China's spirit. The article notes that Xi Jinping first put forward the formulation in 2021 at the centenary of the Party, and that the 20th Party Congress (2022) wrote "carrying forward the great founding spirit" into its theme. Zeng argues that the spirit is both the starting point of the Party's lineage of spirit and its guiding thread, expressing the Party's political character.

The piece is organised around two attributes of the founding spirit, which Zeng calls narrative and theoretical. It first traces the spirit to the founders' own intellectual paths, citing Li Dazhao, Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and Liu Shaoqi on how they came to Marxism. It then reads the 32-character formula in two halves, drawing on Mao's writings, Engels's graveside speech, early Party congress documents and recent statements by Xi.

Zeng argues that "source" has two senses: origin ("源头") and root ("本源"). As origin, the spirit stems from the Party's creation and from a national awakening in which Marxism was combined with China's concrete realities and traditional culture. As root, its first two phrases, on upholding truth and ideals and on the original aspiration and mission, answer what the Party is to do, namely its political ideal and goal. Its last two phrases, on fearlessness in struggle and on loyalty to the Party and to the people, answer what the Party is, namely its political essence and foundation. Zeng links these to the Party's growth from about fifty members to nearly 100 million and to what the author calls the twin miracles of rapid growth and long-term stability.

Zeng concludes that the founding spirit answers the fundamental question of what the Communist Party is and what it intends to do, summarises the political nature of a Marxist party, and points to the focus of Party political building. On this view it will encourage the whole Party to move forward and provide political assurance for building a strong country and national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media present the founding spirit as the root of the Party's spiritual lineage, together with the historical quotations used to support that reading.
quoteEn: The great founding spirit gives a concentrated answer to the fundamental question of what the Communist Party of China is and what it intends to do, sums up the political nature of a Marxist party, and implies the focus and point of application of the Party's political building.
quoteZh: 伟大建党精神集中回答了“中国共产党是什么、要干什么”这个根本问题，概括了马克思主义政党的政治属性，暗含了党的政治建设的着眼点与着力点

glossary.en: great founding spirit of the Party
glossary.explanation: A formulation Xi Jinping introduced in July 2021: upholding truth and ideals, practising the original aspiration and mission, fearing no sacrifice in struggle, and being loyal to the Party and the people. Official discourse presents it as the source of the Party's lineage of spirit.
The official term for the series of named "spirits" of the Party's history, such as the Yan'an spirit, which are traced back to the founding spirit.
Official phrase for the Party's founding purpose: seeking happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the Chinese nation.
The official name for China's development path, promoted since the 20th Party Congress (2022) as distinct from Western modernization.

t: Fine conduct shows the Party's personality strength
zh: 优良作风彰显党的人格力量
paras: Wang Yu's commentary, published in Study Times in June 2025, asks how the Communist Party of China wins public trust and secures its long-term rule. The author argues that, alongside the "power of truth" embodied in correct theory, the Party has a "power of personality" that shows itself chiefly in its fine conduct, and that sustained work on conduct is therefore essential in the new era.

The piece first defines "personality strength" as the outward effect of inner moral qualities, which attracts and unites followers. It then names the three fine styles in which this strength is concentrated. It ends with a historical survey of Party conduct-building from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

Wang's central claim is that the power of truth and the power of personality complement each other: theory without personality strength is pale and unconvincing, while personality strength gives theory its reach. The three fine styles are linking theory with practice, maintaining close ties with the masses, and criticism and self-criticism. In the author's account, these respectively guard against dogmatism, keep the Party serving the people, and let it correct itself, creating a virtuous circle between Party and people.

Wang concludes that conduct-building is the key route by which the Party shows its personality strength, because ordinary people judge the Party by the behaviour of the Party members around them. The article credits the eight-point rule (2012), the campaign against the "four malpractices" and long-term institution-building with renewing Party and government conduct. It also calls for perseverance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media link conduct-building to the Party's legitimacy and public support.
quoteEn: Strengthening conduct-building is the key route by which the Communist Party of China displays its powerful personality strength.
quoteZh: 加强作风建设是中国共产党展现强大人格力量的关键途径。

glossary.explanation: Rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012 to curb extravagance, bureaucracy and formalism among officials. Official accounts present them as the starting point of the conduct-building campaign.
Formalism, bureaucracy, hedonism and extravagance, the four faults of Party conduct targeted by the campaigns launched in 2013.
The Party's term for efforts to improve the work style and behaviour of its members and officials. It is treated as part of Party building.

t: Extending full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the grass roots
zh: 推动全面从严治党向基层延伸
paras: This short commentary, published in Study Times in June 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection to keep extending full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the grass roots. Qi argues that the grass roots are the foundation of the Party's governing position, so Party building and grass-roots governance must be guaranteed by rigorous Party discipline.

The article is organised around three tasks: making anti-corruption work in people's everyday surroundings tangible to ordinary people, fostering an atmosphere in which grass-roots cadres dare to act, and ensuring that livelihood policies are carried out locally. It opens with the 'tigers and flies' anti-corruption approach and ends with policy implementation.

On corruption, Qi argues that 'petty corruption' at the grass roots must be brought within the anti-corruption campaign, since unresolved cadre corruption would impair state governance and weaken the Party's credibility. Extension downward means greater intensity, not just wider coverage, and Qi proposes linking discipline inspection and supervision with grass-roots inspection tours. On cadres, Qi notes that the country has over 5.17 million grass-roots Party organisations and that 'lying flat' and reckless action persist. Qi proposes positive incentives, fair selection and promotion, training and job rotation. On livelihood policy, Qi proposes making policy delivery a key assessment indicator, holding inactive cadres accountable and opening channels for public oversight.

Qi concludes that grass-roots cadres must unite Party spirit with the people's interests, so that people feel the Party's care through concrete benefits. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media present the grass-roots dimension of Party discipline and anti-corruption work in 2025.
quoteEn: The grass roots are the end-point of the state governance system and the front line on which the Party consolidates its governing base; if corruption among grass-roots cadres is not effectively resolved, it will impede the normal operation of the governance system, weaken the Party's governing credibility and affect its cohesion.
quoteZh: 基层是国家治理体系的末梢，也是党巩固执政基础的前沿，基层干部腐败问题得不到有效解决，会妨碍国家治理体系的正常运行，削弱党的执政公信力，影响党的凝聚力。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the Xi Jinping era, used since 2014, for stricter Party discipline, anti-corruption work and cadre management at all levels.
Xi Jinping's shorthand for pursuing both senior officials ('tigers') and low-level officials ('flies') in the anti-corruption campaign.

t: Historical experience of Party membership building during the War of Resistance
st: The period of the nationwide war of resistance against Japan
zh: 全民族抗战时期党员队伍建设的历史经验
paras: This short commentary asks how the Communist Party of China handled the tension between expanding its membership and maintaining its quality during the nationwide War of Resistance against Japan. Wang argues that the Party resolved this creatively. According to the article, membership grew from just over 40,000 at the start of the war to more than 1.2 million by 1945, while the Party's vanguard character and purity were preserved.

The article is organised around three experiences: balancing breadth with vanguard quality in recruitment standards, combining theoretical education with practical training, and combining strict discipline with care for members. Wang draws on Party resolutions of 1935–1941, the 1942 rectification campaign and the Seventh Party Congress.

Wang traces how recruitment standards shifted. The Wayaobao meeting (1935) made willingness to struggle for Party policy the main criterion, and a 1938 resolution called for recruiting members tenfold and a hundredfold. After rapid expansion harmed quality, a 1939 decision urged quality over quantity. Wang then describes ideological education, the rectification campaign and practical tests such as rent reduction, production drives and guerrilla warfare. Finally, Wang points to a disciplinary system applied equally to ordinary members and leaders, paired with a policy of "examination and promotion in equal measure" and the principle of curing the illness to save the patient.

Wang concludes that these practices provided an organisational guarantee for victory in the war and in the New Democratic Revolution, and contributed to Marxist party-building theory. The author also holds that they offer lessons for advancing the new great project of Party building in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed overview of wartime Party recruitment, education and discipline, with references to key Party documents.
quoteEn: achieved a dialectical unity of breadth and vanguard quality in the Party's membership
quoteZh: 实现了党员队伍广泛性与先进性的辩证统一

glossary.explanation: An ideological and organisational campaign launched by the Party in Yan'an in 1942. It targeted dogmatism, sectarianism and other perceived errors and promoted criticism and self-criticism.
Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution, roughly 1919–1949, led by the proletariat and aimed at overthrowing imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism.

glossary.zh: 党的建设新的伟大工程
glossary.pinyin: dǎng de jiànshè xīn de wěidà gōngchéng
glossary.en: new great project of Party building
glossary.explanation: A formulation, in use since the 19th Party Congress (2017), for strengthening the Party's organisation, ideology and conduct in the new era.

t: The landmark significance of the Seventh Party Congress in the history of Party building
zh: 党的七大在党的建设史上的里程碑意义
paras: Marking the 80th anniversary of the Seventh Party Congress (April–June 1945), Li Ying, a researcher at the Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee, argues in this newspaper commentary that the congress was a landmark in the history of Party building. Li notes that Xi Jinping visited the congress site at Yangjialing in Yan'an in October 2022 and called for telling its story well. In Li's account, the congress developed Mao Zedong's thinking on Party building, substantially revised the Sixth Congress constitution, and formally formed the Party's first generation of central collective leadership with Mao Zedong at its core.

The article has three main sections. The first reviews Mao's reports and speeches at the congress, including On Coalition Government, the oral political report and the concluding speech. The second examines the 1945 Party Constitution and its changes from the 1928 version. The third traces how the leadership collective took shape, from the Zunyi Meeting through the 1943 reorganisation of central bodies to the election of the Seventh Central Committee.

On Mao's thinking, Li stresses the 'three work styles': integrating theory with practice, close ties with the masses, and self-criticism, which Mao presented as marks distinguishing the Party from all other parties. Li also covers Mao's treatment of Party spirit and individuality as a dialectical unity, relations among different groups of cadres, and speaking truthfully. On the constitution, Li identifies four innovations: a General Programme added for the first time; a clear definition of the Party's nature; the first statement of four duties and four rights of members, with rules on age and on leaving the Party; and a fuller formulation of democratic centralism with 'four subordinations'. On leadership, Li argues that Mao's position was reached through correct leadership and recognised by Liu Shaoqi, Ren Bishi, Chen Yi and others.

Li concludes that these measures reflected the Party's ideological, political and organisational maturity, established Mao Zedong Thought as the guiding ideology, and displayed the institutional strengths of a Marxist party. After the congress, Li says, the united Party advanced to the victory of the new-democratic revolution in 1949. Read the original if you want an official Chinese account of how the Seventh Congress is presented in Party-history writing, especially on the 1945 constitution and the formation of Mao's leadership collective.
quoteEn: The Seventh Congress also has landmark significance in the history of Party building.
quoteZh: 七大在党的建设史上也具有里程碑意义。

glossary.explanation: The Seventh National Congress of the Communist Party of China, held in Yan'an from April to June 1945. It adopted a new Party constitution and wrote Mao Zedong Thought into it as the guiding ideology.
The Party's official term for the adaptation of Marxism-Leninism to Chinese conditions, associated with Mao Zedong and formally adopted as guiding ideology at the Seventh Congress.
The Party's organisational principle combining election and discussion from below with unified, centralised leadership and discipline.
Mao's 1945 summary of the Party's distinguishing practices: integrating theory with practice, close ties with the people, and self-criticism.

t: Grasp the problem and you grasp the concrete
zh: 抓住了问题也就抓住了具体
paras: This short commentary, published in Study Times on 25 June 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's remark that grasping the problem means grasping the concrete, and applies it to improving Party conduct (作风建设). Zhu argues that ordinary people judge conduct not by the number of meetings, speeches or documents but by which problems actually get solved. The author presents problem-oriented, detail-focused work as a distinctive feature of conduct-building in the new era.

The piece opens by noting that the Party's history of victories is tied to its ability to seize the key problem of each period. Zhu stresses that problems are concrete, change over time, and that yesterday's remedy may become today's new ailment. The main body then sets out four pairs of distinctions cadres need to draw, before a brief closing call.

The core argument is that problems must be classified before they are solved, and that principle should not be used to answer concrete complaints from grassroots people. Zhu separates matters of principle, where there is no room for compromise (political direction, the people's interests, national security), from flexible matters that allow local experimentation. Individual problems are to be mined for general lessons, while general problems need top-level design. Problems at one link in a chain are distinguished from problems of the whole process, and simple problems, which call for quick action, from deep and complex ones, which need systemic and lasting mechanisms.

Zhu concludes that internalising this approach is a basic skill for leading cadres facing new contradictions. Telling the 'genus' from the 'species' of a problem is described as the key to the concrete, and the author expects governance to improve as countless specific problems are handled by category. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-press commentary translates Xi Jinping's problem-oriented rhetoric into guidance for cadres' working methods.
quoteEn: Today the problems of conduct raised by cadres and the public, especially at the grassroots, are all very specific; one cannot answer the specific with principle, but must respond to them one by one, classify them scientifically and solve them concretely.
quoteZh: 当前，干部群众特别是基层群众反映的作风问题都很具体，不能以原则来应对具体，要一一回应、科学分类、具体解决。

glossary.explanation: A long-running Party campaign theme concerning the work style and discipline of Party members and officials, including opposing formalism and bureaucratism.
A working principle emphasised by Xi Jinping: policy and work should start from identifying and solving real problems.

t: Grasping Party spirit, Party conduct and Party discipline together
zh: 坚持党性党风党纪一起抓
paras: This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in June 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's formulation that Party spirit, Party conduct and Party discipline form an organic whole: Party spirit is the foundation, conduct the outward expression and discipline the safeguard. Li Yu argues that handling the three together, and linking the correction of work style, the enforcement of discipline and the fight against corruption, summarises practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and deepens understanding of how a Marxist ruling party is built. In Li's account it is also a key lever for the Party's self-reform.

The article has two parts. The first traces the idea from Engels's first use of "Party spirit" in 1845, through the Communist Manifesto and Marx and Engels's 1879 letter to Bebel, to Lenin's remarks on discipline at the ninth congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks). It then follows the Chinese Communist Party's own experience, from the Three Main Rules of Discipline and Eight Points for Attention to the reform era. The second part sets out practical requirements.

Li argues that Xi's formulation combines treating symptoms and root causes, and combines inner consciousness with outer norms. It sets up a dialectical path from cultivating Party spirit, to forming work style, to shaping discipline, and so supports tackling cases where misconduct in work style and corruption are intertwined. Li proposes three practical principles. The first is systematic thinking, with overall advance and breakthroughs on key points. The second is making the effort regular and long-term, attending to small details such as gift-giving and club hospitality. The third is leading from above, with leading cadres as the "critical few".

Li concludes that grasping the three together is essential to keeping the Party advanced and pure. Li calls for integrating this work into everyday tasks, linking it to assessment systems and coordinating the organisation, propaganda and discipline-inspection bodies. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of the theoretical lineage and practical agenda behind the Party's current campaign on conduct, discipline and anti-corruption.
quoteEn: Grasping Party spirit, Party conduct and Party discipline together is a key measure for keeping the Party forever advanced and pure.
quoteZh: 坚持党性党风党纪一起抓，是永葆党的先进性和纯洁性的关键举措。

glossary.explanation: The principled stand, loyalty and political character expected of Party members. Chinese Marxism traces it to Engels's use of the term in 1845.
The Party's style of work and behaviour, including its ties to the masses and its handling of formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance.
The rules and disciplinary regulations binding Party members, enforced by discipline-inspection bodies.
A term prominent under Xi Jinping for the Party's efforts to correct its own problems and strengthen itself without external pressure.
A phrase for leading cadres, whose example is regarded as decisive for the conduct of the Party as a whole.

t: Origins, strategies and effects of the Communist Party of China's emotional mobilisation in the Yan'an period
zh: 延安时期中国共产党情感动员的缘起、策略及效应
source: Journal of Yan'an University (Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 2
paras: Most studies of the Communist Party of China's mass mobilisation follow a class-struggle line and focus on political and economic dimensions. Li Dan argues that this neglects emotion. The article takes emotional mobilisation, defined after Bai Shuying as the process of using emotional work in interaction to arouse, stimulate or change people's cognition, attitudes and evaluations. It asks why the Party mobilised emotions in the Yan'an period, how it turned feeling into revolutionary action, and what followed, so as to explain from the angle of emotional identification why the Party was able to succeed.

The article has three parts: the origins of emotional mobilisation, its strategies and its effects. The evidence is drawn mainly from statements by Mao Zedong, Ren Bishi, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai and Xie Juezai, from Zhao Chaogou's reportage Yan'an Yi Yue (A Month in Yan'an), from wartime pictorial publications and from border-region education regulations. It also cites Elizabeth Perry's work on the Chinese revolution and emotion.

Li identifies three emotional obstacles in the early Yan'an years: a latent national consciousness, passive revolutionary morale marked by fear and defeatism, and hesitant attitudes towards the Party after Guomindang propaganda against it. Li then sets out five strategies that, in the article's account, escalated step by step: improving material life through land distribution and relief to lay an emotional foundation; arousing national sentiment; shaping the image of the Party through Mao Zedong, the disciplined army and model figures such as Norman Bethune, Zhang Side and labour heroes; intensifying anger by publicising Japanese atrocities, including in photographs; and political education. Education also regulated emotion, for example by curbing the killing of prisoners and, through the rectification movement, by unifying feeling.

Li holds that emotional mobilisation helped the revolution succeed, citing Perry's view that the Party beat the Guomindang partly by mobilising popular emotion. It also deepened popular emotional identification with the Party, including its leader, policies and character, and enriched understanding of Mao Zedong Thought, with Mao portrayed as an expert in emotional mobilisation. Li adds that emotion worked together with other forms of mobilisation, and that it is gradual and long-term but, once aroused, the most fundamental and lasting. Read the original if you study Yan'an-period mass mobilisation, Party propaganda or the role of emotion in Chinese revolutionary history, and want the primary sources the author draws on.
quoteEn: Emotional mobilisation tends to be gradual and long-term, but once emotion has been aroused, its role and effects are often the most central, the most essential and the most lasting.
quoteZh: 情感动员往往表现为一定的渐进性与长期性，但是一旦情感被激发，其发挥的作用与起到的效果往往也是最核心、最本质、最持久的。

glossary.explanation: The use of emotional appeals and practices to change people's attitudes and move them to act. The article adopts Bai Shuying's definition from recent Chinese scholarship.
An ideological campaign launched in Yan'an around 1942 to unify the Party through study, criticism and self-criticism, targeting subjectivism and sectarianism.
The Party's official term for Mao's theory adapted to Chinese conditions, largely formed during the Yan'an period.

t: The roots of the Party's spirit of self-reform in fine traditional Chinese culture: an exploration
zh: 党的自我革命精神的中华优秀传统文化根脉探析
paras: The article asks how the Communist Party of China's spirit of self-reform is rooted in fine traditional Chinese culture. Huang and Zhang present that spirit as a concrete outcome of the Two Integrations in the field of Party building. They argue that it fits closely with four traditional ideas and has turned them from static cultural 'genes' into a dynamic political practice.

The article has four main sections, each pairing a traditional value with an element of Party discourse. The first links the 'historical cycle' question, which Huang Yanpei put to Mao Zedong in 1945, to a consciousness of hardship and potential danger. The second links the 'unique problems of a large party' to the moral character of self-scrutiny in solitude. The third links the 'four selfs' (self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation) to the idea of discarding the old and establishing the new. The fourth links the 'sitting an exam' spirit to the ceaseless striving of the Chinese nation. Classical sources such as the Book of Changes, Confucius, Mencius, Mozi and Wang Yangming are set beside speeches by Xi Jinping and earlier Party leaders.

The authors' central move is to read each Party practice as a modern continuation of a classical ethic. Self-reform is the Party's 'second answer' to the historical cycle, after Mao's 'new path of democracy', and the authors tie it to the maxim of preparing for danger in times of peace. Criticism and self-criticism, inspection tours and the Party's rectification and education campaigns are read as updated forms of 'being watchful over oneself when alone' and of correcting faults. Revisions of the Party Constitution and of Party regulations, the Eight-point Regulation and the emphasis on study are cast as inheritors of the reformist tradition. Xi's phrase that self-reform is 'always on the road' is read as the contemporary form of the ancient ideal of self-strengthening.

Huang and Zhang conclude that the self-reform spirit has moved from fit with traditional culture to combination and then to fusion, achieving the 'creative transformation and innovative development' of that culture. They state that this cultural root gives full and rigorous self-governance of the Party a deep foundation. In their view it also supplies spiritual strength for resolving the problems unique to a large party and for building a Marxist party that stays in power long-term. Read the original if you want to see how Party-building theory is justified through Chinese classical sources, with the specific classical phrases it uses for each pairing.
quoteEn: The Party's spirit of self-reform is highly compatible with the traditional Chinese spirit of preparing for danger in times of peace, of self-scrutiny in solitude, of discarding the old and establishing the new, and of ceaseless self-strengthening.
quoteZh: 党的自我革命精神与中华优秀传统文化中的居安思危、慎独自省、革故鼎新、自强不息精神具有高度的契合性

glossary.explanation: A formula in Party theory for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second integration, with traditional culture, was stressed by Xi Jinping in 2023.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The slogan for the Party's strict discipline and anti-corruption drive since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
The pattern in which dynasties rise quickly and then collapse. Huang Yanpei raised it with Mao Zedong in Yan'an in 1945, and the Party treats escaping it as a basic question of governance.

glossary.en: unique problems of a large party
glossary.explanation: A phrase introduced by Xi Jinping in his report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It refers to the problems that arise from the Party's size and long period in power, later elaborated as the 'six ways of staying'.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: The value, historical evolution and basic experience of the Communist Party of China's building of cultural leadership
zh: 中国共产党文化领导权建设的价值意蕴、历史演进及基本经验
source: Ideological and Political Education Research (思想教育研究), 2025 no. 4
paras: Xiao and Ge take up the Party's cultural leadership (cultural hegemony in the Gramscian register, rendered in Chinese as the Party's "cultural leadership"), a proposition Xi Jinping put forward in the new era. They argue that existing scholarship concentrates on the new era, theoretical bases and practical paths, and that the topic should be examined across the Party's century-plus history. Their thesis is that building cultural leadership strengthens the Party's governing position and ideological foundation, and that its history yields lessons for propaganda and cultural work today.

The article is organised in three parts: the value of cultural leadership, its historical evolution, and the basic experience drawn from it. The historical section moves through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. It cites Lenin, Marx and Engels, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping.

On value, the authors contend that cultural leadership is an inherent requirement of consolidating the Party's core leadership, a political guarantee for taking on a new cultural mission, and the key to holding the dominant say in ideological work. They argue that it supports cultural subjectivity through the Two Integrations, the goal of a cultural powerhouse by 2035, soft power and cultural security. Historically, they trace a line from left-wing cultural organisations and Yan'an literary policy, through control of the media and the "Double Hundred" policy, to the Three Represents and the new era's emphasis on core socialist values. From this they derive four lessons: comprehensive Party leadership over cultural work, backed by law and institutions; the guiding position of Marxism in ideology; a people-centred orientation; and resolving the dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western, to achieve cultural innovation.

The authors conclude that the Party has built cultural leadership step by step through winning, constructing, consolidating and improving it, and that this experience offers guidance for building a cultural powerhouse. They call for firmly holding leadership, management and discourse power in ideology, countering Western non-Marxist currents and historical nihilism, and reconciling a unified guiding ideology with cultural diversity. Read the original if you want a periodised, officially aligned account of how the Party conceptualises its cultural leadership from 1921 to the present, with references to key Party documents.
quoteEn: Upholding the Party's cultural leadership is an inherent requirement of consolidating the Party's core leadership position.
quoteZh: 坚持党的文化领导权是巩固党的核心领导地位的内在要求

glossary.explanation: The Party's leading position in cultural and ideological work. The term overlaps with Gramsci's cultural hegemony; Xi Jinping formulated it as a formal proposition in the new era.
Xi Jinping's formula of combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. The "Second Integration" is the latter.
Policy announced by Mao Zedong in 1956 encouraging "a hundred flowers blossoming" in the arts and "a hundred schools contending" in scholarship, under Party leadership.
Jiang Zemin's thinking holding that the Party represents advanced productive forces, the orientation of advanced culture and the fundamental interests of the people.
A twelve-term set of values (including prosperity, democracy, harmony, patriotism) promoted by the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

t: The people-centred character of the Chinese Communist Party's self-reform
zh: 中国共产党自我革命的人民性意蕴阐析
paras: Liu Dongxu and Huang Rongsheng ask in what sense the Chinese Communist Party's "self-revolution" (rendered here as the Party's self-reform) has a "people-centred" (renminxing) character. They argue that this character is the foundational one among its several attributes. It follows from the Party's essential nature as a Marxist party, and it runs through each of the four "selfs" named in official documents: self-purification, self-improvement in the sense of perfecting itself, self-renewal and self-elevation.

The article opens with a review of Chinese scholarship since Xi Jinping first used the term in 2015. That work covers the term's origins, meaning, features and experience, and a few studies treat its people-centred side. The authors say they draw on political science, Party history and Marxist philosophy, guided by Xi Jinping's thinking on Party self-reform and by the Party's practice over more than a century. They also tie the discussion to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and to Chinese modernization. The body has five parts: the origin, then one part for each of the four "selfs".

On the origin, the authors cite Marx and Lenin to argue that genuine "people-centredness" belongs to proletarian parties, while bourgeois parties use it as a cover for class interests. The Party, in their account, has no special interests of its own, which gives it the courage to correct itself. It also aims to safeguard and develop the fundamental interests of the great majority. Self-purification is then linked to a mission of responsibility to the people: listening to their voices, dealing with fading original aspiration, lost ideals and corruption, and filtering out "impurities". Self-improvement rests on relying closely on the people, taking in their views, and repairing the Party's body, strengthening its mechanisms and broadening its functions. Self-renewal means decisions that reflect popular wishes and acceptance of popular oversight, which the authors present as the "second answer", alongside democracy, to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Self-elevation means accepting the people's judgement, protecting their interests, and building the skills to serve them.

The authors conclude that self-reform and people-centredness are mutually reinforcing and that the Party's long-term governance depends on both. They present their reading as theoretical support for studying the Third Plenum's decisions, raising the Party's leadership of deepening reform and Chinese modernization, and rallying the people behind building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how official Party-building discourse links self-reform to the people, with its supporting citations from Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping.
quoteEn: Self-reform, as the distinguishing mark separating the Chinese Communist Party from other parties, stems not only from the Party having no special interests of its own, but also from its aim of better safeguarding and advancing the fundamental interests of the broadest masses of the people.
quoteZh: 自我革命作为中国共产党区别于其他政党的显著标志，不仅源于党没有任何自己的特殊利益，同时也源于自我革命旨在更好地实现维护发展最广大人民的根本利益。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping first used in 2015 and later made central to Party-building discourse. It refers to the Party's continuing effort to correct itself, discipline its members and fight corruption. The Party's own English renderings include 'self-reform' and 'self-revolution'.

glossary.zh: 自我净化、自我完善、自我革新、自我提高
glossary.pinyin: zìwǒ jìnghuà, zìwǒ wánshàn, zìwǒ géxīn, zìwǒ tígāo
glossary.explanation: The 'four selfs' that Party documents name as the aims of the Party's self-reform. The article structures its argument around them.
The official name for the Party's development path, promoted especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022), which stresses features that differ from Western modernization.

glossary.en: historical cycle of rise and fall
glossary.explanation: Refers to the 1945 'cave dialogue' between Mao Zedong and Huang Yanpei about how to avoid the pattern of dynastic rise and decline. Mao answered 'democracy'. Xi Jinping later added self-reform as a 'second answer'.

t: An institutional path for leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform
st: An analysis based on the "spillover effect" of intra-Party regulations
zh: 以党的自我革命引领社会革命的制度路径研究
zhSub: 基于党内法规“溢出效力”的分析
source: Journal of Nanjing Normal University (Social Science Edition), 2024 no. 6
paras: The 20th Party Congress report (2022) calls for "leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform". Wang asks how this leadership can be given an institutional and practical form, not only an ideological one. The article argues that intra-Party regulations, through what it calls their "spillover effect" beyond the Party, are the main institutional channel linking the two revolutions.

The article has three parts. It first defines "spillover effect" and sets out the relationship between that effect and the two revolutions. It then analyses the institutional logic of the leadership relationship. Finally it examines concrete institutional arrangements, using named regulations such as those on united front work, inspection tours, discipline inspection and joint Party–government documents.

Wang defines spillover as an extension of the scope of a regulation's force: in space, in persons and in subject matter. Social revolution is read, following Xi Jinping, as a new movement of social construction that consolidates the existing superstructure and can only be led by the Party. Because intra-Party regulations govern both "Party building" and "Party leadership", Wang argues, they mediate between self-reform and social revolution. The institutional logic has two strands: effect moving from inside the Party to outside it, and from self-discipline to discipline of others. The Party restrains itself, and its regulations then guide society mainly through broad direction and only limited direct regulation. Wang insists that such spillover must not replace state law. In practice, the author says, spillover works through Party leadership, rigorous self-governance and Party–government cooperation. It also raises the Party's revolutionary leadership capacity through leadership regulations, the Party's leadership system and "hybrid" Party regulations issued jointly with state organs.

Wang concludes that the spillover effect is a distinctive strength of the legal system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and operates through both authorising and prohibiting provisions. In the article's account, this dual effect strengthens the Party's capacity to lead and also sets the direction and aims of social revolution. Read the original if you study Party-building theory, intra-Party regulations or how Chinese scholars link Party discipline, the legal system and social governance.
quoteEn: The spillover effect of intra-Party regulations objectively exists, but it must not expand arbitrarily, and the spilled-over force of intra-Party regulations must never replace the force of law.
quoteZh: 党内法规“溢出效力”客观存在，但不能肆意扩张，溢出的党内法规效力绝不能代替法律效力

glossary.explanation: A term stressed in Xi Jinping-era Party discourse for the Party's continuous self-purification, improvement and renewal, presented as the second answer to the problem of the historical cycle of rise and fall.

Formal rules issued by Party bodies, such as the Central Committee and its departments, to regulate Party leadership and Party building. They are enforced through Party discipline and are distinct from state law.
Here the Marxist term is read, following Xi Jinping, as a new movement of social construction under Party leadership rather than the overthrow of the existing political order.
The Party's work of building ties with non-Party groups, such as democratic parties, religious figures, overseas Chinese and ethnic minority representatives.

t: A precious asset for Party conduct in the new era
zh: 新时代作风建设的宝贵财富
paras: This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in June 2025, asks how the revolutionary culture of the Communist Party can inform efforts to improve Party conduct today. Huang and Qiao argue that revolutionary culture holds rich ideas on conduct, and that its glorious traditions and fine style remain a spiritual asset for the new era.

The authors draw on episodes from the Jinggangshan period, the Long March, the Yan'an rectification movement and the early People's Republic. They cite Mao Zedong's "single lamp wick", Zhou Enlai's "ten family rules", the "Three Rules of Discipline and Six Points for Attention" and the "six provisions" of the Second Plenum of the Seventh Central Committee.

The argument is organised around four qualities. Firm conviction and the courage to win supply the ideological foundation. Putting the people first and serving without selfishness give conduct its purpose. Seeking truth from facts and self-reform are described as the key path, with the Yan'an rectification movement presented as a model of criticism and self-criticism against subjectivism, sectarianism and "Party formalism". Hard struggle and dedication are called the essential requirement. For each, Huang and Qiao set a present-day demand, including the Two Upholds, solving people's pressing concerns, investigating conduct and corruption together, and rejecting hedonism and extravagance.

The authors conclude that cadres should keep applying the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. In their view, revolutionary culture should nurture the original aspiration, strengthen resolve and give Party members a loyal, clean and responsible character, adding "red momentum" to building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link revolutionary history to current campaigns on Party conduct.
quoteEn: For Chinese Communists, revolutionary culture contains the spiritual code of where we come from and where we are going, and it is a precious spiritual asset for the Party's conduct building.
quoteZh: 对中国共产党人来说，革命文化蕴含着我们“从哪里来、向何处去”的精神密码，是党的作风建设的宝贵精神财富。

glossary.explanation: A political formula from 2018 that calls on Party members to uphold Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Party Central Committee and the whole Party, and to uphold the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership.
An ideological campaign led by Mao Zedong from 1942 in Yan'an. It used criticism and self-criticism to target subjectivism, sectarianism and Party formalism.
Rules adopted by the Central Committee in December 2012 to curb bureaucracy, extravagance and formalism among officials, and a basis for later Party conduct campaigns.

t: Studying closely Xi Jinping's important statements on strengthening the Party's work style
zh: 深学细悟习近平总书记关于加强党的作风建设的重要论述
paras: Writing in connection with the Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, Song Fufan argues that Party members must study Xi Jinping's statements on the Party's work style closely. The commentary opens from the premise that the Party's style is its image and bears on its survival. Song contends that these statements give scientific guidance for making work-style building a regular and long-term practice in the new era.

The piece has three parts. The first sets out the basic answers Xi's statements give on work style. The second explains why the campaign matters for building a high-calibre cadre corps, for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and for advancing Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The third lists practical requirements for the campaign.

Song's central claim, taken from Xi, is that work-style problems are at root problems of Party spirit (dangxing) and, at their core, of the Party's relationship with the people. Hence work style must be built by tempering Party spirit and by bringing Party and masses closer together. For the first, Song names firm ideals and convictions, a correct handling of public and private interests, rigorous intra-Party political life, and a thorough spirit of self-reform. For the second, Song names the mass line, genuine feeling for the people, and cadres' position as public servants. Song presents work-style building as the breakthrough point of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012), starting from the eight-point regulation.

Song's practical requirements are these: leading cadres, as the 'key minority', set an example; they hold correct views of power, of achievements and of career; the 'four undesirable work styles' (formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism, extravagance) are corrected; work-style correction, discipline and anti-corruption are pursued together; and the effort is made routine and long-term through institutional mechanisms. Song also calls for positive incentives alongside tolerance of error and correction. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Central Party School scholarship presents Xi Jinping's work-style discourse and the logic of the 2025 campaign.
quoteEn: Work-style problems are in essence problems of Party spirit, and Party spirit is also what plays the decisive role.
quoteZh: 作风问题本质上是党性问题，起决定作用的也是党性。

glossary.explanation: A set of rules on official conduct adopted by the Politburo in December 2012, covering matters such as meetings, travel, frugality and closeness to the masses. It is the starting point of the post-2012 work-style campaigns.
The ideological and moral qualities expected of a Communist Party member, including loyalty to the Party's principles. Chinese Party writing treats it as the foundation of good conduct.
Formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, named in the 2013 mass-line campaign as the main work-style problems to be corrected.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: Official term for the strategy, prominent since 2012, of strict Party discipline and anti-corruption, treated as one of the 'Four-Pronged Comprehensive Strategy'.
The Party's working method of drawing on the people's views and serving their interests. It dates from the Mao era and is described as the Party's lifeline.
The official term for China's path of modernization, set out in the 20th Party Congress report (2022).
Official term for leading cadres, whose conduct is held to set the tone for the whole Party.

t: Governing the Party with a reform spirit and strict standards
zh: 坚持用改革精神和严的标准管党治党
source: Renmin Luntan·Xueshu Qianyan (People's Tribune · Academic Frontiers), 2025 no. 6
