paras: Tang Huangfeng and Liu Linfeng ask why the Communist Party's level of leadership matters for the further comprehensive deepening of reform and how it can be raised. Taking up the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which names the Party's leadership level as a core aim and its overall leadership as the first principle of reform, the authors argue that this level directly determines whether reform succeeds or fails. They propose a three-part account: the underlying logic, the internal mechanism, and the strategic path.

The article is organised in three sections. The first sets out the logic under three heads: fidelity to scientific socialism's principle of Marxist party leadership, the Party's accumulated experience of leading reform and opening up, and the Party's mission and responsibility in the new era. The second examines the mechanism through which leadership acts on reform, in four dimensions: direction and path, strategy and tactics, policy and institutions, and organisational and personnel support. The third turns to practical paths. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Deng Xiaoping, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, and cites figures on the Party's organisation and on the Central Commission for Comprehensively Deepening Reform.

In the authors' reading, the Party sets direction by holding the line on fundamentals and the people-centred stance, sharpens strategy through sound judgement of complex conditions and national planning, and supplies policy and institutional frameworks. They cite the central reform leading body, set up in 2013, which they say has held 72 meetings and approved over 600 documents, together with decision-making, coordination and supervision mechanisms. They also point to a Party organisation of more than 99 million members and to cadre and talent management. Under the Party's leadership, they argue, reform moved from local experiments to systematic integration.

For the new journey, the authors call for four improvements. These are the central leadership's overall design, coordination and integrated advancement of reform; the ability of Party committees at each level to produce replicable, extendable experience, including through the mass line and pilot schemes; the mobilisation of cadres and members; and supervision, inspection and follow-up of implementation. They conclude that institution-building should be the main thread and that the whole Party must keep a strategic and historical initiative in raising its leadership level. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party-building scholarship links leadership capacity to reform implementation.
quoteEn: Raising the Party's leadership level in comprehensively deepening reform upholds and develops the basic principles of scientific socialism, accords with the general laws of reform and development, and is a strategic choice that meets the people's expectations and withstands the test of practice.
quoteZh: 提高党对全面深化改革的领导水平，坚持并发展了科学社会主义的基本原理，顺应了改革与发展的普遍规律，是符合人民期待且经得起实践检验的战略选择。

glossary.zh: 中央全面深化改革委员会
glossary.en: Central Commission for Comprehensively Deepening Reform
glossary.explanation: The Party body that designs and coordinates reform, chaired by Xi Jinping. It was created in 2013 as a leading group and renamed a commission after 2018.

t: Continuing to extend full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the grassroots
zh: 持续推动全面从严治党向基层延伸
paras: This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection to "continuously extend full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the grassroots". Li Junwei argues that grassroots Party organisations underpin all Party work and its combat effectiveness, and that closing the "last mile" of Party discipline requires clear responsibilities, stronger grassroots supervision and lighter burdens on local cadres.

The article has three parts. The first describes extension to the grassroots as a distinctive feature of Party governance in the new era. The second sets out priority tasks. The third explains how such governance consolidates the Party's long-term rule.

In the first part, Li holds that the Party has combined a focus on the "critical few" (senior cadres) with discipline over the "vast majority", passing responsibility down level by level. Li says that the Party has built up branches and made grassroots organisations "fortresses", and that campaigns against corruption in poverty relief, land requisition and similar areas won public trust. The priority tasks are to make Party committees bear primary responsibility, in line with the responsibilities of functional departments and discipline inspection bodies, and to deal routinely with misconduct and corruption close to ordinary people, such as school meals, village collective assets and funeral-sector abuses. Li also calls for integrating supervision (discipline inspection, inspection tours, auditing, big-data tools), extending inspections to villages and communities, and implementing the 2024 regulations on curbing formalism to reduce burdens on the grassroots.

Li concludes that Party requirements must reach every link of grassroots governance, every branch and every member, through stricter education, management and Party life. Li also holds that results must benefit the public, since "the people's hearts are the greatest politics", with cadres' conduct serving as the barometer of Party conduct. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how the Central Party School frames grassroots Party discipline, supervision and burden reduction in 2025.
quoteEn: The people's hearts are the greatest politics; to keep extending full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the grassroots, the test must be whether it responds to what the people think, worry about and hope for, and resolves the prominent problems they complain of most.
quoteZh: 民心是最大的政治，持续推动全面从严治党向基层延伸，就要把顺应群众所思所想所忧所盼、解决好群众反映强烈的突出问题作为检验标准。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: Official slogan since the 18th Party Congress (2012) for strict Party discipline, anti-corruption work and organisational management, one of the "Four Comprehensives".
Official phrase for senior and leading cadres, who are held to higher standards of conduct and supervision.
The duty of Party committees and their leaders to run Party discipline in their own jurisdiction, distinct from the supervisory responsibility of discipline inspection commissions.

glossary.zh: 整治形式主义为基层减负
glossary.pinyin: zhěngzhì xíngshì zhǔyì wèi jīcéng jiǎnfù
glossary.en: curbing formalism to reduce burdens on the grassroots
glossary.literal: rectifying formalism to lighten the load on the grassroots
glossary.explanation: A campaign to limit excessive paperwork, meetings, inspections and online reporting demanded of local cadres by higher levels.

t: The Party's leadership of urban work: historical review and lessons
zh: 党领导城市工作的历史回顾与经验启示
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2024 no. 11
paras: Xue Zelin starts from the fact that China's urbanization rate passed 60% in 2019, which the author takes to mark a middle-to-late stage of urbanization. The article asks how the Party's historical experience of urban work can be summed up so that the idea of the "people's city" runs through all urban work and points to a modernized path of urban governance. Xue's answer is that two keywords, "the people" and "development", run through seventy-five years of practice, and that four lessons follow.

After a short survey of existing studies, organised around the Party's centenary and the seventy years of the People's Republic, the article builds a three-dimensional analytical framework. It draws on Xi Jinping's remarks on the people's city, his call for systems thinking and the policy cycle of formulation, implementation and evaluation. Xue then reviews key urban-work meetings and documents in three periods: socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. A final section sets out a path for people's-city building under Chinese modernization.

In the framework, formulating the policy of building a people's city is the policy-making stage. The principle that the people's city is built by the people is the implementing tool, and the principle that it is built for the people is the evaluation standard. Xue reads the three periods through this lens, from the shift from consumer to producer cities, through the focus on urban economic growth, to the new-era aim of urban governance modernization. From this Xue draws four lessons: upholding the Party's leadership, putting the people first, seeking truth from facts, and building consensus and unity of purpose. The author also links urban governance models to successive industrial revolutions and argues that the fourth, digital one gives China a chance to explore its own urban path.

Xue concludes that urban work must follow the Party's leadership and a people-centred stance. Policy formulation should meet the era's mission, given what the author calls unprecedented urbanization, ageing and digitalization. Implementation should operate at the macro, meso and micro levels, from functional positioning to "people's livelihood projects". Evaluation should treat residents as the principal body, with rights to be informed, to participate and to supervise. Read the original if you study Chinese urban policy, the Party's official account of its urban work, or how the people's city concept is being turned into an analytical framework.
quoteEn: Although the strategic priorities and policies of the Party's urban work changed many times over seventy-five years of struggle, each time the adjustment was made accurately and promptly on the basis of seeking truth from facts and of actual work needs.
quoteZh: 虽然在75年奋斗历程中，我们党城市工作战略重点和政策发生了多次变化，但每次都基于实事求是，立足实际工作需要准确及时做出的政策调整。

glossary.literal: important concept of the people's city
glossary.explanation: A concept associated with Xi Jinping's 2019 Shanghai visit, summed up as "the people's city is built by the people and for the people". It is presented as the guiding principle of urban work in the new era.
The official term for China's own path to modernization, given prominence at the 20th Party Congress (2022).
Application to cities of the goal of modernizing the national system and capacity of governance. It stresses refined, precise and systematic management.
A long-standing Party principle of basing policy on actual conditions. It is associated with Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping.

t: Chinese Communists' understanding and critique of capitalist modernization
zh: 中国共产党人对资本主义现代化的认识与批判
paras: How should a latecomer country relate to the modernization that the capitalist West pioneered? Liu Mingming argues that Chinese Communists have never worshipped or copied capitalist modernization. Instead, the article says, they have insisted on 'surpassing through critique'. Liu holds that copying it would only make a relatively backward country a dependency, and that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation therefore requires a new road of modernization that sublates the capitalist one.

The article begins with the failure of the late Qing and republican-era schemes (from 'Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for use' to wholesale Westernization) advanced by the landlord class and the bourgeoisie. It then sets out four features of the Communists' critique: its proletarian standpoint, its comprehensive scope, its dialectical method and its aim of transcendence. It draws on the Communist Manifesto, Mao Zedong's 1944 remarks on industrialization and several statements by Xi Jinping.

In Liu's account, the critique is comprehensive because capitalist modernization is characterised as expansionist and predatory, materialist, destructive of the balance between humans and nature, and polarising in wealth. Liu adds that it rests on a 'centre–periphery' structure of exploitation that can enrich a few but not deliver common prosperity. The method is dialectical: Communists separate what is specific to the capitalist system (colonial expansion, materialism, polarisation, ecological imbalance) from the shared achievements of human civilization (advanced science and technology, scientific management, cultural accomplishments), which they say should be learned from. Liu argues that Chinese modernization surpasses the capitalist model by keeping a socialist direction, competing openly in the capitalist world market, and correcting capitalism's distortions, without implying that other countries must follow China's path.

Liu concludes from the standpoint of historical materialism that this transcendence is objectively necessary. Chinese modernization grew out of the critical inheritance of capitalist achievements, so Liu warns that wholesale negation of Western modernization would harm it. Capitalist modernization cannot resolve the contradiction between socialized production and private ownership. Liu says Chinese modernization removes this obstacle by keeping public ownership dominant and pursuing common prosperity, and that Party leadership and Marxism supply its political and cultural guidance. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-aligned scholarship frames the critique of Western modernization and the case for Chinese modernization as its successor.
quoteEn: Chinese Communists have never blindly worshipped or imitated capitalist modernization, but have persisted in surpassing it through critique.
quoteZh: 中国共产党人对资本主义现代化从来都不是盲目崇拜和模仿，而是坚持在批判中超越。

glossary.explanation: An official concept, developed especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022), describing China's own path to modernization as distinct from Western models. It is characterised by a large population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony with nature and peaceful development.
A goal of socialism in Chinese Party discourse, meaning prosperity shared by all rather than by a few. It has been given renewed emphasis under Xi Jinping.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's central national goal, presented as restoring China's strength and standing after the 'century of humiliation'.

glossary.en: 'Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for use'
glossary.explanation: A late Qing reformist formula for adopting Western technology while preserving Chinese institutions and values as the foundation.

t: Further deepening reform comprehensively and adhering to institution-building as the main thread
zh: 进一步全面深化改革与坚持以制度建设为主线阐论
paras: Xu Yaotong takes up a principle in the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization: that further comprehensive deepening of reform must "adhere to institution-building as the main thread". Xu treats this as a new formulation and the core idea of the Decision. The article argues that the two are dialectically linked: reform needs institution-building as its main line, and institution-building depends on further deepening reform.

The article has three parts. The first traces a historical lineage from Marx and Engels, through the Paris Commune, to the Chinese Communists from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping. The second analyses the six components of "further comprehensively deepening reform" in the Decision: historical position, requirements of the times, guiding thought, overall goal, principles and tasks. The third parses the phrase "adhere to institution-building as the main thread" and what it implies for method.

Xu reads Marx and Engels as holding that socialism is a developing, constantly reforming society with no ready-made blueprint, so that reform and institution-building are ordinary, permanent tasks. Xu argues that each of the Decision's six components ties back to institutions, with the seven areas of focus essentially being institutional systems. Xu also glosses "main thread" as three things: main purpose, main axis and leading role. The article counts 187 uses of "institution" in the Decision. For method, it follows the Decision's formula: strengthen top-level design, advance breaking and establishing together, and establish the new before breaking the old. It also separates three tiers of institutions. Fundamental institutions are to be consolidated, basic institutions improved, and important institutions innovated through new supply.

Xu concludes that reform must carry institution-building through its whole process, across all fields and mechanisms, and into every step and procedure, under the rule of law. Officials are urged to build institutional awareness and act by the rules. Xu presents this as continuing a long line of Party practice, from Deng Xiaoping's call for a more mature and fixed set of institutions to Xi Jinping's stress on institution-building. Read the original if you want a Party-theory exposition of the Third Plenum's institutional logic, with its historical genealogy and its textual breakdown of the Decision.
quoteEn: To further deepen reform comprehensively, one must adhere to institution-building as the main thread; and to adhere to institution-building as the main thread necessarily requires and relies on further comprehensively deepening reform.
quoteZh: 要进一步全面深化改革，就要坚持以制度建设为主线；而要坚持以制度建设为主线，则必然需要和依靠进一步全面深化改革。

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept of a modernization path with Chinese characteristics, prominent in Party documents since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.literal: taking institution-building as the main line
glossary.explanation: A principle added to the reform principles in the 2024 Third Plenum Decision. It makes building and refining institutional systems the organising line of reform.

t: The conception of history in the Communist Manifesto and the development of modern society
zh: 《共产党宣言》的历史观与现代社会发展
paras: This short commentary asks what conception of history the Communist Manifesto sets out and why it still matters. Liu argues that the Manifesto, besides fixing communism as a goal, gives a scientific statement of the materialist conception of history, which explains both how modern society came into being and where it is heading.

The article first draws on the Manifesto's account of the origin of modern bourgeois society. It then turns to the Manifesto's forecast of future society. It closes by pointing to the 1872 German preface, which says that the general principles remain correct while their application depends on historical conditions.

Liu reads the Manifesto as tracing the bourgeoisie to the growth of productive forces and relations of production within feudal society. The Manifesto credits the bourgeoisie with a "very revolutionary part": it created enormous productive forces and opened up world history through the world market. The article then identifies three signs of crisis. These are the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation, the opposition of capital and wage labour with its periodic overproduction crises, and the creation of the proletariat as the bourgeoisie's "gravediggers". From this Liu draws the Manifesto's conclusion that the bourgeoisie can no longer rule. Only proletarian revolution can end exploitation, and it leads to an association in which the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all.

Liu concludes that the Manifesto's conception of history shows the scientific character and truth of Marxist theory. Rereading it after more than 170 years is said to help strengthen historical self-confidence, historical consciousness, historical mission and historical initiative. Read the original if you want a concise, orthodox summary of the Manifesto's historical materialism as presented in a Chinese Party-theory outlet.
quoteEn: This scientific conception of history still has indelible theoretical significance and practical value today, and it demonstrates the scientific character and truth of Marxist theory itself.
quoteZh: 这一科学的历史观在今天仍然具有不可磨灭的理论意义和实践价值，它彰显了马克思主义理论本身的科学性和真理性。

t: The Party-admission oath ceremony over a hundred years: theoretical interpretation, forms of practice and functional value
zh: 百年历程中的入党宣誓仪式：理论阐释、践行方式、功能价值
paras: This article examines the oath-taking ceremony through which new members join the Communist Party of China (CPC). Gao and Lu treat it as a mandatory step in recruiting members and as a solemn pledge to the Party, the country and the people. They argue that, across more than a century, the ceremony has moved from a rough early form to a settled one and then to continuing refinement. They present it as a basis for the "major honours system" of a large Party and country, and for telling the CPC's story to the world.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the ceremony's theoretical sources and basic attributes. The second surveys four forms of practice: the regular ceremony, joining at the front line, secret admission and posthumous recognition of membership. The third assesses the ceremony's functions at the level of the individual, the group and the Party as a whole. Cases range from the Anyuan miners' club in 1922 to Zou Taofen (1944), Qiu Shaoyun (1952) and a pandemic-era recognition in 2021. A short closing section links the ceremony to Xi Jinping's 2021 renewal of the oath.

Gao and Lu trace the ceremony directly to the Statutes of the Communist League drafted by Marx and Engels in 1847, which set out a question-and-answer admission procedure. In their account, it reached the CPC partly through the Russian Social-Democratic Labour Party and Lenin. They identify three stable attributes: class character, shown in portraits, the singing of the Internationale and oath wording; popular character, shown in oath content and the growing number of non-members attending; and advanced character, shown in adaptable forms and Marxist guidance. Procedures varied by period, for example in the object of salute, until the 12th Party Congress (1982) made the Party flag the national standard. The clenched-fist gesture is described as the constant element.

On function, the authors argue that the oath strengthens each member's political belief and sense of duty, builds a collective organisational culture and ideological identity through its symbols, and gives the Party a fuller public image. They conclude that the ceremony is an important result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They call for further work on its meaning and on members' understanding and observance of the oath. Read the original if you study Party building, political ritual or the history of CPC admission practices and want a Chinese-language account with many historical examples.
quoteEn: The Party-admission oath ceremony is an important result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and a foundational link in the honours system of a large Party and country.
quoteZh: 入党宣誓仪式是马克思主义中国化时代化的重要成果，也是大党大国荣典制度的基础性环节。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: An official formula for the Party's project of applying Marxism to Chinese conditions and to current circumstances. It is used to present Party theory and practice as a continuing development of Marxism.

glossary.pinyin: dà dǎng dà guó róngdiǎn zhìdù
glossary.en: honours system of a large Party and country
glossary.literal: honours-and-ceremonies system of a great Party and great country
glossary.explanation: A phrase for the system of state and Party honours and ceremonies. The authors treat the oath ceremony as one of its foundations.

glossary.literal: joining the Party on the firing line
glossary.explanation: An exceptional admission, in war or disaster, in which the usual procedure is shortened for someone who has shown courage or merit.
The Party's practice of granting membership after death to a person who died for its cause and had asked to join. Party regulations set the approval procedure.

t: Zhu De's understanding of and reflections on talent work in the early years of the People's Republic
zh: 新中国成立初期朱德对人才工作的认识与思考
paras: How did the early People's Republic try to solve its shortage of skilled people, and what did Zhu De contribute? Zhang Feng, an associate researcher at Yangzhou University, argues that Zhu De, a leading member of the Party's first generation of central leadership, gave sustained attention to talent work after 1949. Zhang holds that his many statements and proposals helped launch and develop the new state's talent enterprise and still offer historical lessons for today.

The article draws on Zhu De's speeches, inscriptions, telegrams and letters from roughly 1949 to 1956. It is organised in four parts: the urgency and importance of talent work; the use of former professional and technical personnel; the training of the country's own modernised talent; and the principles of talent cultivation. Cases range from engineers and scientists to air force, navy and military-academy personnel, young people and women.

Zhang's first move is to show why talent mattered. The author cites a figure of fewer than 50,000 science and technology personnel with university education in 1949, and reads Zhu De's repeated calls for technical skill as tied to three needs: industrialisation, scientific development and a modernised national defence army. Second, Zhang reports Zhu De's view that former Guomindang-era experts, including air force and navy technicians, should be used after a process of 'unity, education and remoulding', and that this was a political task. Third, Zhu De is said to have insisted on self-reliant training: running regular schools, especially military academies, and encouraging youth and women to become specialists, even while Soviet help was welcomed. Two principles run through this: political and professional competence must be united ('politics plus technology'), and theory must be combined with practice.

Zhang concludes that Zhu De, moved by hopes for national strength and popular wellbeing, laid out guiding ideas and a blueprint for the sustained development of talent work. In the author's assessment, this shows the foresight of the older generation of proletarian revolutionaries on a question bearing on the fate of the Party and state. Read the original if you study early PRC cadre and technical-personnel policy, Zhu De's thought, or the history of military modernisation and education, and want a documented account from Party sources.
quoteEn: Zhu De knew well that the key precondition and crucial element in modernising the army was modernising the army's talent.
quoteZh: 朱德深知，实现军队现代化的重要前提和关键要素是实现军队人才的现代化。

glossary.explanation: An early PRC policy formula for dealing with former Guomindang-era intellectuals, technicians and officials: win them over, educate them politically and change their outlook so they could serve the new state.

t: Goals and strategies of institution-building in the context of further comprehensively deepening reform
zh: 进一步全面深化改革视域下制度建设的目标体系与策略方法
source: Scientific Socialism (科学社会主义), 2024 no. 6
paras: Li Xiaoyu takes up institution-building as the main thread of the reform agenda set out by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article asks what problems current institution-building faces, what goals it should be anchored to, and which strategies and methods can achieve them. Li argues that institution-building is the central line of further comprehensively deepening reform, and that it should rest on six goals and be pursued through a set of differentiated methods.

The article has three parts. The first sets out why institution-building is necessary. The second builds a framework of goals and checks it against current conditions in China. The third discusses strategies and methods: who supplies institutions, what drives institutional innovation, which principles apply and which concrete paths exist. Li draws on Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping, Lenin, Weber, Huntington, Douglass North, and Acemoglu and Robinson, and illustrates the argument with cases such as the Zhejiang reforms and market segmentation.

Li gives three reasons for necessity: bringing the strengths of the socialist system into play, building a modern socialist great power, and meeting great-power competition, which the author describes as ultimately competition between institutions. Criticising indicators such as the World Bank's governance index for ignoring national conditions, Li holds that governance has general, national and task-specific attributes. From these Li derives six goals: completeness, unity, hierarchy, systematicness, coordination and adaptability. On methods, Li argues that the centre should lead on fundamental, top-level institutions, while local governments, enterprises and individuals innovate in concrete ones. Innovation is driven by crisis, development needs and opening up. Li also classifies paths into six types: filling gaps, consolidating, strengthening implementation, regulating and adjusting, improving, and abolishing.

Li concludes that a new form of reform is emerging, guided by Party leadership, problem orientation, top-level design, systems integration, institutional and mechanism reform, and a focus on reshaping relationships. The author maintains that continuous institutional innovation will provide the impetus and institutional guarantee for Chinese modernization. The author also stresses that reform is never finished and must be carried through. Read the original if you want a Chinese-journal account of how institution-building is theorised and classified under the 2024 reform decision, with a detailed typology of reform measures.
quoteEn: Institutional advantage is a country's greatest advantage, and institutional competition is the most fundamental competition between countries.
quoteZh: 制度优势是一个国家的最大优势，制度竞争是国家间最根本的竞争。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's model of national development, which it presents as distinct from Western modernization. It has been prominent in Party documents since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
The reform programme launched at the 18th Central Committee's Third Plenum in 2013 and extended by the 2024 Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee.
The practice of planning reform comprehensively from the central leadership down, as opposed to piecemeal or purely local experimentation.

t: Paths for advancing the Party's self-reform through ideological building
zh: 以思想建设推进党的自我革命的路径考察
paras: Chen Si and Li Zhiyong ask how ideological building (sixiang jianshe) can drive the Communist Party of China's self-reform. They start from the 20th Party Congress (2022) claim that self-reform is the Party's "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Their thesis is that the problems self-reform must address share a root in ideals and convictions, so ideological building is both a key lesson of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era and a necessary measure for the future.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the internal logic linking ideological building to self-reform. The second surveys four historical periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third proposes five directions for further work.

On the theoretical side, the authors argue that ideological building gives self-reform three things: theoretical guidance, because practice and theory advance in a cycle; value orientation, because self-reform is meant to lead the "great social revolution"; and a method, because corruption, the "four winds" and disloyalty are all traced to weakened ideals. Self-reform is therefore described as first of all an ideological revolution. The historical survey presents a continuous practice: rectifying erroneous lines (the 1935 Zunyi Meeting), Mao Zedong's principle of building the Party ideologically, the Yan'an Rectification Movement, the 1950s rectification campaigns including the Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan case, the full Party rectification of 1983, and the centralised education campaigns of the new era. The authors credit the new-era emphasis on making officials unwilling to be corrupt for laying an ideological basis for the anti-corruption campaign's "overwhelming victory".

For the future the authors call for firmer ideals and convictions, adherence to the Two Integrations so that practical innovation drives theoretical innovation, theoretical armament that combines concentrated and routine education, and attention to the "critical few" leading cadres, including family conduct. They also call for learning, practice and assessment mechanisms that make the work regular and long-term, combining ideological building with institutional governance. Read the original if you want a systematic official-academic account of how Party theorists link ideological education to anti-corruption and Party discipline, with a historical periodisation from 1921 to 2024.
quoteEn: The Party's self-reform is first of all an ideological revolution, in which ideological building makes all Party members firm in their ideals and convictions and strengthens their courage and confidence to carry out self-reform.
quoteZh: 党的自我革命首先是一场思想革命，就是通过思想建设使全体党员坚定理想信念，增强进行自我革命的勇气、底气

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The slogan for the Party-discipline and anti-corruption drive that has run since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It covers ideological, organisational, stylistic and disciplinary measures.
One of the Party's core areas of self-construction. It covers theoretical study and education in ideals and convictions for members and cadres.
The formula of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. The second integration was added in 2023.
The four undesirable work styles targeted since 2012: formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance.

t: An analysis of the historical starting point of the modern transformation of Chinese civilization
zh: 中华文明现代转型的历史起点析论
source: Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育), 2024 no. 12
paras: When did the modern transformation of Chinese civilization begin? Chen Dianlin and Liu Ming take up this question, which they describe as a foundational problem for tracing the evolution of Chinese civilization since the modern era, and on which they say scholars have reached no consensus. Using the perspective of the Second Integration, they argue that the starting point cannot be a single event. It is a historical period running from the May Fourth Movement to the founding of the Communist Party of China.

The article first surveys six existing views. Three tie the starting point to the old-democratic revolution: the Opium War, the 1911 Revolution and the First World War. Three tie it to the new-democratic revolution: the spread of Marxism, the founding of the Party and the founding of the People's Republic. The authors criticise each in turn. They then examine the question through three lenses: its time and space, its concrete cultural form, and its agent. A further section looks at the historical, cultural and practical circumstances, drawing on early Party figures such as Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, Qu Qiubai, Li Da and Zhou Enlai.

The authors argue that the Opium War brought national crisis but did not yet reach Chinese values and ethics. They hold that the 1911 Revolution was undone by Yuan Shikai's restoration, and that the Party's founding aimed first at class struggle. They also hold that the founding of the People's Republic marks a later stage rather than a beginning. Drawing on Marx and Engels, they present transformation as driven by the shift from a smallholder agrarian mode of production to industrial modernity. In their account, traditional culture has a dual character, as national spirit and as feudal ideology. They see its critical sublation as the way forward, with Marxism supplying the key and sharing common values with Chinese tradition. The Party, as the vanguard of the proletariat, is the agent, and early Party writers identified the proletariat as the leading force.

The authors conclude that three dimensions converge in the period from the May Fourth Movement to the Party's founding. These are intensifying national crisis and modernizing pressure, the linking of Marxism with Chinese cultural elements, and the Chinese working class's emergence as a political actor whose cultural mission the Party affirmed. They present this as a historical basis for building a modern Chinese civilization today and for adapting Marxism to Chinese tradition. Read the original if you want a systematic review of Chinese scholarly positions on periodising Chinese civilization's modernization, and an example of how the Second Integration is used as an analytical framework.
quoteEn: The historical starting point of the modern transformation of Chinese civilization should be a historical period in which several dimensions converge.
quoteZh: 中华文明现代转型历史起点应是多维聚合的历史时段

glossary.explanation: A formula introduced by Xi Jinping in 2023, referring to combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture. It is the second of the Two Integrations, the first being Marxism with China's concrete realities.
The Hegelian and Marxian idea (Aufhebung) of negating something while preserving and raising its valuable content to a higher level.

t: The "Two Integrations": rationale and path for building a Party-building discourse system
zh: “两个结合”：党建话语体系构建的理与路
paras: Sun Zhaohong asks how the Chinese Communist Party should build and refine its discourse on Party building (the concepts, phrases and narratives used to describe and guide its own construction). The article argues that the discourse system has grown through the Two Integrations, meaning the combination of Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. In the new era, Sun contends, the system must continue to rest on this method so that it has a "soul" of truth, "roots" in culture and "strength" in practice.

The article is organised in three parts, one for each of these three dimensions: theory, culture and practice. Each part first sets out why that dimension is the foundation of Party-building discourse and then explains how the Two Integrations should be applied to it. Sun draws on Party history from the Marxist-Leninist doctrine of party building and Mao Zedong's sinification of Marxism, through Deng Xiaoping's institutional reforms, to Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

In the first part, Sun treats Marxism as the "soul" of the discourse, carried forward through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and now guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In the second part, traditional culture is the "root". Sun's example is "seeking truth from facts", an old phrase whose meaning the Party has enriched, and Sun stresses that the two sources must "fit" each other and form a new "cultural living organism", not a mere assembly. The "two vanguards" formulation (the Party as vanguard of both the working class and the Chinese people and nation) is offered as an instance of this synthesis. Sun adds that traditional culture must be screened, since feudal clan-based networks are said to feed corruption. In the third part, practice is the source of the discourse. Sun traces the progression from "ideological party building" to institutional governance and the "new great project", and treats the Party's self-reform as the latest innovation. Sun says discourse must summarise historical experience and address current problems, such as the "six how-to-always" challenges facing a large party.

Sun concludes that a Chinese Party-building discourse needs Marxist theory, cultural subjectivity and practical problem-solving together, since Western party theories cannot explain the Party's experience. The Two Integrations, Sun argues, should produce a distinctive discourse that answers how a long-governing Marxist party is to be built and offers the Party's answer to corruption as a global problem. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory journal links discourse construction to the Two Integrations, with examples of specific Party-building terms.
quoteEn: "Integration" does not mean simply adding Marxism to fine traditional Chinese culture; it is the Party combining various conditions and resources, cultural ones included, to carry out comprehensive innovation in theory, practice, institutions and discourse.
quoteZh: “结合”，不是把马克思主义与中华优秀传统文化简单相加，而是中国共产党结合各种条件和资源（包括文化条件和资源）进行综合的理论创新、实践创新、制度创新、话语创新。

glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula for combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second integration was added to official discourse in 2021–2023.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official description of the Party's ongoing effort to fit Marxist theory to Chinese conditions and to the demands of the current era.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's current guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
Official term for the Party's efforts to discipline, correct and renew itself, presented since the 2010s as the answer to the problem of the historical cycle of rise and decline.

t: The historical characteristics of the CPC's promotion of the spirit of historical initiative in the new era, and their practical implications
zh: 新时代中国共产党发扬历史主动精神的历史特点及其现实启示
source: Journal of the Party School of the CPC Hangzhou Municipal Committee, 2025 no. 2
paras: Ding Junping and Yang Yating ask how the Communist Party of China has put the "spirit of historical initiative" into practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and what that practice implies today. They argue that the Party has taken the initiative in four ways: in achieving major results, in shouldering its historical mission, in drawing lessons from history and in opening up bright prospects. In their account this is a correct choice for national development and Party building, and it supports the Party's new tasks in advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization.

The article first traces how Xi Jinping has used the concept of "historical initiative". It dates his first new-era use to 2013 and counts 13 mentions in nine speeches in 2021–2022. It also cites a mention in the explanation of the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The authors then review the existing literature, which they say mostly follows a "formation–promotion" pattern and pays little attention to new-era practice. The main body sets out four historical characteristics, and a closing section draws four implications.

In the authors' reading, the four characteristics are as follows. First, the Party leads great change with a strong sense of political responsibility, sustained by ideals and convictions and by its mission. Second, it follows a people-centred development philosophy, treating the people's aspiration for a better life as its goal. Third, it summarises history using scientific methods, linking different periods, balancing success and failure, and applying the lessons creatively, as in the third historical resolution and its "ten affirmations". Fourth, it opens up prospects by judging the trend of the times, through the "two overall situations", the three major questions of the era, and timed goals such as the Two Centenary Goals. The authors present these as showing the Party's strategic and theoretical initiative.

The authors draw four implications. The Party should hold to Marxist belief and use Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to strengthen conviction. It should lead the great social revolution through the Party's self-reform. It should draw strength from the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists that begins with the founding spirit of the Party. And it should respect the people's principal position and learn from their wisdom. They conclude that the spirit of historical initiative will continue to be promoted and will help the Party answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Party theorists frame "historical initiative" in Xi-era documents and of the research literature on it.
quoteEn: The scientific approach by which the CPC insists on self-reform accords with the core essence of its insistence on promoting the spirit of historical initiative.
quoteZh: 中国共产党坚持自我革命的科学思路与坚持发扬历史主动精神的核心要旨相吻合

glossary.explanation: A concept in Xi Jinping's discourse, used from 2013 and especially after 2021. It refers to the Party actively grasping historical laws, opportunities and responsibilities rather than reacting passively.
The official name for China's path to modernization, presented since the 20th Party Congress (2022) as distinct from Western models.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's overarching national goal, which the Party links to achieving a strong, modern China by the mid-21st century.
Official phrase for the strategic overall picture of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the profound changes unseen in a century in the world.
Official term for the Party's efforts to correct itself and maintain discipline and purity, stressed under Xi Jinping.

glossary.pinyin: liǎng gè yībǎi nián fèndòu mùbiāo
glossary.explanation: The goals of building a moderately prosperous society by the Party's centenary (2021) and a modern socialist country by the People's Republic's centenary (2049).

glossary.zh: 中国共产党人精神谱系
glossary.explanation: A set of named "spirits" (e.g. the Long March spirit) officially recognised in 2021 as a chain of Party values, with the founding spirit of the Party as source.

t: Decoding the mechanism of cultural confidence and strength through the lens of the Two Integrations
zh: 解码“两个结合”视域下的文化自信自强机制
source: Shanghai School Economics Review (Haipai jingjixue), 2024 no. 4
paras: Sun Shaoyong and Chen Zhongbin ask how the Two Integrations (integrating Marxism with China's specific realities and with its fine traditional culture) relate to the task of building cultural confidence and strength. They argue that the two are closely linked and reinforce each other: advancing cultural confidence and strength is both an inherent requirement and the goal of the Two Integrations. The article sets out the logic of this relationship, explains its internal mechanism and proposes practical paths.

The article has three parts. The first treats the logical relationship, claiming that the two share a common goal (building a culturally strong country), compatible values and the same principal force, the people. The second explains the "endogenous mechanism" under three headings: understanding of laws, creative thinking and grasp of the times. The third sets out four practical paths.

In the central section, the authors argue that the Two Integrations deepen understanding of how fine traditional culture is created, spread and integrated. For example, they say culture tends to spread from high to low positions of value and, as it matures, differences give way to shared elements, which they link to the ideals of harmony in diversity and a common spiritual home for all ethnic groups. They also claim that the Two Integrations widen creative thinking by joining revolutionary culture with the great founding spirit of the Party, traditional moral ideas with the core socialist values, and cultural renewal with modern science and technology. On the grasp of the times, they hold that the Two Integrations answer the demand to strengthen national cultural soft power and bring out the contemporary governing value of traditional culture.

For practice, the authors call for Marxist guidance across cultural work, including cultural undertakings and industries, reform of the cultural system and public cultural services. They also call for deeper interpretation and more innovative expression of fine traditional culture. They want the core socialist values to guide cultural production, social consensus and individual conduct. Finally, they urge exchange and mutual learning among civilizations while upholding a Chinese cultural standpoint, drawing on the Global Civilization Initiative. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship links the Two Integrations to cultural policy and the project of cultural strength.
quoteEn: Advancing cultural confidence and strength is both an inherent requirement of the Two Integrations and their goal.
quoteZh: 推进文化自信自强既是“两个结合”的内在要求，也是其目标指向。

glossary.explanation: A formula in Party theory: integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with its fine traditional culture. The second integration was stressed by Xi Jinping in 2021–2023.
A concept stressed under Xi Jinping: confidence in the value and vitality of China's own culture, including its traditional, revolutionary and socialist strands.
A set of 24 characters formulated in 2012, covering values at the national, social and individual levels, promoted as the guiding values of Chinese society.
An initiative proposed by Xi Jinping in 2023 that promotes respect for the diversity of civilizations, shared human values, and cultural exchange.
A term adapted from Joseph Nye, used in Chinese policy for the international appeal and influence of a country's culture.

t: Party leadership and the rule-of-law character of the "Fengqiao Experience" in the new era
zh: 党的领导与新时代“枫桥经验”的法治属性
source: China Leadership Science (Zhongguo lingdao kexue), 2025 no. 2
paras: The "Fengqiao Experience" began in Fengqiao township, Zhuji, Zhejiang, in the 1960s as a method of resolving disputes locally through mass mobilisation. Zhao Yang and Liu Yongyan ask in what sense its new-era form, shaped since the 18th Party Congress (2012), has a rule-of-law character. They argue that this character grows out of Party leadership: under the Party, the experience applies rule-of-law thinking and methods, inherits traditional Chinese legal culture, and advances the modernization of grassroots governance.

The article has three parts. The first sets out what the rule-of-law character means, both the general features of modern rule of law (supremacy of law, equal protection, checks on power, procedural justice, protection of rights) and its Chinese features. The second examines the conditions that formed it: Party documents from the 18th Party Congress to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Xi Jinping's statements on the experience since 2003, and links to traditional legal culture. The third turns to practice, using cases from Zhejiang and Shandong and the court system.

The authors identify four Chinese features: Party leadership, a people-centred approach, a pluralistic dispute-resolution mechanism that combines rigid legal norms with flexible mediation, and the linking of governance theory to local legal practice. They trace its roots to the traditional ideas of \"fairness, forgiveness and trust in the people\", to \"village-law autonomy\" and to combining virtue with law, which they present as an instance of the Two Integrations. Their cases are the \"three ups and three downs\" decision-making mechanism in Fengyuan village, digital tools such as Wenshang County's online petition system, and one-stop dispute resolution and litigation services in Zhejiang courts. They credit these with shifting governance from ending litigation towards having little litigation at all.

The authors conclude that the new-era Fengqiao Experience is a component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and a practical expression of Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law. They present it as a workable approach to grassroots governance on the rule-of-law track, and call for continuing to uphold and develop it so as to form a pattern of shared contribution, governance and benefits. Read the original if you want a Party-line account of how Chinese legal scholarship ties grassroots mediation to Party leadership, official documents and traditional legal culture, with Zhejiang and Shandong cases.
quoteEn: The rule-of-law character of the new-era "Fengqiao Experience" embodies an organic unity of rule-of-law thinking and the mass line, and of institutional rigidity and cultural flexibility.
quoteZh: 新时代“枫桥经验”的法治属性，体现了法治思维与群众路线、制度刚性与文化柔性的有机统一

glossary.explanation: A model of grassroots dispute resolution that originated in Fengqiao township, Zhejiang, in the early 1960s. Mao Zedong endorsed it in 1963, and the Party has since promoted it as an exemplar of social governance.
Xi Jinping's formula for combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. The second integration is invoked to legitimise drawing on traditional culture.

glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law
glossary.explanation: The body of ideas on law and governance attributed to Xi Jinping and formally set out in 2020. It stresses Party leadership, a people-centred approach and rule of law as the basis of national governance.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology since the 19th Party Congress (2017), written into the Party and state constitutions.

keywords: Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law

t: A historical examination from launching reform to further deepening reform comprehensively
zh: 从实行改革到进一步全面深化改革的历史考察
source: Studies on CPC History (Zhonggong dangshi yanjiu), 2024 no. 6
paras: Chen Jinlong asks how China's reform has evolved from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article argues that this path involved both a changing conceptual content of 'reform' and shifting practical priorities. Tracing it, Chen holds, helps clarify the internal logic of reform history.

The article is a Party-history study in four stages. It begins with reform centred on economic restructuring and early talk of comprehensive reform in the 1980s. It then covers comprehensive and deepening reform aimed at a socialist market economy and the Scientific Outlook on Development (1992–2012). Next it treats comprehensive deepening of reform from the 18th Party Congress (2012), and finally further comprehensive deepening under the banner of Chinese modernization. Chen relies mainly on speeches and documents by Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao, Xi Jinping and Party plenums.

Chen's central move is to show that each stage's reform concept was justified by a different driver. Early reform was tied to the Four Modernizations, opening up and the improvement of socialism; later stages were tied to the market-economy goal, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and then to modernizing national governance, demonstrating institutional advantages, solving prominent problems and the movement of basic social contradictions. Further comprehensive deepening is presented as a two-way relation with Chinese modernization, and as driven by institutional innovation, the principal social contradiction and the development of new quality productive forces. Chen lists the 14 key tasks and 'seven focuses' of the 2024 plenum as expressing this link.

Chen concludes that reform has been gradual, with stage-specific priorities and economic reform always the leading element. In Chen's account, the trajectory shows the Party's historical initiative as a 'mission-driven' party that leads reform and relies on the people. The family of reform concepts that results is said to lay a foundation for an autonomous Chinese body of knowledge about reform. Read the original if you want a documented, quotation-rich account of how official reform terminology developed from 1978 to the 2024 plenum.
quoteEn: From launching reform, comprehensive reform and deepening reform, to comprehensively deepening reform and further comprehensively deepening reform, a complete conceptual system of reform has been built and a cluster of reform concepts has formed.
quoteZh: 从实行改革、全面改革、深化改革，到全面深化改革、进一步全面深化改革，构建了改革的完整概念体系，形成了改革的概念集群。

glossary.explanation: Official concept of China's own path to modernization, set out in the 20th Party Congress report (2022).
Concept promoted by Xi Jinping from 2023, referring to advanced productivity driven by technological breakthroughs and industrial upgrading.
Guiding concept of the Hu Jintao era, stressing people-centred, comprehensive, coordinated and sustainable development.

glossary.zh: 国家治理体系和治理能力现代化
glossary.pinyin: guójiā zhìlǐ tǐxì hé zhìlǐ nénglì xiàndàihuà
glossary.literal: modernization of the national governance system and governance capacity
glossary.explanation: The overall goal of comprehensive deepening of reform set at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013).

glossary.zh: 社会主义市场经济体制
glossary.explanation: The reform goal adopted at the 14th Party Congress (1992), combining market mechanisms with the socialist system.

t: The "three distinctions" and the internal logic of further deepening reform comprehensively
zh: “三个区分开来”与进一步全面深化改革的内在逻辑
paras: Xu Yulu asks how the "three distinctions" (sange qufen kailai), first put forward by Xi Jinping in January 2016, relate to the programme of further deepening reform comprehensively set out at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article argues that the distinctions, which separate honest errors in reform from deliberate or self-interested violations of discipline and law, are an internal part of what that reform needs. They encourage and protect officials who must take risks, so applying them effectively is presented as a precondition for carrying out the plenum's reform agenda.

The article has three sections. The first sets out the meaning and current value of the three distinctions as a form of combining strict management with care for cadres. The second analyses their logical link to the reform agenda. The third discusses how to implement them. Xu draws on Xi Jinping's statements, the 2018 General Office guideline on motivating cadres, the Party's accountability regulations, disciplinary rules, local measures in Jinan, Shenzhen and Beijing, and a 2022 model case from the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection.

Xu argues that the distinctions serve three aims. They underpin a precise mechanism for tolerating and correcting errors, so officials dare to act on "breakthrough" tasks. They rest on a developing system of responsibility, so officials can act skilfully on "complex" tasks. They help build a political ecology that supports getting things done, which serves the "clear" tasks. The author then links them to three reform challenges: venturing into "uncharted territory", gnawing at "hard bones", and dissolving "mental and policy shackles". Officials are said to fear conflicting policies, unclear limits and malicious reports. Xu holds that errors from inexperience, uncertain outcomes and changing environments in first-time trials should be tolerated under conditions of motive, circumstances and procedure.

Xu identifies gaps in practice: weak awareness, limited ability to judge motives, vague regulations and a cautious atmosphere. The proposals are to strengthen political consciousness and Party leadership, use systematic thinking, lawful procedure and coordination between departments, build mechanisms for advance risk reporting, clearing officials' names and follow-up visits, and make more use of guiding cases. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-school account of how tolerance for officials' errors is being tied to the post-2024 reform agenda and to concrete disciplinary practice.
quoteEn: The "three distinctions" rely on and act upon an ever-improving system of official responsibility, and in both internal belief and external standards of action they give cadres support for acting precisely on the "complex" agenda of further deepening reform comprehensively.
quoteZh: “三个区分开来”依托并作用于不断完善的履职责任体系，在内部信仰和外部行动标准方面，都为干部在进一步全面深化改革“复杂性”议程中精准作为提供支持支撑。

glossary.explanation: A principle announced by Xi Jinping in January 2016. It separates honest mistakes made in reform and experimentation from deliberate violations or acts for private gain, so that the former can be treated leniently.

Institutional arrangements that allow officials to be excused or given lighter responsibility for certain mistakes while requiring the mistakes to be corrected. Local governments and central bodies have issued rules on it since about 2016.

glossary.en: strict management with care for cadres
glossary.explanation: A Party formula for managing officials. It pairs strict discipline and supervision with support, encouragement and protection.
The reform programme adopted at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee in July 2024. It sets out more than 300 measures to advance Chinese modernization.

t: The historical logic and contemporary mission of building an autonomous knowledge system for CPC history and Party building studies
zh: 建构中共党史党建学自主知识体系的历史逻辑与时代使命
paras: This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in April 2025, asks how the discipline of CPC history and Party building studies should construct its own autonomous knowledge system. Yang Lanjie argues that the task follows from China's modern history and from the Party's record of governance, and that it is a duty of scholars in the field. The author also holds that reforming how the discipline is evaluated is a necessary condition for success.

The article opens with Xi Jinping's April 2022 instructions to philosophy and social science scholars at Renmin University. It then has three parts: the historical logic behind building an autonomous knowledge system, the contemporary mission of the discipline, and the role of new evaluation standards. It refers to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and to the 2024 degree guidelines that set out four second-level disciplines under the first-level discipline of CPC history and Party building studies.

Yang's historical argument is that modern China was pushed into a "catch-up" mentality that applied Western analytical models to Chinese experience and lost subjectivity. In Yang's account, cultural subjectivity has since revived, and the Party's achievements since reform and opening up require a locally grounded explanation. Yang presents the discipline, which centres on "the governance of the Communist Party" and "the governance of China", as one of the most distinctively autonomous fields. For its mission, Yang says it must uphold Party leadership and the people-centred stance, combine historical and political thinking, and offer Party-building experience for a new form of human political civilization. The author says some concepts, such as "political party" and "state governance", are shared with other traditions, while others, such as "the Yan'an experience", are distinctive.

Yang concludes that evaluation of the discipline should stress autonomy and practice. It should not rest on counting talent titles, honours and papers, and should instead integrate moral education, social contribution, and the fit and effectiveness of training, including for Party organisation cadres. The author expects this to join professional development with social application and theory with practice. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Party-school-affiliated scholar frames disciplinary autonomy, evaluation reform and the Party-building field.
quoteEn: CPC history and Party building studies revolves around \"the governance of the Communist Party of China\" and \"the governance of China\", and is a systematic body of theory and knowledge on the Party's history and its own building.
quoteZh: 中共党史党建学围绕着“中国共产党之治”与“中国之治”展开，是党的历史和自身建设的成体系的理论和知识

glossary.en: CPC history and Party building studies
glossary.explanation: A first-level academic discipline in China's degree system that combines the history of the Communist Party with the study of Party building. The 2024 guidelines divide it into four second-level disciplines.
A slogan in Chinese social science policy calling for concepts and theories rooted in Chinese practice rather than borrowed from Western scholarship.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in 1978.

glossary.en: the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee
glossary.explanation: A Party meeting held in July 2024 that adopted a decision on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization.

t: Establishing a seeking-truth-from-facts style of study throughout the Party
st: Revisiting Mao Zedong's "Reform Our Study"
zh: 在全党树立实事求是的学风
zhSub: 重温毛泽东《改造我们的学习》
paras: This short commentary in Study Times revisits Mao Zedong's 1941 report "Reform Our Study" (改造我们的学习), delivered to cadres in Yan'an on 19 May 1941 and later included in volume three of the Selected Works of Mao Zedong. Li Youxin argues that Mao's criticism of subjectivism, and his call for a style of study based on seeking truth from facts and linking theory with practice, still offers guidance for making improvement of Party conduct regular and long-term.

The article has three parts. It first sets out the wartime background in which Mao proposed reforming study, then summarises Mao's contrast between the subjectivist attitude and the Marxist-Leninist attitude, and finally treats investigation and research as the base for changing Party conduct. It closes by linking this to current Party campaigns.

Li explains that by the War of Resistance the Party had become a large mass party with many new members and cadres of uneven theoretical training. Mao's 1938 call for a Party-wide study competition improved theoretical levels but exposed a separation of theory from practice. Li reports Mao's charge that subjectivists neglect present conditions and Chinese history and study theory for its own sake. Against this stands the Marxist-Leninist attitude, in which one starts from objective reality and seeks its internal laws. Li stresses Mao's reinterpretation of the traditional phrase "seeking truth from facts" (实事求是), and his judgement that subjectivism is an enemy of the Party, the working class, the people and the nation. Li presents investigation as the basic skill that makes this attitude concrete, citing Mao's line that without investigation there is no right to speak.

Li concludes that Mao's text was a key step in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, and that its emphasis on investigation remains a "family heirloom" for Party members. The article ties this to the current study and education campaign on the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, whose first item is improving investigation and research, and to Xi Jinping's remarks that style problems are at root problems of Party spirit. Li calls on cadres to go to the grassroots, keep close ties with the people, and so secure a sound style of work for Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party press uses a Yan'an-era text to support present-day campaigns on Party conduct.
quoteEn: To put seeking truth from facts and linking theory with practice into concrete effect, one must master the basic skill of investigation and research.
quoteZh: 要具体地做到实事求是、理论联系实际，就要掌握调查研究这个基本功。

glossary.literal: seek the truth in actual matters
glossary.explanation: A phrase from traditional Chinese textual scholarship that Mao reinterpreted in 1941 as starting from objective reality and finding its laws. It later became a core principle of Party ideology.
A 1941 report by Mao Zedong to Yan'an cadres criticising subjectivism and dogmatism in Party study. It was an early text of the Yan'an rectification movement.
In Party usage, an attitude that acts on assumptions, book knowledge or enthusiasm rather than on investigation of actual conditions. Mao treated it as covering dogmatism and empiricism.

A set of rules on official conduct issued by the Central Committee after the 18th Party Congress (2012), aimed at curbing formalism, extravagance and bureaucratism. The first point concerns improving investigation and research.
The Party's term for applying Marxism to China's concrete circumstances and developing it in that context. Mao's Yan'an-era writings are treated as foundational for it.
The official term for China's path of modernization, promoted by the Party since the early 2020s as distinct from Western models.

t: The proactive logic of "upholding the Party's cultural leadership" in the new era
zh: 新时代“坚持党的文化领导权”的主动逻辑
source: Teaching and Research (教学与研究), 2025 no. 1
paras: Liu Shuijing and Zhang Pan take up the idea of "upholding the Party's cultural leadership", which Xi Jinping put forward as a formal category at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development on 2 June 2023. The authors treat it as a question bearing on ideological security, cultural sovereignty and the fate of the Party and state. Their thesis is that the proposition is the product of the Communist Party's own initiative, and that it carries a historical, a value-based and a practical "proactive logic" (zhudong luoji).

The article is organised in three parts, one for each logic. The first traces the Party's handling of cultural leadership through four periods: the New Democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The second sets out the value of cultural leadership in four dimensions: Party building, national development, cultural innovation and mutual learning among civilizations. The third lists five practical lines of work.

On the historical logic, the authors present each period as a stage in winning, consolidating and extending leadership over culture. They cite Mao Zedong's call for a "national, scientific and mass" culture led by proletarian thought, the "Double Hundred" policy, the reform-era principle of "grasping both hands", and the new-era concepts of cultural confidence and the Two Integrations. On the value logic, they argue that cultural leadership strengthens the Party's authority and the moral legitimacy of its rule. They add that, through the "second integration", it supports the cultural form of Chinese modernization and a more equal, open world civilizational order. On the practical logic, they identify five pairings: Party spirit with the people's standpoint, positive publicity with struggle in public opinion, mainstream with diverse cultures, offline with online positions, and Party committee responsibility with the participation of many actors.

The authors conclude that only by understanding this proactive logic and upholding the Party's overall leadership of propaganda, ideological and cultural work can the Party consolidate its governing position more deeply. They add that this will strengthen the cohesion of the Chinese nation and produce new achievements in Chinese culture. The article follows official discourse closely and gives a systematic account of how Party theorists frame cultural leadership. Read the original if you want a compact survey of the Party's current framing of cultural leadership, with its periodisation and the policy measures it names.
quoteEn: The cultural leadership of a proletarian party has never been achieved through political and economic struggle alone. It is won by spreading advanced scientific ideas and culture to gain broad social recognition and support, a method that has more attraction, influence and appeal for the people.
quoteZh: 无产阶级政党的文化领导权从来不是单纯通过政治和经济斗争手段来实现的，而是通过传播科学先进的思想文化来获得社会的广泛认可和支持，这种方式更能对人民群众产生吸引力、影响力、感召力。

glossary.explanation: The Communist Party's leading role in the cultural and ideological sphere, related to the Gramscian idea of hegemony. Xi Jinping named it explicitly in June 2023.
The formula of combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's specific realities (the first integration) and with China's fine traditional culture (the second integration).
The official term for China's own path of modernization, promoted since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
Confidence in China's culture and its socialist cultural path. It was added to the "Four-sphere Confidence" (path, theory, system, culture) under Xi Jinping.
The policy announced in 1956 encouraging a "hundred flowers" in the arts and a "hundred schools" in scholarship, within limits set by the Party.

t: The Party's historical experience in combating formalism and bureaucratism
zh: 我们党力戒形式主义、官僚主义的历史经验
paras: Liu Yan and Wang Peng ask what the Communist Party of China's century-plus struggle against formalism and bureaucratism can teach the present. Citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), they call both practices major enemies of the Party's mission in the new era. They argue that the Party has stayed vigilant and adapted its response to each new form of the problem.

The article reviews the Party's record from the New Democratic Revolution through reform and opening up to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It draws on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and organises the experience under four headings: building an ideological defence, perfecting the institutional system, cultivating a good work style, and emphasising supervision by the masses.

On ideology, the authors trace formalism and bureaucratism to wavering ideals and convictions, and cite Mao's view that formalism comes from idealism and a weak grasp of Marxism. They point to Yan'an rectification, Deng's ideological struggle and Xi's stress on Party spirit. On institutions, they follow Deng's claim that style problems cannot be solved without fixing institutions, and describe a system of Party regulations and laws covering education, regulation, restraint and punishment. On style and supervision, they note that the core problem is detachment from reality and the masses. They list the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, the campaign against the "four undesirable work styles", and efforts to ease burdens on the grassroots. They also stress public supervision and the use of public satisfaction in assessing cadres.

The authors conclude that these four measures together form the historical experience that is relevant to opposing formalism and bureaucratism today and to advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed overview of how Party discourse links anti-bureaucratism to ideology, institution-building, work style and mass supervision.
quoteEn: Formalism and bureaucratism arise because some Party members and cadres have wavering ideals and convictions. They do not, or not fully, put the cause of the Party and the people first, and are keen to perform for superiors, unaccountable to those below, indifferent to results, and calculating their own personal interests.
quoteZh: 形式主义、官僚主义产生的根源，在于一些党员干部理想信念出现了动摇，干工作不是或不完全是以党和人民的事业为重，热衷于对上表现、不对下负责、不考虑实效，打个人的“小算盘”。

glossary.explanation: In Party discourse, a work style that stresses appearances, paperwork and procedure over practical results. It is paired with bureaucratism as a standard target of Party rectification.
A style of leadership marked by detachment from the masses, arbitrary command and indifference to real problems. The Party treats it as a persistent ailment.
Rules on work style adopted by the Central Committee in December 2012, shortly after the 18th Party Congress. They curb extravagance, excessive meetings and formalistic practices among officials.
Formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance. The Party has campaigned against them since 2013.
The Party-wide rectification campaign of the early 1940s, led by Mao Zedong. It targeted subjectivism, sectarianism and Party formalism.
The official name for the Party's current development path and national goal, set out in Xi Jinping-era documents.

t: Multidisciplinary perspectives on research into CPC Party building and their integration
zh: 中共党建研究的多学科视角及其融合
source: Journal of East China Normal University, 2025 no. 1
paras: Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), scholars from many disciplines have studied the Communist Party's own construction, yet they rarely talk to one another. Wang Keyuan reviews how political science, sociology and management studies each approach Party building, sets out their strengths and weaknesses, and argues that the field has become fragmented. The article proposes ways to integrate the disciplines, prompted by Xi Jinping's January 2022 call to improve the discipline, academic and discourse systems of Party building research.

The article has four sections. The first three survey one discipline each. Political science works with concepts such as the "mission-driven party", with arguments for why Party leadership is necessary in modernization, and with empirical study of leadership and governing methods. Sociology examines organisational embedding in new economic and social organisations, the co-optation of new social strata such as private entrepreneurs, and a "spatial turn" in grassroots Party building. Management studies covers Party self-governance, Party-led grassroots governance and digital tools in Party work. The fourth section assesses all three and proposes integration.

Wang's critique is specific to each field. Political science, in this account, relies on grand narratives and selective historical evidence, and its concepts are not distinctive: "mission-driven party" echoes Nanni's missionary/broker distinction, and every ruling party "governs". Management studies coins labels such as "integrated governance" while neglecting historical precedents like the Yan'an-era unified leadership system. Sociology is richer and more finely grained, but borrows Western spatial theories uncritically. Wang adds that traditional Party history scholars work mainly from texts and leaders' speeches, while other disciplines favour institutional analysis or surveys, and the two groups seldom read each other's work or attend each other's meetings.

Wang concludes that integrating the disciplines would produce a three-level framework of discourse, institutions and practice. Discourse means what leaders say and demand, institutions means the designs that follow, and practice means how those designs actually operate. Wang treats all three as indispensable and links the integration to the aim of "using scholarship to speak about politics", which balances academic depth with political character.
