Read the original if you want a map of how Chinese political scientists, sociologists and management scholars frame Party building, and where a Chinese author finds that work weak.
quoteEn: In fact, integrating the knowledge of the above disciplines on CPC Party building can yield a three-level logical framework of \"discourse–institutions–practice\".
quoteZh: 实际上，将上述四个学科关于中共党建的知识融合起来，就能形成“话语－制度－实践”三层次的逻辑框架。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese political science describing the CPC as a party driven by a historical mission, such as national rejuvenation, rather than by vote-maximising. The article notes it resembles Nanni's "missionary party" category.

t: Leading and safeguarding the building of world-class universities with Chinese characteristics through full and rigorous Party and university governance
zh: 以全面从严管党治校引领保障中国特色世界一流大学建设
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in 2025, Zhang Jun, Party secretary of Beijing Institute of Technology and a member of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, asks how full and rigorous self-governance of the Party can lead and safeguard the building of world-class universities with Chinese characteristics. Zhang argues that the Party's self-reform and stricter Party management in universities are consistent with, and necessary for, better performance in education, science and talent work. The article takes its cue from Xi Jinping's speech at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection.

The article has three parts. The first sets out why the Party's self-reform must continue, drawing on the Party's history, the demands of Chinese modernization and the idea of escaping the 'historical cycle' of rise and decline. The second examines the political considerations behind tightening Party governance in universities, looking at their mission, their internal and external situation and the problems Zhang identifies. The third proposes concrete measures.

Zhang's central claim is that self-reform is the Party's distinctive strength, from the Yan'an rectification campaign to the anti-corruption drive since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In universities, Zhang says, Party governance matters more because of the 'Two Great Situations', international rivalry over science and talent, and growing resources and integrity risks. Zhang names shortcomings in supervision: weak political development, thin ideological and political education, insufficient transmission of responsibility, and corruption in research, construction and admissions. The proposed remedy has three strands: making the Party's overall leadership effective, including the president responsibility system under the Party committee and ideological education; institutionalising the fusion of Party-building with academic work through comprehensive, specialised and deeper inspection tours, extended to secondary-level Party organisations; and making rigorous governance long-term through discipline education, institutional constraints and the 'Three不 [not daring, not able, not wanting] to be corrupt' approach.

Zhang concludes that a systematic approach to Party governance, covering all content, personnel, responsibilities and institutions, should turn the Party's leadership advantage into an advantage in building world-class universities. The article is a Party-internal programmatic statement from a university leader and discipline official rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want to see how Party discipline and inspection work are linked to higher-education policy in current official discourse, including the specific mechanisms proposed for universities.
quoteEn: We must address Party spirit, Party conduct and Party discipline together, strengthen the ethos of schools and study and the ethics of teachers, correct the stubborn ills of the 'four undesirable work styles', remove the soil and conditions in which corruption breeds, and create a clean and upright environment for teaching and nurturing students.
quoteZh: 必须坚持党性党风党纪一起抓，加强校风学风、师德师风建设，纠治“四风”顽疾，铲除腐败滋生的土壤和条件，营造风清气正的教书育人环境。

glossary.explanation: A concept stressed by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress: the Party's capacity to correct itself and purge corruption and misconduct from within.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party-discipline and anti-corruption programme pursued since 2012, covering political, ideological, organisational and conduct requirements.
The official term for China's path of modernization, set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022) as the Party's central task.
The national programme to build world-class universities and disciplines. The article uses the term for the participating institutions.

glossary.zh: 党委领导下的校长负责制
glossary.pinyin: dǎngwěi lǐngdǎo xià de xiàozhǎng fùzé zhì
glossary.en: president responsibility system under the Party committee
glossary.explanation: The university governance arrangement in China's public universities, in which the president manages the institution under the leadership of the university Party committee.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: The Third Plenum of the 20th Party Congress shows firm resolve to see reform through to the end
zh: 党的二十届三中全会彰显将改革进行到底的坚强决心
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2024 no. 11
paras: Li Junru takes up Xi Jinping's description of the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) as showing 'firm resolve and strong sense of mission' to carry reform through to the end. The article argues that the plenum, the tenth Third Plenum since reform and opening up began, marks a new stage in China's reform, and that 2024 was distinguished by the Party's determination in preparing, adopting and implementing its Decision.

The piece has three parts. It first distinguishes 'reform', 'comprehensively deepening reform' and 'further comprehensively deepening reform'. It then considers why this distinction matters, through a brief historical comparison of Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi. Finally it reviews 2024: the drafting process, Xi's May inspection in Shandong, the plenum of 15–18 July, and the follow-up in Politburo meetings, policy documents and legislation.

Li's central argument is that 'comprehensively deepening reform' is not merely 'reform' with adjectives added. Drawing on Deng's 1992 southern tour remarks and Xi's 2013 statements, Li reads it as reform aimed at 'governance', that is, modernizing the system and capacity of national governance. The 2024 phase keeps that overall goal but adds a new theme, Chinese modernization. Li periodises the shift: Mao 'organised' the people, Deng made them 'lively', and Xi's 2013 phase stressed 'lively yet orderly'. The 2024 plenum, in Li's account, begins a stage in which national governance and social development are better matched. Li illustrates this with the planned Private Economy Promotion Law, which protects private firms' rights while setting legal and ethical obligations.

Li concludes that the 300-plus reform measures, the dense flow of documents, laws such as the decision to raise the statutory retirement age gradually, and opening-up steps such as visa-free transit and the removal of foreign-investment restrictions all show the Party means to follow through. Li reports that the measures improved confidence and economic recovery after the Politburo meeting of 26 September, and that some foreign firms expanded investment in China. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-school reading of how the 2024 plenum relates to earlier reform stages, together with a chronological record of its implementation.
quoteEn: 'Comprehensively deepening reform' is not a continuation of 'reform' in the general sense, but reform put forward on the basis of Deng Xiaoping's reform thinking and strategic conception, one considered 'from the overall perspective of the system and capacity of national governance'.
quoteZh: “全面深化改革”不是“改革”一般意义上的延续，而是根据邓小平的改革思想和战略构想提出的，“从国家治理体系和治理能力的总体角度考虑”的改革

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's path of modernization, set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022). The Party presents it as distinct from Western models of modernization.

glossary.zh: 国家治理体系和治理能力现代化
glossary.pinyin: guójiā zhìlǐ tǐxì hé zhìlǐ nénglì xiàndàihuà
glossary.en: modernizing the system and capacity of national governance
glossary.literal: modernisation of the national governance system and governance capacity
glossary.explanation: A goal set by the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), alongside improving socialist institutions with Chinese characteristics. It is treated as the overall objective of 'comprehensively deepening reform'.
The reform programme launched at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), covering all fields of reform rather than a few. The 2024 plenum framed its agenda as continuing it.

t: A sharp ideological weapon for strengthening Party conduct in the new era
st: Studying General Secretary Xi Jinping's important expositions on strengthening Party conduct
zh: 新时代加强党的作风建设的锐利思想武器
zhSub: 学习习近平总书记关于加强党的作风建设的重要论述
paras: Writing as the Party's official historian, Qu Qingshan takes up Xi Jinping's body of statements on Party conduct (作风建设). Qu presents them as a theoretical resource for the 2025 campaign of study and education on implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, which runs from the spring session of the National People's Congress to July. The article's thesis is that these statements form a coherent theory, part of Xi's thinking on Party building and on the Party's self-reform, that guides the campaign.

The article is organised in three parts. The first covers why conduct matters, what kind of problem it is and what its core is. The second covers the main measures, the key tasks and the 'critical minority' of leading cadres. The third covers effective methods, purposes and institutional guarantees. Qu quotes Xi extensively throughout, including his March 2025 remarks in Guizhou and Yunnan, and cites the monthly publication of data on violations of the eight-point regulations, which had reached its 137th consecutive month.

In Qu's reading, Xi holds that Party conduct determines whether the people support the Party and whether its cause succeeds. Conduct problems are at bottom problems of Party spirit (党性), measured by the distinction between public and private interest, and at their core they concern the Party's relationship with the people. The eight-point regulations are described as a long-term, strict starting point. The campaign against the 'four undesirable work styles' (formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance) is a continuing task, to be pursued without 'fatigue syndrome' and against new covert variants. Leading cadres must set an example from the top down, and Qu stresses that Xi's own conduct is held up as a model.

For the longer term, Qu reports Xi's call to link correcting conduct, enforcing discipline and fighting corruption, and to investigate and handle conduct problems and corruption together. Conduct work should extend to study, writing and meeting styles, and should shape social customs through a combination of moral advocacy and a 'negative list' of prohibitions. Party committees and discipline commissions bear defined responsibilities, supported by regularised institutions and technological supervision. Qu concludes that conduct building is never finished and urges Party members to study these texts and carry out the campaign thoroughly. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-history reading of how Xi's conduct theory is organised and presented at the start of the 2025 campaign.
quoteEn: Conduct building has only a continuous tense and never a completed one; it is by no means an expedient measure but an eternal task.
quoteZh: 作风建设只有进行时，没有完成时，决不是权宜之计，而是永恒的课题。

glossary.explanation: A set of rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012, shortly after the 18th Party Congress, to curb officials' extravagance, formalism and bureaucratism. It covers matters such as meetings, travel, receptions and contact with the public.
Formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, which Party discourse identifies as the main conduct problems to be corrected since 2012.
A phrase used by Xi Jinping for leading cadres, whose conduct is said to set the tone for the whole Party and society.
An official concept holding that the Party can keep itself clean and effective through its own continuous internal rectification, rather than through external checks.
The quality of loyalty to the Party's ideals, principles and organisation expected of members; here treated as the underlying basis of good conduct.

t: Improving the system of intra-Party regulations from the perspective of the Marxist systems view
zh: 马克思主义系统观视角下的党内法规制度体系完善
paras: The article asks how the system of intra-Party regulations can be further improved now that the Party has declared it "relatively complete". Meng and Wang argue that this system should be treated as a genuine "system" in the sense of the Marxist systems view. On that basis, they say, its problems can be diagnosed and fixed as a whole rather than regulation by regulation.

The authors first review the official definition of the system, from the 2017 Opinions on strengthening intra-Party regulation to the 2021 additions, and note that existing scholarship has seldom applied systems thinking to it. They then describe the system through four features: wholeness, structure, function and openness. For each feature they set out current difficulties, and then propose remedies. Engels on nature as an interconnected totality is their main classical reference.

In their account, the system has a vertical hierarchy (the Party constitution, central regulations, ministerial regulations, local regulations) and a horizontal "1+4" framework of four blocks: organisation, leadership, self-development and supervision. The authors identify several problems. Some regulations are dormant or conflict with newer rules. The concepts "intra-Party regulation system" and "intra-Party regulation institutional system" are used interchangeably. Substantive rules lack procedural counterparts. The blocks overlap, and the self-development and supervision blocks far outnumber the leadership and organisation blocks. The system's "value rationality" is neglected. Drafting is insufficiently democratic and lacks technical standards.

The proposed remedies are to plan the whole system and clarify its concepts. The authors also call for filling gaps, for example with regulations on ideological and political work, and for supporting rules for the United Front regulations. They would reclassify overlapping provisions, shifting the focus from "no rules to follow" to good rules and good governance, and open drafting to rank-and-file members. They also propose a technical drafting standard, piloted locally. They conclude that only by abandoning "fragmented" thinking can the system be optimised. Read the original if you study Party-building, intra-Party regulation or how Chinese legal scholarship applies systems theory to the Party's own institutions.
quoteEn: Improving the system of intra-Party regulations is a systematic undertaking in which efforts must come from many directions and pull the same way.
quoteZh: 完善党内法规制度体系，是一个多方发力、同向发力的系统工程。

glossary.explanation: The body of formal rules governing the Communist Party's own organisation and conduct. It is defined as organised around the Party constitution, with democratic centralism at its core.
The structure adopted in 2017: the Party constitution plus four blocks of regulations on organisation, leadership, self-development and supervision/guarantees.

t: Between substance and function: source problems from the perspective of a "policy history of reform and opening up"
zh: 体用之间：“改革开放政策史”视野下的史料学问题
source: Studies of CPC History (Zhonggong dangshi yanjiu), 2024 no. 6
paras: Zhao Nuo takes up a methodological problem in the emerging study of the history of reform and opening up: how to find direction in a mass of sources when core archives are limited and peripheral materials are abundant. The article argues that researchers should choose research questions first, so that the questions guide where to look. Zhao proposes the "policy history of reform and opening up" as the point where sources and questions meet, and holds that sources and questions are mutually constitutive ("substance and function") rather than separate.

The article first justifies policy history. Zhao says policy is the link between theory and practice and a baseline in the sources, and describes the decades since 1978 as an "era of policy". Zhao then sets out three working strategies, each with examples drawn from the author's own research: extending the time frame, moving down to local archives, and connecting policy history with neighbouring fields. The examples are price reform, the household contract responsibility system in the provinces, and the 1982–1988 institutional reform of the State Council.

Zhao's core claim is that policy history has been dismissed as a dull account of meetings and documents, but can be made productive. Treating policy as "policy chains" and "policy networks" lets researchers reuse already published materials such as leaders' works, document collections and periodicals. For price reform, this reveals a "triangular balance" among price stability, social stability and growth. Local archives, in Zhao's account, show that the usual "breakthrough, central approval, full roll-out" narrative and the reform/conservative divide are too crude. Provincial decisions came in three waves with uneven timing, and Shandong's leaders promoted reformers while avoiding open controversy. Finally, "peripheral sources" such as reference books, diaries, letters, periodicals, film and poetry can be combined with institutional, intellectual, cultural and social history, and some may become core sources.

Zhao concludes that the history of reform and opening up needs source work organised around a sense of direction chosen through research questions. The article recommends policy history as the way to do this and warns against anxieties about fragmentation, arguing that a few focused topics are what the field needs now. The aim, Zhao says, is to join theoretical and practical lines of history and to trace the historical logic of governance. Read the original if you work on the sources and methods of Party history or reform-era history and want concrete guidance on archives, document collections and local materials.
quoteEn: The agonising over whether questions or sources are the substance and which the function has little real meaning; the two are not opposed poles in simple cooperation, but often permeate each other and serve as each other's substance and function.
quoteZh: 议题与史料孰为体、孰为用的纠结实际意义不大，二者不是两端对持、简单合作的关系，常常是相互浸润、互为体用的。

glossary.explanation: The policy course launched at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in 1978, introducing economic reform and opening to the outside world.
A traditional Chinese philosophical pair, in which "ti" is the fundamental essence and "yong" its practical application. The author uses it to describe how research questions and sources relate.
The rural reform of the late 1970s and 1980s that let farm households contract land and output from collectives. It is widely seen as a landmark of reform and opening up.
The author's term for tracing one policy across a long time span, to see continuities and breaks between earlier and later decisions.
The author's term for the set of related policies issued together in the same period, which should be studied in relation to one another.

t: The Seventh Party Congress and the establishment of Mao Zedong Thought as the Party's guiding ideology
zh: 党的七大与毛泽东思想指导地位的确立
paras: Marking the 80th anniversary of the Seventh National Congress of the Communist Party of China (held in Yan'an, April–June 1945), Han Zhenfeng asks why that congress matters and how it came to establish Mao Zedong Thought as the Party's guiding ideology. Han argues that the congress summed up more than twenty years of the new-democratic revolution, set a correct line, programme and tactics, overcame erroneous ideas within the Party and wrote Mao Zedong Thought into the Party constitution. In this account, the result was unprecedented unity on the basis of Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought. The piece is a short commemorative commentary from the Guangming Daily.

The article has four parts. It first recounts the long preparation and the proceedings of the congress, including the reports by Mao Zedong, Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi and Zhou Enlai. It then traces the formation of Mao Zedong Thought in stages: germination (1921–1927), formation (1927–1935), maturity (1935–1945) and later development. A third part follows the emergence of the term "Mao Zedong Thought" itself, and a final part assesses the congress's significance.

Han contends that the congress had been repeatedly postponed since 1931 partly because of war conditions and partly because the Party was not ideologically united on major questions. In Han's reading, the Yan'an rectification movement removed dogmatism, subjectivism and sectarianism, and the Sixth Plenum's resolution on historical questions prepared the ground by affirming Mao's leadership. Han then follows the concept from Zhang Ruxin (1941) and Deng Tuo (1942) to Wang Jiaxiang's 1943 article, which first used the term "Mao Zedong Thought". The Seventh Congress constitution defined it as the thought unifying Marxist-Leninist theory with Chinese revolutionary practice, and Liu Shaoqi's report on the constitution summarised its content in areas such as new democracy, the peasantry, the united front, revolutionary war and Party building.

Han concludes that establishing Mao Zedong Thought as the guiding ideology scientifically summed up the revolution's experience and expressed the Party's ideological, political and organisational maturity. The author presents it as the start of independent theoretical creation and as the guide that led to the founding of the People's Republic and to the foundations of socialist institutions. The piece uses the framing of the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Read the original if you want a concise official-style account of how Party historiography presents the Seventh Congress and the genealogy of the term "Mao Zedong Thought".
quoteEn: Establishing Mao Zedong Thought as the guiding position across the Party reflected the Party's ideological, political and organisational maturity, marked the start of its independent theoretical creation, and realised the integration of Marxism's basic principles with the actual conditions of the Chinese revolution.
quoteZh: 确立毛泽东思想在全党的指导地位，集中反映了我们党在思想上、政治上、组织上的成熟，标志着我们党开始独立自主地进行理论创造，实现了马克思主义基本原理同中国革命实际相结合。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official term for the Chinese adaptation of Marxism-Leninism associated with Mao Zedong. It was written into the Party constitution in 1945.
An ideological campaign in the Party from 1942 onward, aimed at dogmatism, subjectivism and sectarianism. Party historiography treats it as preparation for the Seventh Congress.
Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution (roughly 1919–1949) led by the proletariat against imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism, as a step towards socialism.

t: The functional positioning of intra-Party regulations in relation to intra-Party power
zh: 论党内法规之于党内权力的功能定位
paras: Liu Changqiu asks what function intra-Party regulations (dangnei fagui) should serve in relation to power inside the Chinese Communist Party. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), governing the Party according to regulations has been heavily stressed, and the author notes that many scholars treat the regulations mainly as a means of restraining intra-Party power in order to protect Party members' rights. Liu argues that this view is one-sided. The article's thesis is that the regulations have two dimensions: they must both declare and safeguard intra-Party power and regulate and restrain it, and the two functions are unified in serving the Party's political needs.

The article has four parts. It first reviews the existing scholarship and traces the rights-centred habit of thought in modern jurisprudence that Liu holds responsible for the one-sided emphasis. It then sets out the two-dimensional positioning, treating declaring and safeguarding power as the primary function and regulating and restraining it as an important one. The third part argues that both functions serve the Party's political needs, using Party history from 1921 to the post-2012 period. A short conclusion draws out implications for institution-building.

Liu draws on political science and jurisprudence to argue that law gives power its authority and so sustains order, and that restraint of power rests on this. Unlike state law, which is rights-based, intra-Party regulations are said to give priority to members' obligations, strengthening discipline, the authority of the Party Central Committee and unified action. Liu also holds that unchecked intra-Party power invites abuse, corruption and policy errors, so the regulations must set conditions, procedures and responsibilities, which Liu presents as an expression of the Party's self-discipline and self-reform. Historical examples include Mao Zedong's 1938 call for detailed intra-Party rules against factionalism, the 1955 supervisory commissions and Deng Xiaoping's remarks on Party rules.

Liu concludes that the apparent conflict between the two functions is a dialectical unity. Regulation design should seek a "golden mean" between safeguarding and restraining power, rebalancing the intra-Party power structure by dividing and allocating powers sensibly. Liu credits the regulatory system built since 2012 with strengthening centralised leadership while curbing corruption. Read the original if you study Party-building theory or intra-Party law and want to see how a Chinese legal scholar justifies a power-strengthening function for Party rules alongside the rights-protection view.
quoteEn: Intra-Party regulations must both declare and safeguard intra-Party power and regulate and restrict it, and their institutional design must strive for a balance between the two.
quoteZh: 党内法规既要宣示和保障党内权力，同时又要规范和限制党内权力，其制度设计须努力实现两者之间的平衡。

glossary.explanation: Rules adopted by the Communist Party of China to govern its own organisation and members, such as the Party Constitution, regulations and guidelines. Since 2014 they have been counted as part of the socialist rule-of-law system.

glossary.en: governing the Party according to regulations
glossary.literal: governing the Party in accordance with rules
glossary.explanation: The principle of running the Party through intra-Party regulations, emphasised in official discourse since the 18th Party Congress (2012) alongside governing the country according to law.
In the article, the authority that Party organisations hold over lower organisations and members, defined as a form of organisational public power.

keywords: governing the Party according to regulations

t: Building an anti-corruption institutional system with Chinese characteristics for the new era
st: An interview with Lu Pinyue, senior professor at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics
zh: 构建新时代中国特色反腐败制度体系
zhSub: 访上海财经大学资深教授鲁品越
paras: This is an interview with Lu Pinyue, senior professor at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, who has researched the topic. It was published in Marxist Studies (2025, no. 3). Lu takes up why corruption has been an unsolved problem throughout history and why, in Lu's account, only socialism under the Communist Party's leadership can build an anti-corruption system that treats both symptoms and root causes.

The interview has four parts. It first explains why anti-corruption matters and why old systems failed, then analyses the causes and types of corruption under the socialist market economy. It next sets out the essential features and basic architecture of the new-era system, and finally examines the "three-no" mechanism (not daring, not being able, not wanting to be corrupt). The interviewer's questions follow this order, and Lu quotes Xi Jinping extensively throughout.

Lu argues that the essence of an institution is set by its principal contradiction. In exploiting-class systems, whether imperial China, the Kuomintang or capitalism, anti-corruption responds to popular pressure while protecting the rulers' fundamental interests. Lu cites "skinning and stuffing" under the Ming and, for capitalism, political donations, lobbying, the "revolving door" and asset-declaration schemes. Under socialism, by contrast, the Party's anti-corruption will, which represents the people, is said to dominate absolutely over a small minority seeking illegal gain. Lu describes the architecture as "one foundation" (full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, Party leadership and the people first), "two answers" (popular supervision of power and the Party's self-reform), the "three-no" mechanisms, and correcting the "four undesirable work styles". The "three-no" system is the central link. Lu pairs strict supervision with protection of officials who err in good faith, and rejects "high salaries to nurture honesty", locating the real cause of corruption in lost conviction.

Lu concludes that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has made a major contribution to this age-old problem. Lu holds that the system will keep developing alongside the building of a modern socialist country and that high-pressure anti-corruption must continue, since power always carries the risk of corruption. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theoretical account of how Chinese scholars explain the logic, types and institutional design of the current anti-corruption campaign.
quoteEn: Anti-corruption is indeed an age-old problem for human society, because the risk of corruption always accompanies public power.
quoteZh: 反腐败的确是人类社会的千古难题，因为腐败风险总是与公共权力相伴而生。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: Party-building policy emphasised since the 18th Party Congress (2012), stressing strict discipline, supervision and anti-corruption within the Communist Party.

glossary.pinyin: bù gǎn fǔ, bù néng fǔ, bù xiǎng fǔ
glossary.literal: not daring to be corrupt, not able to be corrupt, not wanting to be corrupt
glossary.explanation: Official formula for anti-corruption: deterrence through punishment, institutional constraints on power, and cultivation of ideals and integrity.
Formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, targeted by the Central Committee's eight-point rules adopted in 2012.
Official concept that the Party itself must purify and improve itself, presented as the second answer, after popular supervision, to the historical cycle of rise and decline.

t: The roots of the Party's spirit of self-reform in fine traditional Chinese culture
zh: 党的自我革命精神的中华优秀传统文化根脉探析
paras: Huang Gang and Zhang Jing ask how the Communist Party's spirit of self-reform relates to fine traditional Chinese culture. They argue that this spirit is a concrete result of the Two Integrations in the field of Party building. In their account, it is rooted in traditional ideas and moral norms that the Party has inherited and carried forward. They present this as theoretically and practically significant for the full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era.

The article is organised around four traditional cultural qualities, each paired with a contemporary Party concept. The first is a consciousness of hardship and danger, linked to the "historical cycle" question. The second is moral self-scrutiny in solitude, linked to the "difficulties unique to a large party". The third is renewal by discarding the old, linked to the "four selves". The fourth is ceaseless self-strengthening, linked to the "examination" spirit. Each section draws on classical sources such as the Book of Changes, the Analects, the Zuo Commentary and the Daodejing, alongside speeches by Xi Jinping and Mao Zedong.

The authors present self-reform as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of dynastic rise and fall, after the "new path of democracy" that Mao gave in 1945. Concepts such as bottom-line thinking, risk prevention, criticism and self-criticism, and the inspection system are read as modern versions of old ideas about vigilance, self-examination and mending one's faults. The four "selves" (self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation) are tied to the Book of Changes idea of renewal, with the Party's institution-building, repeated revisions of the Party Constitution, the Central Committee's eight-point regulations and its emphasis on study cited as evidence. The authors claim that the Party's self-reform gives these culturally inherited traits a dynamic form.

The authors conclude that the Party's self-reform spirit fits closely with the traditional values of preparedness against danger, self-reflection, renewal and perseverance. They describe a progression from fit to integration to fusion, which they say achieves the creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional culture. In their view, this cultural foundation supplies spiritual strength for resolving the difficulties unique to a large party and for building a Marxist party that stays in power over the long term. Read the original if you want to see how Party-building theory is tied to classical Chinese sources and to Xi Jinping's formulations.
quoteEn: The Party's spirit of self-reform is highly consistent with the traditional Chinese spirit of preparing for danger in times of peace, self-scrutiny in solitude, renewal by discarding the old, and ceaseless self-strengthening.
quoteZh: 党的自我革命精神与中华优秀传统文化中的居安思危、慎独自省、革故鼎新、自强不息精神具有高度的契合性

glossary.explanation: A concept stressed since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and by Xi Jinping, referring to the Party's efforts to cleanse, correct and renew itself from within. It is presented as the Party's second answer to the historical cycle.
The formula of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second integration was emphasised by Xi Jinping from 2021–2023.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name of the Party's anti-corruption and discipline campaign since 2012. It covers ideological education, institution-building, supervision and discipline.
The pattern in which regimes rise quickly and then decline. It was raised by Huang Yanpei in a 1945 talk with Mao Zedong in Yan'an and is used in Party discourse as a problem the Party must escape.

glossary.en: difficulties unique to a large party
glossary.literal: problems unique to a large party
glossary.explanation: A formulation Xi Jinping put forward in the 20th Party Congress report (2022). It refers to the governance challenges arising from the Party's huge size and its long time in power.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: The Communist Party of China's leadership of rural moral development: historical achievements and experience
zh: 中国共产党领导乡村道德建设的历史成就与经验
source: Mao Zedong Deng Xiaoping Theory Studies, 2024 no. 12
paras: Zhang Zhitao asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has led moral development in the countryside over more than a century, and why it has succeeded. The article argues that rural moral development has been an important and distinctive part of the Party's work in the countryside. Its theoretical roots lie in the Marxist classics, and its historical changes follow a consistent logic. Zhang presents this as a reference for the current drive for rural revitalization.

After a short review of existing studies, the article has three parts. The first draws on Marx and Engels to trace the theoretical origins of the Party's approach. The second follows four historical periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third sets out the logic behind these changes.

In the first part, Zhang reads Marx and Engels as treating morality as a "practical-spiritual" mode of grasping the world, with a normative character that can push society forward or hold it back. Marx and Engels, Zhang says, criticised peasant consciousness as selfish, narrow, scattered and conservative, and held that it can only change when socialised large-scale production replaces small-peasant production. They also made the free and all-round development of the human being the final aim. For the historical part, Zhang lists measures in each period. These include women's emancipation, campaigns against opium and gambling, literacy drives, collectivist education, the Dazhai campaign, the rural civilisation drives, the core socialist values, the protection of traditional villages, and the integration of self-governance, rule of law and rule by virtue.

Zhang identifies four constant principles in the Party's approach: Marxist guidance, the Party's leading role, a people-centred position, and keeping pace with the times. On the last, the Party adjusted rural moral work to each period's principal contradiction and historical task. Zhang concludes that the century of experience has moved rural morality from traditional to modern forms and has adapted Marxist rural moral theory to Chinese conditions. The author calls for adherence to Marxist guidance, the goal of agricultural and rural modernization, and innovation in both practice and theory. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-by-document account of CPC rural moral policy from the 1920s to the 2020s, as the Party's own scholars present it.
quoteEn: The key to the success of the CPC's rural moral development lies in its skill in formulating suitable, well-targeted policies and measures according to the principal social contradiction and the different historical tasks that arise from it.
quoteZh: 中国共产党乡村道德建设能够取得成功，关键就在于善于根据社会主要矛盾以及所形成的不同历史任务，有的放矢地制定与之相适应的政策、措施。

glossary.explanation: A national strategy announced at the 19th Party Congress in 2017 to modernise agriculture and the countryside. It covers industry, ecology, culture, governance and living standards.
A set of twenty-four characters in twelve values at the national, social and individual levels, promoted by the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as the common value consensus.

glossary.en: integration of self-governance, rule of law and rule by virtue
glossary.literal: combination of autonomy, rule of law and rule of virtue
glossary.explanation: A model of rural governance (the "three governances") endorsed at the 19th Party Congress in 2017. It combines village self-government, legal norms and moral guidance.
The Party's official judgement of the main tension in society at a given stage, which defines its central tasks. The article lists four formulations, from the revolutionary period to the new era.

t: Standardising the Party's leadership of legislative work: theoretical explanation, practical challenges and paths for improvement
zh: 党领导立法工作规范化：理论阐释、实践挑战与优化路径
source: Chinese Leadership Science (中国领导科学), 2025 no. 2
paras: Zeng and Xia ask how the Party's leadership of legislation can move from general principle to concrete, operable rules. Their thesis is that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party's leading role in lawmaking has been firmly affirmed, but procedures for exercising it remain underdeveloped. They argue that building explicit procedural norms is both a requirement of the rule of law and an internal requirement of the Party's overall leadership.

The article has four parts. It first offers a theoretical account of why such standardisation is needed, drawing on Peng Zhen's views on turning Party policy into state law. It then examines practice, using the 2023 Criminal Law Amendment (XII) as an example. Next it identifies problems in the preparatory stage, in coordination with legislatures and in protecting legislative powers. It closes with proposals for improvement.

In the authors' account, Party policy is the guide and basis of legislation: mature, tested policies are raised to law through statutory procedure. They present the Party's role as macro-level leadership, setting direction and approving major legislative matters, not managing details. They identify three gaps. Party rules say little about the form of legislative proposals or the review of legislative plans, which vary across localities. The roles of Party committees, Party groups in people's congress standing committees and the congresses themselves are poorly defined, as are the rules for requesting instructions and reporting. Finally, there is no systematic procedural guarantee of the legislature's leading role. The authors say that joint Party-government documents, and Party committees deciding matters that belong to people's congresses, weaken congress authority.

Zeng and Xia propose collective, documented and carefully considered legislative proposals instead of individual leaders' remarks, and a regulated process for reviewing legislative plans. They call for clearer duties for congress Party groups and a standard system of requesting instructions and reporting, with registration, supervision and accountability, and defined categories of major matters. They also want stronger support for congress deputies and for the review of draft laws, and wider use of grassroots legislative liaison points as part of whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want a Chinese legal-scholarly view of the procedural gaps in Party–legislature relations and the reforms proposed.)
quoteEn: Party leadership of legislation means collective leadership of legislation by Party organisations, not the personal leadership of individual Party leading cadres.
quoteZh: 党领导立法是党组织集体领导立法，而不是党的领导干部个人领导立法。

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2019 that describes China's democracy as covering every stage of political and legislative life, including consultation and participation beyond elections.

glossary.en: system of requesting instructions and reporting
glossary.explanation: A Party practice by which subordinate bodies seek guidance on major matters before acting and report back afterwards. In legislation it governs how congress Party groups consult Party committees.

t: Deepening understanding of the laws governing the Party's theoretical innovation
zh: 深化对党的理论创新的规律性认识
paras: This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in March 2025, asks what regularities govern the Communist Party of China's theoretical innovation. Zhao Fuke starts from the 20th Party Congress (2022) task of opening up new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The author also cites the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which stressed advancing theoretical innovation "on a new starting point". Zhao argues that richer results in the new era require a deeper grasp of five regularities.

The article is organised under five headings: the fundamental method of the Two Integrations; a people-first value orientation; systematisation and scholarly grounding of theory; answering practical questions and guiding practice; and the unity of being rooted in China with having the world in view. Zhao draws on Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation of the "sinification of Marxism", Xi Jinping's speeches since 2021, and the Party's recent theoretical documents.

Zhao presents the Two Integrations (combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture) as the fundamental method, with Marxism as the "soul" and traditional culture as the "root". Theory is said to come from the people's creative practice, so innovation must go among the masses and be followed by theoretical study and education. On systematisation, Zhao says innovation shows itself in "identifying concepts" and linking them into judgements and principles. The example given is the Party's self-reform, which Zhao says advanced Marxist party-building theory. Theory must also answer the questions of the era, such as what kind of socialism to uphold and how to build a long-governing Marxist party, and so guide practice.

Zhao concludes that the Party's innovation both solves China's problems and contributes to humanity's. Starting from "what we are doing" is said to have produced the judgement that socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era and the path of Chinese modernization. Concern for the world is said to have produced the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind and the three global initiatives. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists frame the logic of theoretical innovation under Xi Jinping.
quoteEn: The Communist Party of China's theoretical innovation ultimately originates from the practice of life of the people.
quoteZh: 中国共产党的理论创新归根结底来源于人民群众的生活实践。

glossary.explanation: Formula in which Marxism is combined with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Xi Jinping first stated it in full in 2021, and the 'second integration' was stressed in 2023.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: Official phrase for the continuing process of fitting Marxism to China's conditions and to the contemporary era. Mao Zedong first raised the 'sinification of Marxism' in 1938.

Xi-era concept holding that the Party must continually purify and reform itself, tied to anti-corruption and strict Party discipline. Presented as the answer to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall.
Official term for China's own path of modernisation under Party leadership, put forward as the way to achieve national rejuvenation.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept of international relations, promoted since 2012–2013 as a framework of shared development and security.

t: Identification and resonance: the communication and promotion of the spirit of the 1935 Zunyi Conference
zh: 认同与共鸣：1935年遵义会议精神的传达与宣介
paras: Writing for the 90th anniversary of the Zunyi Conference (January 1935), Zhang Xudong asks how a decision reached by the top leadership in three days became a shared conviction across the whole Red Army. The article argues that the turning point was completed only when the conference's spirit was conveyed to every officer and soldier, consolidated through promotion, and finally accepted as a unified consensus. Zhang's thesis is that effective communication of major decisions depends on timeliness and accuracy, but above all on winning ideological identification and emotional resonance.

The article has three parts. The first examines how the conference's spirit was 'conveyed' (chuanda) at the central level and at the unit level. At the central level these means were attendance at the conference, oral briefings, telegrams and documents, and assemblies held from Zhaxi to Gouba and Huili. The second part examines 'promotion' (xuanjie) through proclamations, the Red Army newspaper Hongxing, and propaganda teams. The third part analyses the identification and resonance this produced, drawing mainly on memoirs and diaries of commanders and soldiers.

Zhang's central distinction is that conveying was largely passive reception, while promotion invited active participation. Conveying relied on cadre reports, study of the Resolution, its Outline and the 'Letter to All Red Commanders and Fighters', and layered discussion in which cadres criticised the 'Left' line from their own experience. Promotion used concise, mobilising proclamations, editorials and reports of victories in Hongxing, and propaganda teams with 'agitation sheds', slogans and shouted appeals. Drawing on recollections by figures such as Liu Bocheng, Xiao Ke, Nie Rongzhen and Fang Qiang, Zhang then argues that soldiers identified with the new ideological line, the new military line of active defence and mobile warfare, and the new organisational line centred on Mao Zedong. In Zhang's account, this endorsement was a rational choice as well as an emotional response, in contrast with the 'Left' line's harsh struggles and punishments.

Zhang concludes that the Zunyi Conference achieved its turn from top to bottom only through this process of conveying and promotion, and that its internal implementation deserves study at the meso and micro levels as well as in general assessments. The lesson drawn is that major decisions require attention to timely, accurate and well-chosen means of communication, with a focus on ideological identification and emotional resonance. The author cites Xi Jinping's 2015 call to make good use of the conference's historical experience. Read the original if you want a source-based account, drawn from Long March memoirs and diaries, of how the Zunyi decisions were passed down through the Red Army and how official Party history interprets that process.
quoteEn: For major decisions and deployments, one must attend to the methods of conveying and promoting them, and even more to ideological identification and emotional resonance.
quoteZh: 重大决策部署，既要讲究传达与宣介的方式方法，更要重视思想认同与情感共鸣。

glossary.explanation: An enlarged meeting of the CPC Political Bureau held in Zunyi, Guizhou, in January 1935 during the Long March. Official Party history treats it as the turning point at which Mao Zedong's leadership of the military line was established.

The label official Party history gives to the leadership line of Wang Ming and others before Zunyi, criticised as dogmatist and adventurist. The article associates it with positional defence in the fifth anti-encirclement campaign.
A military doctrine associated with Mao Zedong. It favours mobile and guerrilla warfare to destroy enemy forces, in contrast to passive, positional defence.
The top-down relaying of a decision or the spirit of a meeting to lower levels. The article treats it as the first, largely passive stage of dissemination.
Propaganda and presentation of a decision through proclamations, media and cultural forms. The article treats it as the second stage, which turns reception into active participation.

t: The basic course and experience of ruling-party building since the founding of the People's Republic of China
zh: 新中国成立以来执政党建设的基本历程与经验
source: Marxist Theory Discipline Studies (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2025 no. 2
paras: Liu Honglin asks what a Marxist ruling party is and how one should be built, which the article treats as the basic question of Party building. Liu argues that over more than 75 years the Communist Party of China has deepened its grasp of the laws governing its own construction, and has found in self-reform a second answer to the historical cycle of rise and decline. The article sets out to draw lessons from this course for the Party's self-reform, for solving the problems unique to a large party, and for advancing national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization.

The article is a historical survey in three periods: the period of socialist revolution and construction, the era of reform and opening up and socialist modernization, and the new era. Liu frames each period around the problems Party building faced. These include power alienation and corruption, separation from the masses, the 'fear of incompetence' and ideological or institutional rigidity. A short conclusion draws out general lessons.

For the first period, Liu describes open Party-building, the setting up of Party committees and groups in state organs, rectification campaigns, the Three-Anti campaign (the first concentrated anti-corruption drive), cadre training and discipline inspection bodies. The Eighth Party Congress (1956) is presented as a systematic plan for ruling-party building. For the reform era, Liu stresses reform of Party and state leadership systems, the creation of intra-Party regulations, improved Party style, anti-corruption work, ruling-capacity and ruling-theory building, and themed education campaigns. For the new era, Liu stresses top-level design, the Central Eight-point Regulation, a stricter approach to cadres, responsibility systems and about forty intra-Party regulations. Liu describes these as moving Party governance from 'lax and soft' to 'strict and firm' and as forming a system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

Liu concludes that popular support decides the rise and fall of a party, and that winning it depends on the Party's own condition and on what it delivers for the people. Party leadership, Party building and the Party's cause are said to be mutually reinforcing, so Party building must change with the times while keeping to problem-orientation, goals and mission. Its results are ultimately to be tested by the masses' approval, through progress in Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a periodised, document-by-document account of how Party building is presented in official Chinese Party historiography from 1949 to the present.
quoteEn: Party leadership, Party building and the Party's cause are mutually reinforcing, and ruling-party building must keep pace with changing circumstances and the demands of the times.
quoteZh: 党的领导、党的建设、党的事业是相辅相成的，执政党建设必须根据形势变化与时代要求与时俱进

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan and policy programme associated with Xi Jinping since 2012. It covers discipline, anti-corruption, Party style, and the development of intra-Party regulations.
The official idea that the Party can purge and renew itself without external checks. It is presented as the 'second answer' to the historical cycle of rise and decay.
The official name for China's development path, set out in Party documents from the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
A set of rules issued in December 2012 requiring officials to improve their work style and keep close to the people. It curbs formalism, bureaucracy, extravagance and hedonism.

glossary.en: historical cycle of rise and decline
glossary.explanation: The idea, associated with a 1945 exchange between Mao Zedong and Huang Yanpei, that regimes tend to flourish and then collapse. Party leaders say supervision and self-reform allow them to escape it.
The policy launched at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in 1978. It shifted the focus of work to economic development and brought market reforms and opening to the outside world.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: Strengthening the livelihood foundation of building a leading education country
zh: 厚植教育强国建设的民生根基
paras: Duan Meijuan, writing in the People's Daily in March 2025, takes up one of the six attributes that Xi Jinping assigned to a "leading education country" at the National Education Conference: the capacity to safeguard people's livelihood. The article argues that this capacity expresses the people-oriented character of education. Building a leading education country, Duan contends, requires making public education services more inclusive, accessible and convenient, and resolving the pressing educational concerns of ordinary families.

This is a short Party-press commentary, organised in three steps: the meaning of livelihood-protection capacity, the weak links that hold it back, and the practical requirements for strengthening it. It draws on Xi's statements on education and on the record of the Party Central Committee since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It closes with a short passage on the author's own institution, Hunan Women's University.

On meaning, Duan reads livelihood-protection capacity as embodying a people-centred philosophy of development, the idea that educational fairness underpins social fairness and justice, and a higher quality of educational supply. Duan then names three weaknesses: high-quality resources are still insufficient and unevenly distributed, notably between city and countryside; special groups, including left-behind children, children with disabilities and migrant workers' children, are inadequately served; and evaluation still leans on exam scores, so that private tutoring persists despite the "double reduction" policy. The proposed remedies follow these gaps: rebalance resources through fiscal transfers, paired cooperation and teacher rotation; reform evaluation and integrate vocational and general education; and strengthen funding, legal and digital support.

Duan concludes that the work must be guided by Xi Jinping's statements on education and carried out with strict implementation, so that the results of education reform reach all people more fairly. Universities are urged to take on livelihood responsibilities, and Hunan Women's University is offered as an example. It says it links its disciplines to social needs through cooperation with industry and serves women's development. Read the original if you want an example of how official commentary frames education policy in terms of livelihood and fairness, and of the policy measures it lists.
quoteEn: Strengthening livelihood-protection capacity means speeding up the building of an education open equally to everyone, and paying more attention to the balanced allocation of high-quality educational resources across regions, between urban and rural areas, among schools and among groups.
quoteZh: 增强民生保障力，意味着要加快建成平等面向每个人的教育，更重视优质教育资源在区域、城乡、校际、群体之间的均衡配置

glossary.explanation: A goal set out by Xi Jinping at the National Education Conference in 2024. It describes an education system that supports national strength and national rejuvenation.
One of the six attributes of a leading education country listed by Xi. It refers to education's ability to meet people's everyday needs and ensure fair access.
A 2021 policy to reduce students' homework burden and off-campus tutoring, including tighter regulation of private tutoring companies.

glossary.zh: 以人民为中心的发展思想
glossary.pinyin: yǐ rénmín wéi zhōngxīn de fāzhǎn sīxiǎng
glossary.explanation: A principle associated with Xi Jinping that makes the people's wellbeing the aim of development.

t: Upholding the people-centred governing philosophy
zh: 坚持以人民为中心的执政理念
paras: This short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (25 March 2025) asks what the people-centred governing philosophy of the Communist Party of China means and why it matters. Zhang Fuwen argues that it answers the questions of whom the Party governs for, whom it relies on, why it governs and how. In Zhang's account, it is both an innovative development of Marxist party-building theory and a contemporary form of the Party's fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly.

The article first places the philosophy in the Marxist tradition and in the Party's history. It then shows how it appears in the Party's governing practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and ends by linking it to the Party's founding mission, leadership and Party discipline.

Zhang argues that Marxism treats the proletarian party as an instrument of the people's interests and state organs as "public servants", not masters. On this basis the author says the Party represents no interest group or privileged stratum, and takes bringing benefit to the people as the essence of governing. The author cites the poverty-alleviation campaign as evidence, and describes governing as "for the people" and "reliant on the people", a dialectical unity realised through the mass line, now extended online in the age of artificial intelligence. Zhang assigns three roles: the founding mission is the value thread, strengthening Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is an important support.

Zhang concludes that the Party's purity, advanced character and governing capacity are not innate. They must be maintained through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform, so that the people-centred philosophy can be upheld. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists link the people-centred philosophy to Party building and discipline.
quoteEn: The Communist Party's governance is not a \"solo performance\" by Party members and cadres, but a \"grand chorus\" that relies on and mobilises the people.
quoteZh: 中国共产党执政不是广大党员干部的“独角戏”，而是依靠人民、动员人民的“大合唱”。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the Xi Jinping era, from about 2014, for stricter discipline, anti-corruption work and internal supervision within the Communist Party.
An official concept stressing that the Party must continually correct its own faults and purify itself without external pressure.
A working method associated with Mao Zedong in which Party cadres gather the views of ordinary people, turn them into policy and take them back to the people.
The Party's official formula for its founding purpose, to seek happiness for the Chinese people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: The Zunyi Conference: from historical event to historical landmark
zh: 遵义会议：从历史事件到历史标志
source: Teaching and Research (Jiaoxue yu Yanjiu), 2025 no. 3
paras: Marking the 90th anniversary of the Zunyi Conference of January 1935, Huang asks why this meeting, unlike many historical events, became a lasting landmark in the history of the Communist Party of China. The author's answer is that it saved the Party, the Red Army and the revolution at a critical moment. In Huang's account, it did so by effectively establishing Mao Zedong's leadership and the leading position of a correct Marxist line, which opened a stage of independent and self-reliant problem-solving.

The article has four sections. It first examines why the Party leadership before Zunyi was neither stable nor mature. It then treats the conference's organisational result, Mao's leading position, and its political result, the correct line. A final section draws out the conference's historical standing and its lessons for the present. Huang draws on Party resolutions, speeches by Mao, Zhou Enlai, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping, Comintern documents and Xi Jinping's remarks.

Huang contends that before Zunyi the Party lost independence organisationally, because the Comintern repeatedly reshaped its leadership. It also lost independence ideologically, because Comintern resolutions and Soviet experience were turned into a dogmatic "international line" detached from Chinese conditions. Zunyi, the author argues, ended this rule in fact, building on the Tongdao, Liping and Houchang meetings. The Comintern later endorsed Mao's leadership, and the Party defeated Zhang Guotao's splittism. Huang stresses that the conference corrected the military line, and that Mao's later writings, including On Practice and On Contradiction, and the Yan'an rectification movement deepened the political and theoretical reckoning.

Huang draws four lessons. The Party needs a strong and mature central leadership core; the author links this directly to the Two Establishes and to Xi Jinping's position today. It must keep to independent and self-reliant development, which the author connects to Chinese modernization. It must integrate Marxism with China's concrete realities and with traditional Chinese culture, avoiding dogmatism. It must hold to a correct political line, namely the Party's basic theory, line and strategy. Read the original if you want an official Party-history interpretation of Zunyi and how it is tied to present-day leadership doctrine.
quoteEn: A party that has lost both its organisational independence and its ideological independence is bound to be immature and unstable, and bound to suffer setbacks and failure.
quoteZh: 一个丧失了组织的独立性，又丧失了思想的独立性的政党，必然是不成熟的、不稳定的，必然要遭到挫折和失败。

glossary.explanation: A formula from the Party's 2021 historical resolution. It affirms Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Central Committee and of the whole Party, and the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought.
The official term for China's path of development under Party leadership. It is presented as distinct from Western models of modernization.
An ideological education campaign launched in 1942 in the Party's wartime base. It targeted dogmatism and subjectivism and consolidated Mao Zedong's leadership.

t: The operating logic and optimisation paths of rural grassroots Party building in leading rural revitalisation
zh: 农村基层党建引领乡村振兴的运作逻辑与优化路径
paras: Liu Xiaoli asks how rural grassroots Party building can effectively lead rural revitalisation, a strategy launched at the 19th Party Congress (2017) and reinforced by the 20th Party Congress (2022) emphasis on strengthening the grassroots. The article argues that Party leadership works through three linked logics (structure, process and function), and that current weaknesses in each can be remedied by targeted reforms.

The article opens with a survey of existing scholarship, grouped into four perspectives: organisational embedding, authorisation and empowerment, structure and institutions, and structure–function–organisational capacity. Liu finds that most studies summarise local experience or discuss methods, and that the overall logic and a systematic path are underdeveloped. The author then builds a "structure–process–function" framework. The article moves through the operating logic, the problems found in practice and proposed paths of improvement.

On operating logic, Liu holds that Party leadership builds a "one core, many actors" community of revitalisation, with the Party playing a "meta-governance" role across levels and sectors. It re-engineers mechanisms of value, interest and power to integrate social forces, and it exercises five capacities: political leadership, ideological guidance, development promotion, mass cohesion and social service. Political leadership is said to be the core and to determine the others. Liu identifies three problems: imbalance in structure (strong Party and government, weak enterprises and society), weak adaptability in process (poor coordination, rigid institutions, tensions among culture, economy and politics), and insufficient fit in function, where Party building "floats above" revitalisation as "two skins".

Liu proposes widening and diversifying Party-organisation coverage, for example in industrial bases, associations and among migrant members. The author also proposes organisational linkage mechanisms, "Party–mass roundtables" and shared-interest communities, and a shift from rigid "embedding" to "integration". Further proposals are to strengthen political functions, ideological guidance under socialist core values, farmers' initiative through the mass line, incentive and mediation systems, and service provision. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-school account of how grassroots Party building is conceptualised and prescribed in rural revitalisation policy.
quoteEn: Political leadership is the core category of grassroots Party building's leadership of rural revitalisation; mass cohesion, development-promoting capacity, ideological guidance and social service are its concrete means.
quoteZh: 政治领导力是基层党建引领乡村振兴的核心范畴，群众凝聚力、发展推动力、思想引领力和社会服务力是基层党建引领乡村振兴的具体方式

glossary.explanation: A national strategy announced at the 19th Party Congress (2017) to promote agricultural and rural development and narrow urban–rural gaps.
The practice of using Party organisational work to guide and steer economic and social tasks, here rural revitalisation.
A governance formula in which Party organisations form the leading core while governments, enterprises and social organisations take part.
A concept from governance studies meaning the governance of governance, here used for the Party's role in coordinating other actors.
A Party working method, associated with Mao Zedong, of going among the people, drawing on their views and mobilising them.

t: What counts as important research on CPC history?
st: Rethinking the problem of "fragmentation"
zh: 究竟何为重要的中共党史研究?
zhSub: “碎片化”问题再思考
source: Studies on the History of the Communist Party of China (Zhonggong dangshi yanjiu), 2024 no. 6
paras: Ying Xing asks what makes research on the history of the Communist Party of China (CPC) important, at a time when the field is flooded with submissions and publications that the author finds heavy on process and detail but light on problems, structure and weight. Ying argues that fragmentation will not be cured by gathering more sources: the field needs historical insight (shishi) of the kind valued by Chinese historiography, not merely the accumulation of archival material. The article presents its answer as five questions.

Ying opens with a survey of Chinese historiographical criticism from Liu Zhiji to Chen Yinke, Qian Mu and Liu Xianxin. The survey is meant to show that many historians rejected the claim that history is simply the study of sources. The five questions then ask what the most important Party-history sources are, why political history matters, why comparison matters, which theory to borrow, and why the study of "wind and momentum" is needed. Examples come from Chen Yinke, Foucault, Weber, Fei Xiaotong and Wang Fansen, along with Red Army history.

Ying makes three main moves. First, important sources are those with overall significance for the Party's thought and line, such as congress resolutions, Party constitutions and records of cadres trained in the Soviet Union, rather than whatever is convenient. The author criticises "hometown Party history", which picks subjects by ease of access. Second, political history, with organisational and intellectual history, is the centre of Party history, and Ying reads even Foucault's work on marginal groups as political history. Comparison is what lets a study move from a case to general conclusions instead of "seeing the small through the small". The author illustrates this with the Red Army's first honorary titles for combat units, awarded in the Sichuan–Shaanxi base area in 1934. Third, Ying warns against "middle-range theory" and urges sustained work on classical thinkers such as Marx, Tocqueville, Weber and Foucault. The author adds that theory can "discover" concepts in the sources as well as invent them, and that historians should combine the "solid" study of facts with the "hollow" study of climate and trends.

Ying concludes that fragmentary studies with reliable sources and clear interpretation still have scholarly value, but that research differs in quality. Those who want to go beyond fragmentation must ask whether their topics carry enough weight, and should not rely on convenient sources or rapid output. Important research, the author says, "blows the wind" and does not merely receive it. Read the original if you want to understand a leading sociologist's critique of current Party-history scholarship, or the way Chinese historiographical and Western theoretical traditions are used to set methodological standards for the field.
quoteEn: Important research is what blows the wind, not what is merely blown by it.
quoteZh: 所谓重要的研究，就是“吹风者”，而非“受吹者”。

glossary.explanation: A concept from traditional Chinese historiography, ranked by Liu Zhiji alongside talent and learning. It means the ability to grasp the meaning and larger significance of historical events.

The author's term for Party-history research that picks its subject because it is the researcher's home area or easily accessible. It is modelled on the author's earlier criticism of "hometown sociology".

A term from Western social science for theories that sit between grand theory and empirical description. The author treats it as producing fragmented theory that handles historical complexity crudely.

glossary.literal: observing the wind and gauging the momentum
glossary.explanation: A method drawn from the historian Liu Xianxin, in which historians study the climate and trends behind concrete facts. The author presents it as a complement to evidence-based research.

t: A semiotic reading of how the Chinese Communist Party's Red newspapers shaped the revolutionary spirit
zh: 中国共产党红色报刊塑造革命精神的符号学解读
paras: Su Jie and Wang Fei ask how the Party's Red newspapers of the New Democratic Revolution period used signs to shape and spread the revolutionary spirit, a mechanism they say existing research has treated only thinly. They argue that linguistic and visual signs, combined in layered structures, conveyed revolutionary ideas, stirred popular feeling and built consensus. The study is framed by the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to build socialist ideology with strong cohesion and leadership.

The authors take the Soviet-area newspaper Red China (Hongse Zhonghua) as their case. Section one identifies its linguistic signs (keywords, slogans, editorials) and visual signs (illustrations, mastheads, typefaces, layout), then examines how they combine within and across categories. Section two applies Peirce's tripartite account of the interpretant to issue 242, and section three draws historical values and present-day lessons. Saussure, Eagleton and Geertz are used as theoretical support.

The central argument is that meaning is produced through relations between signs. The authors report that the paper's 172 illustrations broadly follow a conflict frame of enemy, us and friend, and that mastheads fuse fonts, a map of China, a five-pointed star and the Party emblem into a single visual narrative. Using Peirce, they treat the intentional interpretant as the Party's mobilising intent, set out in headline, body text and calls to action in issue 242. The effective interpretant is the audience's emotional resonance and cognitive reading, and the communal interpretant is the shared consensus and collective action that embed the spirit in group memory.

The authors credit Red newspapers with three historical values: spreading revolutionary theory in concrete cultural symbols, strengthening identity through hero and martyr imagery, and passing revolutionary culture across generations. For the present they draw two lessons for Party media: keep a concise, forceful vernacular style, and stay close to people's livelihood, now extended through the "online mass line". They tie the latter to the Marxist principle of the people's character and to Mao Zedong's idea of newspapers run for the masses. Read the original if you want a worked example of applying Peirce-style semiotics to Party press history, with close description of Red China's mastheads and front pages.
quoteEn: By presenting revolutionary heroes and major events symbolically, Red newspapers turned these symbols into society's collective memory, allowing the revolutionary cultural tradition to continue through history.
quoteZh: 红色报刊通过符号化展示革命英雄人物、重大事件等内容，将这些符号转化为社会的集体记忆，使革命文化传统得以在历史进程中延续。

glossary.explanation: Press organs published by the Communist Party during the revolutionary era, such as Red China, used for propaganda and mobilisation.
The set of values attributed to the Party's revolutionary history, such as struggle, sacrifice and service to the people, which official discourse promotes as a heritage.
Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution, roughly 1919–1949, led by the proletariat against imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism.
A principle in Party discourse that media and policy must serve the people's fundamental interests; the 20th Party Congress report calls it an essential attribute of Marxism.

t: Strengthening "Three New" Party building to raise the effectiveness of primary-level governance
zh: 以加强“三新”党建提升基层治理效能
paras: Wang Yang, a deputy dean at a university school of Marxism, takes up a practical problem in a short commentary in Guangming Daily. China's new economic organisations, new social organisations and new employment groups (the "Three New") are growing quickly, and the author asks how Party building in these areas can raise the effectiveness of primary-level governance. The thesis is that strengthening "Three New" Party building turns the Party's leadership advantages into concrete results in governance. In Wang's account, this also consolidates the Party's governing foundation and the base of national governance.

The piece cites Xi Jinping's call to give priority to Party building in these three areas, and the 2025 Government Work Report's pledge to improve urban and rural primary-level governance. It is organised in three parts. The first concerns institutions and mechanisms for "Three New" Party building. The second concerns extending Party organisation and work into these fields. The third concerns widening the ways in which "Three New" Party organisations and members can play a role.

On institutions, Wang calls for a chain of "overall leadership, systematic advancement, coordinated operation, and responsibility". Party committees at each level would oversee the work, supported by task forces, joint meetings, assigned contacts and performance assessment. Regional and sector-based coordination would be built around parks, business districts and buildings, and mechanisms such as "blow the whistle and report in" would be extended to these fields. On coverage, Wang proposes embedding Party organisations in grid-based management, using a "whole life cycle" model of registration, entry, empowerment and exit. For delivery drivers and similar workers, the author proposes function-based Party organisations, and uses trade unions, the Communist Youth League and women's federations, together with online one-stop platforms, to mobilise people. On roles, Wang urges flexible education such as livestreamed courses, finer-grained services that protect labour rights, industry-chain and association Party building, and consultation platforms. These platforms would carry demands upward and policy and resources downward, and they would support a governance community in which everyone has responsibility.

Wang concludes that Party leadership can be put into practice at the grassroots through better coordination, wider organisational coverage and fuller use of Party members in emerging sectors. The article presents these as measures for building a governance community in which "everyone has responsibility, does their part and shares in the benefits". Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented statement of how Party-building language is applied to platform workers, private firms and social organisations at the neighbourhood level.
quoteEn: Strengthening "Three New" Party building and raising the effectiveness of primary-level governance is an inherent requirement for further consolidating the Party's governing foundation and the root of national governance, and for promoting high-quality development of social work in the new era.
quoteZh: 加强“三新”党建，提升基层治理效能，是进一步夯实党的执政基础和国家治理根基，推动新时代社会工作高质量发展的题中应有之义。
