The article argues that self-reform should be read through the Marxist view of revolution, as a continuing, internally necessary part of the proletarian party's revolutionary practice. On this reading it is not a one-off campaign. Writing in early 2023, Zeng links the idea to the Party's historical experience and to the "two great revolutions" of the new era.

The article has three parts. The first defines self-reform within Marx's and Engels's accounts of revolution: dialectical negation of oneself, political revolution and social revolution. The second sets out why self-reform arises, under three headings: the proletariat's historical emergence, the historical mission of its party, and revolutionary strategy. The third turns to practice and gives five requirements for self-reform under the Party. It draws on Lenin, Deng Xiaoping, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping.

Zeng's central move is to separate two tasks of the proletarian party. In political revolution the task is confrontation and destruction, and the proletariat must also shed the "old filth" of the society it grew up in. In social revolution the task shifts to construction, and the party must become both a revolutionary party and a governing party, as Lenin's call for self-education under the New Economic Policy is said to show. Zeng then argues that self-reform is necessary because of the proletariat's class character, because of the party's historical mission, and because it is part of revolutionary strategy, which must raise the party's own consciousness and capacity.

On this basis Zeng calls for self-reform that holds to the fundamental direction of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It should grasp the new features of the new era, rely on the people's主体 position, recognise that social revolution is long and arduous, and carry forward a spirit of self-reform. The article presents the Soviet collapse as a case of drift from the socialist direction, and credits full and rigorous self-governance of the Party with strengthening the Party's ties to the people. It also calls for combining "breaking" (tackling corruption) with "establishing" (institution-building). Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic grounds the Party's self-reform in classical Marxist theories of revolution.
quoteEn: Self-reform, as a necessary element, forms part of the inner logic of the proletarian party's historical mission, and is also an inevitable expression of the party's vanguard character and scientific nature.
quoteZh: 自我革命作为必要内容构成了无产阶级政党的历史使命的内在逻辑，也是无产阶级政党先进性和科学性的必然表现。

glossary.explanation: Official term for the Party's continuing effort to purify and improve itself, especially against corruption and ideological slackness. It was stressed in Party documents under Xi Jinping.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: Official slogan for the Party's drive for discipline, anti-corruption and internal supervision since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
Official formulation pairing the great social revolution led by the Party with the Party's own great self-reform, said to be carried out together.

t: Model, paradigm, exemplar: the methodological lessons of the third historical resolution for research on the history of New China
zh: 范本、范式、范例：第三个历史决议对新中国史研究的方法示范
source: Contemporary China History Studies (Dangdai Zhongguoshi Yanjiu), 2022 no. 4
paras: Zhu Hanguo asks what the third historical resolution, adopted by the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee in November 2021, offers as method for scholars studying the history of the People's Republic. The article contends that the resolution sets a standard for such research in three ways: it supplies a model (the 'grand view of history'), a new paradigm (the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation) and a set of methodological exemplars drawn from the correct view of Party history.

The article has three main sections. The first sets out four perspectives on New China's history that follow from the grand view of history. The second reviews the two existing paradigms in the field, a 'national history' paradigm and a 'socialist history' paradigm, citing scholars such as Zhu Jiamu, Cheng Zhongyuan, Li Li'an and Zhang Qihua and works such as the five-volume Draft History of the People's Republic of China. The third draws three methodological lessons from the resolution's correct view of Party history.

Zhu argues that the grand view of history places New China within five thousand years of Chinese history, within the century of Party struggle, within the history of the world socialist movement and within contemporary world history. Against the two existing paradigms, Zhu presents the resolution as proposing a 'rejuvenation paradigm' that divides the period into three phases (to the start of reform and opening up, to the 18th Party Congress of 2012, and the new era since then), each laying foundations for national rejuvenation. On method, Zhu calls for viewing history in concrete, objective and connected terms, so that the periods before and after reform and opening up are not set against each other. Zhu also calls for grasping the main theme and main thread, allowing several themes such as rejuvenation and modernization to coexist, and for treating errors in context. The Cultural Revolution is a nationwide error to be fully rejected, but Zhu holds that its period cannot be dismissed wholesale. The first thirty years' achievements are the 'mainstream' and the errors 'tributaries'; Zhu cites Taiwan's high-school textbooks as an example of one-sided negation.

Zhu concludes that research on New China's history has moved from its founding through development to maturity, and that the resolution is a classic text on how to understand, analyse and write history. Its historiographical attitudes and methods, in Zhu's view, are an example for deepening the field. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese historian of the Party and the People's Republic translates the 2021 resolution into research method and into positions on the periodisation and evaluation of the pre-reform decades.
quoteEn: Viewed across more than seventy years, the history of New China is a history of realizing the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and the founding of New China, reform and opening up, and the entry of socialism with Chinese characteristics into a new era are three monuments along the way.
quoteZh: 纵观 70 多年的新中国史，就是一部实现中华民族伟大复兴的历史，新中国成立、改革开放、中国特色社会主义进入新时代，是其进程中的三座丰碑。

glossary.explanation: The 2021 Central Committee resolution on the major achievements and historical experience of the Party's century of struggle. It follows the 1945 and 1981 resolutions on Party history.
A approach promoted by Xi Jinping that places events in long time spans, wide space and broad context. The article presents it as an expression of historical materialism.
The official goal of restoring China's national strength and standing. The resolution presents it as the central theme of modern Chinese history.
The policy launched at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in 1978, introducing market-oriented economic reform and engagement with the outside world.
The official stance, stressed by Xi Jinping from 2021, that Party history should be assessed through historical materialism, with attention to its main theme and mainstream.

keywords: two periods before and after reform

t: Tracing the concept of "the spirit of historical initiative" and the logic of its evolution
zh: “历史主动精神”概念溯源及其演进逻辑
source: Journal of Beijing Administration Institute, 2022 no. 6
paras: The 2021 Party resolution on the major achievements and historical experience of the Party's first century uses the phrase "the spirit of historical initiative" twice, once for the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and once for the Chinese people. Hou and Lü ask where the concept comes from and how it took shape. They argue that its roots lie in Marx's notion of the proletariat's "historical initiative", and that it developed through Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao into a defining trait of the Party under Xi.

The article has three main parts. The first traces the idea in Marx and Lenin, including Marx's 1871 letter on the Paris Commune and Lenin's comments on the Russian revolution of 1905. The second sets out the Chinese context, moving from the Chinese people's passage from \"spiritual passivity\" to initiative, through Mao's \"conscious dynamic role\", to the reform era. The third covers the concept's formal establishment and its content since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and ends with proposals for the future.

In the authors' reading, Marx and Lenin treat the proletariat's historical initiative as heroism, self-awareness of its mission, revolutionary capacity and creative remaking of society according to objective laws. They contrast this with utopian socialists, who they say treated workers as passive. Lenin's Saturday volunteer labour is presented as an example that moves the concept's focus towards Communists. Mao's \"conscious dynamic role\" is treated as the key link in China: it joins respect for objective laws with the mobilisation of the people and cadres. The authors say Jiang Zemin first formally used the term in 1989, when speaking of the working class. They list six features of the spirit under Xi, including dialectical-materialist method, a people-centred stance, theoretical innovation, Party study campaigns, global strategic vision and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. They condense its meaning into five elements: a scientific spirit that respects laws, a spirit of the people as subject, conscious initiative, foresight and a spirit of responsibility.

The authors conclude that the achievements of the decade since 2012 result from this spirit, and that it must be turned from an idea into practice as the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation enters a critical stage. They propose five dialectical pairings to guide this: Party leadership and the united front; respect for laws and respect for the people; theoretical and pioneering innovation; assessing the situation and seizing momentum; and the Party's self-reform and social revolution. Read the original if you want a detailed genealogy of this official concept, from Marx's letters to the 2021 resolution, and the Party-theory framing around it.
quoteEn: The spirit of historical initiative has a distinctly generative character; it is the result of the combined action of the historical, theoretical and practical logics of the Party's century of leading the people forward.
quoteZh: 历史主动精神具有鲜明的生成性品格，是党百年来团结带领人民砥砺奋进的历史逻辑、理论逻辑、实践逻辑综合作用的结果

glossary.explanation: A phrase in the Party's 2021 historical resolution for the proactive, self-aware attitude of the Party and people in shaping history. The authors trace it to Marx's term "historical initiative".

Mao Zedong's term in On Protracted War for people's ability to act on the world by forming ideas, plans and policies from objective facts. The authors treat it as a step in the formation of the concept.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The slogan for the Party's discipline and anti-corruption drive since 2012, part of the "Four Comprehensives" strategy.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The long-term national goal in official Party discourse, associated with the "two centenary goals".
The Party's official formulation for its own internal rectification and discipline. Xi Jinping presents it as the answer to the "historical cycle" of dynastic decline.

t: A historical-materialist interpretation of the Communist Party of China's self-reform
zh: 中国共产党自我革命的历史唯物主义阐释
paras: Dai Yuqi takes up the Party's self-reform (自我革命, often rendered "self-revolution"), which official discourse presents as a defining trait and advantage of the Communist Party of China. Dai notes that existing scholarship concentrates on its practical significance, value, measures and comparative advantages, and argues that its historical-materialist interpretation is underdeveloped. The article's thesis is that self-reform can be explained through three strands of historical materialism: social epistemology, the mass view of history, and practical dialectics. Dai also contends that ancient ruling classes and Western electoral parties could only adjust themselves, not carry out self-reform, because of their class standpoints and interests.

The article has four parts. The first treats the origins of self-reform, the second its value, the third its methodology, and the fourth its prospects. The first part traces self-reform through four periods: new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second part draws on Marx, Engels, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping on the people's standpoint and the mass line. The third part works through problem- and goal-orientation, and criticism and struggle. The last looks ahead to the Party's second centenary goal.

In the first part, Dai argues that social being, in the form of world conditions, national conditions and Party conditions, determines the theme of self-reform in each period, while consciousness actively responds to it. Examples include ideological Party-building in the Yan'an rectification, discipline and style in the 1950s, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era. The second part holds that self-reform rests on the people's standpoint and the mass line. Dai presents popular supervision as an external constraint and self-reform as an internal one, and says the two are organically united as answers to the question of escaping the historical cycle. The third part sets out the dialectic of problem-orientation and goal-orientation. Dai names self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-enhancement as the Party's capacities, and warns against both a view that self-reform is unnecessary and an excessive one.

Looking ahead, Dai calls for perfecting the institutional norms of self-reform, with the Party constitution and democratic centralism at the core, plus high-quality personnel and strict supervision. Dai also urges tackling the \"unique problems of a large party\" raised at the 20th Party Congress (2022), and says the Party should further deepen whole-process people's democracy. Dai suggests this would offer a \"Chinese approach\" and a new model for party politics elsewhere. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school-style account of self-reform is built from Marxist philosophical categories, with detailed periodisation of the Party's campaigns.
quoteEn: Without self-reform, democratic supervision loses its effect; without democratic supervision, self-reform loses its test in practice.
quoteZh: 缺乏自我革命，民主监督就会失去作用效果；缺乏民主监督，自我革命就会失去实践检验。

glossary.explanation: A term in official Party discourse for the Party's capacity to identify and correct its own faults and to renew itself. It has been emphasised especially since 2012 and was written into key documents of the 19th and 20th Party Congresses.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party-discipline and anti-corruption drive under Xi Jinping since 2012. It covers ideology, organisation, conduct, discipline and institution-building.

glossary.en: unique problems of a large party
glossary.literal: problems unique to a big party
glossary.explanation: A phrase first used in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It refers to the challenges of governing and managing a party with over 90 million members.

Official term, promoted by Xi Jinping since 2019, for the claim that democracy in China operates across all stages of governance (elections, consultation, decision-making, supervision) rather than only at elections.
A principle of Party work associated with Mao Zedong. It holds that the Party must gather views from the masses, turn them into policy and carry them back to the masses.

t: Telling good stories to shape an image
st: A century of the Communist Party of China's external publicity work
zh: 讲好故事塑形象
zhSub: 中国共产党对外宣传的百年历程
paras: Published in the journal Party Building (Dangjian) in early 2023, this article takes up the Party's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which called for building Chinese discourse and narrative systems, telling China's story well and presenting a credible, lovable and respectable China. Zhai surveys the Communist Party of China's external publicity work (duiwai xuanchuan) over a hundred years. The author argues that the Party has consistently adapted this work to changing international conditions, national circumstances and Party circumstances, and that it has created a favourable international climate of opinion for revolution, construction and reform.

The account is chronological and divided into four stages. The first covers the revolutionary years from the early 1920s to 1949, from the Comintern congresses to the Long March, the War of Resistance and the Liberation War. The second covers the early People's Republic under Cold War isolation. The third covers reform and opening up from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the 16th and 17th Party Congresses. The fourth covers the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

Zhai's central claim is that each stage had a distinct task. Before 1949, the Party worked through limited channels and foreign journalists such as Edgar Snow, whose Red Star Over China is cited, to counter Nationalist propaganda and win international support. After 1949, the aim was to break the Western bloc's blockade and replace the image of a semi-colonial country, through foreign-language publications, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and public diplomacy. Under reform and opening up, the Party introduced a spokesperson system and press conferences and answered Western criticism with white papers on human rights and Tibet. Since 2012, the article describes a broader, multi-actor publicity pattern involving the Belt and Road Initiative, cultural exchanges, documentaries and the circulation of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China in 37 language editions. It also describes publicity struggles over trade, Hong Kong, Taiwan and human rights.

Zhai concludes that the achievements of this work rest fundamentally on the strong leadership of the Party Central Committee and the guidance of its theory. The author calls for implementing the 20th Party Congress's requirements under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, so as to strengthen international communication, the appeal of Chinese culture and the persuasiveness of Chinese discourse. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed periodisation of the Party's foreign-facing propaganda and the cases it highlights at each stage.
quoteEn: Looking back over the hundred-year course of external publicity work, from small to large and from weak to strong, the fundamental reason for all these historic achievements lies in the strong leadership of the Party Central Committee and the scientific guidance of the Party's guiding thought.
quoteZh: 回顾外宣工作由小到大、由弱到强的百年历程，种种历史性成就的取得，根本在于党中央的坚强领导和党的指导思想的科学指引。

glossary.explanation: The Party-state's term for communication aimed at foreign audiences, often shortened to waixuan. It covers foreign-language media, press briefings, white papers and cultural exchange; the English equivalent 'propaganda' has a more neutral sense in Chinese.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017 at the 19th Party Congress.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.
A Chinese international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative, proposed by Xi Jinping in 2013.

glossary.en: the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence
glossary.explanation: Principles of mutual respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence, publicised by China in the 1950s.
Official government policy documents; the State Council Information Office issues them to state China's positions to domestic and foreign audiences.

keywords: Xi Jinping: The Governance of China

t: Theoretical foundations for advancing the new great project of Party building in the new era
zh: 新时代深入推进党的建设新的伟大工程的理论依据
paras: Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wang Chuanli asks what theoretical grounds support the Congress report's decision to keep up full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and to push forward the new great project of Party building in the new era. The article argues that these arrangements are not only policy but apply and enrich Marxist doctrine on party building, as part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

Wang takes four parts of the report in turn and matches each to a classical Marxist principle. Upholding the centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee is tied to Engels's view of authority. Forging minds and souls through Party theory is tied to the theory of inculcation. Stricter discipline and conduct is tied to the vanguard character of the Party. Unceasing self-governance is tied to the theory of permanent revolution. The article draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Xi Jinping, and on episodes from Party history.

In the first part, Wang reads Engels's On Authority as showing that more social cooperation requires more authority. Wang argues that China's higher degree of socialisation, with big data and artificial intelligence, makes the case for the Central Committee's authority stronger, and that this is compatible with democratic centralism. In the second, Wang follows Lenin's What Is to Be Done? to hold that socialist consciousness must be brought to workers from outside. By the same logic, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era could not arise spontaneously from the masses and must be summed up by outstanding leaders, with Xi as its main founder. In the last part, Wang cites the "four tests" and "four risks" and the "four-fold 'until'" and "four-fold 'to'" formulas of Marx and Engels. Wang reasons that, as a disease can recur, corruption and bad work styles can rebound even after the anti-corruption campaign's reported "overwhelming victory".

Wang concludes that the Marxist theory of permanent revolution supplies the basis for continuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and for using the Party's self-reform to lead social revolution. In Wang's account, Party members must therefore keep their revolutionary spirit, purge corrupt elements, overcome privilege and preserve the purity of the proletarian vanguard. Read the original if you want to see how a Tsinghua Marxism scholar ties the 20th Congress's Party-building agenda to Engels, Lenin and the theory of permanent revolution.
quoteEn: The Marxist theory of permanent revolution provides the theoretical basis for the Communist Party of China's unremitting full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and its unremitting efforts to "lead social revolution through the Party's self-reform".
quoteZh: 马克思主义的不断革命论，为中国共产党不懈地全面从严治党和不懈地“以党的自我革命引领社会革命”提供了理论依据。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It covers Party discipline, ideological education, work style and anti-corruption.
The Party's official term for its own internal rectification, used to justify continued discipline and anti-corruption work.

glossary.zh: 党的建设新的伟大工程
glossary.pinyin: dǎng de jiànshè xīn de wěidà gōngchéng
glossary.en: new great project of Party building
glossary.explanation: A phrase used since the 19th Party Congress (2017) for Party-building work in the new era. It echoes an earlier Party slogan from the 1980s about a "great project" of Party building.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the continuing project of fitting Marxist theory to Chinese conditions and to contemporary circumstances.

glossary.literal: concentrate the heart, cast the soul
glossary.explanation: A slogan in the 20th Congress report for using the Party's current theory to unify members' beliefs and ideals.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想

t: The Second Party Congress and the Party's mass work
zh: 中共二大与党的群众工作
paras: Marking the 100th anniversary of the Second National Congress of the Communist Party of China (1922), this newspaper commentary asks what the congress contributed to the Party's mass work (qunzhong gongzuo). Li Chuanbing argues that the congress made a pioneering exploration of how to work among the masses, and that revisiting it helps summarise historical experience and grasp the characteristics and rules of mass work. Li ties this to the people-centred approach to development in the new era.

The article opens with the Resolution on the Party's century of struggle adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). It then has two main sections. The first covers how the Second Congress deepened theoretical understanding of the importance of mass work. The second covers the policies it set. A closing section assesses the historical contribution of these ideas.

In Li's account, the congress's resolution on Party organisation defined the Party as a large "mass party" and a vanguard that must not become a "minority of communists" cut off from the masses. Li holds that the congress also analysed Chinese social classes in a scientific and realistic way. It affirmed the leading role of the workers, treated the peasantry as the largest element of the revolution, saw the bourgeoisie as having a revolutionary side while noting its tendency to compromise, and counted handicraftsmen and small shopkeepers as participants. On this basis it proposed a democratic united front and measures on Party discipline, trade unions and youth work. Li stresses that the proletariat's temporary alliance with democrats was not surrender to the bourgeoisie.

Li concludes that these ideas guided the mobilisation of workers, students and youth after the congress and helped bring about the first high tide of the revolution. They are also presented as a theoretical precedent for the Party's mass line and for the united front, later named one of the Party's "three magic weapons". Read the original if you want a short, official-style account of how Party historiography now links the 1922 congress to the mass line and united front doctrine.
quoteEn: The Second Congress set the task of building the Party into a revolutionary, mass-based proletarian party.
quoteZh: 中共二大提出把党建设成为一个革命的群众性的无产阶级政党的任务

glossary.explanation: A Party working method, associated with Mao Zedong, of gathering the views of the people, turning them into policy and returning to the masses to implement it. It is often summarised as "from the masses, to the masses".
The Party's strategy of building alliances with other classes, parties and groups against a common enemy. It is traditionally listed among the Party's "magic weapons".
The alliance policy adopted at the Second Congress in 1922. It proposed uniting workers, peasants, the petty bourgeoisie and the bourgeoisie against imperialism and warlords.
The Party's work of mobilising, organising and communicating with ordinary people, such as workers, peasants and youth.

t: Persistently and thoroughly advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
zh: 持之以恒深入推进全面从严治党
paras: Published in Guangming Daily on 15 September 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, this commentary takes its starting point from Xi Jinping's remarks to a seminar of provincial and ministerial leaders. Li Lifeng argues that the Party, as the world's largest Marxist governing party, can consolidate its long-term rule only by pursuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party without letup. The article presents this as the means by which the Party's self-reform can lead social revolution.

The piece has three parts. The first presents full and rigorous self-governance as a great practice of self-reform in the new era. The second explains why the effort is "always on the road". The third sets out concrete directions for opening up a new realm of self-reform.

Li's central reasoning is that self-governance serves the Party's founding mission and its great struggle, cause, project and dream. The article names the "four tests" and "four dangers" as long-lasting, and treats the Party's willingness to correct its own errors as the reason it has endured. It points to global turbulence and to the pressures of national rejuvenation, and it says that impurities in political stance, thinking, organisation and conduct remain unresolved. Quoting Xi, it holds that the struggle against corruption is still fierce and that the Party can ensure it never degenerates only by sustained effort. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the article says, this effort has ended lax governance and found a way to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall.

Li proposes six lines of action. They are: political development as the guiding principle, including the Two Upholds and the Two Establishes; ideological development through study of Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; stricter discipline and conduct, including the eight-point regulations; a sustained, zero-tolerance anti-corruption campaign targeting both "tigers" and "flies"; stronger Party organisations and a cadre corps willing to struggle; and a system of Party regulations and supervision. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official press framed self-governance and anti-corruption on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: Full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is the great practice of the Party's self-reform in the new era, opening a new realm of self-reform for a century-old Party.
quoteZh: 全面从严治党是新时代党的自我革命的伟大实践，开辟了百年大党自我革命的新境界。

t: Guidance by Marxist scientific theory as the Communist Party of China's distinctive political character and strong political advantage
zh: 马克思主义科学理论指导是中国共产党的鲜明政治品格和强大政治优势
paras: This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 19 September 2022, ahead of the 20th Party Congress, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that being guided by Marxist scientific theory is the Party's distinctive political character and strong political advantage. Ruan and Chen argue that, in the end, the reasons the Communist Party of China "can do it" and socialism with Chinese characteristics is "good" come down to the fact that Marxism "works".

The piece has three sections. The first presents Marxism as the choice of history and of the Chinese people since the Opium War of 1840. The second runs through four historical periods: new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third looks ahead to the continuing task of developing Marxism in China.

In the first section the authors say that capitalism, reformism, liberalism, social Darwinism, anarchism, pragmatism and other currents were each tried and failed to resolve China's fate. The Chinese people therefore chose Marxism and the Party formed from its union with the workers' movement. The relationship is described as reciprocal: the Party did not fail Marxism, because it has defended, upheld and developed it through successive theoretical achievements, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Marxism did not fail the Party, because the Party grew from weak to strong under its guidance. The authors write that the Party was founded, flourished and grew strong through Marxism. For each period they pair a theoretical innovation with a historic leap: "standing up", "becoming prosperous" and "becoming strong".

The authors conclude that Marxism is not dogma but a guide to action, which must be adapted to China and to the times (adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times) in order to take root. They hold that this adaptation is far from finished, since contemporary change exceeds what the classical authors could imagine and China is still in the primary stage of socialism. The Party's theoretical mission is to keep combining Marxist principles with China's realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, opening up new horizons for twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars framed Marxism's role in the Party's legitimacy on the eve of the 20th Party Congress (2022).
quoteEn: The Communist Party of China was founded because of Marxism, has prospered because of Marxism, and has grown strong because of Marxism.
quoteZh: 中国共产党因马克思主义而立，因马克思主义而兴，因马克思主义而强。

An official thesis that China is still in an early, long-lasting stage of socialism, marked by underdeveloped productive forces. It underpins the Party's reform-era policies.

t: Achievements and experience of the Communist Party of China in pioneering innovation during a century of struggle
zh: 中国共产党在百年奋斗中坚持开拓创新的成就和经验
source: Contemporary Economic Research (Dangdai jingji yanjiu), 2022 no. 1
paras: Taking its cue from the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over a century, this article asks how the Communist Party of China has sustained innovation in its hundred years of struggle. Cheng Enfu and Sun Shaoyong argue that the Party's history is a continuous process of innovation, and that this has been a fundamental reason for its successes. They summarise achievements and lessons in four fields: theory, practice, institutions and culture.

The article opens with the revolutionary heroism and optimism of the New Democratic Revolution, which the authors present as a spiritual precondition of victory. It then takes each of the four fields in turn. For each, it sketches the historical record from Mao Zedong through reform and opening up to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), and then lists several lessons. The institutional section also reviews the framework set out by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019).

On theory, the authors credit the Party with adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They name three lessons: proceed from national conditions and combine Marxism with Chinese realities and traditional culture; be problem-oriented; and keep thought liberated while opposing opportunism and dogmatism. On practice, they stress strengthening Party leadership, putting the people at the centre, and holding to a scientific worldview. On institutions, they call for fidelity to objective laws, integration with national governance, and firm enforcement, including keeping power and capital 'in the cage of institutions' and opposing private capital monopoly and disorderly expansion. On culture, they stress the dialectic of economic base and superstructure, the policy of letting a hundred flowers bloom, and reliance on the people.

The authors conclude that innovation in all four fields has given the Party a body of experience that underpins the building of a modern socialist country and national rejuvenation. They present these lessons as a guide for deepening understanding of the laws of Communist Party rule, socialist construction and social development. They also call for cultural works to avoid pursuing ratings, box office or circulation alone, and to follow socialist core values. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned overview of how Chinese scholars summarise the Party's innovation record across theory, practice, institutions and culture.
quoteEn: The history of the Communist Party of China is a history of continuously advancing theoretical innovation and theoretical creation.
quoteZh: 中国共产党的历史，就是一部不断推进理论创新、进行理论创造的历史。

t: Staying clear-headed and resolute in solving the problems unique to a large party
zh: 时刻保持解决大党独有难题的清醒和坚定
paras: This newspaper commentary, written after the 20th Party Congress (2022), takes up Xi Jinping's call to remain clear-headed and resolute in solving the problems unique to a large party. Liu Zhiming argues that, for the world's largest Marxist governing party to keep the people's support and consolidate its long-term rule, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party must be treated as a permanent strategic task. Any relaxation, the author warns, risks a rebound.

The article moves in three steps. It first presents the willingness to carry out the Party's self-reform as a tradition and a lesson of a century of struggle. It then explains why a problem-oriented, cautious attitude is still needed, citing the speech by Xi at the second plenary session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (2023 session of the new Commission). It closes with five practical directions for the new journey.

Liu's central claim is that the Party's strength lies not in avoiding mistakes but in correcting them through criticism and self-criticism, democratic centralism and service to the people. On this reading, the Party has no interests apart from those of the nation and people, which is why it can face its own problems. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the author says, the anti-corruption campaign and rigorous self-governance have solved many prominent problems. Even so, impure thinking, politics, organization and work style persist, and the "four tests" and "four dangers" remain. Liu presents the Party's self-reform as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall, and says only the Party itself can defeat it.

Liu calls for the Party to keep to its original aspiration and mission and to unify thinking, will and action under the Party Central Committee, with the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. The author also proposes strengthening governing capacity and rule-based Party governance, sustaining cadres' drive through both strict management and encouragement, and building self-correcting mechanisms around the Party constitution and organizational life. The last proposal is a healthy political ecology, starting with how officials are selected and promoted. Liu is confident that the Party will keep renewing itself through self-reform. Read the original if you want an example of how a CASS Party-building scholar presents the official line on the Party's self-reform after the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: The Party's greatness lies not in never making mistakes, but in never shying away from its ailments: it actively conducts criticism and self-criticism, dares to face problems, has the courage to reform itself, and possesses a very strong capacity for self-repair.
quoteZh: 党的伟大不在于不犯错误，而在于从不讳疾忌医，积极开展批评和自我批评，敢于直面问题，勇于自我革命，具有极强的自我修复能力。

t: Staying clear-headed and resolute in tackling the problems unique to a large party
zh: 时刻保持解决大党独有难题的清醒和坚定
paras: This newspaper commentary, published in Hunan Daily and posted in January 2023, takes up a formula from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): to keep the people's support and consolidate its long-term governing position, the Party must stay clear-headed and resolute about the problems unique to a large party. Liu Zhiming argues that this is a strategic response to the question of what kind of long-ruling Marxist party to build and how to build it. In Liu's reading, the Party must see the task through and carry its great self-reform to the end.

The piece has three parts. The first presents the courage for self-reform as a tradition and a lesson of the Party's century of struggle. The second explains why the problems remain pressing under long-term rule. The third sets out five areas of work for the new journey, drawing mainly on Xi Jinping's remarks at the Second Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection.

Liu's central claim is that the Party's strength lies in its capacity to correct itself rather than in avoiding mistakes. Liu credits this capacity to the Party's people-centred commitment, democratic centralism and criticism and self-criticism, and says the Party has no interests of its own apart from those of the nation and the people. Liu accepts that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since 2012 has solved many problems. Even so, the author argues, impurity in thinking, politics, organisation and work style persists, and the "four tests" and "four dangers" will endure. Liu treats the Party's self-reform as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and decay, and says only the Party itself can defeat it.

Liu proposes five measures: remember the founding mission; unify thinking, will and action through the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; improve governing capacity through institutional and rule-based Party building; sustain officials' drive through incentives; and uncover and fix problems through democratic centralism and criticism and self-criticism. A healthy political ecology depends on proper selection of officials and a sound political culture. Liu concludes that a governing Party led by Xi Jinping's core will keep renewing itself. t: The Chinese Communist Party's changing understanding of modern China as "semi-colonial"
zh: 中国共产党对近代中国“半殖民地”社会性质的认识历程
paras: Zhai Yu takes up a question of Party history: how and when the Chinese Communists came to describe modern China as "semi-colonial", the first half of the "semi-colonial and semi-feudal" formula that became the standard characterisation of China's modern society. The article argues that the Party's semi-colonial designation was largely an independent judgement made from its own observation of China. It was not a conclusion handed down by the Comintern, although Lenin's usage inspired it.

The article begins with the standard account of the formula and its consequences for the targets and tasks of the revolution. It then traces the term from Lenin's writings of 1915–1920 through the early Party. It examines Tian Cheng's 1921 pamphlet, Zhang Tailei, Chen Duxiu, Cai Hesen, Zhang Guotao and Qu Qiubai, and the documents of the Second and Third Party Congresses. It ends with Mao Zedong's usage from 1923 and his 1939 text On the Chinese Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party.

Zhai makes three main moves. First, Lenin's "semi-colony" meant a state's semi-independent international position, whereas the Chinese formula extended it to the nature of society. Second, Zhai corrects claims in the literature about priority. Tian Cheng's 1921 pamphlet, not Cai Hesen or Chen Duxiu, is likely the first use by a Chinese person in China. The Second Congress (1922) documents already called China semi-colonial about five months before the Comintern's Fourth Congress did the same. They did not use the term "semi-feudal" or the full formula, which the Second Congress documents lack. Third, usage was uneven. Leaders such as Qu Qiubai and Li Lisan still wrote "colony" after 1922, while Party documents were more consistent and in 1928 even influenced a Comintern resolution.

Zhai presents Mao as the most consistent user of the term, who never used "colony" for China beforehand. In the 1930s Mao treated China as semi-colonial overall but with colonial parts, notably the north-east after Japan's invasion. Zhai concludes that the formula was already in frequent use by Mao in the year or two before 1939, so the 1939 text did not originate it, though it gave the systematic theoretical statement. The origin of "semi-feudal" and of the fixed wording is left for a separate study. Read the original if you study early CPC history, the Party's relationship with the Comintern, or the textual genealogy of the "two halves" theory.
quoteEn: The designation of China as semi-colonial shows that even in the Party's founding period the Communist Party already had the theoretical ability to think independently about China's problems, and did not simply view modern China's social nature according to the Comintern's definitions.
quoteZh: 对中国半殖民地的定位显示出即使在创党初期，中国共产党已经具有独立思考中国问题的理论素养，并没有完全按照共产国际的定义来看待近代中国的社会性质。

glossary.explanation: The standard Chinese Marxist characterisation of Chinese society from 1840 to 1949, under imperialist pressure while retaining feudal social relations. It underpins the claim that the revolution had to be anti-imperialist and anti-feudal.
Shorthand for the semi-colonial and semi-feudal theory of modern Chinese society. It was given systematic form in Mao Zedong's 1939 writings.
The Moscow-based international organisation of communist parties (1919–1943), to which the early CPC was affiliated.

t: Pressing ahead with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party without pause: taking responsibility for solving the problems unique to a large party
st: Studying Xi Jinping's important speech at the Second Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection
zh: 一刻不停推进全面从严治党 在解决大党独有难题上担当使命责任
zhSub: 深入学习领悟习近平总书记在二十届中央纪委二次全会上的重要讲话精神
source: China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News, 19 January 2023, p. 5
paras: This commentary, published in the China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News on 19 January 2023, is a study piece on Xi Jinping's speech at the Second Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The author argues that the speech gives the fundamental guidance for advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. In the author's account, the speech sets out why the problems unique to a large party arise, how they show themselves and how to resolve them. Discipline inspection and supervision bodies, the author says, must therefore keep a clear head and firm resolve in tackling them.

The piece has three parts. The first explains the demand to keep up the fight against these problems and to see the Party's self-reform through to the end. The second covers the goals and tasks of building a system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The third turns to the priority tasks of Party conduct, clean governance and the anti-corruption struggle, and to the high-quality development of discipline inspection and supervision work.

The author lists six problems unique to a large party: keeping the original aspiration and mission; unifying thought, will and action; maintaining governing capacity; keeping up a spirit of enterprise; spotting and correcting its own errors; and sustaining a clean political ecosystem. The author says these call for treating full and rigorous self-governance as a long-term strategy and rejecting any hope that the tone will soften. The author describes the self-governance system as covering every aspect of Party building and rests it on institutions and Party rules. For discipline bodies, the author sets out six tasks: concrete, precise and routine political supervision; persistent enforcement of the central Party's eight-point regulations against the 'four undesirable work styles'; stronger discipline; a protracted anti-corruption fight that stresses 'one who is in charge' and 'flies' (petty corruption); a sounder Party and state supervision system; and a disciplined, loyal inspection corps.

The author concludes that these bodies, as political organs, must support the Party's overall leadership and the Two Upholds. They must also make sure the decisions of the 20th Party Congress (2022) are carried out, and must reform themselves so that the Party never degenerates. The text is an authoritative official reading, not an independent analysis. Read the original if you want to see how the Party's discipline apparatus presented its tasks at the start of 2023, including its list of the six problems and its priorities for supervision and anti-corruption work.
quoteEn: Because full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform are always on the road, full and rigorous self-governance must be treated as the Party's long-term strategy and an eternal task.
quoteZh: 全面从严治党永远在路上，党的自我革命永远在路上，决定了必须把全面从严治党作为党的长期战略、永恒课题

t: Deeply grasping the important experience of Party building in the new era
zh: 深刻把握新时代党的建设的重要经验
source: Jiguan dangjian yanjiu (Research on Party Building in Government Organs), 2022 no. 12
paras: Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Chen Zhigang asks what lessons can be drawn from the decade of Party building since 2012. Chen argues that under the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, the Party has been strengthened through a series of new ideas and strategies, has reversed what the article calls a lax and soft approach to Party discipline, and has found a path for escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. The article presents six lessons as valuable for understanding the laws of Communist Party governance and for advancing the "new great project" of Party building.

The article is a commentary organised in six numbered sections, each stating one lesson: upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership; adhering to fundamental principles while breaking new ground; leading full and rigorous self-governance of the Party with political building; upholding the Party's nature and purpose; problem orientation; and a systemic approach to self-reform. Each section combines extended quotations from Xi Jinping with the author's summary of measures taken since 2012.

In Chen's account, the first lesson is that the Party's leadership has been extended from political, ideological and organisational leadership to leadership over all work. It rests on the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, which Chen presents as the decisive factor behind the decade's achievements. Chen lists theoretical innovations, including the move from strict Party governance to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and from the "two musts" to the "three musts". These are said to have solved the problem of self-supervision and given a "second answer" to the historical cycle question. Chen links the Party's closeness to the people (the mass line, whole-process people's democracy, common prosperity) with an uncompromising anti-corruption stance. The article also describes a "combination of punches" of self-reform: political, ideological and institutional building, work-style rectification, and anti-corruption work.

Chen concludes that these hard-won experiences must be continued and developed so that the Party remains the strong leadership core of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Chen calls for continued work on formalism and bureaucratism, corruption in key projects and posts, and new mechanisms for supervising top leaders. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-building lessons of the Xi era, as presented in a Chinese Party-building journal in late 2022.
quoteEn: Adhering to fundamental principles while breaking new ground is the secret of Marxism's enduring vitality, and also the secret of the steady progress of all the undertakings of the Party and the state.
quoteZh: 坚持守正创新，这是马克思主义永葆生机活力的奥妙所在，也是党和国家各项事业不断顺利发展的奥妙所在。

glossary.explanation: A formula from the 2021 Party history resolution and the 20th Party Congress. It affirms Xi Jinping's position as core of the Central Committee and the Party, and the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought.
The requirement that Party members firmly uphold the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee and Xi Jinping's core position.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The slogan for the Party's discipline and anti-corruption drive since 2012. It covers ideological, organisational, work-style and institutional building.
The official term for China's democratic model, which stresses people's participation at every stage of governance rather than only in elections.
An official goal of broadly shared wealth, promoted as a defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
Refers to the dynastic pattern of rise and decline, which Huang Yanpei raised with Mao Zedong in 1945. Party texts say that self-reform is the answer.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: The Communist Party of China's creation of a new form of rule-of-law civilization: a historical narrative
zh: 中国共产党创造法治文明新形态的历史叙事
source: Social Sciences in China (中国社会科学), 2022 no. 12, pp. 45–58
paras: Fu Zitang asks what is new about the rule-of-law civilization created under the Communist Party of China (CPC) over its first century. Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Fu argues that Chinese modernization includes a Chinese path of rule-of-law modernization, and that the Party's century of struggle has produced a new form of rule-of-law civilization. In the author's account this form breaks what Fu calls the West's monopoly over narratives of legal modernization.

The article follows the Party's history from its Second Congress (1922) through the Jinggangshan land law, the Soviet-era constitutional outline, the 1954 constitution, the post-1978 reform period and the Xi Jinping era. It is organised around three dimensions of innovation: mechanisms, texts and discourse. Fu calls mechanisms the fundamental driving force, texts the visible result and discourse the inner construction. A closing section compares this with Western legal development.

On mechanisms, Fu holds that the Party's leadership of law is a matter of constitutional fact. Fu traces the shift to governing in accordance with law and describes a mechanism in which the Party leads legislation, ensures law enforcement, supports the judiciary and takes the lead in obeying the law. Fu treats "is the Party or the law greater" as a false question and says the real one is whether power or law is greater. On texts, Fu sets out four moments: dawn, new beginning, system and codification. The last is marked by the 2020 Civil Code and by planned codes in administrative, environmental and educational law. On discourse, Fu points to two successive "sixteen-character" formulas, to rule-of-law faith, to good law and good governance, and to the "rule-of-law system" as an original category.

In conclusion, Fu contrasts China's path with Western ones. Mechanisms are described as "autonomous" rather than home-grown or transplanted. Texts are said to follow neither common law nor civil law. Western legal discourse is described as stagnant and facing a "discourse deficit". Fu says the Chinese form favours exchange and mutual learning among civilizations over a clash of civilizations or imposed models. Fu calls for continued work guided by Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned periodisation of Party legal history and its main concepts, or an example of how Chinese legal scholarship frames comparison with the West.
quoteEn: Innovation in rule-of-law mechanisms is the foundation of Chinese-style rule-of-law modernization.
quoteZh: 法治机制创新为中国式法治现代化之本

glossary.explanation: Official term for China's own path of modernization under Party leadership. It was stressed in Xi Jinping's 2021 speech and in the 20th Party Congress report (2022).
Principle that the Party must exercise its ruling position through the constitution, laws and Party regulations. It was made the Party's basic mode of governance in 2004.
Concept from the Fourth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2014). It covers legal norms, enforcement, supervision, safeguards and Party regulations.
Formula holding that good governance requires good law. It appears in the 19th and 20th Party Congress reports.

keywords: Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law

t: The Communist Party of China and the four historic leaps of Chinese modernization
zh: 中国共产党与中国式现代化的四次历史性跨越
paras: Following the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this article asks how the Communist Party of China has advanced and extended Chinese modernization, which it defines as socialist modernization led by the Party. Huang Yibing argues that the Party's century of effort can be read as four historic leaps, each setting the course for the next. The article appeared in the journal Dang de wenxian (Party Literature) in late 2022 and was posted online in January 2023.

The article moves chronologically. It begins with the failed modernization attempts after the Opium War of 1840 and the democratic revolution led by the Party. It then covers the Mao-era drive for the "four modernizations", Deng Xiaoping's "Chinese-style four modernizations" and the three-step strategy, and finally the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The last part sets out Xi Jinping's remarks on Chinese modernization, the 20th Congress's plans, and the significance of the Chinese path for socialism and for the world.

Huang's core argument is that modernization could not succeed in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, so the Self-Strengthening Movement, the reformers and Sun Yat-sen's camp all failed. Citing Mao Zedong, Huang holds that new productive forces require prior revolution of the relations of production and superstructure, so national independence and liberation were the precondition. After 1949 the Party built an independent industrial system, avoided what it calls the Soviet one-sided emphasis on heavy industry, and set the four-modernizations goal. Deng's formulation, tied to the idea of a moderately prosperous society, adapted the goal to China's conditions. Huang credits the post-2012 period with five Chinese features of modernization, five major principles, and a comprehensive blueprint covering the economy, politics, culture, society and ecology.

Huang concludes that Chinese modernization, as the article describes it, enriches modernization theory, offers a new path for governing a socialist state, widens routes to modernization for developing countries, and contributes to a community with a shared future for mankind. The text closes by calling for firm adherence to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and to the Party's leadership in building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want an official Party-history account of how the leadership periodises Chinese modernization and links it to the 20th Congress line.
quoteEn: China's modernization must take the winning of national independence and the people's liberation as its fundamental premise and foundation.
quoteZh: 中国的现代化必须以争取民族独立和人民解放为根本前提和基础。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official term for China's path to modernization, defined as socialist modernization led by the Communist Party. It was given a systematic formulation at the 20th Party Congress in 2022.
The goal of modernizing agriculture, industry, national defence and science and technology. Zhou Enlai announced it as a national strategic goal in 1964–65.
A Confucian-derived term for a comfortably-off society. Deng Xiaoping used it from 1979 as the medium-term target of Chinese modernization.

Deng Xiaoping's strategy, formalised at the 13th Party Congress in 1987: double GNP and secure subsistence, reach a moderately prosperous level by 2000, and basically achieve modernization by the mid-21st century.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for international relations and global governance, used as a guiding idea of Chinese foreign policy.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology since 2017, written into the Party and state constitutions.

t: Comprehensively advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation requires continuing to uphold and strengthen the leadership of the Communist Party of China
zh: 全面推进中华民族伟大复兴必须继续坚持和加强中国共产党的领导
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (Sixiang lilun jiaoyu daokan), 2022 no. 12
paras: Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhu Jiamu asks why the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation must continue to rest on the leadership of the Communist Party of China. Taking up the Congress report's statement that the key to building a modern socialist country lies in the Party, Zhu argues that Party leadership was the decisive factor in past progress and remains indispensable for the next stage. The article appeared in a journal on ideological and theoretical education.

The article has three parts. The first reviews modern Chinese history to claim that only the Party was qualified to lead national rejuvenation. The second sets out seven contributions the Party made to that goal since its founding. The third turns to the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the tasks and risks ahead, and the practical, legal and theoretical grounds for Party leadership.

Zhu's core reasoning is historical and class-based. Earlier efforts, from the Taiping movement to the 1911 Revolution, failed for lack of an advanced class and a correct path. In Zhu's account the bourgeoisie could not lead, so the working class, joined with Marxist intellectuals, formed the Party, which carried both socialism and anti-imperialism and feudalism. Zhu lists seven contributions: a socialist path, the political precondition of independence, three historic opportunities (the Korean War, the opening to the United States, and opening up), a stable environment, fitting development strategies, progress on national unification, and a revitalised national spirit. Zhu then argues from Marxist base-and-superstructure theory that public ownership as the main body of the economy explains China's one-party leadership under multi-party cooperation, and the Party's absolute command of the army. Zhu rejects multi-party electoral competition as the measure of democracy, calling Party leadership the primary form of whole-process people's democracy.

Zhu concludes that without Party leadership there would have been no revolutionary victory, no new China and no rejuvenation. Zhu stresses that the remaining tasks are harder: modernization, unification, world peace and common prosperity, amid domestic problems and external pressure the author attributes to US-led hegemonism. Zhu calls for upholding Party authority and the Party's self-reform, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how a senior Party historian grounds Party leadership in history, class analysis and Marxist theory after the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: Therefore, Party leadership and democracy are not only not in contradiction; on the contrary, Party leadership is the primary form through which people's democracy is realised.
quoteZh: 因此，党的领导与民主不仅不矛盾，相反，它是人民民主的首要实现形式。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China to national strength and prosperity after the 'century of humiliation'. It is closely tied to the Chinese Dream and to the two centenary goals.
A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2019. It describes the Party's claim that democratic participation runs through the whole policymaking cycle, not only elections.
A goal of shared wealth for all the people, emphasised under Xi Jinping as a defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
The official name for the Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership, public-sector predominance and a market economy.

t: Advancing the new great undertaking of Party building
st: Studying General Secretary Xi Jinping's important statements on Party building in the new era
zh: 推进党的建设新的伟大工程
zhSub: 学习习近平总书记关于新时代党的建设工作重要论述
paras: This article is a study-and-exposition piece on Xi Jinping's statements about Party building since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It asks what guides, structures and secures the Party's work in the new era. Wu argues that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has strengthened Party cohesion, and that the task is to build a Marxist governing party that can stay in power over the long term.

The text is organised in three parts. The first sets out the fundamental guidance: guiding thought, the main thread and the overall goal. The second describes a strategic layout of seven areas: political, ideological, organisational, conduct, discipline and institutional building, plus the anti-corruption struggle. The third discusses three safeguards: serious intra-Party political life, methodological innovation through inspection and supervision, and the responsibility of Party committees.

Wu treats long-term governance as the decisive question among the three major propositions of the Xi-led leadership. The author points to the Soviet Communist Party and India's Congress Party as former ruling parties that lost power, and presents Xi's thinking as a way to avoid that fate. The main thread is strengthening long-term governing capacity, advanced nature and purity. The overall goal is a strong leadership core, which Wu says is needed to unite a large, diverse country and build value consensus under a socialist market economy. Political building comes first, and the author calls it the Party's fundamental building. Wu draws on Chinese history, such as the late-dynasty corruption of land annexation and the ancient censorate. The author contrasts the censorate, which served imperial rule, with the Party's inspection and supervision system, which is said to answer to the Party and the people. Wu also reads the Party's internal regulations as drawing on traditional Confucian moral requirements. Democratic centralism is described as requiring both democracy and centralisation. Wu says its weaknesses appear as unchecked "top leaders" and as inadequate implementation of higher-level intentions.

Wu concludes that advancing Party building must take account of a complex international and domestic situation and of diversified interests under the market economy. The author calls on the Party to hold to self-reform, to preserve its advanced nature and purity, and to let self-reform lead social revolution toward a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned overview of how Party-building priorities in the Xi era are categorised and justified.
quoteEn: Without a strong leadership core, the culture of the Chinese national community could not be forged, strong cohesion and fighting capacity could not take shape, and still less could there be a strong capacity for social organisation and mobilisation.
quoteZh: 没有一个坚强的领导核心，就铸就不了中华民族共同体的文化，就形成不了强大的凝聚力战斗力，更不可能有强大的社会组织动员能力

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan adopted under Xi Jinping after 2012 for tightening Party discipline, conduct and anti-corruption work across the whole Party.
A phrase used in Party discourse for the Party's continuing effort to correct its own faults and maintain discipline without outside pressure.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official long-term national goal of restoring China's strength and international standing, closely associated with Xi Jinping's Chinese Dream.
The Leninist organisational principle of the Communist Party, combining discussion and the minority's obedience to the majority and to higher bodies.
A Party system in which central inspection teams visit regions and departments to examine discipline and corruption; resident supervision (派驻) places supervisory bodies inside agencies.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: Relying on the Party's self-reform to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall
zh: 依靠党的自我革命跳出历史周期率
paras: How can a Marxist party that has ruled for a long time keep its nature and purpose and escape the cycle of dynastic rise and fall? Yan Xiaofeng, writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), argues that the Party's self-reform is the "second answer" to this question, following Mao Zedong's first answer of supervision by the people. The article presents self-reform as the deepest logic of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and as the key conclusion on building a long-ruling Marxist party.

The article has four sections. It first sets out why the cycle is a fundamental problem, drawing on imperial dynasties, peasant uprisings and the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party. It then traces the Party's search for an answer from the Yan'an "cave conversation" of 1945 to the present. A third section reviews six areas of Party building under Xi Jinping: political, ideological, conduct and discipline, anti-corruption, organizational and institutional work. The last draws four conclusions about building a long-ruling party.

Yan reads the cycle through historical materialism: earlier ruling groups represented a minority and so could not resolve their conflict with the people, and could not reform themselves. The two answers form an organic whole, with supervision by the people acting from outside and self-reform from within. Yan argues that supervision by the people supplies the political guarantee and motivation for self-reform, while self-reform internalises that supervision. Each is incomplete without the other. In Yan's account the Soviet party failed because it became a privileged bureaucratic group unable to reform itself.

Yan concludes that a long-ruling Marxist party must hold to a Marxist view of power ("the country is the people"), have no special interests of its own, and keep its founding mission. It must also keep the resolve to turn the blade inward so that the Party does not change in nature, colour or flavour. Anti-corruption is described as the most thorough form of self-reform, and Yan stresses that self-governance "is always on the road". Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theoretical account of how the 20th Party Congress framed self-reform as a way out of the historical cycle.
quoteEn: The organic combination of supervision by the people and self-reform makes up the complete answer to escaping the historical cycle; neither can be dispensed with.
quoteZh: 人民监督和自我革命的有机结合，构成跳出历史周期率的全面答案，二者缺一不可。

glossary.explanation: A term the Party uses for its capacity to purify, improve and correct itself. It is presented officially as the second answer to the historical cycle.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The Party's slogan since the 18th Party Congress (2012) for tightening discipline, conduct and anti-corruption work across the Party.
The 1945 Yan'an talk between Mao Zedong and Huang Yanpei, in which Mao said democracy and supervision by the people would let the Party escape the historical cycle.

t: How the Communist Party of China came to understand modern China as "semi-colonial"
zh: 中国共产党对近代中国“半殖民地”社会性质的认识历程
paras: The article asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) arrived at the "semi-colonial" half of the standard characterisation of modern China as "semi-colonial and semi-feudal". Zhai Yu argues that the judgment was largely the Party's own independent conclusion, reached from its reading of China's circumstances, and not a verdict handed down by the Communist International (Comintern). Lenin supplied the term, but early CPC figures applied it to China before Comintern documents did.

Zhai first sets out the standard theory and Lenin's use of "semi-colony" between 1915 and 1920. The article then corrects several claims in the CPC-history literature about who first used the term, taking in Chen Duxiu, Cai Hesen, Zhang Tailei, Qu Qiubai, Zhang Guotao, Li Lisan and Mao Zedong. It follows the Second, Third and Fourth Comintern-related meetings and the CPC's Second and Third Congresses, and ends with Mao's writings of the 1920s and 1930s.

On priority, Zhai holds that Cai Hesen was not the first to apply the term to China, since Chen Duxiu did so a month earlier in 1922. A pamphlet signed "Tian Cheng", dated June 1921, probably contains the first use by a Chinese author inside China. Zhai also argues that the Second Congress (1922) used the idea of China as a semi-colony months before the Comintern's Fourth Congress did, so the common claim that Comintern meetings gave the CPC this view is, in Zhai's account, historically wrong. Zhai adds that the Second Congress documents do not call China "semi-feudal" or use the fixed phrase.

Zhai then shows that leaders' usage wavered between "colony" and "semi-colony" until the mid-1920s, while Party documents were more consistent and later influenced the Comintern's 1928 resolution. Mao used "semi-colony" consistently from 1923 and tied it to the survival of Red base areas amid imperialist rivalry. In the 1930s he warned that Japan sought to turn China into a full colony, and Zhai notes that Mao's 1939 essay The Chinese Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party gave the systematic statement of the theory, though he had used the phrase earlier. Zhai leaves the origins of the "semi-feudal" half for separate study. Read the original if you are interested in CPC history, the Comintern's role in early Party thought, or detailed source-based disputes over who first used key terms.
quoteEn: The CPC's characterisation of modern China as a semi-colony was more an independent judgment, which its members made on the basis of their own observation of China's national conditions and international position.
quoteZh: 中国共产党人对近代以来中国的半殖民地定性更多地是他们根据自己的观察对中国的国情和国际地位作出的独立判断。

t: The Communist Party of China and the four historic leaps of Chinese modernization
zh: 中国共产党与中国式现代化的四次历史性跨越
source: Documents of the Party (Dangde wenxian), 2022 no. 6
paras: Written after the 20th Party Congress (2022), this article asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has advanced and extended Chinese modernization over a century. Huang Yibing argues that the process can be read as four historic leaps, each led by the Party: finding the correct direction, striving for the "four modernizations", defining a distinctively Chinese version of them, and now building a modern socialist country in all respects. The article stresses that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization under Party leadership and rejects both a closed, rigid old path and a path of changing the Party's banner.

The article follows a chronological structure. It begins with failed modernizing projects after the Opium War (the Self-Strengthening Movement, the reformers around Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, and Sun Yat-sen's industrial plans) and then the New Democratic Revolution. It moves to the Mao-era industrial system and the "four modernizations", then to Deng Xiaoping's "Chinese-style" modernization, the "three-step" strategy and the goal of a moderately prosperous society. The last section covers the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the 20th Congress blueprint.

Huang's central claim is that modernization in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal China was impossible without first revolutionizing the social order. Citing Mao Zedong, the author holds that new productive forces cannot grow under imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism, so national independence and popular liberation were preconditions. Later leaps are presented as continuous adaptation to national conditions, from avoiding the Soviet pattern of neglecting light industry and agriculture to Deng's modest "xiaokang" target. For the present, Huang summarises Xi Jinping's statements on the five features of Chinese modernization, its essential requirements and five major principles, and the Congress's plans in the economy, politics, culture, society and ecology.

Huang concludes that Chinese modernization offers a new path for socialist governance and gives developing countries an alternative to the Western model. The author describes it as a "parallel" process, with industrialization, informatization, urbanization and agricultural modernization advancing together, in contrast to the "serial" Western sequence. The article also presents it as a peaceful path that contributes to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want an official-line, Party-history narrative that links the Opium War, Mao, Deng and Xi into a single account of modernization just after the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: China's modernization must take the winning of national independence and the liberation of the people as its fundamental precondition and foundation.
quoteZh: 中国的现代化必须以争取民族独立和人民解放为根本前提和基础。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the CPC's model of socialist modernization, elaborated especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as having distinctive features, such as a huge population and common prosperity, and as distinct from Western models.
A traditional term that Deng Xiaoping used from 1979 for a modest, comfortable standard of living as China's modernization target. It later became a goal of building a moderately prosperous society.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for China's foreign policy and vision of international relations, stressing common interests and cooperation.

t: The Party's century of struggle has profoundly shaped the course of world history
zh: 党的百年奋斗深刻影响了世界历史进程
paras: Taking its cue from the 2021 Party resolution on the major achievements and historical experience of the Party's first century, this commentary asks how the Communist Party of China's hundred years of struggle have affected world history, and why it has become the world's largest governing party with major global influence. Feng argues that the Party's work is an integral part of humanity's progress and that its influence rests on three foundations: the advantages of the socialist system, great development achievements and the spirit of self-reform. The piece appeared in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), no. 23, 2021.

The article has two parts. The first sets out the forms the influence takes: the Party's record on peace, justice and win-win cooperation; its role in inter-party exchanges, in world socialism and in international organisations; and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. The second part explains the underlying logic under three headings: the political foundation, the material guarantee and the source of momentum.

In Feng's account, Chinese modernization has created a new form of human civilisation and shown that no single model of modernization exists, giving countries that want both development and independence a fresh option. Feng credits the Party with leading world socialism after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and with maintaining regular contact with more than 500 parties and political organisations.
